News.title: Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
News.content:
"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

The government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

Burnham said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

News.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
News.content:
As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times, external, the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around Â£500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report, external, Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver â or at least begin to deliver â on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow â and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

News.title: Home secretary plans to tackle 'perception of two-tier policing'
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is to announce stronger guidance on police impartiality to tackle what she calls the "corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing".â¯

She will tell a conference of police chiefs that they should avoid what she calls "misguided attempts at course correction" where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

Recent complaints about alleged two-tier policing have mostly come from those on the right in politics.

They have pointed to the arrest of Henry Nowak as he was dying after being stabbed by Vickrum Digwa who had accused him of racism.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued that white people are treated differently by police because of their race. But critics say this claim risks overlooking the longâstanding experiences of black and minority ethnic communities.

Some senior police figures have also strongly rejected the claim of two-tier policing.

Mahmood will announce a new national standard is being developed "to ensure all members of the public are treated equally", said the Home Office.

"Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed," she will say.

But Mahmood will announce "clear, comprehensive guidance" on police impartiality, which reinforces that officers must apply the law consistently to avoid what she called "motivated actors" whipping up the idea that there's two-tier policing.

Mahmood will say that community engagement can mean going to a residents' association meeting and having tea and biscuits - or samosas - but it shouldn't mean engaging with activists pushing an agenda.

"Leave the politics to the politicians," she will say. "And we will leave the policing to you."

The home secretary will add that more needs to be done to tackle inequalities in policing, highlighting the persistently low proportion of black police officers.

However, she will state that some "well-intentioned approaches", such as the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, "have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing".

"As a Muslim home secretary, no one can doubt that equality in policing, and in our forces, matters to me," she will say.

"But we must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

"To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing "does not mean treating everyone the same."

Jo Noakes who leads the College of Policing, the standards-setting body for the police, said it will issue new guidance for officers that will make clear on impartiality in Spring.

She said: "Policing must act in a way that maintains public confidence, which is dependent on officers and staff exercising their powers without fear or favour...

"Impartiality cannot be seen in isolation but needs to be considered alongside how policing acts with fairness and inclusion - both in its own ranks and with the public."

News.title: Harry Styles, Cher, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish to headline Glastonbury 2027
News.content:
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.

It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.

In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.

Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.

At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.

Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.

Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.

She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.

In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.

Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.

Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.

She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.

Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.

More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

News.title: AI used to find security flaw in Java, world's third-largest programming language
News.content:
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is the world's third largest programming language used by 90% of the world's Fortune 500 companies like Apple and Amazon, and many banks, hospitals and governments.

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" the incidents are related.

More recently, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update.

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

That adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed.

Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes. And at this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

News.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
News.content:
"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Friday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small stepsâ¦ to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

News.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
News.content:
The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around Â£800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of Â£12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

News.title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
News.content:
The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.

But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.

People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.

But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).

Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."

"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.

"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."

So why is she back swimming in it?

"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

News.title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
News.content:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

News.title: Voy at-home test kit adverts banned over low testosterone claims
News.content:
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.

It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.

Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.

The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds, external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.

Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.

Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.

Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".

At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.

News.title: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health
News.content:
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.

Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.

And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.

Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.

"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.

"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."

Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.

People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

News.title: Is there any more snow on the way for England and Scotland?
News.content:
Snow fell across parts of Northern England and southern Scotland on Tuesday, following the first widespread Met Office weather warning for snow of the season.

Around 1-3cm fell for most locations, which threatened to cause travel disruption for some major routes.

But with milder air spreading in across the UK, and the ground still relatively warm at this time of year, much of that has already melted.

So was this just a brief taste of the season ahead, or is there more snow on the way?

News.title: BBC drama Shetland to return for 12th series
News.content:
The BBC detective drama Shetland is to return for a 12th series, with filming starting next year.

The new six-part series will see the return of Ashley Jensen, playing DI Ruth Calder, and longstanding cast members Steven Robertson as DS Sandy Wilson and Lewis Howden as PC Billy McCabe.

But DI Tosh McIntosh will be a notable absence because one of the original stars, Alison O'Donnell, leaves the drama at the end of the current series following a 13-year stint.

She has promised a "memorable" departure from the show, with the first episode leaving fans in suspense as she was left trapped in a locked water tank.

Further casting details for the next series will be announced in due course.

The show, filmed both in Shetland and at locations in mainland Scotland, averaged seven million viewers across 2025.

Anita Vettesse will take over as lead writer on the new series, which will be produced by Angus Sharpe and distributed internationally by ITV Studios.

The TV series, adapted from the novels by Ann Cleeves, was first broadcast on BBC One in March 2013.

DI Jimmy Perez, played by Douglas Henshall, was the central character for the first seven series, with Ashley Jensen then joining as DI Calder in 2023.

News.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive Â£1m to scale up their projects.

One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

News.title: Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said he plans to set out his proposed options to reshape the UK's future relationship with the EU next month.

Downing Street had been facing pressure to specify when the prime minister would take this step, after he previously said he would do so "around" a summit taking place in Brussels this week.

Burnham will travel to the meeting with the EU this Friday, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

However, it is understood he will not indicate any preference at this stage which of the long-term options he could back in future.

Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said Burnham would be wasting his premiership by reopening arguments about Brexit.

Speaking to Sky News, Burnham said: "I'm in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal - that's what I'm doing this week. We'll see how it goes.

"And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU."

He added this would be set out "alongside" the 10-year plan for the economy that he has promised to unveil before Parliament breaks for Christmas.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Negotiations for the deals to be unveiled on Friday began under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, but Burnham has indicated he believes the UK's Brexit deal needs to be revised further.

Making his first major foreign policy speech on Monday night, Burnham told his audience: "After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship.

"This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next Parliament."

In September, Burnham told the Labour Party conference he would "take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners".

Asked on Tuesday whether Burnham was now "hitting the brakes" and pushing any announcement of options back further into the future, a No 10 spokesman said earlier: "I don't accept that characterisation."

And speaking to Sky News, Burnham rejected the idea he was stepping back, arguing he was "doing exactly what I said".

"I will set out next month what the next phase looks like, and that is exactly what I said at my conference speech."

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy has said Labour should go into the next election promising to rejoin the EU.

Writing in The Times on Tuesday,, external he said the prime minister's conference speech in Liverpool "didn't only ignite a debate around joining the EU - it blew the door wide open".

"Burnham is right to break glass on the European question because membership is the greatest growth accelerator the government has available."

News.title: What are the laws behind letting your kids off school to play GTA 6?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The highly-anticipated release of the Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) video game has left schools across the UK worried about a potential rise in absences.

The latest iteration of the action-adventure game, developed by Rockstar Games, will launch on Thursday.

In preparation for the so-called “GTA flu” (where children pretend to be ill so they can skip classes and play the game), several schools and trusts have sent letters to parents.

“Whilst we understand that the release of a highly-anticipated game can generate considerable excitement among young people, we would like to remind families that students are expected to attend school as normal,” one letter read.

“Any absence for the purpose of gaming or leisure activities will be recorded as an unauthorised absence.”

open image in gallery Schools worry that the game may lead to an increase in unauthorised absences ( Rockstar Games )

Another letter is reported to have urged parents to maintain normal bedtimes to ensure children arrive at school “rested” and ready to learn.

What are the laws behind letting your child play truant for the day?

According to the UK government, local councils and schools can use “various legal powers” if your child is missing school “without a good reason”.

Authorised absences tend to cover situations such as physical or mental illnesses, exceptional circumstances or medical appointments that cannot be arranged outside of school hours.

This includes a Parenting Order, which requires parents to go to parenting classes.

“You’ll also have to do what the court says to improve your child’s school attendance,” the government’s website states.

If the council thinks you need support getting your child to go to school but you’re not co-operating, they can apply to a court for an Education Supervision order.

This is where a supervisor is appointed to help get your child into education.

open image in gallery You can be fined for letting your child skip school if you don’t have a ‘good reason’ ( Getty/iStock )

If the local authority is concerned your child is not getting an education, they can get a School Attendance Order.

You’ll have 15 days to provide evidence that you’ve registered your child with the school listed in the order or that you’re giving them home education. If you do not, you could be prosecuted or given a fine.

Local councils can also issue each parent a fine of £80 , rising to £160 if it is not paid within 21 days.

If parents get to three fines in a three-year period, the penalty increases to £160.

“If you do not pay the fine in 28 days you may be taken to court for keeping your child out of school,” the

If your child is off school 3 or more times within the 3 years you will not be fined but may be taken to court.

If you’re taken to court, you could get a fine of up to £2,500, a community order or a jail sentence of up to three months.

News.title: Democrat beats both Dan Sullivans in Alaska Senate race as final midterms result called
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Democrat has won the Alaska Senate race, completing her party’s sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

Mary Peltola defeated not one, but two Dan Sullivans in the closely watched contest, the ninth Senate seat the Democrats flipped.

​The Republican nominee and incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan was battling both Peltola and two other Republicans, including one named Dan J. Sullivan who later appeared on the ballot without a party affiliation.

​During the two week vote count, Peltola maintained a steady lead over now-outgoing Senator Sullivan.

Mary Peltola has officially won the US Senate election in Alaska ( Getty )

​In a statement released on November 17 announcing her victory, Peltola spoke about a theme that had formed the bedrock of her campaign: the cost of living.

​“Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table,” she said.

“Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.”

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, meaning voters can name candidates in the order of their preference. A voter’s secondary choices are used to determine a winner if no candidate crosses the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election.

Voting data analysed by the BBC showed that over a third of Dan J. Sullivan’s voters left their second choice blank, with Peltola being their second most popular choice.

Peltola received almost double the second-choice votes as the incumbent Senator Sullivan.

However, Republicans, including President Trump, have long claimed that having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot could confuse voters.

More follows on this breaking news story...

News.title: Glastonbury 2027 to be headlined by Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender will headline Glastonbury in 2027, it has been confirmed – making them the youngest headliners in the history of the festival.

North Shields-born singer-songwriter Fender, 32, will play Friday on the Pyramid stage. Former One Direction star Styles, 32, plays the Pyramid stage on Saturday, while the 24-year-old American singer-songwriter Eilish headlines on Sunday night.

This will mark Eilish’s second headlining slot at the festival, having become the youngest-ever Glastonbury headliner in 2022. She previously played the Other stage in 2019.

Styles has never performed at Glastonbury, while Fender was due to perform at the 2020 event, which was cancelled due to Covid.

In a major coup for the festival, Cher will perform in the Sunday afternoon legends slot.

Next year’s event, which will take place in Somerset between Wednesday 23 to Sunday 27 June, will be the first Glastonbury in two years. The festival took time off for its regular fallow year in 2026. In a statement, festival organiser Emily Eavis – daughter of the festival’s co-founder Michael – expressed her excitement over the new line-up.

“We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what’s to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists,” she said.

Harry Styles has previously curated the Meltdown festival (Ian West/PA) ( PA )

A host of other acts have also been announced, with Kraftwerk making their Glastonbury debut on the West Holts stage, along with debut appearances by US singer-songwriter Sombr, British soul singer Sienna Spiro and the Slovakian pop star Adéla, best known for her internet-bending summer track “Nicole Kidman”.

Lily Allen, FKA Twigs, Lola Young, Teddy Swims, Christine and the Queens, Massive Attack and Flo will also appear, as well as Kacey Musgraves, Thundercat, Robyn, and Ezra Collective. Rap legends De La Soul, The Streets, and experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine will additionally perform.

General admission tickets to Glastonbury 2027 sold out in under an hour in October, though anyone who didn’t manage to get tickets will have another chance when the Glastonbury resale takes place in April.

The speedy sale time didn’t manage to beat the previous record from 2014, when 120,000 tickets were snapped up in 26 minutes.

The second sale on Sunday 4 October took place days after coach tickets to the festival sold out in less than 30 minutes, with hopeful festival-goers thrown off by a major change to the buying system.

Shortly before the coach tickets sale kicked off, fans noticed that users could no longer log in on multiple devices, with a registration code producing just one queue number.

The change appears to be an attempt to tackle bots. However, it also scuppered the plans of fans who use a “syndicate” system where groups of friends use the same registration code to try and better their chances.

More to come...

News.title: Energy bills to rise by more than £400 in shock new forecast
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Household energy costs are set to soar by more than a quarter in January as experts warned a typical bill could jump by more than £400 due to the Iran war.

Experts at Cornwall Insight have predicted Ofgem’s energy price cap will rise by 26 per cent to £2,166 a year on January 1, up £443 on the level between October and December to hit the highest since 2023.

It said the government’s £100 household energy payment announced in the Budget for homes in council tax bands A to D in England is not included in the forecast because it is a one-off payment made outside the price cap.

Ofgem will announce the quarterly price cap level for January to March on November 25.

Releasing the forecast, Craig Lowrey, retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, said: “After already climbing in October, energy bills look set to rise again in the new year, and the timing could hardly be worse, with colder weather in January pushing up energy use and households already dealing with the cost-of-living crisis.”

( PA )

The market intelligence firm says that rising costs continue to be driven by conflict in the Middle East, with oil and gas trade disrupted worldwide since February.

Mr Lowrey said: “Once again, the cause lies thousands of miles away, yet another reminder of how events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.

“While the £100 Household Energy Payment and the removal of VAT from electricity bills will be welcomed, ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East.”

Official figures released on the same day as the forecast show that inflation in the UK reached 3.6 per cent in August, which analysts say is driven primarily by rising energy costs.

Sophie Hale, research director at the Resolution Foundation, said: “Another global energy shock has delivered a further blow to UK living standards in October, pushing inflation up to its highest level in a year.

“The worst may be yet to come as energy costs spread to the prices of other goods and services. Any further support this winter must be more accurately targeted at the households who need it most.”

This is a breaking story and is being updated

News.title: NS&I Premium Bond holders made to repay prize money after £500,000 blunder
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands of Premium Bond holders have had prizes clawed back from them by National Savings and Investments (NS&I) after it admitted to mistakenly paying out over £500.000.

The government-backed bank said it had overpaid £518,000 to around 3,500 customers following its prize draw in May due to duplicated payments. The majority of this was automatically reversed, but around £1,600 remains to be paid back.

An NS&I spokesperson said: “In May this year, due to a technical error, duplicate Premium Bonds prize payments were made to around 3,500 Direct Saver accounts.

“We contacted all account holders and apologised for the inconvenience caused and cancelled the duplicate payments.”

One customer said his money was held after he won a £1,700 prize but was overpaid £325, with his accounts being frozen until this was returned, The Times reported.

Thousands of Premium Bond holders have had prizes clawed back from them by National Savings and Investments (NS&I) after it admitted to mistakenly paying out over half a million pounds ( Getty )

Under consumer laws, anyone overpaid by NS&I is not entitled to keep their payment and must return it. However, it may be possible for them to appeal to the bank for compensation over its error.

It comes after NS&I revealed earlier this year that it had mistakenly withheld £367m from thousands of bereaved families due to an “operational failure” to trace the savings accounts of many bereaved customers.

Around 34,000 estates were affected by the issue, the bank has said, with the compensation process expected to be completed in the first half of 2027.

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Earlier in November, NS&I said more than £3 million in repayments and compensation had been issued to 613 estates so far.

It has also confirmed that the issue has been resolved for current and new bereavement claims from January, with measures introduced to ensure the error is not repeated.

The episode led to the resignation of former NS&I chief executive Dax Harkins, who had been in the post for three years.

Premium Bonds are an investment product offered by the bank, which is owned by the government. Millions of savers are entered into its prize draw every month to win cash prizes ranging from £25 to £1 million, with two millionaires made at every draw.

Savings held with NS&I do not accrue interest as with regular bank accounts, but are put up against a random digital prize picker.

There are now 22 million people taking part in the government-backed savings scheme, holding more than £137bn.

News.title: David Lammy backs calls for UK to rejoin European Union
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham has been urged by former foreign secretary David Lammy to campaign on a promise to rejoin the EU at the next election.

Writing in The Times, Mr Lammy, who also served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir Starmer, said the prime minister’s Liverpool speech "blew the door wide open" on the debate.

He said: "Burnham’s Labour should go into the next election clear that its intention is to rejoin the EU.

"Forming the next government would give it the mandate to begin formal negotiations.

"Once a deal is agreed, this should be put to the people. Unlike the last referendum, the public should have the opportunity to decide between two clearly defined choices."

This intervention arrives as Mr Burnham prepares for a major UK-EU summit in Brussels amid renewed examination of Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

The PM promised at his Labour conference address in September that he would lay out options to the nation around the time of the November meeting.

( AFP/Getty )

However, with the Brussels summit approaching on Friday, Mr Burnham appeared to delay that schedule.

In a speech on Monday, the PM said he would start a discussion with the bloc on options after the summit, before presenting options to the public at a later date.

Pressed on whether reopening the Brexit topic had become toxic, the Labour leader told Sky News on Tuesday: “I’m in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal. That’s what I’m doing this week. We’ll see how it goes.

“And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU.

“And I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.

“But I don’t agree with you at all, actually, that it’s a toxic debate.”

He repeated his pledge to stick to the 2024 Labour manifesto’s red lines – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement – before a general election and that the “British public will be in charge of whatever comes next”.

He denied changing the timeframe he had laid out in September, saying: “I will set out next month what the next phase looks like.

“And that is exactly what I said at my conference speech.”

Mr Burnham also launched an attack on Tory former prime minister Boris Johnson, who, alongside Lord Cameron, cautioned him against returning to the bloc.

News.title: Christopher Nolan: Why I don’t believe in director’s cuts
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Christopher Nolan is one of the world’s leading directors, who has steered many films to acclaim and overwhelming box-office success. But, according to the Oscar-winning filmmaker, he doesn’t actually “do anything” on set.

“It’s a weird thing,” Nolan told me in Los Angeles, ahead of the film’s home entertainment release on Wednesday (18 November). “As a director, you’re not doing anything; all you’re really doing is asking other people to do [things] and asking [them] to give their best and bring together something that you haven’t seen before, hopefully.”

Nolan attributed the overwhelming success of The Odyssey, his billion-dollar adaptation of Homer’s epic poem, filmed entirely on IMAX, to the creatives he assembled alongside producer (and wife) Emma Thomas. These included production designer Ruth de Jong, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson and sound mixer Willie Burton – all names to expect on Oscar nomination morning in January.

open image in gallery ’Directors don’t do anything’: Christopher Nolan sheds light on his collaborative filmmaking process ( Getty )

The special features on The Odyssey’s home release are an enlightening accompaniment to the film, showcasing the lengths Nolan went to pull off a series of impressive feats. The result was a global haul of $1.84bn – the biggest film of his career, surpassing The Dark Knight Rises (2012), which made $1.085bn.

One day before the interview, during a Q&A moderated by lead star Matt Damon on the Universal Studios lot, Nolan’s team noted how the director set strict time limits for tasks they initially considered impossible. However, when the creatives got to work, they achieved what he had asked of them. Nolan shared his view on his process, telling me that “the reality of being a director is not taking no for an answer”.

“A lot of it is like, ‘Yes, on the face of it, that wouldn’t work, but what if we look at it a different way? What if we re-approach it?’ And just asking people to continually reassess what’s possible – and that can come across as being a taskmaster or being a bit hard on people. But certainly with the crew on The Odyssey, it was just a joy to work with them all because there was a lot of pride in people coming up with incredible solutions.”

The reality of being a director is not taking no for an answer Christopher Nolan

Thomas, who has produced all of Nolan’s films since his 1998 debut Following, expressed slight concern that people might think they’re “really harsh taskmasters”.

But she said that, in her experience, actors and crew members “really like it when a director knows what they want and what they need”. Case in point: the fact that all of the creatives frequently return for more. “So it can’t be too bad,” Thomas levelled. “Everyone appreciates the fact that Chris shoots for the moon,” she continued, “and sometimes we get that, sometimes we don’t, but the end movie is always better because of the high standards that he sets for all of us.”

Thomas added that the reason Nolan is “so special as a director” is because “he does not ask anybody to do anything that he wouldn’t do himself”. On The Odyssey, a rigorous experience that Damon branded the toughest filmmaking experience of his career, Nolan wasn’t sitting in a tent watching the action on a monitor; he was standing alongside his cast and crew members amid adverse weather conditions, be it extreme heat or torrential rain.

open image in gallery ‘He doesn’t ask anybody to do anything that he wouldn’t do himself’: Christopher Nolan mucking in with cast and crew on ‘The Odyssey’ ( Universal Pictures )

Nolan is still in the process of deciding what film he’ll make next, but if there’s any pressure to go bigger than The Odyssey, he’s not showing it. In fact, he doesn’t look at it in such binary terms.

“There’s a lot of different factors that swim around in terms of choosing a project, and so you never quite know where you’re going to land,” he said. “I certainly don’t view films as big or small or those kinds of categories. It’s really, to me, about story and genre and how you might approach something in a new way. You’re always looking for an opportunity like that, but story has to drive everything.”

As for whether there could be a director’s cut of The Odyssey, Nolan gave a firm no, revealing “there’s a lot of deleted scenes scrumpled up in the wastebasket that no one will ever see”.

“I don’t really believe in director’s cuts,” he explained. “I want to stand by the film that goes out. As a writer-director, I try to do a lot of that weeding out. There aren’t many scenes that were shot. On a film like this, to spend a day shooting something on top of a mountain or in the rain or on a boat or whatever that isn’t gonna be in the film, I would really rather not do that. And so I wanna stand behind the cuts of the films that are put out there.”

open image in gallery Matt Damon led the acting charge as Odysseus in ‘The Odyssey’ ( Universal Pictures )

Nolan maintained that it’s his job “to fight for the cut of the movie right ‘till it goes into theatres”, adding: “That’s what I’ve always done.”

‘The Odyssey’ will be available to watch at home from Wednesday (18 November).

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.
