News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” the ASA added.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

The ASA launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.

News.title: ‘I lost my family when I contracted HIV’: why virus is still taboo in Iraq
News.content:
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.

The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.

His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.

“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph, his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”

The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.

When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.

He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.

“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.

To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.

News.title: Bosses ‘increasingly reluctant’ to hire as employment costs soar
News.content:
Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in 12 years outside the pandemic as employers braced for the impact of the Government’s workers’ rights reforms.

Vacancies dropped by 22,000 to 690,000 in the three months to October, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This was the lowest since February to April 2021 – and the worst performance since the three months to September 2014 when taking out the impact of Covid lockdowns.

Bosses are grappling with higher employment costs in addition to the Government’s looming deadline to implement the Employment Rights Act on Jan 1. Under the changes, a cap on claims for unfair dismissal will be scrapped and the time a worker needs to have been employed before they can make a claim will be cut from two years to six months.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “The problem isn’t that businesses are firing workers. It’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them.”

News.title: Wall Street slides as Nvidia casts shadow over tech stocks
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Asian stocks fell sharply at the start of a huge week for AI following the shock exit of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang over a string of extramarital affairs.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi fell 3.6pc and Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.4pc after another night of drama for the $4tn (£3tn) chip giant.

Just hours after Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, called for a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia , it emerged Mr Huang was considering a possible comeback.

Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, were among prominent figures to sign a public letter demanding that Nvidia “bring Jensen back”.

Meanwhile, several unnamed tech executives set up a “war room” to coordinate a “Stand With Jensen” campaign, according to The Financial Times.

The Wall Street Journal also reported overnight that Nvidia could be looking to scale back some of the aggressive financing it has deployed to prop up other AI companies.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies said: “These concerns are more real and are likely to have an impact on a number of companies in the supply chain.”

Taiwan’s Taiex, a beneficiary of the global AI frenzy, sank 6pc, with shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC down 5.7pc.

Allies in Silicon Valley, including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, have pushed for Mr Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia despite an ongoing investigation into his conduct by the company’s board.

The chip giant will unveil its latest quarterly results on Tuesday after triggering a wave of turmoil for the tech sector.

AI giant Anthropic is expected to list in New York this week with a valuation of $1.4tn, doing so at a time when valuations are coming under pressure.

By Monday morning, several major AI supplies had suffered a drop in their share price, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung down 4.3pc and 4.5pc, respectively.

OpenAI investor SoftBank Group also slipped 3.7pc, while memory maker Kioxia dropped 7.7pc. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron was also down 7.1pc.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “Nvidia’s results tomorrow may outweigh everything and will largely put a bow on a bumper earnings season in what has been a bumpy period for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Asian stocks mostly fell Monday as the tech sector struggled to recover from the crisis at Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang stepped down.

Mr Huang, a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The 63-year-old’s departure raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a build-out that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

Reports that Mr Huang was in talks for a spectacular return to the hotseat, did not appear to be having much of an impact in Asia, with Taiwan’s Taiex index plunging 6pc as chip giants TSMC and MediaTek were hammered.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 3pc owing to steep losses in SK hynix and Samsung, while Japan’s Nikkei lost more than 2pc with Advantest plunging 11.1pc and Kioxia 7.7pc.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Manila and Jakarta, though Hong Kong, Mumbai and Wellington rose.

Sports.title: National League side rehire former manager less than a YEAR after sacking him for losing 11 games in a row
Sports.content:
Next

NATIONAL LEAGUE whipping boys Gateshead have rehired former manager Alun Armstrong after advertising their head coach job on social media.

Armstrong’s first spell ended in January after losing 20 of his 32 games in charge.



ELEVEN of those defeats came one after another in a dismal run that led to him stepping aside.

Armstrong moved into a Head of Football Development Role while former Newcastle goalkeeper Rob Elliot successfully steered the Tynesiders clear of relegation last term.



Ex-Sunderland midfielder Lee Cattermole was appointed to lead Gateshead into this campaign, but his reign lasted less than four months.

Cattermole, 38, won one, drew two and lost 11 of his 14 games at the helm, giving him a grim win rate of 7.1 per cent.

Last week, Gateshead put out a statement on social media encouraging coaches with a Pro License and previous experience in management or assistant management to send in their CVs.

But they ended up turning back to Armstrong, hoping that he will fare better in a new era for the previously cash-strapped club, which was bought out by US private investors Flacks Group earlier this month.

Gateshead-born Armstrong faces a gargantuan task, with the club sitting 13 points from safety, having scored nine goals in their 16 league games thus far – half as many as any other side in the division.

But the returning boss said: “It is an opportunity that I could not turn down.

“What’s going to happen to this place is really exciting. The players are going to get the best tools possible and this club has never had that, which is great.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino says he is ‘following my heart’ in farewell message to USA as he jets in to start work at Man Utd

MAURICIO POCHETTINO has penned an emotional farewell letter to USA fans following his final game as manager.

The Argentine officially agreed to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United boss last week.



It was announced that the 54-year-old’s reign at Old Trafford would begin after he concluded his duties with the USMNT.

Poch signed off from the job in style early this morning, guiding his former troops to a 2-0 (8-0 on aggregate) Concacaf Nations League quarter-final win over Haiti.



The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager was visibly emotional after the final whistle as he bid goodbye to fans at the TQL Stadium in Cincinnati.

And the emotions of the moment were still raw when he took to Instagram to issue a farewell statement to fans.



It read: “It is never easy to say goodbye, especially after everything we experienced together.

“I always wanted the opportunity to coach in the USA, and I was very happy to have this chance with the national team.

“Two incredible years, with so many great moments and experiences that will stay with me always.

“From the challenges we faced at the Gold Cup to the excitement of the USA hosting the World Cup, and now finishing our time by reaching the semi-finals of the Nations League, I am proud of what we achieved.

“When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone.

“I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team.

“Not everything in football can be measured by results, and I believe we have helped build something important for the future of soccer in this country.

“This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally.



“I have discovered a wonderful country, made new friends and enjoyed so many of the traditions.

“Every time I hear Country Roads, I will forever think of all of you with a smile.

“Thank you to the players, staff, everyone at @usmnt and all the supporters. Especially to those who believed in us and gave us this opportunity.

“Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to.



“I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.

“I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves. Thank you 🇺🇸.”

Pochettino will take over a club in dire straits from top to bottom.

But he’s relishing the job of bringing the glory days back to the Theatre of Dreams.

ASHLEY YOUNG says Manchester United should forget building a new team around Bruno Fernandes – and go for Morgan Gibbs-White instead.

New boss Mauricio Pochettino has a big decision looming over his Portuguese skipper who has turned down two new contract offers at Old Trafford.



He turned 32 earlier in the autumn and is having a below-par season for the Red Devils by his high standards.

While Young, 41, played on at the top level until he was 40, he feels the time is right to start looking to the future rather than relying on Fernandes.

United blew their summer budget on three midfielders in Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos – but Young thinks they need to spend again.

Gibbs-White has been heavily linked with moves to Tottenham and Manchester City in recent years but is still at the City Ground.

He added: “There’s a lot of players there that shouldn’t be playing for Manchester United, shouldn’t be in that squad.

PAUL INCE claims Manchester United’s midfield have “no legs” and accused them of “wasting” £50million on Andrey Santos.

Former Old Trafford star Ince says the “basket case” Red Devils are too lightweight in the middle of the park and lack power.



Along with Santos from Chelsea, Youri Tielemans arrived from Aston Villa and Carlos Baleba joined from Brighton in a £155m midfield revamp.

The trio have been locked in a battle with Kobbie Mainoo and captain Bruno Fernandes for the three central positions.



This is just one of the problems new head coach Mauricio Pochettino will have to try to solve when he starts work on Wednesday after jetting in from the USA.

Guv’nor Ince, who won seven trophies in his six years at United, told SunSport: “Fernandes is a world-class player but has got no legs.

“Mainoo, he’s got no legs. So where are the legs in the middle of the park? If you’re going to be a top team, you’ve got to have legs.

“Those players, they’re not powerful. They’ve got no legs. The times you see them running back to their goal.”

Brazilian Santos, 22, signed for United in July despite being sent out on loan four times by Chelsea and generally used as a squad player by the Blues.

The Red Devils moved for him because he fit their age profile and had Prem experience.

Santos has started just four of United’s ten Premier League games and was an unused sub in the thrilling 4-4 draw with Aston Villa before the international break.

Sports.title: Paul Ince insists Mauricio Pochettino has the ‘nous’ to succeed at Man Utd and slams ‘bizarre’ poisoned chalice excuses
Sports.content:
Next

PAUL INCE believes Mauricio Pochettino has the “nous” to nail it at Manchester United.

New boss Pochettino, 54, jets into Manchester on Wednesday before taking his first training session on Thursday in preparation for the crunch Premier League clash at Liverpool on Sunday.



The former Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea chief has coveted the United job for more than a decade.

But it seemed like that ship had sailed — until the club decided to move for the Argentine this month.



Well-placed sources say Poch only came under consideration as Michael Carrick’s replacement within the last few weeks, despite his two-and-a-half-year exile from club management.

Having taken the USA to the World Cup last 16 in the summer, he will take over at his fourth Prem club with Man Utd in 18th — lower than when Southampton hired the former defender in January 2013.

Red Devils legend Ince, 59, castigated the club in 2018/19 for not appointing Poch as Jose Mourinho’s replacement — and has urged his former employers to staunchly back their new manager now.

Ince, who won seven major trophies in six seasons at Old Trafford, said: “I’ve met Pochettino a few times, a lovely, lovely man. Really, really kind, humble man, very approachable.

“I spent about 20 minutes talking about football, X, Y and Z. And, for me, he’s a top, top manager. It’s going to be a tough job for him. It really is. But it must be an exciting job for him.

“I hear these words about it being a poisoned chalice, which is mad. You’re at one of the biggest clubs in the world, and it’s the poisoned chalice managing Manchester United? It’s bizarre.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“We know at Spurs he did a very, very good job. The likes of Harry Kane, Dele Alli and Mousa Dembele, top, top players. Have United got these players? I’m not sure they have.

“But the question is, if you’re going to sack someone like Carrick, who was out there? There’s only him, Antonio Conte, Julian Nagelsmann, people like that.

“So people say, ‘Is he the right man for the job?’ You can only answer that question in two years.



“He’ll be great. Settle the players down. There’s a lot of issues that need to be sorted out. Has he got carte blanche on what he does? To say, ‘I’d bring the players in, I’d do this’?

“Recruitment has been absolutely terrible and the decision-making from the hierarchy has been terrible. It needs someone who’s got a bit of nous at Manchester United, and he’s the man to do that.”

Pochettino will be joined at United by son Sebastiano and Silvia Tuya, both fitness coaches. At Tottenham, Poch had SIX fitness coaches. United are 19th out of 20 clubs for total distance covered this season.

Carrick did not have his own fitness coach and ensured United players always had a day off the day after a game.

Previous managers Ruben Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Mourinho and Louis van Gaal insisted on recovery sessions the day after matches.



Ince was a tireless box-to-box midfielder for United at the start of their period of dominance under Sir Alex Ferguson in the early 1990s — and he has been staggered by their questionable work-rate this season.

He pinpointed the Red Devils’ 1-1 draw at Fulham on September 20 as the moment he realised that the players’ fitness was not up to scratch.

Ince, speaking via Freebets.com, added: “Do you know what started ringing bells for me? When they played Fulham away.



“From the kick-off that Fulham had, they had 46 passes and a shot on goal without a Manchester United player touching the ball.

“Now, when you’re talking about away from home, you want to make a statement. So United not touching the ball for 46 passes . . .

“There’s got to be something wrong here. It’s not the way they play football. Is it the fact that they’re very pedestrian in their passing, a lot of square passing?

“But 46 passes and you haven’t even touched the ball, that’s unheard of. That got the alarm bells ringing.

“And the problem you get now is that, as it’s been highlighted, and the players see it, the players say, ‘We’re not working hard enough’.



“I don’t believe a player ever goes on to the pitch and says, ‘I’m not going to work hard, I’m not going to try for the team’. I could never envisage a player thinking that way.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“And as it’s been highlighted, you then get players running around like lunatics to show they’re working hard. And all of a sudden, they’re just getting picked off.

“It is alarming — not working hard, running hard, doing the right things. And that’s probably the reason why they are where they are.”

Sports.title: Who will England play in Nations League quarter-finals?
Sports.content:
Next

ENGLAND’S win over Spain on Sunday saw them top their Nations League group over the World Cup winners.

The Three Lions held on for a fantastic 3-2 win in Madrid as Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored the goals.



It was Spain’s first defeat in 43 matches – ending their stunning run under Luis de la Fuente.

The victory means England are now seeded in the Nations League quarter-final draw.



Who can England face in Nations League quarter-finals?

With England having now topped the group over Spain, they have set up a potential quarter-final showdown with Belgium, Holland or Norway.

Each of the four group winners from League A will be drawn against a runner-up from a different group, meaning England will avoid Spain no matter what.

France, Germany and Portugal topped the other groups, so Tuchel’s side will avoid all of those in the last-eight.

The draw for the knockout stage of the Nations League is due to take place on Friday, November 20 at 11am GMT.

The quarter-finals will be two-legged ties, with the first match on March 25-27 and the return leg on March 28-30.

Sports.title: Vitor Matos QUITS Championship promotion race with Swansea to join Strasbourg
Sports.content:
Vitor Matos QUITS Championship promotion race with Swansea to join Strasbourg

French side Strasbourg made an official approach for Vitos Matos on Monday and the 38-year-old Portuguese coach has decided to leave Swansea City after less than a year

View 2 Images Vitor Matos is leaving Swansea for Strasbourg (Image: Cameron Smith/Getty Images)

Vitor Matos has quit Swansea City, trading in a promotion push in the Championship for a move to Strasbourg.

‌



‌



As reported by WalesOnline, Matos has agreed to take over from Hugo Oliveira at the French club. Oliveira is understood to have taken training as usual on Tuesday, but is now poised to be sacked and replaced.

‌



Matos took training with Swansea on Tuesday too, but has made up his mind to ditch the Welsh club, who sit sixth in the Championship. Swansea have fought hard to keep hold of their manager and will be due compensation of around £5million.

‌



The 38-year-old has been in charge of Swansea for just under a year. They finished 11th last season, prompting Matos to sign a new contract until 2030.

Swansea, who host West Brom on Saturday, have made a strong start to the 2026/27 Championship season and sit just three points off Birmingham City in top spot, despite losing their last two matches.

But Strasbourg's official approach for Matos on Monday set the wheels in motion, and although the departure has not yet been announced, the Portuguese coach is moving to France.

‌



Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1, just two points above the relegation zone after a poor start to the season. The sister club of Chelsea brought in Oliveira to replace Gary O'Neil in the summer after he left for Ipswich Town.

Oliveira has returned just three wins in 10 league games and patience has run out during the current international break.

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 2 Images Hugo Oliveira has struggled at Strasbourg (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Swansea started the season on fire and Matos won the manager of the month award for August. And despite their form tailing off, he has been linked with a move away from south Wales.

Matos was one of the names linked with Crystal Palace before they replaced Pierre Sage with Thomas Frank. Asked about the Palace links in October, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."

Article continues below

Swansea have been well aware of the interest in their promising young manager, with chief executive Tom Gorringe addressing the subject in a recent interview. "The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch," Gorringe said.

"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that [But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta delivering on Arsenal promise after Gunners strike triple agreement
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta delivering on Arsenal promise after Gunners strike triple agreement

Three Arsenal players have agreed to sign new long-term contracts, showing the club's commitment to helping Mikel Arteta build a dynasty at the Emirates Stadium

View 3 Images Mikel Arteta has been given a triple boost (Image: Pavel Lebeda/Soccrates/Getty Images)

It's one of football's universal truths: to win the title is hard, to retain it is even harder.

‌



‌



But after 10 games, Arsenal are sitting pretty five points clear at the top of the Premier League table. Barring a 3-0 drubbing at Brighton and their shock defeat to Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup, Mikel Arteta and Co. have largely kept their foot on gas.

‌



The same goes off the pitch, too. It's emerged that the trio of David Raya, Declan Rice and Jurrien Timber have all reached agreements with Arsenal over new contracts.

‌



Securing the futures of key players has been a common theme since Arteta established the spine of his team circa 2023 and began regularly competing for major honours. In the last 18 months, Bukayo Saka, William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes have all signed long-term contracts. Strike while the iron is hot, goes the old adage.

Black Friday special! Click here to sign up to Mirror+ for just £1 a month!

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



To boot, Arteta extended his stay at the Emirates last month by penning a new deal until 2030. It's clear that the Arsenal manager and his players are in it for the long haul, and want to create the 'dynasty' that Arteta is targeting.

"This is what we want to create right now," the Gunners boss affirmed in an interview with Men In Blazers at the beginning of the season. "It has to be the ambition from the owners of this football club and everybody on the board, to every staff member and ultimately the players. Then you have to show that with facts and actions."

‌



The trio of impending contract extensions back up Arteta's message, one which is even helping bring players into the project.

Will Arsenal create a dynasty? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

‌



View 3 Images Arsenal have reached agreements with both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice (Image: Rich Linley - CameraSport via Getty Images)

"Since the first time I spoke to him, he wants to make a dynasty here, trying to win everything as possible," £75million summer signing Bruno Guimaraes explained. "I am always very excited of his idea."

‌



The Brazilian midfielder added: "I don't have like one target - we go for everything. I think the potential we have in this team is unbelievable.

"I don't want to put targets, we need to think game again and let's see how far we can go, but with this team, I have a big chance of winning trophies."

‌



Easier said than done, of course, with Arsenal already out of one competition this season. But any potential dynasty will also depend on the strength - or lack thereof - among their rivals.

View 3 Images David Raya is poised to sign a new contract with Arsenal (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

‌



Manchester City have a serious punishment for financial breaches looming over them, while Liverpool, Manchester United, Chelsea and Tottenham have each appointed new managers and kicked off transition periods in 2026 - two in crisis-ridden United's case. Right now, Brighton are closest to Arsenal when it comes to league position.

There's also somewhat scarce competition on the continent. Paris Saint-Germain are Europe's top dogs but needed penalties to beat Arsenal in last season's Champions League final. The Gunners have also shown that they're a match for Bayern Munich, having recently earned a 2-2 draw in Germany.

Article continues below

Yet winning the Premier League remains Arsenal's top priority, as they look to become only the second team since 2009 - after City - to retain the English crown. Back-to-back titles would go a long way to cementing a dynasty and given that their best players are sticking around, who'd bet against them?

Sports.title: It's time to end the 'let's laugh at Sol Campbell' pile-on after latest viral clip
Sports.content:
It's time to end the 'let's laugh at Sol Campbell' pile-on after latest viral clip

Sol Campbell has found himself at the centre of more mockery following a recent appearance on Piers Morgan's 'Football Uncensored' show and now the ridicule is starting to become a bit uncomfortable

View 2 Images Sol Campbell has unfairly become a figure of ridicule

At first, Sol Campbell's confusing remarks, rambly anecdotes and explanations were humorous. Now it's all become a bit cruel.

‌



‌



Campbell was a top-quality, world-class central defender, an experienced England international, and an Arsenal Invincible during his heyday and he deserves respect. Naturally, Tottenham supporters will disagree.

‌



But since briefly dipping his toes into management with Macclesfield Town and Southend United, the 52-year-old has found himself the centre of widespread mockery.

‌



That ridicule obviously dates back much further than his short-lived coaching career but in recent years, it's been rather prevalent.

Despite launching his own podcast and documentary series, Legends Corner TV, Campbell still has his moments in front of the camera. There is just no getting away from that.

He once tipped France to win the 2018 World Cup quarter-final between Brazil and Belgium during a Sky Sports News broadcast and mistakenly claimed he was in charge of Southampton during a post-match interview while bossing Southend.

‌



Teen footballer dies after being hit in the head by ball during match READ MORE :

During a recent appearance on The Overlap, the former Gunners stopper went viral for revealing that he once considered leaving Tottenham as a youngster for Nottingham Forest.

The problem was, when pushed for further background, Campbell indicated there was no approach, no actual conversation and seemingly suggested the proposition was purely fantasy.

‌



Unsurprisingly, the clip in question blew up on social media and it was no surprise to see Piers Morgan quiz Campbell on the whole debacle during his latest Football Uncensored show.

After being shown the footage, Campbell set the record straight, replying: “What’s the problem?! It’s Forest, European champions, a top team… I was 18!”

‌



Simon Jordan added with a smirk: "You should have said that then you silly sod!"

Morgan said: "If you responded the way you just had, it wouldn't have gone viral."

‌



Campbell replied: "That's the thing with the internet."

The point is, the mockery continually just goes over Campbell's head. He doesn't understand what it is that people find funny.

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 2 Images Sol Campbell watches back the original clip from The Overlap

‌



When the laughter enters such a territory, it's time for the joking to stop.

Morgan's in-depth interview with Campbell - plus Jordan - covered a vast range of topics including his controversial move to Arsenal, England's 3-2 win over Spain, the lack of opportunities black managers receive within English football and more.

‌



But unfortunately, even though the dialogue was compelling, it will be best remembered for Campbell struggling to understand the concept of combined XIs or the segment posted online of Morgan and Jordan picking Campbell's brains on the Forest ordeal.

That is what will likely drive the most numbers and because Morgan and Jordan are two very intelligent and engaging big-name media figures, it comes across as if they're having a laugh at Campbell's expense as he's not on the same intellectual level.

‌



Where he is so perplexed and bewildered by it all, it makes for really uncomfortable viewing. If Campbell wants to promote and continue building his own media profile and platform, he should be allowed to do so without judgement.

In fact, just a brief scroll of his Legends Corner channel unveils a sit-down interview with Italian striker icon Christian Vieri. There are also interviews with Dwight Yorke and Andy Cole as the forward pair reminisce on their physical battles with the commanding centre-half.

Article continues below

Campbell can cut a complex figure in the sense that at times, he is difficult to understand. There are often missing gaps in his stories but everyone is different and not everybody is blessed with the gift of being an eloquent speaker. It feels like time he is finally cut some slack.

Sports.title: Man Utd and Mauricio Pochettino have decision to make over wonderkid on nightmare loan
Sports.content:
Man Utd and Mauricio Pochettino have decision to make over wonderkid on nightmare loan

Manchester United looked to have signed the next big thing in young striker Chido Obi from Arsenal but the youngster has struggled out on loan in the Eredivisie

View 4 Images Mauricio Pochettino has decisions to make ahead of January

It's over two months since Chido Obi signed for Willem II on loan and he's still not scored a single goal for the Dutch club.

‌



‌



First loans can be notoriously difficult for young players, but Manchester United's young striker Obi has faced more than a few speed bumps since moving to the Netherlands, having been thrust into a team that has had three managers this season and looks destined for relegation.

‌



United insert break clauses into the contracts of each young player they send on loan, say The Manchester Evening News. They can be activated in the January window, and the club will consider recalling Obi from a nightmare spell.

‌



Willem have played 12 games in the Eredivisie, losing nine and drawing three, leaving them rooted to the bottom of the table and staring at an immediate return to the Dutch second tier after being promoted.

Last season, Willem were the third-best team in the Eerste Divisie and only managed to get promoted through the play-offs, so it's not a surprise that they have suffered some shocking results.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Obi was on the pitch for a 3-0 defeat to Excelsior and a 5-1 hammering against Ajax, and was on the bench when PSV won 7-0. He's only been on loan for eight weeks, but it has been a brutal reintroduction to men's football.

‌



United knew it would be a struggle for Willem to retain their top-flight status, but still decided to send Obi on loan there. There wasn't much interest in the young striker, and the Eredivisie was seen as an appropriate setting for the next stage of his development.

Reacting to Obi's arrival, Willem's technical director Freek Heerkens said: "Chido is a young, talented striker who is at an important moment in his development.

‌



"He has been able to develop in a top-level sports environment at Manchester United over the past few years and is now eager to gain experience. We can help him with that, and the Eredivisie is an excellent platform for it.

"At the same time, with Chido, our squad is bringing in a striker whose qualities can be of value to the team."

‌



View 4 Images Chido Obi has yet to score since joining Willem II on loan

Obi made eight first-team appearances under Ruben Amorim in 2024/2025, but he was played out of necessity due to injuries, not because he was seen as ready to play at that level on a permanent basis.

‌



The decision was made to play Obi exclusively in academy fixtures last season, with a view to assessing his situation over the summer before confirming his next steps, as he still had a lot to work on.

Obi was initially frustrated to be spending the campaign playing academy fixtures, but he was told to get his head down, and that pre-season could be an opportunity to impress Michael Carrick.

‌



He scored 20 goals and, crucially, improved his off-the-ball work. However, he didn't improve enough to earn a role with the first team this season because he still wasn't ready to contribute at that level.

It was agreed Obi would be sent on loan, and a sensible decision was made to find him somewhere abroad, with academy staff recognising they would be setting him up to fail by sending him down the English football leagues, where he would struggle with the physicality.

‌



The Eredivisie seemed like the perfect environment for Obi to continue to learn, but Willem's struggles have made life difficult for him.

While Obi has scored twice for Willem in behind-closed-doors friendlies, he has not been considered ready to start once for Willem, and their recent caretaker manager publicly questioned his defensive work.

‌



View 4 Images Obi made a handful of first-team appearances under Ruben Amorim (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

Adrie Koster took caretaker charge after John Stegeman, who was in charge when Obi signed, was sacked. Speaking after a cup game in which Obi played the final 24 minutes, he admitted frustration with his defensive responsibilities when Willem went down to ten men.

‌



"It is partly a matter of mindset, but also of youthful exuberance," said Koster. "That boy has never experienced anything like this before. He doesn't do it on purpose either, so we shouldn't focus everything on him. This is simply part of his learning process. But we are going to talk to him about it."

The headline of the Dutch newspaper that published the quotes, VoetbalPrimeur, read: "Koster sees problem with Manchester United loanee."

‌



Koster's comments were not as harsh as the headline made them out to be, and his opinion didn't matter much because he was a caretaker, but his situation has not improved since Jurgen Streppel's appointment.

Obi has been an unused substitute in both of Streppel's games in charge. It's obviously early days in his tenure, but United will look to recall the young striker in January if he is not getting any minutes.

‌



View 4 Images Pochettino is now calling the shots at Manchester United (Image: JC Ruiz)

Alexander Isak once spent a half-season on loan at Willem from Borussia Dortmund. Nobody expected Obi to become the 'next Isak' after his spell in the Netherlands, but more was anticipated from him at this stage.

‌



Even if Obi is recalled from his loan with Willem and spends the second half of the season playing academy fixtures, he can still have a bright future, but it would be fair to suggest his future may be away from United.

United fans were giddy when Obi was signed from Arsenal in 2024. Obi's transfer to United was described by sources as a "genuine coup", and he ripped apart defences in a prolific first season, but his peers have caught up to him physically, which has negated his biggest strength.

Article continues below

It was always going to be a challenge for Obi to replicate his goalscoring form in the men's game, and there may be a few more speed bumps to come on his journey.

Sports.title: Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray steps away from job due to health issues
Sports.content:
Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray steps away from job due to health issues

Blackburn Rovers have announced that manager Tony Mowbray has left the club due to health issues with the 62-year-old addressing fans in a statement

View 2 Images Tony Mowbray has left Blackburn Rovers due to health issues (Image: Jorge Horsted/NurPhoto)

Tony Mowbray and Blackburn Rovers have announced that the 62-year-old has left his role as manager due to health issues.

‌



‌



Mowbray, who enjoyed a five-year spell at Ewood Park between 2017 and 2022, returned to the club in the summer. He had been diagnosed with bowel cancer in February 2024 before returning to football at West Bromwich Albion in early 2025 after receiving the all-clear.

‌



A statement confirming the news was shared on Tuesday morning. Mowbray said in the statement: “Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as Head Coach of Blackburn Rovers.

‌



“I’m immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I’ve loved working with them.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



“Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you’ve given me. It’s been a pleasure working alongside you.

“To the fans, thank you for the way you’ve supported me and the team this season. I’ve always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

‌



“I’m grateful to the Owners and Suhail for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

“I’d ask that you give me and my family privacy at this time. Thank you for your understanding.”

‌



View 2 Images Mowbray returned to Ewood Park for a second spell in June

Mowbray had overseen a strong start to the season despite Blackburn being tipped to struggle and financial difficulties. He departs with Rovers sat 13th in the Championship table, winning six and drawing three of his 15 games at the helm.

‌



It has been confirmed that Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds will take responsibility for first-team duties at Blackburn in an interim capacity following Mowbray's departure.

The Blackburn owner, Balaji Rao, said: “Our thoughts are with Tony and his family as he steps back from his duties to focus on his health.

‌



“Through our many meetings over the years, we’ve come to know Tony well and grown very fond of him. We’ve always admired his professionalism, his dedication and the passion he brings to his work at Blackburn Rovers.

“Tony, please know that you have our unconditional and unwavering support. We send you and your family our love and strength, and we will do all we can to support you through this time.”

Sports.title: Richard Masters issues plea to Premier League clubs over Man City sponsor threat
Sports.content:
Richard Masters issues plea to Premier League clubs over Man City sponsor threat

The Premier League's legal war with Manchester City doesn't only involve the club itself but has ramifications for their sponsors such as Etihad Airways and Etisalat

View 2 Images Richard Masters leads a five-person Premier League board (Image: Michael Regan/Getty Images)

The Premier League's five-person board of directors, led by chief executive Richard Masters, is asking clubs for legal protection should Manchester City's sponsors decide to sue them personally.

‌



‌



A league-wide meeting on Thursday will reportedly see the board make a request for clubs to cover their legal expenses, potentially worth billions of pounds, if a corporate defamation case is brought against them.

‌



It's been almost two months since an independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenue by £900million through what it described as 'sham' contracts with sponsors between 2008 and 2019. Masters added in a damning statement that City - who were charged in February 2023 but deny any wrongdoing and have appealed the verdict - had 'systematically broken Premier League rules for nearly a decade'.

‌



City's stadium and front-of-shirt sponsor, Etihad Airways, responded within 24 hours by saying that it was considering legal action against the Premier League, with the airline making several complaints. Meanwhile, fellow sponsors Etisalat - a telecommunications company worth more than £40bn - said on Monday that it viewed the findings related to Etisalat as 'entirely false and defamatory', and was considering its legal options.

Black Friday special! Click here to sign up to Mirror+ for just £1 a month!

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



The Premier League has come to realise that its board - comprised of Masters, Alison Brittain, Mai Fyfield, Dharmash Mistry and Matthew Ryder KC - is not equipped with indemnity from legal action from a third party, such as one of the sponsors. A report from the Times claims that league chiefs will seek to change that at Thursday's planned meeting with all 20 clubs in London.

It's explained that the change would see Premier League clubs collectively pay for legal expenses and any damages that could follow successful legal action from one of City's principal sponsors or any other third party. The document in question - which was sent to clubs for consideration ahead of the meeting - makes no mention of City, the club's sponsors or the 115 charges case.

‌



View 2 Images Etihad Airways threatened the Premier League with legal action in September (Image: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu via Getty Images)

While insiders reportedly view the move as a response to Etihad's legal threat, the Premier League maintain that the league is always looking to protect the board's ability to make decisions that are in the best interests of the league and its clubs. Article 35 of the Premier League's articles of association currently states that a director's legal expenses will only be reimbursed if they win a case.

Article continues below

Sponsors could also opt to take action outside of the UK, with corporate defamation claims in the United States known to have risen above the billion-pound mark. There, both sides are required to pay their own legal fees irrespective of the outcome.

Sports.title: What's still to play for in 2026 as F1 hits Vegas?
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season has three races left to go with the Las Vegas Grand Prix opening the final triple header of the year this weekend.

For the first time since the final five rounds of 2023, both world championship battles are settled before the end of the season after Mercedes wrapped up the Constructors' Championship last time out in Brazil to go with Kimi Antonelli's winning of the drivers' crown the week before in Mexico.

But that doesn't mean there aren't other important battles to be won, and key questions to be answered, elsewhere through the field before the chequered flag falls on this season in Abu Dhabi on December 6...

Who will finish second to Antonelli?

While the battle to be world champion is the only one that truly matters for drivers each year, there is personal and competitive pride at stake in finishing as high up as possible in the standings, even if the drivers may not always talk this fact up.

While the new world champion holds a mighty and unassailable lead of 111 points, his rivals behind are more tightly packed together in the battle for the best-of-the-rest positions.

Just 18 points covers the drivers in second, third and fourth places in the championship, while second through to sixth are split by 33 points.

Drivers' Championship - Battle for second 2) Max Verstappen, Red Bull - 279 points



3) George Russell, Mercedes - 262 points



4) Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari - 261 points



5) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari - 249 points



6) Lando Norris, McLaren - 246 points

In a position that had looked highly unlikely at mid-season, it is Max Verstappen (279 points) who holds second place heading into the final three rounds thanks to a run of eight consecutive podium finishes that has included three race wins.

That kind of form will make the Dutchman hard to dislodge from what would be a sixth successive top-two championship finish stretching back to 2021.

But George Russell (262 points) and Lewis Hamilton (261 points) are close enough to still harbour hopes of each finishing second themselves.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Sky Sports' The F1 Show, Damon Hill says that Ferrari 'could win the Drivers Championship and the Constructors Championship' if they 'put all their eggs behind Lewis Hamilton'

For Russell, regaining the second place he has held for much of the year would at least provide a positive note to end a difficult season in team-mate Antonelli's wake, while Hamilton would be able to point to a four-place improvement on his 2025 campaign as showing firm signs of progress for both himself and Ferrari heading towards 2027.

One of Verstappen, Russell and Hamilton is most likely to finish second as it stands, but neither fifth-placed Charles Leclerc (249 points) nor sixth-placed Lando Norris (246 points), the winner of the last race in Brazil, can yet be definitely counted out of that battle with a maximum of 75 points left up for grabs.

In all this is also the sub-plot of which Ferrari driver finishes higher in the standings. Hamilton has been their lead championship runner since the Canadian Grand Prix in May, but Leclerc - who was comfortably the team's top scorer in 2025 - cut the gap to his team-mate to 12 points in Brazil.

Will Red Bull or McLaren finish third in lucrative teams' battle?

While trophies are also on offer for the drivers who finish second and third in the standings, which will be presented at the FIA Awards in Shanghai in December, the battle for places between the 11 teams in the Constructors' Championship offers a more substantial prize.

It is the finishing order in the standings which determines teams' prize money. That means that every extra position gained, or place retained, equates directly to a team's money earned at the end of the season.

Ferrari are not yet officially secure in second but, with a buffer over third place of 95 points, that position could be confirmed in Las Vegas.

But the battle for third between Red Bull and McLaren will run potentially all the way to the chequered flag in Abu Dhabi.

Constructors' Championship standings 1) Mercedes - 652 points



2) Ferrari - 510 points



3) Red Bull - 415 points



4) McLaren - 398 points



5) Racing Bulls - 114 points



6) Alpine - 69 points



7) Haas - 31 points



8) Audi - 28 points



9) Williams - 12 points



10) Aston Martin - 7 points



11) Cadillac - 0 points

At one point in late summer, outgoing champions McLaren had been looking likely to make a fist at chasing down Ferrari for second, but a troubled triple header across Azerbaijan, Malaysia and Singapore dropped them into the clutches of a resurgent Red Bull, who then overtook them for third at the United States Grand Prix.

They both scored 33 points last time out in Brazil and are separated by 17 points.

Elsewhere, and while not officially secure, Racing Bulls are on course for a best-ever finish of fifth with Red Bull's sister team holding a 45-point buffer over Alpine.

Alpine will almost certainly finish sixth, but seventh place is still up for grabs with just three points separating Haas and Audi.

Williams, Aston Martin and Cadillac all looked poised to stay in their current respective positions of ninth, 10th and 11th barring some unexpected big end-of-season results.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The funniest celebrity encounters at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Who will finish with crucial momentum for 2027?

While 'momentum' certainly isn't as easy to measure as world championship placings, it's something all teams will be hoping to feel they carry into this winter off the back of the season's final three races.

That's particularly important this year as, unlike last winter, the rule changes afoot for 2027 are not revolutionary. There are changes to the both aerodynamic and engine regulations, which will see the power split shift to 58-42 in favour of the internal combustion engine, but they are not as substantial as the complete reset we saw at the start of 2026.

Late-season performance in 2026 has more chance of being maintained into 2027, while upgrades brought by teams across the final months of this season will have been with a view to development direction for next year too.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater gives his verdict on a wet Sao Paulo GP, where Lando Norris won in the wet, Max Verstappen fought from the back and Mercedes took the constructors' title

The fact that the season is finishing with a battle at the front in which the competitive order from race to race between Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren is not predictable, certainly bodes well for next year.

Indeed, fresh from securing the team's first constructors' championship in five years, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff cautioned: "It looks like the most maybe competitive era that is about to start because the teams have become so professional in capability and resource that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore."

Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur sees it a similar way, saying of the competitive end to 2026: "I think it's good for the championship, good for the show.

"Probably it will be true next year and the following years with the convergence of performance."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player New angles of Lando Norris shattering his champagne bottle on the podium after winning the Sao Paulo Grand Prix

New champions Mercedes have only won one of the last five races since introducing an aerodynamic upgrade at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia which they had hoped would reassert their dominance from earlier in the season. It hasn't. The Silver Arrows are now set to introduce their long-awaited ADUO-allowed turbo upgrade in Vegas, although have played down the likely performance gain it will deliver.

Wolff added: "It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship.

"And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year. So, for me, the 2027 season has started now."
