Sports.title: Wales beaten by 10-man Portugal as Neto scores but is sent off
Sports.content:
Wales ended their Nations League group campaign with a 3-2 defeat against 10-man Portugal in Cardiff after Chelsea's Pedro Neto was sent off.

Although there was little riding on the contest, with Wales guaranteed a League A relegation/promotion play-off in March and Portugal having qualified for the quarter-finals, the two sides produced an entertaining spectacle.

Portugal skipper Bruno Fernandes blasted the opener after 11 minutes, but that was immediately wiped out by David Brooks' ninth goal for Wales.

Sorba Thomas broke free to put Wales ahead before the break, but again there was a quickfire response as Neto pounced to restore parity.

Substitute Carlos Forbs stroked Portugal ahead in the final quarter, and the visitors had to negotiate the final 16 minutes a player short after Neto was sent off after receiving two yellow cards in the space of two minutes.

Image: Portugal's team captain Bruno Fernandes encouraged team-mate Pedro Neto to leave the pitch

Wales finish bottom of League A4 with one win and five defeats, and end a disappointing 2026 with a solitary victory, three draws and six losses from 10 games.

Portugal, meanwhile, finish the campaign as group winners as they earned their first win since Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement.

How Wales lost five-goal thriller...

Image: Portugal's team captain Bruno Fernandes encouraged team-mate Pedro Neto to leave the pitch

Craig Bellamy's side had lost 1-0 in Lisbon in September in a game that was to prove Ronaldo's last for Portugal.

Ronaldo's subsequent retirement from international football probably had an impact on the attendance at Cardiff City Stadium, with some seats unfilled, despite the game being officially declared a sell-out.

There would be no clean sheet for Danny Ward on his 50th appearance as Joao Neves robbed Josh Sheehan and Fernandes lashed home from the edge of the box.

Wales responded immediately with Rubin Colwill twice involved, first setting up Harry Wilson for a shot Diogo Costa blocked with his legs and then Brooks, who swept home his ninth international goal, and second in two games.

Wales hit the front five minutes before the break after Brooks worked a one-two with Wilson before releasing Thomas, who advanced from his own half to slot past Costa.

The lead lasted three minutes as Neto lost Jay DaSilva from Trincao's cross to finish at the far post.

Image: Pedro Neto equalised for Portugal before half-time

A breathless first half was not finished as Wilson hit the roof of the net from halfway with Costa retreating frantically, and the Leeds midfielder then forced a sprawling save from the Portugal goalkeeper.

Portugal regained the lead 20 minutes from time when Club Brugge winger Forbs - wearing Portugal's new-styled number seven shirt in the post-Ronaldo era - collected Ben Cabango's poor header and stepped inside Ben Davies to find the bottom corner.

Neto clattered into Brennan Johnson just one minute and 59 seconds after being booked, but Portugal held on for a fifth Nations League win to seal top spot.

Bellamy: That summed up the group for us

Wales head coach Craig Bellamy to BBC Sport:

"We knew in moments we were going to have to suffer due to the quality they have. The intensity wasn't there. We have a lot of players who don't play week in, week out a high-tempo game in such a short space of time. It's not ideal.

"We knew that at moments, when we win it, the spaces open. There were moments that worked really well. It summed up the group for us - really good moments for us; we make a mistake - at this level, these are normal things that happen.

"But also, that final moment. These teams have that profile to hurt you. At both ends, that last bit has caught us a bit in this group.

"Rubin Colwill is really good. There are times where he takes too many touches. You can't do that against this type of team. Five, six, seven - no! When he motors like he has, the ability to be a real top-end player. I'm very critical of him; I do love him.

"But I know there's more. That's why I wanted to play him in this A league. He's going to have to prove himself."

Wilson: We were better team in large spells

Wales forward Harry Wilson to BBC Sport:

"For large parts, we played really well again. At times in the first half, we had to suffer. They're a great team full of world-class stars. At times in our shape, we were comfy.

"But look at our three goals. We're disappointed. But for large parts we were really, really good again.

"We knew from the start it was going to be tough. The first game in the group against Portugal, we showed we belong. Against Norway, we beat them. In large spells tonight, we were the better team.

"Going forward or defending the goal a bit better, that's what we've got to focus on. We're going toe-to-toe with these teams; our shape is good off the ball."

Sports.title: A clash to savour at Ffos Las on Wednesday
Sports.content:
Cheltenham's loss is Ffos Las' gain on Wednesday as old rivals Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir are set to face-off on chase debut and At The Races' Declan Rix previewed the contest.

You always need a bit of luck in this game, no matter what your role or ability. While the elements have unfortunately conspired against those at Exeter so far this season, Ffos Las is the beneficiary of what they are calling The Welsh Arkle on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports Racing.

The race got a huge boost with the somewhat surprise addition of 2026 Supreme Novices' Hurdle winner Old Park Star, a high-profile non-runner on Cheltenham's Saturday card due to the ground being deemed too quick. His inclusion means we have a huge early season clash with an old foe in Sober Glory, last season's unlucky Supreme runner-up.

The inclusion of Old Park Star is no doubt bad luck for those connected to Sober Glory et al; after all, the Henderson-trained horse was meant to run last Saturday, but it's a huge stroke of luck for Ffos Las and indeed, Sky Sports Racing. Exciting early season clashes like this are incredibly rare for novice chasers in Britain - and in general given the monster that the Cheltenham Festival has morphed into - so it's understandable there is a bit of a buzz around the industry ahead of the five-runner Golwg Gwendraeth Beginners' Chase, due off at 13:18pm.

Ground and weather

As of 8.37am on Tuesday, on the back of 16mm since 6pm on Monday, the ground is officially Good (good to soft in places), but with significant rain due. According to the BHA site, tomorrow's forecast reads as, 'blustery with persistent rain, heavy at times throughout the day'. Hopefully it leads to beautiful soft ground which the horses will get through nicely.

The big guns

As the official ratings and betting suggests, Old Park Star (155; 4/6) and Sober Glory (153; 15/8) are the standouts and are set to renew their rivalry having served up a fantastic Cheltenham Festival curtain raiser in March, along with Mydaddypaddy back in third. At the line, the winning margins were 1½ lengths and a nose, with the also reopposing Baron Noir (146; 10/1), Wednesday's third favourite, a further 6 lengths back in fourth.

Wednesday's prices and a glance at the formbook in black and white could lead you down the garden path of just siding the unbeaten hurdler Old Park Star, but replaying the final flight of their Supreme clash is wise, given it had such a significant impact on the race.

Heading to the last in the Supreme, Sober Glory looked to have everything in trouble with a good 1½+ lengths lead before he put in an extra stride, hit the hurdle and landed steeply, losing critical momentum. It was a huge shame for his connections because up to that point he had jumped so well and looked the best horse in the race going to the last.

That mistake cost him dearly, along with many punters having been a huge gamble from 16/1 in the morning to an SP of 9/2. The Philip Hobbs & Johnson White yard clearly felt like they had their charge in great order, produced him beautifully on the day only for that famous last flight on the Old Course at Prestbury Park to scupper a dream start to the 2026 Festival.

His disappointing run 31 days later at Aintree is easily excused on the back of a long season after a huge Cheltenham run and now with his attentions turned to chasing, this former Irish point-to-point winner for Cormac Doyle rates an exciting prospect for the upcoming campaign for owners Brocade Racing.

Standing in his way again is fellow six-year-old Old Park Star, who, to be fair, didn't exactly ping the final flight in the Supreme himself, also putting in an extra stride which led to the son of Well Chosen landing awkwardly but crucially, not losing as much momentum as Sober Glory.

That saw him stay unbeaten in four hurdle starts, after wins at Kempton, Cheltenham and Haydock, showing good versatility in terms of the tracks he could handle along with also displaying tactical adaptability. Having jumped right in places on debut, his hurdling got better and slicker as the campaign progressed and he looked a straight-forward character throughout.

Having been put away after Cheltenham, Old Park Star's attentions now to turn chasing, a game he possesses the physical scope and athleticism for, although unlike Sober Glory he has no point-to-point background. While not ideal, it's possibly a good sign that Nicky Henderson was willing to pitch him into Grade 2 company at Cheltenham on chasing debut before the ground ruled him out.

A horse said to be big and weak last season, there could be much more to come from Old Park Star, his trainer's comments of 'he's still a shell of a horse' last year continually playing on my mind. If he was able to achieve what he did last season when weak, you cannot but be excited about him after another summer on his back.

Chasing to put manners on Baron Noir?

Baron Noir is certainly no no-hoper against Old Park Star and Sober Glory, with 7½ lengths and 6 lengths, respectively, to find with the leading pair, especially if he has settled down for a summer's break and/or fences curb his keen-going ways.

It's in his breeding to be highly-strung, being by Vadamos out of a Dylan Thomas mare, but he's a horse with plenty of ability and it was a clear sign of the belief his trainer Alan King had in him to run in a Supreme when only rated 130.

While essentially well-held at the line, the six-year-old shaped better than the distance beaten, not getting up the hill as well as his Wednesday rivals. With that in mind, the much flatter nature of Ffos Las should suit.

He too has no point-to-point background, but with the King yard ticking along nicely, he is certainly worth a market check.

Skelton pair make up the field

It's not often you would get prices of 33/1 about a Grade 2-winning novice hurdler from the Skelton yard who looks all-over a chaser on novice chase debut, but that's the task facing Carlenrig. His odds are not just about the horses he is taking on, but also the trip, mind.

A winner of the Grade 2 Bristol Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham last December, he showed a good attitude to win over that 3m trip. On the back of that given his unexposed nature, he looked a big player in the River Don Novices' Hurdle at Doncaster 42 days later - despite carrying a penalty - but having been a stinking drifter (4/1 out to 14/1), fell two out when his race looked to be run.

The former winning Irish pointer picked up a small injury that day and hasn't been seen in 298 days so this looks like a starting point to get his campaign up and running.

Stablemate Bobby's Nelson has his first run for the Skeltons and should be more at home over this 2m trip. He also looks a chaser physically and his three-quarter of a length defeat to Baron Noir last December at Uttoxeter doesn't half look bad now; indeed, you could argue he is overpriced at 80/1 on that effort, but is probably best watched.

A bet?

In truth, this looks a race to watch for the future, but if forced to have a bet, at the prices, it would certainly be SOBER GLORY. I don't think it's far fetched to say he looked the best horse in the Supreme before his final flight mistake, and with his point-to-point background, might have a jumping experience edge over Old Park Star. That said, the Hobbs and White yard are only operating at a 5% strike-rate currently, for all they've had plenty of others run well. Either way, I am very much looking forward to seeing how all these horses take to fences.

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel says goodbye to Man Utd with Real Madrid move close
Sports.content:
JJ Gabriel has announced he is leaving Manchester United as he looks forward to his "next chapter" at Real Madrid.

Sky Sports News revealed earlier this month that Real have reached an agreement to sign the 16-year-old prodigy from United.

One source has told Sky Sports News a deal to take Gabriel to Real Madrid could be finalised in the next two to three days.

Gabriel is registered with Manchester United's academy until the end of the season but Real Madrid are intending to sign him in January.

There is a FIFA loophole that allows European clubs to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have a European passport which Gabriel qualifies for through both parents.

In a farewell post on Instagram he said: "Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020. as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams.

"Here I grew as a player and as a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Real Madrid transfer target JJ Gabriel scores sublime goal for Man Utd u21s against Leicester u21s in Premier League 2.

"You gave me moments I'll always treasure. To every coach, every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.

"As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything. JJ."

Gabriel did not make a competitive first-team appearance for United, but did make a senior appearance in United's pre-season friendly defeat to AC Milan this summer.

The teenager requested to leave United in September and has not trained with the club since. When Gabriel's camp made it clear he wanted to move on, they asked to be de-registered immediately for the player to become a free agent.

Sky Sports News understands a big factor as to why Gabriel is leaning towards a move to Real Madrid is because he and his camp are confident there is a clear pathway to the first team at the Bernebeu.

Man Utd ready to move on from Gabriel saga despite losing teenage star

Sky Sports News' Dan Khan:

"Those on the outside of Carrington's walls will understandably view Gabriel's impending departure as a major blow for Manchester United. The reality, however, is that it has been expected for some time.



"Gabriel and his family have no longstanding ties to United as a club. He was not born and raised in the north of England, where a sense of local connection might have carried greater weight in his decision to stay.



"Over the last 12 months, United have pulled out all the stops to convince Gabriel and his family that there was a pathway to the first team. They met Sir Alex Ferguson, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. Gabriel also trained with the senior squad and made his first-team debut at the age of 15 against Atletico Madrid in pre-season.



"Ultimately, it was not enough to keep him at the club. As disappointing as it will be to lose a talent of Gabriel's calibre, United will no longer have to make further concessions to accommodate a young player and his family - a situation that can risk upsetting the balance of an entire academy system.



"There is a wider consideration, too. Parents and agents connected to other academy players will inevitably take note when they see one individual receive such tailored treatment. It can create expectations that are difficult for a club to manage across its youth system.



"This situation now appears to be reaching its conclusion. But the focus will soon shift to the 16-year-old himself. His talent is undeniable, but will the circus surrounding his exit become a hindrance to his development, or will it prove to be little more than a footnote in what could be a long and illustrious career?



"Time will tell. And I imagine Jose Mourinho will have something to say about it, too."

'He could have been a superstar' - Merse on Man Utd losing Gabriel

Image: Gabriel did not make a single competitive appearance for Man Utd's first-team

Sky Sports' Paul Merson:

"This kid's a good player. He could have been a superstar. Man Utd will be gutted.

"This rule has got to change. I think it's because his mum and dad have got an Irish passport that he's allowed to go abroad. And that needs to change.

"Manchester United have worked on this kid, made him the player he is. Obviously, he'd have been gifted at the same time.

"The thing is, he's going to Real Madrid. I said Manchester United are one of the biggest clubs in the world. He's going to the biggest club in the world. It's not like there's not a player in the world who wouldn't go to Real Madrid.

"You ask any player who's playing in the Premier League, if Real Madrid come for you, it's very rare you turn them down. Great opportunity for the kid."

Sports.title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
Sports.content:
After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. I think it’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

View image in fullscreen Maheta Molango: ‘Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.’ Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian

Then there is the question of integrity. Last summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer, establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says, “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “I think we live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on. They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people and a lot of people who have a good product. I think we need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

Sports.title: Portugal’s new No 7 Forbs channels Ronaldo for winner as Wales are denied
Sports.content:
One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese Football Federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.

For Wales, a Nations League relegation playoff double-header awaits in March, with Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia and Herzegovina – who knocked them out of World Cup qualifying this year – all potential opponents in Friday’s draw in Switzerland. Afterwards Craig Bellamy stressed the importance of keeping elite company to accelerate improvement but reiterated that he will not be in the job beyond Euro 2028, after which his contract expires.

“If we want to develop as a ­football nation and continue to move ­forward, we have to be playing against the best teams,” Bellamy said. “It’s only going to improve us. I was the best manager going in [Group] B, finished top … how good am I? Now I’m in [Group] A, we’ve played quite well, but I’m crap. It’s about playing the best teams, that’s how we’re going to get better. I won’t be here for the next Nations League, I won’t be the manager then, so I’m doing it for the next one.”

This was a welcome victory for ­Portugal, who advanced to the quarter-finals as group winners after a bruising 4-1 home defeat by Denmark in Braga. Turn a new page and all that. There were plenty of positive takeaways for Wales too. David Brooks cancelled out Bruno Fernandes’s opener and Wales seized the lead through Sorba Thomas, who applied the ­finish after a slick team move. But Neto, who picked up two bookings inside two minutes, the second for a foul on Brennan Johnson, levelled before half-time. Bellamy’s side were fun and, at times, freewheeling but Forbs had the final say with a neat run and finish.

Bellamy stressed the importance of locking down Vitinha and João Neves, two of his favourite players, but Wales did not allow the Paris Saint-Germain pair to have things all their own way. It was a ludicrously open game and, approaching the half-time interval at 2-2, a stray Renato Veiga pass supplied the all-action Harry Wilson with a speculative opportunity from halfway. Wilson intercepted the ball and, after taking a touch to roll it into the opposition half, the Leeds midfielder launched a marvellous left-foot lobbed effort towards goal, his 45-yard shot skimming the roof of Diogo Costa’s goal net.

View image in fullscreen Sorba Thomas put Wales 2-1 up, although their lead lasted only three minutes. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Portugal may have levelled a few moments earlier, Neto easily beating Jay Dasilva in the six-yard box to prod in Francisco Trincão’s brilliant cross, but Wilson’s attempt at the audacious was another gentle reminder of Portugal’s precarious state. After suffering their heaviest competitive home defeat against Denmark on Saturday, Portugal were again susceptible defensively. Before Thomas capped a scintillating team move to seize the lead on 40 minutes, Wilson twice went close, Diogo Dalot making a desperate block for the first.

This was an entertaining contest for which it was worth braving the winter conditions. When Fernandes picked his spot on 11 minutes, sending an unerring strike into the top corner, Portugal appeared in the groove. But Wales responded two minutes later when Brooks, who scored with a superb dinked finish in Norway, dug out another clever effort. Wilson saw a shot repelled by Costa but when the ball squirted free Rubin Colwill had the presence of mind to calmly square for Brooks, who squeezed a left-foot shot into the far corner. Colwill, a fan favourite here for Cardiff, thoroughly enjoyed his first Wales start under Bellamy.

Colwill impressed in a deep midfield role alongside Josh Sheehan of Bolton, whose former clubmate Aaron Collins, now of MK Dons, arrived from the bench midway through the second half for his debut. Portugal, meanwhile, introduced João Félix and the Club Brugge winger Forbs, the latter wearing the tweaked No 7 shirt that will always be ­synonymous with Ronaldo. An unmarked Ben Cabango, who replaced Joe Rodon as a precaution at half-time, went close to earning Wales the lead with a header. The weary look on Costa’s face as he pawed Cabango’s header away from goal for a corner said it all.

The moment Forbs surged on to a loose Cabango header and then at Davies before applying a low finish provided light relief on an uncomfortable night. For Wales, a challenging campaign ended as it began, with a heartening defeat by Portugal.

“Look, it’s a £1.2bn squad against a £170m squad,” Bellamy said. “I live in the real world. I’m beyond happy. I couldn’t ask for more. Against a top team, if you make a couple of mistakes as we did, you will get punished. We’ve offered a really good version of ourselves, we’ve been a massive part of this group. It’s just about those fine margins.”

Sports.title: Nations League roundup: Devenny’s divine strike lifts Northern Ireland to top tier
Sports.content:
A wonder strike from Justin Devenny earned Northern Ireland top spot in Nations League Group B2 and promotion to the top tier of the competition. The Stoke player fired home on the volley from the edge of the area to earn a 1-1 draw away to Hungary, who would have leapfrogged Michael O’Neill’s side in the group with victory.

Northern Ireland had fallen 1-0 behind after a 35th-minute goal from the striker Barnabas Varga, who slotted home when one-on-one with the goalkeeper Pierce Charles after a defensive mix-up. The goal ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign and also sent Hungary to the top of the group in the live standings.

But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for O’Neill’s young outfit, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders. As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation – with Rajmund Toth firing over late on – but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of their campaign.

“It’s a great feeling for us,” said O’Neill, who had to watch the game from the stands as he served a touchline ban. “We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.

“We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 [qualification] but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we’ve given against some very good teams, it’s very encouraging.”

In Wales’s group, Norway snatched a quarter-final berth thanks to Erling Haaland’s 96th-minute penalty against Denmark. It was Haaland’s second and completed a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down as the Danes were pipped for second place in Group A4.

Denmark, who began the day in second place in the standings and needed to avoid defeat to reach the knockout phase, led 2-0 inside 14 minutes through Rasmus Højlund and Pierre-Emile Højbjerg.

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland celebrates his winning penalty as Norway pipped Denmark to a quarter-final berth. Photograph: Oliver Hardt/UEFA/Getty Images

But Haaland pulled one back before half-time and, after Martin Ødegaard’s 83rd-minute equaliser had set up a grandstand finish, the Manchester City striker scored from the spot in the sixth minute of added time after the video assistant referee had ruled Joachim Andersen had handled in the area.

The two nations finished level on nine points and although Denmark had a better goal difference, Norway progressed on their head-to-head record after also winning the reverse fixture 3-2.

“It’s one of the crazier football years,” Haaland told TV2. “It’s fun to be a part of finishing it off in style. Ståle [Solbakken, Norway’s coach] said ⁠it before the match: ‘Let’s just get a good finish now to a completely indescribable football year.’ It’s fun to be Norwegian.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Norway’s latest success came ​on the back of their memorable World Cup run, when Haaland ‌and Ødegaard led the country to the ‌quarter-finals in their first appearance at the tournament for 28 years. “It’s completely fantastic and fun,” Haaland said. “I should have had a hat-trick today, ‌but I’m happy with two goals, so that’s totally fine.”

The Republic of Ireland beat 10-man Kosovo 3-0 at the Aviva Stadium to go ahead of the visitors in the standings for Group B3 to secure second place and a spot in the promotion playoffs. The win also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month’s qualifying draw for that competition.

View image in fullscreen Troy Parrott celebrates his first spot-kick with Jayson Molumby and Adam Idah. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

Kreshnik Hajrizi’s first-half handball on the line earned the Kosovo defender a red card and allowed Troy Parrott to bury the resulting penalty. The Republic were awarded a second spot-kick early in the second period after a foul by the goalkeeper Arijanet Muric, with Parrott again scoring. Jack Moylan’s header from a Liam Kitching cross made it 3-0.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, the red card incident sparked by Moylan’s cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott. His effort – clearly goalbound – was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately sent off.

Sports.title: Peter Storey, Arsenal Double winner and England international, dies aged 81
Sports.content:
Arsenal have paid tribute to Peter Storey, a key member of their 1971 Double-winning team, after the death of the former England midfielder at the age of 81.

Storey was part of the Bertie Mee team that secured the First Division title and FA Cup in a season that remains one of the most celebrated in Arsenal’s history and played 501 times for the club. That places him eighth on their appearances list.

Storey, who represented England on 19 occasions from 1971-73, earned respect for his uncompromising approach and versatility, also featuring at right-back.

View image in fullscreen Peter Storey playing for England against Scotland at Wembley in May 1973. Photograph: Ed Lacey/Popperfoto/Getty Images

Storey died in hospital after a short illness, surrounded by his family. Arsenal said: “Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of 1970-71 Double winner Peter Storey. All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.”

Born in Surrey, Storey began his career at Arsenal and made his debut shortly after his 20th birthday in 1965. He is fondly remembered by the club’s fans for scoring a stoppage-time penalty in the 1971 FA Cup semi-final against Stoke that forced a replay and kept the Double dream alive.

Storey left for Fulham in 1977 and retired eight months later when his contract was cancelled, going on to own a pub in north London. He was later convicted of several criminal offences, including financing a plot to counterfeit gold coins and smuggling pornography. He released an autobiography, True Storey: My Life and Crimes as a Football Hatchet Man, in September 2010.

Storey’s family said: “We are deeply grateful for the many kind messages, tributes and good wishes we have received. It has been a great comfort to see the affection and respect in which he was held by so many, both within the football community and beyond.”

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney says he contemplated taking own life during playing career
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated taking his own life. The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life.

“I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

View image in fullscreen Wayne Rooney celebrates after scoring England’s opening goal in the 2014 World Cup qualifying match against Poland at Wembley Stadium in 2013. Photograph: Laurence Griffiths/Getty Images

“I got to a place where you’re contemplating suicide. You just didn’t want to be around anyone. I didn’t want to see people in the streets. I didn’t want to go into shops. I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else [I] really struggled with it.”

Quick Guide How do I 

Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, said the issues he faced occurred at the height of his career. “You don’t want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it,” he said. “Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man if you like for doing that.

“I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I’ve just had a young son, I’ve just been married. It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn’t. It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.”

Rooney, who is currently featuring on the ITV show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, credits his wife, Coleen, with helping him turn the tide. “Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it.”

Sports.title: ‘I’m entering to win’: Philippe Diallo launches campaign to topple Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Philippe Diallo, Europe’s candidate to fight Gianni Infantino for the Fifa presidency, said he had received “strong signs of support from other continents” as he launched his campaign in Paris on Tuesday.

The French Football Federation president also said he had contacted Kozo Tashima, who announced his candidacy this month, and would try to convince him to “join forces”. Diallo did not indicate whether he would explicitly be asking Tashima to stand aside. “Our approaches are based on the same assessments and the same values,” he said.

Diallo revealed the first figure from Uefa to encourage him to mount a late challenge had been the Football Association chair, Debbie Hewitt. With strong European backing, the 63-year-old has secured 55 of the 106 votes needed to unseat Infantino, the favourite in March’s election.

“With the unanimous support of Uefa, I already have a large base of votes,” Diallo said. “It’s now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents. Since yesterday, I’ve had strong signs of support from other continents which will be revealed in the coming days.”

Diallo’s candidacy was ratified by the FFF’s executive committee on Tuesday, one day before the deadline to declare for the election. Tashima, the Japan FA’s honorary president, is the only other person to have said they will take on Infantino. “Initially I wasn’t running,” Diallo said, “but the insistence of my European colleagues, as well as others, led me to accept the proposal.”

Diallo has worked in French football since 1992, chairing the lobby group Union des Clubs Professionnels de Football for almost 30 years before joining the FFF in 2021. He was elected president two years later, having initially stepped up in an interim capacity.

He is also very familiar with the inner workings of Fifa, having been a judge in its dispute resolution chamber for more than two decades.

View image in fullscreen Philippe Diallo’s candidacy caps several months of him very publicly distancing himself from Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Ashley Landis/AP

“I have the experience, the conviction and the values to make my candidacy a credible alternative to the current Fifa leadership,” he said. “I’m entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win. What has happened over the last few months has shocked the footballing world and does not match our vision for the future of football.”

Diallo, who formally withdrew the FFF’s support for Infantino in September, said he was “aware of the responsibility” of his candidacy: “I’m doing this to be in line with everything that we’ve been saying since this summer, and even before that.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Diallo reiterated his criticism of Infantino and railed against what he described as “solitary governance” at Fifa. “The great issues of football are being decided behind the scenes, with no transparency, without consulting the stakeholders,” he said.

According to Diallo, recent events have “damaged football’s image, its credibility, and have introduced the poison of division”. He cited the Fifa Peace Prize, the lifting of Folarin Balogun’s red-card suspension during the World Cup, the extended half-time break during the final and the failed World Cup sell-off plan.

Diallo indicated he had not spoken with Infantino in months. “The last time I saw him was at the World Cup, when he came to a few France matches,” he said. “Unfortunately he didn’t take the opportunity to share some of his projects with us. I considered that to be an act of defiance.”

Diallo said he would go into detail on his manifesto on 6 December at the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in Belfast. “My vision is that of open governance,” he said. “It’s one where the authorities truly play their role and the president is in charge of vision and strategy but leaves the day-to-day management to the secretary general. I think that certain stakeholders, namely the clubs and players, need to be more directly involved.”

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel confirms Manchester United exit: ‘You gave me moments I will always treasure’
Sports.content:
JJ Gabriel has announced his departure from Manchester United by posting a farewell message to the club on social media.

The teenager, who has not played a competitive game for the first team, joined as a 10-year-old in 2020 but has been absent since he requested the cancellation of his registration in September before he turned 16, on 6 October.

It has been widely reported that he will join Real Madrid and while he made no mention of his intended destination, his goodbye video on Instagram appears to have taken him closer to a move to the Spanish giants.

Gabriel said in the video: “Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here I grew as a player and a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

“You gave me moments I will always treasure. To every coach and every member of staff, to my teammates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.

“As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything, JJ.”

Gabriel had remained registered to United, who are understood to be ready to explore legal options against the youngster’s next club over a possible breach of regulations.

The 16-year-old is the son of former Republic of Ireland international, Joe O’Cearuill, and last season became the youngest winner of United’s Jimmy Murphy Award, for their young player of the year.

United had hoped to persuade the teenager to stay but it appears his hat-trick-scoring turn against Sabah on his Uefa Youth League debut, on 10 September, will be his final appearance for the club. Gabriel shone in that 5-0 victory although his representatives were disappointed he was not registered to play later that day in the Champions League fixture against the champions of Azerbaijan.

The teenager was due to appear in the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton the next week but had seemingly decided upon a new direction by that point. Gabriel would have become the club’s youngest player in a competitive match in that tie, having appeared off the bench for Michael Carrick’s side in an August friendly against Atlético Madrid.

Sports.title: Wiegman cites young talent as key to new England deal after calling up Goodwin
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman says the potential in England’s emerging young players helped convince her to extend her contract until the end of 2029’s European Championship.

The Lionesses head coach, whose previous deal was due to expire next year, gave first senior call-ups to the striker Isobel Goodwin and goalkeeper Katie Cox on Tuesday as she named her squad for December’s two-leg World Cup qualifying playoff against Ukraine.

Speaking to the media for the first time since she signed her new contract in October, Wiegman described the Football Association as “a trailblazer with the women’s game and a great federation to work for” and said: “I’m really happy with the team but also talents coming through, which is exciting, and there’s now some high potential, and hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players, if not already. And I hope to have a part in that, too, and have a contribution to that. While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited.

“The majority of their development is happening [at their clubs] but when they come to our environment, I hope to have a little part of that contribution.”

The Dutchwoman has led England to three consecutive major tournament finals, lifting two European titles, since taking charge in 2021 on a deal to 2025. Asked whether she had expected that to become an eight-year stay, she said: “No. I thought: ‘Four years, that’s a long time.’ Then it became six years and that looks like it’s becoming eight years. I would never have expected all of the things that we have reached.”

Will she call it a day in 2029? “Well, I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know! I don’t plan that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”

Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Taylor Hinds (Arsenal), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Poppy Pattinson (London City Lionesses), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)



Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Grace Clinton (Manchester City), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Ella Toone (Manchester United), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)



Forwards: Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea), Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Isobel Goodwin (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal) Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Wiegman, whose latest 25-player squad includes 10 players with fewer than 10 caps, watched from the stands at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday as Goodwin scored for London City Lionesses with a terrific finish against Arsenal. She said of the 23-year-old: “We always knew she’s a huge talent [with] a high potential. We’re watching a lot of games over periods of time, all the time, so we [had] kept an eye on her anyway, but I think it also helped that she had that great goal and a great performance last Sunday.

“She has some different qualities. She’s really fast too. She can head – she showed that also in attacking set plays and defending set plays also – and she can score goals. Does she need to step up to the next level? Absolutely. But you can tell that she’s improving.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wiegman was unable to call upon several injured players, including Lauren James and Alex Greenwood. She included Manchester United’s Ella Toone, who was initially left out of September’s squad before being recalled for the playoff against Greece. Wiegman said of Toone: “She has impressed us really well. She responded really well. And going back to [her] club, she’s done well too. And that’s what has been fed back to me too.”

Cox is rare in getting an England call-up while playing in the second-tier WSL2. The 20-year-old is on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea.

The Lionesses face Ukraine on neutral territory in Spain in the away leg on 1 December before playing them at Wembley four days later.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino boards a private jet to Manchester with a promise that Man City's dominance of the city rivalry is 'gonna change'... and a bizarre declaration of his love for Country Roads!
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino made a promise to end Man City's dominance as Man United manager in his last interview as United States national team coach on Tuesday evening. The new manager is currently in the air as he prepares to start his new job on Wednesday after landing at 11.30am. Pochettino took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet chartered by the club after his final match on American soil, which saw the US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati. But before becoming airborne, Pochettino had time for a final statement Stateside, after being taunted that 'Manchester is blue, and will always be blue' by one of his interviewers. 'No way,' he shook his head. 'You will see.' 'Give me time. Give me time and then that - that's going to change.' Mauricio Pochettino shared his promise to end Man City's dominance in Manchester in his final television interview as United States national team manager The Argentine took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet last night and is due to land at 11.30am Pochettino also shared a poignant farewell message to his US set-up, days after breaking down in tears in a press conference ahead of his penultimate time in charge. Man United fans may also have been pleased to read of Pochettino's new-found love of John Denver's song Country Roads in his goodbye message, a song which is played before kick-off at Old Trafford. 'It is never easy to say goodbye, especially after everything we experienced together.' Pochettino captioned a carousel of photos of his time in the role. 'I always wanted the opportunity to coach in the USA, and I was very happy to have this chance with the national team. Two incredible years, with so many great moments and experiences that will stay with me always. 'From the challenges we faced at the Gold Cup to the excitement of the USA hosting the World Cup, and now finishing our time by reaching the semi-finals of the Nations League, I am proud of what we achieved. 'When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team. Not everything in football can be measured by results, and I believe we have helped build something important for the future of soccer in this country. 'This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally. I have discovered a wonderful country, made new friends and enjoyed so many of the traditions. Every time I hear Country Roads, I will forever think of all of you with a smile. 'Thank you to the players, staff, everyone at (the US national team) and all the supporters. Especially to those who believed in us and gave us this opportunity. 'Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy. 'I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves. Thank you USA.' Pochettino had previously explained his emotions as stemming from how difficult the decision had been to leave the national team and re-start at Old Trafford. ‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said on Friday. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy. ‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay. ‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward. ‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives. ‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.' Man United first made contact with Pochettino following their breathless 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in their last match before the international break. The Man United hierarchy had previously given former head coach Michael Carrick a stay of execution amid a worrying start to the season, but as they prepared to head into the two-week pause in the relegation zone, the board became keen to make a change. An agonising wait for Carrick followed, with the club legend taking training for multiple sessions at the start of the week as his future was openly mulled by executives including CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox. After the duo returned from Monaco, where they had flown to speak to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe about Carrick's future, the 45-year-old was finally despatched last Thursday morning. Pochettino's United States farewell match went off in pitch-perfect style, which allowed thoughts to quickly move to the next task at hand after the final whistle. Christian Pulisic helped make sure that Pochettino's reign in charge ended on a high note The manager will now focus his attentions on getting Man United out of the relegation zone 'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino said after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.' Travelling with Pochettino are outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott, while his assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield. Man United paid a staggering £10million to cleave Pochettino and his staff away from the United States, after the head coach signed a new contract with the national team in the wake of this summer's World Cup. The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday. Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati. 'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'

Sports.title: 'There was blood everywhere. I've still never been given a cause of death': Robin Smith's widow Karin on the mystery around England legend's passing, his final days and his fight with alcoholism
Sports.content:
'There was blood everywhere. I've still never been given a cause of death': Robin Smith's widow Karin on the mystery around England legend's passing, his final days and his fight with alcoholism

Karin Lwin began dating Robin Smith in circumstances that might have made others think twice.

When Lwin came home one day in 2011 to their mutual apartment block, she saw Smith brooding by the pool, ‘staring out at the South Perth lights’, and asked what was up. He said he was reflecting on his cricket career, his ‘lost’ sporting family – then picked up two bottles of vodka and said he was going to throw himself into the Swan River.

‘Don’t drink that, and don’t throw yourself off a bridge,’ she told him. ‘I’ll be here tomorrow, and every day until you’re OK. So, yeah, that’s when we started dating.’

It is almost a year since Smith, the much-loved former England batsman, was found dead at his home by family members, aged 62. For Lwin, though, the grief feels raw and vivid.

Sitting outside the local coffee shop where they would hang out, she alternates between cherished memories of a decade and a half together, and tears for a life cut short while she was on the other side of the world.

On the day Smith died, Lwin was in Belgrade, Serbia, undergoing stem-cell treatment for multiple sclerosis. Smith had wanted to donate his own stem cells, but the heavy drinking that nearly killed him in 2024, when he was in hospital for seven months with cirrhosis, ruled out the possibility.

Karin Lwin with Robin Smith, the former England cricketer who died last year. ‘He was the love of my life,’ Lwin says. ‘Considerate, loving, kind, empathetic'

Lwin, who still wears her diamond engagement ring, says she doesn’t know the cause of Smith's death despite asking for the autopsy report

Smith was an England icon with a fearsome cut and pull, who played 62 Tests and averaged 43 with the bat

In the last message he sent her, he promised to collect her from Perth Airport on December 5 last year. They had been unable to agree how to fund his anti-drinking medication: she was happy to pay, he didn’t want her to. Lwin, now 59, tells me: ‘He said, “We’ll talk about it on the 5th, when you return”. But I knew he wouldn’t take a cent from me.’

The discussion never took place. On December 1, Smith was found unresponsive at home by his son and daughter-in-law, who spoke on the phone to Lwin, 8,000 miles away in Serbia. According to Lwin, she was told: ‘We opened the door of his apartment, and we had never seen so much blood in our life. There was blood everywhere.’

Lwin says the police were called, though there was no sign of a break-in. Neither was there any indication he had been drinking. There has never been any suggestion of suicide. Even now, though, she says she doesn’t know the cause of death, despite asking for the autopsy report: ‘I was never given an explanation at all.’

To add to the poignancy, the two were planning to get married, with Smith hoping to tie the knot before Christmas this year, preferably in a church back in Hampshire. Lwin had previously resisted thoughts of a wedding until he got his drinking under control. She still wears a diamond engagement ring.

Above all, she remembers a caring, sensitive man whose on-field persona – all muscular square cuts and an average of 43 from his 62 Tests – belied a chronic lack of confidence. ‘Every time there was something drastic, it weighed on him.’

When Smith was asked to speak to Andrew Flintoff’s England Lions squad at Lilac Hill on the day after the Test team had blown the first Ashes Test in Perth in November 2025, he was wracked with self-doubt.

Lwin says: ‘He told me, “I’m a nothing". I said, “Don’t be ridiculous. You’re not a nothing. You’re an icon of English cricket. Go and speak to your English cricket family”.’

Smith (centre) was asked to speak to the England Lions last year during the Ashes, and went down a storm

In an inscription in Smith's autobiography, The Judge, he wrote: ‘My darling Karin, this story of my life would never have been possible without your support'

In the event, Smith went down a storm with the Lions, and was still emotional when he spoke about the experience with me that afternoon – partly because he was touched by the players’ response, partly because he was worried Karin might not make it home from her stem-cell treatment. Just over a week later, Smith would be dead.

Karin's relations with his family are not straightforward, with brother Chris – who won eight Test caps for England in the 1980s – telling the Daily Telegraph earlier this year that Robin ‘just had his finger on the self-destruct button… there was nothing more any of us could do that might have turned him around’.

Lwin argues: ‘Chronic alcoholism is a disease. It’s not just a choice.’ But she also knows Chris’s concern came from a place of love for a man she says was ‘kind, compassionate and always eager to learn about everyone... he had a full heart’.

She also mentions more than once the moment Smith’s ex-wife, Kath, squeezed her hand sympathetically during his funeral in Perth, and says Chris’s wife, Julie, sent her a locket of Robin’s famous crinkly hair, which earned him the nickname 'Judge'.

After the funeral, Lwin asked Hampshire chairman Rod Bransgrove to take Smith's ashes back to England and scatter them at the Rose Bowl, the county’s HQ, where the Robin Smith Suite houses members on matchdays.

And she will visit the venue in July, when England and Australia contest the fourth Ashes Test – and the first staged in Southampton. ‘He (Smith) asked me to promise that I would go,’ she says. ‘He also wanted to pass on some batting tips to the England guys after watching them in the Perth Test last year, and explain to them what they did wrong.’

In an inscription in Smith's autobiography, The Judge, ghost-written by the journalist Rob Smyth but with contributions from Lwin on the psychological aspects, he wrote: ‘My darling Karin, this story of my life would never have been possible without your support.

Karin alternates between cherished memories of a decade and a half spent with Smith and tears for a life cut short

‘You were by my side at my lowest point in my life, loved and encouraged me to capture my mojo. You wrote beautifully and accurately to bare my soul to the cricketing world.’

And he would be thrilled to see the effects of her stem-cell treatment. Having been confined to a wheelchair, in which Smith would spin her around to music, Lwin can now walk with the aid of a stick.

‘He was the love of my life,’ she says. ‘Considerate, loving, kind, empathetic, always with a philanthropic mindset.

'He wanted to help everyone if he could, and was much loved by young cricketers he coached in Perth. I feel their pain, as well as I feel mine.’

For confidential support, call Samaritans on 116 123, visit samaritans.org or visit https://www.thecalmzone.net/get-support

Sports.title: How Mauricio Pochettino's culture shock tactics will resurrect Man United: From 'Murderball' training that leaves players throwing up to telling Harry Kane to slim down and why even the smell of the kit must be spot on
Sports.content:
When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

Rangnick replied that he was certain it could. The German was, of course, proved very wrong.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

Heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

But no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

Mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

The good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

Son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' says Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’

On arrival this week, for example, he will renew acquaintances with Luke Shaw, one of his old Southampton players signed for Louis van Gaal at United back in 2014. Shaw – the club’s only real left back – is 31 now and recovering from injury.

The physical limitations of this United team were clear in the titanic but ultimately rather pitiful 4-4 draw with Aston Villa that proved to be Michael Carrick’s last game in charge just before the international break.

Invited back into a game they trailed 2-0, United’s front four briefly chased the life out of Villa when Unai Emery’s team were in possession. For 20 minutes, Villa could not get out of their own half.

But the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

At Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

Six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa whose ‘Murderball’ sessions eventually arrived in England during his spell at Leeds United eight years ago. The stated aim is simple.

The likes of Bruno Fernandes (centre) have struggled to maintain the physicality Pochettino will demand across 90 minutes in games this season

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ said former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’

Trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ says Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’

For this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

At United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

Equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new when he landed at Southampton in 2013

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight

There is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

This, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three says everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

Pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as important as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He said, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’

Equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

At Tottenham, Pochettino would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in

Pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment

As strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

These are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like new-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave New World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’

What manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a new manager bounce at Old Trafford.

His relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their new boss

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea

United’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

So, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

Here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

Pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

The man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

But Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate issues, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

Sports.title: Melbourne Cup horse found dead in a skip: Racing world shocked after horrifying discovery - as bizarre explanation is issued for 'respectful burial' blunder
Sports.content:
The racing world has been left in shock after a Melbourne Cup horse who died after suffering severe colic was found in a skip – with the equine specialists who were unable to save the horse only able to offer a baffling explanation.

So You Are was found among the general waste at Cleanaway's Lucas Heights facility in Sydney after the five-year-old gelding died on Monday.

The horse had been rushed to REC Equine Specialists at Randwick for emergency surgery after being struck down with colic.

The specialists euthanised the horse after it became clear he could not be saved – but managing partner Dr Jonathan Lumsden could only apologise 'unreservedly' for what came to pass after his death.

'REC Equine Specialists extends its deepest sympathy to the owners, trainer and connections of So You Are, and apologises unreservedly for the distress caused by footage shared on social media today,' Lumsden told news.com.au.

'On Monday 16 November, So You Are was brought to our hospital for emergency treatment of severe colic. Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanised under anaesthesia. After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried.

Racing NSW stewards are investigating whether a horse found in a skip bin at Lucas Heights was So You Are

So You Are underwent emergency treatment at a specialist equine hospital but could not be saved

'What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry. So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that.

'We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change. We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally.

'We are working with our service provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.

'Effective immediately, we have stopped using this service provider, we are reviewing how the service providers we contract care for horses after death, from collection to final burial, and will share the findings with So You Are's connections and Racing NSW.
