World.title: Hungry, unpaid and afraid: Africa’s journalists pushed to the brink
World.content:
How can a hungry journalist be expected to deliver the facts the public needs? Across Africa, journalists are struggling to survive, working for months without pay and reporting without contracts or protection. This is not just a workplace crisis. It is an attack on the very conditions that make independent journalism possible.

Yet journalists are expected to expose corruption, scrutinise power and verify claims while wondering how they will pay for food, rent or transport to their next assignment. For many, journalism has become a struggle for survival. The consequences are visible in every delayed salary, every unpaid assignment and every story abandoned because the reporter cannot afford to pursue it.

With UNESCO’s support, the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) and its affiliated unions and associations across Africa’s five regions carried out the first journalist-led, continent-wide survey of journalists’ working conditions, labour rights, safety and media freedom. It drew responses from 1,586 journalists in 45 African countries. Among those surveyed, 61 percent said their income from journalism did not meet their basic living needs, 58 percent reported delayed salaries and 62 percent had no written contracts.

Behind these numbers are journalists expected to perform an essential public service without the means to make a decent living. In Central Africa, 55 percent of respondents reported salary arrears lasting three to eight months within a single year.

The deprivation extends beyond pay. Many respondents also reported having no health insurance or paid leave. Freelancers and contributors are among the most exposed. Many lack contracts, predictable incomes and social protections yet are expected to produce regular work and take risks similar to those faced by newsroom staff.



This widespread precarity is corroding the quality of journalism. Investigations require time, travel, secure communications, access to documents and careful verification. Poverty and unpaid work deprive reporters of these basic tools. A newsroom under financial strain has less capacity to check claims, protect sources and follow a story beyond the first official statement. Stories are dropped. Errors are harder to catch. The public is left with a thinner, weaker account of events.

The consequences for information integrity are grave. The FAJ report describes journalists relying on side businesses, borrowed money and allowances from outside sources, including political “per diems”. This does not mean that journalists in precarious work are dishonest. It means poverty wages and financial exposure can create openings for outside interests to influence what gets covered and how. These conditions can allow “brown envelope” practices to flourish. When a journalist’s ability to survive depends on money from a person or institution with a stake in a story, independent reporting is placed under pressure.

The survey shows that these abysmal conditions are already shaping coverage. Eighty-four percent of respondents said they practised self-censorship frequently or occasionally. Sixty-nine percent said threats had led them to avoid certain stories. When a journalist fears losing an already inadequate income, censorship does not need to arrive as a formal ban. It can be the decision not to investigate because the personal cost feels too high.

The danger is physical as well as economic. Sixty-five percent of journalists who took part in the survey had experienced work-related threats or intimidation in the previous three years. More than half rarely or never felt safe reporting, and 78 percent said they had no workplace access to legal support. Journalists are sent to report on dangerous events and uncover uncomfortable truths that powerful interests would rather keep hidden, then are left to face the perilous consequences alone.

Online attacks deepen the crisis. Journalists reported online harassment, digital surveillance and hacking attempts, often without access to digital safety training. Female journalists face additional risks, including sexual harassment, online gender-based violence, unequal pay and exclusion from leadership. When women are driven out of public debate by threats, journalism loses their reporting and the public loses the perspectives they bring. The strain is also evident in journalists’ wellbeing: 44 percent reported frequent burnout, and 47 percent had considered leaving journalism.



The survey’s regional findings highlight delayed or inadequate pay in West, Central and Southern Africa and political intimidation, arrests and legal harassment in East and North Africa. There is no single African newsroom experience: In some places poverty is the most immediate threat; in others, repression and physical danger dominate. Often journalists face both.

Country examples also show that democratic credentials alone do not guarantee decent conditions. The report describes Ghana as having relatively strong democratic credentials yet cites research from 2023 finding that many media workers there earned as little as G500 cedis ($38.80) to 1,000 cedis ($77.61) a month. Freelancers often relied on transport reimbursements, commissions or sponsored content to survive. Elections and democratic institutions matter, but without labour rights, fair pay and protection from pressure, journalists can remain economically vulnerable even in a more open political environment.

There are, however, practical examples of progress. In Mauritania, a government decision in 2025 regularised 1,860 media workers at public media institutions after a sustained campaign by the Association of Mauritanian Journalists with the backing of FAJ and the International Federation of Journalists. These journalists gained permanent contracts, equal pay and benefits, medical coverage, paid leave and retirement benefits after more than 30 years of campaigning for professional and social recognition. In Morocco, a collective agreement signed in February 2023 and negotiated by the National Syndicate of Moroccan Journalists secured a net monthly salary increase of 2,000 dirhams ($201) for eligible journalists with more than four years of experience. These changes show how government action and collective bargaining can put real protections into journalists’ working lives.

Namibia offers another important lesson. Journalists in the survey still described long hours, unpaid overtime and stagnant salaries. But formal registration of the Namibia Media Professionals Union gave media workers a recognised way to organise and bargain collectively. This month, the union secured a substantially improved settlement for workers facing retrenchment at The Namibian newspaper. This does not resolve the wider crisis, but it shows how collective representation can defend workers’ rights in practice.

In Somalia, long one of Africa’s most dangerous countries for journalists, the National Union of Somali Journalists led the development of a national action plan on journalists’ safety adopted in September 2022 after consultations involving journalists, the government and international partners. It sets out a Somali-led framework to strengthen journalists’ safety, media freedom, access to information and protection for female journalists. Its adoption was an important step towards safer working conditions for journalists.

Across the continent, the African Union and its organs have also taken steps to address journalists’ safety and media freedom. Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU commissioner for political affairs, peace and security, has been a vocal advocate for media freedom and journalists’ safety and a leading voice in affirming that professional media are indispensable to democracy and good governance. Over the past three years, the AU Peace and Security Council has increasingly addressed Africa’s media environment. In October, it called for greater protection of journalists, action against impunity and stronger safeguards for access to information.



These examples show what governments, media organisations and multilateral institutions must do. Enforce labour protections. Pay wages on time. Provide written contracts, social protection and legal support. Protect the right to organise and bargain collectively. Treat freelance journalists as workers with enforceable labour rights. Investigate attacks and stop using laws to intimidate reporters. Democratic safeguards and labour protections must advance together. Neither can substitute for the other.

When journalists are forced to choose between pursuing the truth and securing their own survival, the public pays the price: Investigations go unfinished, abuses escape scrutiny and vital facts remain hidden. Fair pay, secure employment and safety are essential to media freedom and the public’s right to know.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Africa’s economic future cannot depend on Washington
World.content:
Trump’s move to exclude South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA shows why Africa must accelerate its own economic integration.

On September 2 , United States President Donald Trump signed legislation extending the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) through the end of 2028, following overwhelming support in Congress. Yet just two months later, on November 2 , his administration announced plans to terminate the eligibility of South Africa and Rwanda for the programme from January 1, 2027.

The decision lays bare the fundamental weakness of AGOA: African economies depend on trade privileges that Washington can withdraw whenever its political priorities change.

AGOA is a US trade law that currently covers 33 eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It was enacted on May 18, 2000, to allow these countries to export thousands of products to the US market duty-free, and was promoted as a strategic mechanism to foster economic growth, expand trade between the US and the continent and encourage economic and political reforms.

AGOA initially delivered promising results. It is estimated to have supported more than 300,000 direct jobs across Africa and 1.3 million indirect jobs. According to a 2024 US Trade Representative report, two-way goods trade between the US and sub-Saharan Africa reached $47.5bn in 2023, including $9.7bn in imports under AGOA and the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP), of which $5.5bn consisted of non-oil products such as apparel and agricultural goods.

However, recent figures point to growing challenges, with some even suggesting a decline. A Congressional Research Service report shows that US imports receiving AGOA duty-free treatment dropped sharply from $7.9bn in 2024 to $5bn in 2025. Another analysis by the German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) noted that the share of US imports from sub-Saharan Africa benefiting from AGOA and GSP preferences plummeted from more than 80 percent in 2008 to roughly 24.7 percent in 2021 amid eligibility uncertainty and short renewal windows.



Only a few eligible sub-Saharan African countries capture most of the programme’s benefits. South Africa is its largest beneficiary, with exports to the US worth billions of dollars annually, while most other eligible countries struggle to make full use of its preferences.

Furthermore, because the US administers the programme’s preferences unilaterally, rather than through a bilateral treaty, Washington can exclude or reinstate any eligible country based on its own assessments and criteria, including market reforms, human rights and labour standards.

Since the programme’s inception, some countries suspended from AGOA have criticised the impact of their removal. Ethiopia’s suspension in 2022, for instance, led to the loss of thousands of garment sector jobs.

In practice, Washington’s geopolitical interests often carry more weight in eligibility decisions than AGOA’s stated criteria.

The Trump administration’s decision to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s AGOA eligibility is a clear case in point. Both countries have pursued policies that conflict with Washington’s interests and that the administration regards as a threat. South Africa has strengthened its economic and political ties with US rivals such as China and Russia, while facing accusations from Washington of obstructing American trade and investment, alongside Trump’s allegations of a “white genocide”.

Rwanda’s alleged support for the M23 rebel group in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has also brought it into conflict with US interests in the region’s critical minerals.

Sharp declines in AGOA import values, unstable US trade policies, and short-term extensions leave African exporters highly vulnerable. Losing AGOA access triggers immediate customs setbacks, including tariff increases of 15 to 20 percent on some products. Ultimately, these unpredictable extensions prevent AGOA from building a self-sustaining African industrial base, making accelerated implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) an urgent priority for the continent.

Africa’s economic vision cannot remain hostage to changing administrations’ policies or unilateral decisions made abroad, as the continent needs to build strategic resilience and economic independence. The AfCFTA is a historic trade agreement signed under the auspices of the African Union (AU) on March 21, 2018, in Kigali, Rwanda, which officially entered into force on May 30, 2019, with trading beginning on January 1, 2021.

The agreement aims to bring African Union member states into a unified market of over 1.3 billion people, with a combined gross domestic product (GDP) exceeding $3.4 trillion.



Relying on a vast regional market would mitigate the impact of external shocks, such as the revocation of preferential trade agreements like AGOA or the sudden imposition of steep tariffs. Given that trade between African nations currently accounts for only about 15–18 percent of the continent’s total trade, the AfCFTA aims to progressively eliminate tariffs on 90 percent of tariff lines, thereby stimulating internal commerce and providing a buffer against declines in Western markets caused by tariff fluctuations.

AGOA and many other external agreements have largely kept Africa in the role of a raw material supplier. In contrast, the AfCFTA encourages the development of regional value chains, where one African nation might produce raw materials, another processes them into finished goods, and the final product is sold to consumers within the continent, with fewer tariff barriers.

AfCFTA has made notable progress in developing the instruments needed for continental trade. The number of countries participating in trade initiatives under the agreement has grown to include South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Tunisia, making use of its preferential tariff arrangements.

The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), launched on January 13, 2022, enables banks and financial institutions to conduct cross-border transactions in African currencies, reducing reliance on foreign currencies such as the US dollar.

The African Union also adopted protocols on competition policy in February 2023 and digital trade in February 2024, aimed at promoting fair competition and facilitating e-commerce. In August 2026, the AfCFTA Secretariat signed an agreement to modernise and digitise customs systems. The AfCFTA Adjustment Fund has also been activated, with an estimated financing requirement of $8bn–$10bn, to support developing countries and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as they adapt to the requirements of the single market.

For AfCFTA to serve its purpose and reduce dependence on volatile global trade agreements that prioritise Western interests over those of Africa, the continent still needs to accelerate economic integration by removing tariff and non-tariff barriers and harmonising trade and regulatory policies to facilitate the smooth movement of goods and services.

To improve local markets, African countries must undertake the costly and risky investments involved in building cross-border infrastructure to reduce the cost of moving goods and services between African countries. Digital energy grids will be essential to this infrastructure, alongside roads and railways.

Africa must shift from simply exporting raw materials to building strong regional value chains focused on local manufacturing and innovation. Meeting the needs of the continent’s vast market would strengthen its economic self-sufficiency and reduce its vulnerability to external political decisions and the expiration of unilateral trade agreements.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemen
World.content:
Share How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemen on social media

Sanaa, Yemen – Mohammed, 19, joined the fighting on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in March this year, battling alongside Houthi forces. The fighting has been relentless over the past few months, as the Houthis advance. The Houthis have faced pro-government forces, as well as Saudi-led coalition air strikes.

They have also faced international sanctions and attempts by Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government to restrict their access to funds.

And yet, speaking during a recent visit to Sanaa, Mohammed said the Houthis were able to continue getting supplies to their fighters.

“It is not always war and death on the battlefield. We have a good time. We eat the best food. We can chew khat. If injured or sick, we will be taken care of. Our commander on the ground makes sure we have the supplies we need,” Mohammed told Al Jazeera.

Throughout a decade of war, Yemen’s Houthi group has developed a range of funding streams, which have enabled it to finance its military operations and tighten its grip on areas under its control.

The Mokha Center for Strategic Studies said in a July report this year that the Houthi financial system generates direct and indirect financial resources and costs worth approximately $2.5bn annually.

That includes around $800m from taxes and customs, $600m from additional fees and levies, $300m from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort, and about $100m linked to mobilisation events, according to the report.

A May research paper from the same institution estimated that nearly 60 percent of collected revenues in Houthi-controlled areas are directed to the security and military sectors.

Diverse funding techniques

As the Houthis’ war grinds on against Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi-led coalition forces, Houthi authorities have employed more fund-generating techniques. Ali Naji, a Sanaa resident, often receives messages on his mobile phone, urging him to contribute to the missile and drone air forces.



“I do not contribute, but thousands of people do, even with 100 Yemeni riyals [$0.19 at the exchange rate set by Houthi authorities in Sanaa]. When these small contributions add up, they make millions, and this funds the war efforts,” Naji, a father of three, told Al Jazeera.

Another method is distributing envelopes to solicit contributions. Last week, Naji was watching the funeral procession of more than 40 civilians who were killed in Sanaa in what the Houthis said were Saudi air strikes.

A Houthi member approached him and handed him an envelope, requesting that he give a voluntary contribution to the war effort. “I did not feel comfortable refusing or returning it empty. I put 1,000 Yemeni riyals (around $1.90) inside the envelope and gave it back.”

When mass rallies are held, a large sheet of cloth is spread on the ground, and people can contribute what they can. “Some give cash. Some donate weapons such as rifles and pistols, or jambiyas [traditional daggers]. From one rally, millions of Yemeni riyals can be raised,” said Naji.

In addition, imported oil has been a major source of revenue for the Yemeni group. In January, the US Department of the Treasury said the Iranian government sold and provided a free monthly shipment of oil to the Houthis using Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates.

With the shipments of Iranian oil, the Houthis continued to acquire a significant amount of revenue through illicit oil sales, generating over $2bn annually, according to the US Department of the Treasury.

Financing recruitment

Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Houthis have established a self-reinforcing system in which “economic control finances coercion, and coercion enables further economic control”.

Their income sources include taxes, customs duties, zakat religious levies, and additional levies, and fuel and telecommunications, said Al-Jeddawy.

“Their control over import permits, fees, and access to foreign currency also gives them considerable leverage over traders and businesses. These resources sustain the security apparatus and patronage networks through which the movement enforces compliance and consolidates its authority,” he added.

Al-Jeddawy noted that the Houthi financial system supports recruitment amid shrinking employment opportunities and unpaid public-sector salaries.



“Joining Houthi forces has become one of the few sources of income available to some young men. Recruitment is accompanied by ideological indoctrination, extending the movement’s influence from military camps into families and local communities. Economic deprivation therefore does more than facilitate mobilisation: it helps the group militarise everyday life and reinforce their authority at the social level.”

A 2024 United Nations panel of experts estimated that Houthi fighters numbered around 350,000, bolstered by the recruitment of fighters sometimes aged under 18.

These resources fund more than recruitment and mobilisation. “The group has expanded its security apparatus, developed increasingly sophisticated weapons, and invested in fortifications, trenches, tunnels, underground facilities, and weapons workshops. This level of continuous militarisation requires considerable and sustained expenditure,” said Al-Jeddawy.

The cost to civilians

Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, said Houthi-run civilian institutions are starved of funds, salaries are not paid regularly, and basic services, such as health and education, continue to deteriorate.

“About one million Yemeni public employees have not received their salaries regularly since 2016. Meanwhile, the group has developed its arsenal and funded its war efforts. When war is a priority, the living conditions of the population become miserable,” Saleh told Al Jazeera.

Roughly 80 percent of the population in Yemen lives below the poverty line, and nearly 22.3 million people depend on some form of humanitarian assistance, according to United Nations reports.

For Mohammed, the Houthi soldier, funding military operations is “a duty” and “a long-term investment”.

“Liberating the country and expelling foreign forces is not free,” said Mohammed. “So, funding fighters and military operations should be every patriot’s priority.”

World.title: What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season
World.content:
India and Pakistan had 42 of the world’s 50 most polluted cities in 2025. Millions now face another toxic winter.

Share What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season on social media

As winter approaches in the Northern Hemisphere, so does smog season, and few places are hit harder than South Asia.

Cities across the region, from New Delhi to Dhaka, are blanketed in a thick grey haze, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeding 350 in several parts of India’s capital last week, a level classed as “hazardous”, according to the air quality monitoring platform IQAir.

In winter, a layer of warmer air can trap cooler air near the ground. Combined with low wind speeds, this stops pollution from vehicles, industry and crop burning from dispersing.

Al Jazeera visualises which cities have the worst air quality, how it is measured, how smog affects your health and what you can do to protect yourself.

What causes smog?

Smog mostly comes from burning fossil fuels, particularly coal, along with exhaust from vehicles and factories, and smoke from forest and crop fires.

Summer smog and winter smog form differently. In summer, sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and other pollutants to form ground-level ozone. In winter, a layer of warm air can sit on top of cooler air near the ground, trapping pollution and stopping it from dispersing.

In South Asia, winter smog is made worse by geography. The Indo-Gangetic Plain, which stretches across parts of Pakistan, northern India, Nepal and Bangladesh, is one of the world’s most polluted regions. Hemmed in by the Himalayas to the north, the plain has weak winds and a shallow layer of air in winter, so pollution has nowhere to go.

How is air quality measured?

The air we breathe is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, but it also contains small amounts of other gases and tiny particles, some of which are harmful.



Monitoring stations track six main pollutants, including ozone, nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter (PM), tiny particles suspended in the air.

The most harmful is PM2.5, particles 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter, about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They can travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

These readings are combined into an Air Quality Index (AQI). The US AQI runs from 0 to 500 and is split into six colour-coded categories:

Green (0-50), good: little or no risk.

good: little or no risk. Yellow (51-100) , moderate: acceptable for most people.

, moderate: acceptable for most people. Orange (101-150) , unhealthy for sensitive groups: children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions.

, unhealthy for sensitive groups: children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions. Red (151-200) , unhealthy: the general public may be affected.

, unhealthy: the general public may be affected. Purple (201-300) , very unhealthy: health risks for everyone.

, very unhealthy: health risks for everyone. Maroon (301+), hazardous: emergency conditions.

Which cities have the most polluted air?

All 50 of the world’s most polluted cities in 2025 were in Asia, according to IQAir, with 42 of them in India and Pakistan.

Loni, on the outskirts of Delhi in Uttar Pradesh state, topped the list with average PM2.5 levels of 112.5 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic metre), more than 22 times the WHO’s recommended limit, followed by Hotan in China and Byrnihat and New Delhi in India.

Vehicles account for 23 percent of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The four Chinese cities on the list are in Xinjiang, where desert dust is a major source.

How does pollution affect your health?

Air pollution, both outdoors and inside homes, is linked to about seven million premature deaths worldwide each year, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Pollutants mainly enter the body through the lungs, where they can cause inflammation, damage cells and weaken the immune system. PM2.5 can also pass into the bloodstream, reaching organs including the heart and brain.

Air pollution is most strongly linked to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer and pneumonia. It can also worsen asthma and reduce lung function, while smoke from cooking with fossil fuels indoors is linked to cataracts.

Long-term exposure has also been linked to dementia and a higher risk of diabetes.

Children, older people, pregnant women and those with heart or lung conditions are most at risk. Exposure during pregnancy has been linked to premature birth and low birth weight.

What can you do to protect yourself?

You can’t control the air outside, but these simple steps can reduce how much pollution you breathe in:



Wear a mask: Use a well-fitting N95 or similar mask outdoors, as cloth masks offer little protection against fine particles.

Use a well-fitting N95 or similar mask outdoors, as cloth masks offer little protection against fine particles. Keep indoor air clean: Close windows on high-pollution days and use an air purifier with a HEPA filter.

Close windows on high-pollution days and use an air purifier with a HEPA filter. Limit outdoor activity: Avoid strenuous exercise outside on high-pollution days.

Avoid strenuous exercise outside on high-pollution days. Check air quality: Check the Air Quality Index (AQI) in a weather app before going out.

Check the Air Quality Index (AQI) in a weather app before going out. Protect those most at risk: Take extra care with children, older people and those with asthma.

How governments are tackling pollution

Governments are trying a range of measures to cut air pollution, particularly in large cities.

Car-free days close city centres to vehicles or limit driving by number plate. Paris held its first car-free day in September 2015, covering about a third of the city. Nitrogen dioxide levels fell by up to 40 percent in some areas, according to monitoring agency Airparif. From 2016, the city also began closing the Avenue de Champs-Elysees to traffic on the first Sunday of each month.

Low-emission zones charge the most polluting vehicles. Within three months of London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) launching in 2019, nitrogen dioxide concentrations at roadside monitoring sites in central London fell by 19.6 percent, according to a University of Birmingham study.

Some cities have targeted household fuel burning. Krakow, Poland, replaced more than 25,000 coal and wood-burning heating devices before banning solid fuels for home heating in September 2019. Average annual PM2.5 levels in the city fell by 40 percent between 2010 and 2021, according to a 2025 study.

World.title: Rafael Grossi is eyeing the UN’s top job. Will US support nuke his chances?
World.content:
The nuclear watchdog chief is seen as technically competent, but questions remain about his plans for UN reform.

Share Rafael Grossi is eyeing the UN’s top job. Will US support nuke his chances? on social media

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) chief Rafael Grossi is eyeing the position of United Nations secretary-general amid a tense race to replace Antonio Guterres.

The Argentinian nominee has finished second in the latest UN Security Council (UNSC) straw poll behind Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes and eight candidates still in the fray.

Grossi, 65, has earned admiration and criticism in equal measure for his IAEA tenure, defined by his hands-on approach to crisis diplomacy in active war zones, but also by accusations of partisanship, levelled against him, especially by Iran.

He is running on an agenda to reform the UN in a way seen as favourable to United States President Donald Trump and his political ally, Argentinian President Javier Milei.

But China and Russia – two of the five permanent UNSC members with veto power – are unlikely to back a candidate so closely aligned with Washington, analysts say, and a global civil society campaign is throwing its weight behind the selection of the first woman to lead the UN in the organisation’s 81-year history.

Transforming the IAEA

Grossi’s legacy at the IAEA and decades-long career as an Argentinian diplomat have cast him as a pragmatic crisis manager.

Since being appointed the UN nuclear watchdog’s director general in 2019, Grossi has been firmly in the front row in moments of international tension, including personally leading inspection teams to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Chornobyl nuclear power plants after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.



Jan Wouters, professor of international law and international organisations at KU Leuven in Belgium, said Grossi has “transformed the technical watchdog into a highly visible, proactive, diplomatic actor”.

“[He] significantly elevated the agency’s global profile through constant shuttle diplomacy and direct engagement with world leaders,” Wouters told Al Jazeera.

In Ukraine, by “focusing on technical safety rather than territorial sovereignty, he successfully brokered eight localised ceasefires between Russia and Ukraine to allow critical plant repairs” during the war, he added.

However, Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez, adjunct professor at the Pompeu Fabra law faculty in Barcelona, Spain, said Grossi’s very active role has “angered” the veto-wielding Russia, which sees him as having overstepped his position as agency head.

To be elected to lead the UN, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour from the 15-member UNSC while avoiding a veto from any of its five permanent members (P5) – China, France, Russia, the US, and the United Kingdom. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGC) then has to sign off on the final choice.

The race is coming down to the wire, as Guterres must leave his post on December 31.

While none of the P5 has publicly announced its preference, the South China Morning Post reported that Beijing has ruled out Grossi for being too close to Washington and would instead back Grynspan.

While Iran is not a member of the UNSC, it has also been vocal in its opposition to Grossi as UN secretary-general. Tehran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, accused the IAEA this month of being overly influenced by the US and European countries in its “one-sided and biased reporting about Iran’s peaceful nuclear programme”.

The IAEA has estimated that Iran was holding 440.9kg (972lb) of uranium enriched to up to 60 percent before the June 2025 Israeli-US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities. While uranium must be enriched to 90 percent to become weapons-grade, the process becomes quick at 60 percent. The amount Tehran has would be enough, if enriched further, to build 10 nuclear weapons, according to the agency.

Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is likely to withstand the criticism, “because the majority of governors of the [IAEA] agree with his approach on Iran”.

“In the context of the UN, probably [this will lead to] a bit of fireworks, but I don’t think it will change many votes,” he said.

Trump’s and Milei’s frontman?

Grossi’s technical ability to lead the UN alone is unlikely to put him much ahead in the race, observers said. Candidates for the post of secretary-general must also be seen as defenders of the UN Charter and the UN’s international law and human rights instruments.



For this reason, support from the Argentinian president is seen as Grossi’s main liability. Milei has framed international institutions as threats to national sovereignty and individual liberty, describing the UN itself as “useless” and its diplomats as “fatally arrogant parasites”.

Since being elected president in 2023, Milei has reignited a longstanding dispute with the UK over the Falkland Islands, a British-administered territory over which Argentina claims sovereignty. Milei has told UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply to the population of the islands, which Argentina calls Las Malvinas.

The Trump administration has also been a fierce critic of the UN, withdrawing Washington from key agencies, slashing UN funding and bypassing the body when it came to launching the war on Iran in February.

Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is seen as close to both Milei and Trump and as someone who could usher in a UN agenda aligned with their foreign policies.

“This will mean, in practice, a shrinking of the UN structure,” Jimenez Martinez said, including merging agencies and reorienting the body around security rather than development.

Grossi has called on world leaders to have the “courage to reform” the institution and lead it into a new era. According to Jimenez Martinez, his insistence on cutting red tape while failing to elaborate on safeguards is unlikely to get him a green light from the UNGA.

Alvina Hoffmann, senior lecturer in diplomatic studies at SOAS University of London, said Grossi is widely seen as a candidate whose “emphasis is on improving the system and cutting overlapping mandates, rather than addressing the structural drivers of inequality”.

He is also seen as someone who focuses on personal leadership, confidential negotiations and preventive diplomacy, “rather than issuing public declarations or condemnations”, which “might come at the expense of being able to call out violations of international law at a time in which international law is increasingly under attack”, Hoffmann said.

Time for female leadership?

According to the tradition of geographical rotation, the UN secretary-general post should next go to a Latin American. Five women are running in the race, and public and civil society pressure is at an all-time high to elect the first woman to the post.

Grynspan ticks both boxes.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society movement advocating for the appointment of the first female secretary-general, said that while electing the next UN chief should be based on merit, this criterion “is not inconsistent with gender considerations”.

UNGA “resolutions and international standards affirm that due regard should be given to achieving gender balance in senior UN leadership”, Donaldson told Al Jazeera.

“In applying these principles, member states should assess candidates not only on their individual competencies and experience, but also on how their personal characteristics and professional trajectories contribute to a leadership that reflects the diversity of the international community.”



“The United Nations has existed for 80 years without ever appointing a woman as secretary-general,” he added. “This persistent imbalance stands in contrast to the organisation’s own commitments to equality, parity and nondiscrimination.”

World.title: FIFA election: Who are Infantino’s challengers, and will he be re-elected?
World.content:
A look at FIFA’s presidential election process, the challengers and key dates, as Gianni Infantino seeks a fourth term.

Share FIFA election: Who are Infantino’s challengers, and will he be re-elected? on social media

The race for next year’s FIFA presidential election has entered a decisive phase this week, with candidates rushing to submit their nominations ahead of the deadline on Wednesday.

Incumbent Gianni Infantino is seeking a fourth term as the head of world football’s governing body, but many in the sport’s fraternity oppose his re-election following his now-aborted plan to sell stakes in future World Cups to private investors.

Standing in Infantino’s way are three challengers: French Football Federation chief Philippe Diallo, top Japanese football official Kozo Tashima, and Ramon Vega, an ex-Switzerland player.

Al Jazeera breaks down everything you need to know about the FIFA presidency and its upcoming elections:

What is the FIFA president’s role?

The FIFA president is the primary representative and ceremonial head of the International Federation of Association Football (FIFA), serving as the lead figure for football’s global governing body.

The president holds the highest position in FIFA’s organisational chart, above the general secretary.

Infantino has been in power since February 2016, succeeding his compatriot Sepp Blatter, who resigned in June 2015. FIFA’s ethics committee had banned Blatter from the sport for eight years for a conflict of interest and disloyalty to the organisation over a $2m payment deal.

In its 122-year history, FIFA has never had a woman as its president. The highest administrative position held by a woman at FIFA was the secretary-general post in 2016, held by Fatma Samoura, a Senegalese diplomat and former United Nations official.

When is the FIFA presidential election, and how does it work?

The next election will be held at the 77th FIFA Congress on March 18, 2027, in Rabat, Morocco.



FIFA holds its presidential elections every four years, staging them at its congress that follows a men’s World Cup – in this case, the 2026 World Cup in North America, won by Spain.

A candidate wins the election based on the backing of individual member nations across six confederations.

There are 211 FIFA member nations. Each holds equal weight in the vote and can support only one candidate per election.

If two candidates are contesting the election, a simple majority of more than 50 percent is needed to win – which translates to the support of 106 member nations.

If there are more than two candidates, a two-thirds majority is required in the first round. Further rounds of voting are held, and the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated each time. This continues until only two candidates remain, and from there on, the candidate with a simple majority wins.

How many votes does each confederation have?

Each member nation in a confederation has one vote. The breakdown of the six confederations’ votes is as follows:

UEFA (Europe): 55

CAF (Africa): 54

AFC (Asia): 46

CONCACAF (North America): 35

OFC (Oceania): 11

CONMEBOL (South America): 10

Candidates require the backing of five national associations to stand in the election, and four men are in the running for the next FIFA president.

Infantino is the highest-profile candidate. The 56-year-old Swiss administrator is seeking a fourth term through 2031.

His closest challenger is Frenchman Diallo, who has the “unanimous” backing of the European national associations. The 63-year-old, the son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the French Football Federation since January 2023.

Japan has fielded a candidate for the first time in history, with Tashima, the Japan Football Association’s (JFA) honorary president, challenging Infantino.

Former Japan international Tashima, who has served on the FIFA Council since 2015 and became JFA president the following year, believes he has a 20- to 30-percent chance of winning the coveted seat in global football.



The list of candidates wraps up with ex-Tottenham Hotspur centre-back Vega, the first to publicly declare his intention to challenge fellow Swiss citizen Infantino.

Arsene Wenger, a French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had been seen as a potential candidate to get Europe’s backing.

The AFP news agency reported that Wenger had been UEFA’s “Plan A” and that Diallo had never been seen as a solution before it became clear the ex-Arsenal boss would not be a candidate.

CONCACAF chief Victor Montagliani had also been mooted as a candidate, but the Canadian later announced his desire to stand for a new term as the head of his confederation, which covers North and Central America and the Caribbean.

Why is Infantino facing opposition?

In July, Infantino faced furious worldwide backlash after an unsuccessful attempt to bring private investors into a proposed FIFA commercial entity that would hold rights linked to competitions, including the World Cup.

UEFA, CONCACAF, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) led the opposition to Infantino and his plan, signing a letter saying football “belongs to no individual”.

But the AFC later performed a U-turn, throwing its weight behind Infantino, who has since apologised for the failed private investment project.

Opposition from UEFA, whose member associations account for 55 votes, and CONCACAF, with 35 votes, could cause minor problems in Infantino’s re-election bid.

UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino, naming Diallo only two days before the official nomination deadline.

What is the controversy with Infantino’s potential re-election?

Earlier this month, Miguel ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Maduro, the former head of FIFA’s governance committee, said Infantino cannot stand for ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌a fourth term as president under the organisation’s statutes.

“Article 33, paragraph two of the FIFA statutes is very clear when it says no person may serve as president for more than three terms,” Maduro told reporters.

“Gianni Infantino has been elected three times; he’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌been president of FIFA for three terms. So, in my view, there’s no way to reconcile another presidency of Infantino.”

Human rights organisation FairSquare also wrote to member associations urging them to declare Infantino ineligible. FairSquare had previously urged FIFA to rule that Infantino was ineligible to seek another term, arguing he has already served ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the maximum three permitted under the body’s statutes.

But Infantino successfully argued that his first spell in charge, when he was elected at an Extraordinary Congress in 2016 following Blatter’s resignation, should not count towards that limit because it completed an interrupted ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠mandate.

In December 2022, the FIFA Council “unanimously confirmed” that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for Infantino, but FairSquare said the reasoning was never made public.



Who is the favourite to win the 2027 FIFA presidential election?

Infantino’s re-election ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠prospects have strengthened significantly in recent weeks.

Last month, the head of Asian football endorsed his bid in a dramatic change of heart, while ⁠⁠⁠support across confederations gives him a commanding position among FIFA’s 211 voting members.

Infantino believes he has the backing of the “vast, vast majority” of member associations, despite criticism of his World Cup sell-off plan.

“I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view,” Infantino told the BBC.

“But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

“I’m just coming back off Tokyo, where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde, where all African countries have endorsed me. I’m speaking to all associations everywhere in the world,” he added.

“There are different points of view; it’s not always easy to bring them all under one roof, but we need to respect – and I do respect – all opinions and all views, and then it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run.”

World.title: Rare video of Brazilian Amazon tribe
World.content:
NewsFeed Rare video of Brazilian Amazon tribe

A new video has emerged showing members of the isolated Awa tribe who live in the remote part of Brazil’s Amazon forest. The group ventured out of the forest and accepted food as aid workers raise concerns about the dangers posed by illegal loggers and hunters.

World.title: Waymo suspends driverless freeway rides across US after California ban
World.content:
California authorities have declared self-driving cars an ‘imminent hazard to public safety’ after traffic incidents.

Share Waymo suspends driverless freeway rides across US after California ban on social media

Waymo has paused its driverless taxi services on freeways across the United States after California temporarily banned the ride-hailing platform on the state’s highways over safety concerns.

A spokesperson for the California-based company – a subsidiary of Alphabet, Google’s parent company – said it has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, but it is “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”.

Waymo implemented the suspension last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they did not say how long it would last.

Along with California, the driverless vehicles will pause highway services in Phoenix, Austin and Miami. Waymo offers rides on city streets in areas including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver.

The spokesperson said the suspension would allow the company to “evaluate our performance” following incidents in California and that it prioritises safety.

One incident on November 6 went viral after video captured on a San Francisco highway showed a Waymo vehicle speeding towards and attempting to pass two police cars, even as their lights were flashing in an intentional bid to slow traffic.

The officers were driving behind a slow-moving construction truck.

The episode led the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) to temporarily ban Waymo vehicles from its highways, effective from November 11.

The DMV, which is responsible for road safety, said its decision was also prompted by a November 5 incident, when three Waymo autonomous vehicles drove into a construction zone in the San Francisco Bay Area.



Waymo said the construction zone incident did not result in injuries or collisions.

‘Corrective actions’ sought

DMV spokesman Jonathan Groveman said in a statement that “similar incidents” occurred on May 18.

“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” he said.

The restrictions “will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates … it has taken effective corrective actions”, the statement read.

Waymo completes half a million trips each week and says it has demonstrated a 95 percent reduction in serious crashes as compared with human-driven vehicles.

It has been testing its vehicles in London since 2016, and has plans to expand into Munich and Madrid in 2027.

World.title: Trump Meets Philippine Leader Before Flying to China
World.content:
Pinned

President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.

Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”

Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.

In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.

The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. The only event of substance on his schedule for the day — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

Mr. Trump also met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.

Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.

Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

Palace history: Mr. Marcos hosted Mr. Trump at Malacañang Palace, where the Philippine leader spent much of his childhood. He left the palace in military fatigues 40 years ago when his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, was ousted. Read more ›

Lily Kuo contributed reporting.

World.title: A tropical Chinese city is half-empty and ready for the summit.
World.content:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities.

When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.

But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”

The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.

Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.

Image Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan and Xi Jinping, China’s leader, at their first meeting in Gyeongju, South Korea, last October. Credit... The Asahi Shimbun, via Getty Images

The Times found that:

China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”

Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.

In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.

Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “enemy state” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.

Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

The analysis covered Chinese state-run and Communist Party-run outlets, including China Central Television, the Xinhua news agency, Global Times and People’s Liberation Army Daily.

Wartime rhetoric surged in discussions of Japan Share of articles or answers about Japan that reference World War II Before Takaichi’s Taiwan remarks in Nov. 2025 One year after Takaichi’s remarks Global Times editorials 23% 72% Defense Ministry briefings 31% 57% People’s Daily 54% 14% Foreign Ministry briefings 38% 13% CCTV Evening News 21% 3% 0 20 40 60 80% 23% 72% Global Times editorials 31% 57% Defense Ministry briefings 14% 54% People’s Daily 13% 38% Foreign Ministry briefings CCTV Evening News 3% 21% 0 20 40 60% Global Times editorials 23% 72% Defense Ministry briefings 31% 57% People’s Daily 14% 54% Foreign Ministry briefings 13% 38% CCTV Evening News 21% 3% 0 20 40 60% Note: For ministry briefings, only spokesperson responses were counted. “Before Takaichi remark” covers data from Aug. 1, 2022, to Nov. 6, 2025; “After” covers Nov. 7, 2025, to Oct. 31, 2026. Sources: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of National Defense, People’s Daily, Global Times and CCTV. Analysis by The New York Times.

China has long been at odds with Japan. But the current scale and coordination of its campaign have little modern precedent, experts said.

“Anti-Japan propaganda is just absolutely everywhere now,” said David Bandurski, executive director of the China Media Project, an independent research group. “It’s a far more focused use of anti-Japanese framing than we’ve seen at any point.”

The Feud Erupts

Ms. Takaichi told Japan’s Parliament on Nov. 7, 2025, that any attempt by China to blockade or seize Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, implying a potential military response. Her comments reflected a long-held Japanese view, but one that has rarely been verbalized.

China reacted furiously. The government urged millions of tourists to avoid Japan, limited the export of some critical minerals, restricted Japanese seafood imports and increased patrols in disputed waters.

Mr. Xi appears to be concerned that Ms. Takaichi, a close American ally who has been a critic of China, could get in the way of China’s military and economic expansion in Asia. Analysts said that he is seeking to drive a wedge between Japan and the United States, as well as countries like Australia, South Korea, India and Britain.

Image Japanese soldiers during a live fire exercise in Gotemba, Japan, in June. Credit... Yuichi Yamazaki/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Ms. Takaichi has accelerated a military buildup to counter China, raising military spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product two years ahead of schedule and loosening postwar rules that restricted the export of weapons. She is expected to push for even more military spending next month as part of a new national security strategy.

A Surge in Propaganda

In the year since Ms. Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan, China has sharply escalated its rhetorical attacks on Japan, according to the Times’s analysis, and there has been a surge in propaganda aimed at both domestic and global audiences.

Since last November, the Chinese Foreign Ministry has publicly accused Tokyo of “remilitarization” or “neo-militarism” at more than 60 briefings, the analysis found. People’s Daily, the Communist Party mouthpiece, cited Japanese “neo-militarism” in 65 articles, and warnings of Japanese “militarism” surged across the outlets we analyzed.

Chinese officials have repeatedly invoked the image of a “gray rhino,” a phrase used in Chinese to describe a looming threat, to characterize Japan. One video that circulated on Chinese news sites, generated by artificial intelligence, shows a rhino, draped in a rising sun flag, wreaking havoc across land and sea.

China Daily, a state-controlled news organization aimed at an international audience, published a cartoon in May showing Ms. Takaichi dressed in samurai armor and carrying a sword. A People’s Daily cartoon describes Japan’s military ambitions as “sugarcoated poison,” showing Ms. Takaichi wrapping skulls to give to children.

The Times parsed more than 20,000 transcripts from the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s briefings since 2013; nearly 400,000 articles in People’s Daily; more than 100,000 items from Guangming Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Global Times and Xinhua; and thousands of published readouts of Chinese leaders’ meetings, state broadcasts, ministry releases and social media trends.

The analysis found that Chinese media has helped amplify official messaging. When interest in China’s feud with Japan faded from April to June and questions from foreign news outlets fell, reporters from state-controlled media in China tried to keep the story alive by asking about Japan at a far higher rate than before.

Image The foreign ministry in Beijing. Credit... Adek Berry/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

In December, a TV reporter from Shenzhen noted that scholars across the region were warning of Japan’s “remilitarization,” prompting a spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry to answer with a list of Japan’s wartime atrocities. In August, on the anniversary of the bombing of Hiroshima, a Xinhua reporter said at a news briefing that “81 years later, Japan’s right-wing forces are stirring, plotting to restore militarism.”

The propaganda has sometimes spilled into the policy arena. When China’s Commerce Ministry placed 80 Japanese industrial, defense and research listings on export control blacklists and watch lists this year, a stated goal was to curb “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism.”

Taking Aim at Takaichi

Mr. Xi’s government has made a point of singling out Ms. Takaichi. A year after taking office, she is still relatively popular at home and has been a vocal supporter of Taiwan throughout her career. She has also built a warm relationship with Mr. Trump.

One tactic used by the Chinese government is to omit Ms. Takaichi’s title, a pointed break with diplomatic protocol. From July through September, officials dropped “prime minister” in six of seven mentions of Ms. Takaichi.

Image President Trump and Ms. Takaichi during a welcome ceremony in Tokyo last year. Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

On Weibo, a popular Chinese social media site that is heavily curated by the government, hashtags that mocked Ms. Takaichi’s wardrobe, emotions, voice or hugging style trended at least 30 times over the past year, the analysis found.

China also appears to be working to foment opposition to Ms. Takaichi inside Japan’s political system. Chinese officials have tried to persuade visiting delegations of Japanese lawmakers and executives recently that Ms. Takaichi does not understand the economic risks of her tough approach to China, and that they should stand up to her, according to two people briefed on the conversations.

After one such meeting in September, Wang Yi, China’s foreign minister, said that it was time for Japan to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leader.

‘Israel of East Asia’

In trying to stir concern about Japan, Chinese scholars have told their counterparts in the West that Ms. Takaichi’s Japan is becoming the “Israel of East Asia.” A delegation of Chinese scholars in South Korea used the phrase during a recent meeting with American scholars, according to David Sacks, an expert on China at the Council on Foreign Relations who took part in the meeting.

Mr. Sacks said his Chinese counterparts repeatedly raised concerns about Japanese militarism. They told the Americans that they feared Japan was seeking to become the most powerful country in East Asia and could draw the United States into conflict.

The aim, Mr. Sacks said, was to push Mr. Trump to “rein in Japan.”

“They want the United States to tell its ally to knock it off and to de-escalate with Beijing,” he said.

During his visit to the White House earlier this year, Mr. Xi suggested that Mr. Trump should join China’s efforts to counter Japan. Mr. Xi invoked World War II to highlight friendship between Beijing and Washington and cited Japan as a common enemy. He described Imperial Japan as “fascist” and “militarist” aggressors.

Help from Russia

China and Russia have increasingly reinforced each other’s attacks on Japan, the analysis shows, using common terms like “remilitarization.”

Analysts say it is all part of President Vladimir V. Putin’s recent pressure campaign against Japan. In August, he made his first-ever visit to islands claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo. Last month, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on espionage charges. And in recent days, Mr. Putin has seized Russian assets of Japan Tobacco.

During a visit to Beijing in May, Mr. Putin signed a statement with Mr. Xi that included a lengthy section devoted to denouncing Japan’s military moves. The statement said, “Japan’s current acceleration of ‘remilitarization’ poses a serious threat to regional peace and stability.” The statement added that Japan should “resist ‘new militarism’ and ‘remilitarization.’”

During an appearance in Moscow last month, Mr. Putin said that he wanted good relations with Japan. But he added, “We are concerned by Japan’s plans for militarization.”

Methodology

The Times collected hundreds of thousands of documents from multiple official Chinese sources: China’s Foreign Ministry briefings, articles from People’s Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Guangming Daily, Global Times, China Daily and Xinhua, as well as Chinese military, ministry, broadcast and social media records. Most sources were downloaded from official websites, and the rest from public digital archives, like the Internet Archive. To quantify the appearance of terms like “remilitarization,” “rearmament” and “neo-militarism” in Foreign Ministry briefings, we used A.I. models developed by Anthropic and Google, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Carbon, to strip out reporters’ questions and measure phrase frequencies per 1,000 Chinese characters. We also used A.I. to separate official statements from third-party quotes, generate initial translations, and classify the topic of news stories, briefing questions and social media trends.

Every quote and translation used in the story was verified against the original Chinese records.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong, and Kiuko Notoya from Tokyo.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong, and Kiuko Notoya from Tokyo.

World.title: Trump’s ‘trade deal’ with Thailand is not a done deal.
World.content:
Pinned

President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.

Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”

Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.

In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.

The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. The only event of substance on his schedule for the day — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

Mr. Trump also met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.

Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.

Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

Palace history: Mr. Marcos hosted Mr. Trump at Malacañang Palace, where the Philippine leader spent much of his childhood. He left the palace in military fatigues 40 years ago when his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, was ousted. Read more ›

Lily Kuo contributed reporting.

World.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
World.content:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

World.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
World.content:
Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones, said "The board does not intend to reinstate him."

Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (Â£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.

The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

World.title: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
World.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.

Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.

Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.

Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.

He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.

"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.

World.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
World.content:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

World.title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
World.content:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
