World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Egypt and the Nile: Transitioning from reactive policy to strategic confrontation
World.content:
The evolving Ethiopian strategy compels Egypt to recalibrate the instruments through which it manages the Nile file, rather than altering its foundational principles. The dispute has moved well beyond a mere technical disagreement over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD); it now represents a concerted effort to parlay physical control over the dam’s floodgates into political leverage over the flows of an international watercourse, setting a precedent for future unilateral projects dictated solely by Addis Ababa.

Against this backdrop, the recent shift in rhetoric by Egypt’s Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation, Dr. Hani Sewilam, carries considerable weight. Egypt is shedding the cautious, overly technical language that characterized years of appeals to negotiations and goodwill, adopting instead a far more forthright framing of the core issue: the dam is not a purely domestic Ethiopian structure, nor does the completion of its construction legitimize a fait accompli or absolve Ethiopia of its binding obligations regarding prior notification, data sharing, and coordination during periods of drought and flooding.

The true value of this recalibrated discourse lies in restoring the issue to its proper context. Egypt does not contest Ethiopia’s right to development, yet it categorically rejects the transformation of that right into unchecked hegemony over a vital resource upon which the survival of downstream nations depends.

Nevertheless, forceful rhetoric alone will fall short unless it is anchored in sustainable, institutionalized policy. First, Egypt must establish a permanent center for intelligence and strategic assessment dedicated to the Nile Basin and the Horn of Africa—one that synthesizes hydrological data and satellite imagery with economic, political, and security analyses. A lack of transparency from Ethiopia should never leave Egypt passively awaiting whatever selective disclosures Addis Ababa chooses to make.

Second, Egypt must channel the documentation of damages into a sustained legal and technical track. In this regard, the newly announced Egyptian-Sudanese committee tasked with assessing the impacts of unilateral operation and pursuing compensation marks a pivotal step forward, provided it is backed by rigorous, evidence-based dossiers for every single incident.

A third track must begin well before ground is broken on any new dams. Egypt should proactively engage international banks, sovereign funds, and engineering firms early on, making it clear that financing infrastructure on an international watercourse without transparent impact assessments and downstream coordination carries severe legal, political, and financial liabilities.

The fourth track centers on cultivating shared regional interests. It is no longer enough for Egypt to merely affirm its respect for the developmental rights of African nations; Egypt must translate that commitment into tangible, on-the-ground projects. Enduring alliances are forged not through diplomatic visits and joint communiqués alone, but through deeply intertwined economic stakes.

Finally, there is the critical imperative of international outreach. While Ethiopia effectively packages its narrative in the compelling idioms of international law, sustainable development, clean energy, and African equity, much of Egypt’s messaging remains largely inward-facing. What is urgently needed is multilingual academic and media output tailored to global universities, financial institutions, the African Union, and the United Nations—content that draws a sharp distinction between collaborative development and development weaponized as an instrument of coercion.

The confrontation required here is neither a call to a war nor a passive surrender to a fait accompli. Rather, it is the cultivation of comprehensive leverage that makes cooperation far more rewarding for Ethiopia than unilateralism, while ensuring the cost of harming Egypt’s interests outweighs any potential gain. If Addis Ababa is translating its rhetoric into an actionable operational framework, Egypt must equally evolve its strategic instruments in defense of its rights. The Nile is not a seasonal dossier to be dusted off whenever a provocative statement is issued; it is an existential imperative that demands permanent, high-level stewardship commensurate with its gravity.

World.title: Police arrest 2 people attempting to traffic 3,391 Egyptian antiquities
World.content:
The Egyptian Interior Ministry foiled the activities of two individuals specialized in excavating and trafficking archaeological artifacts.

The Tourism and Antiquities Police apprehended the pair, seizing 3,391 assorted archaeological items in their possession.

Among the recovered artifacts are hundreds of statues and coins dating back to the Greek and Roman periods, discovered at Tel Dabko site in the Daqahliya Governorate.

Security authorities were notified that two individuals were offering rare artifacts—including historical statues and coins—for sale.

Following intensified investigations and the use of confidential informants, and after completing the necessary legal procedures, security forces were able to apprehend the pair.

The first suspect, 52, is an agricultural worker residing in the city of al-Manzala, while the second suspect, 56, is a mechanical technician residing in the San al-Hagar district of Sharqia Governorate; the latter was also wanted in connection with two court verdicts.

Up to 3,391 Artifacts recovered

Upon searching the individuals, 3,391 artifacts were discovered in their possession.

These included 350 Ushabti figurines of various sizes and shapes, nine statues of different deities, 12 amulets, two scarab-shaped figures, two terracotta pieces, one pottery vessel, and 3,015 coins of various shapes and sizes.

When the seized items were examined by a committee of inspectors from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, it was confirmed that all the objects are genuine artifacts subject to the Law on the Protection of Antiquities.

They date back to the Late Period of ancient Egyptian civilization, while the coins originate from the Greek and Roman periods.

Illicit Excavations

When confronted, the suspects admitted to possessing the artifacts for the purpose of trafficking.

They confessed to having excavated them from a vacant plot of land in the Tel Dabko area—located in the al-Manzala district of Daqahliya —a site protected under the Law on the Protection of Antiquities, which is not open to the public and spans approximately 160 feddans.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: When will mobile phone prices in Egypt decrease? An official explains the situation
World.content:
The Vice Chairman of the Mobile and Telecommunications Division at the Cairo Chamber of Commerce, Walid Ramadan explained on Monday that increasing local mobile phone production and expanding exports could help lower phone prices in the Egyptian market.

During a phone-in with “al-Hekaya,” (The Story) hosted by Amr Adib, Ramadan discussed addressing the challenges faced by manufacturers in order to achieve competitive pricing.

Ramadan added that the rising cost of imported mobile phone components is a key factor affecting production costs.

“Most mobile phone parts are imported; there are supply chains and specific components—such as RAM—that occasionally face shortages, which in turn drives up their prices,” he explained.

Ramadan added that increasing production volume helps companies surpass the break-even point and lower the cost per unit, noting: “As your production quantities grow, you reach the break-even point, which then allows you to lower your prices.”

He pointed out that the Egyptian market requires approximately 20 million mobile phones annually.

The Vice Chairman of the Mobile and Telecommunications Division also emphasized the importance of developing a strategy for expanding exports to markets with which Egypt has trade agreements—a move that would facilitate higher production volumes and lead to cost savings.

What’s behind higher prices for local phones?

Regarding the reasons behind the high prices of some locally manufactured phones—despite the expansion in establishing production facilities—Ramadan explained that local manufacturing does not necessarily imply a reliance on local components, as most phone parts are still imported from abroad.

He urged the Ministry of Industry and Trade to hold meetings with manufacturers to identify the challenges that drive up production costs.

The Vice Chairman added that the government should consider offering incentives to manufacturers—such as relief on energy costs, tax breaks, or export rebates—to help lower production costs and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian-made products.

Ramadan said that increasing production and exports presents an opportunity to transform Egypt into a regional hub for the mobile phone manufacturing and trade industry.

He added that the objective should not be limited to meeting the needs of the domestic market, but should also extend to reaching international markets.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Robert Pattinson chosen as the next James Bond
World.content:
The name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.

After months of intense rumors of a casting battle between some of the entertainment industry’s top names, actor Robert Pattinson, known for his roles in this year’s “The Odyssey” and “The Drama” — not to mention “Twilight” of years gone by — was announced as the next James Bond by Amazon MGM Studios via the official 007 website Monday.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” the 40-year-old British actor said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

The news of Pattinson’s casting was accompanied by a teaser clip of him as Bond — dressed, naturally, in a tuxedo and pointing a gun — as the series’ iconic theme song played.

Pattinson joins an elite club: Just six actors have portrayed 007. Sean Connery first appeared as the suave secret agent in 1962’s “Dr. No.” The most recent was Daniel Craig, who appeared as Bond in five films over 15 years, starting with 2006’s “Casino Royale” and most recently in 2021’s “No Time to Die.”

Production on the next Bond movie, the still-untitled 26th in the series, will begin soon under the direction of French-Canadian director Denis Villeneuve, who is also behind the “Dune” trilogy — the third installment of which costars Pattinson and comes out next month.

“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” Villeneuve said in the statement, adding that Pattinson “has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new.”

To say that Pattinson has had a stellar year is an understatement. In addition to “The Drama” and “The Odyssey,” the actor is also courting awards buzz for his chilling portrayal of “To Catch a Predator” creator Chris Hansen in this fall’s “Primetime.” He’s also been filming as another legendary character, namely Bruce Wayne/Batman, in the upcoming “The Batman: Part II.” (“The Batman: Part II” comes from Warner Bros., which is owned by CNN’s parent company.)

The battle for Bond

Daniel Craig played Bond in five films over 15 years. Nicola Dove/MGM/Everett Collection

Craig’s last turn as Bond in 2021’s “No Time to Die” ended with a closing credit promise that “James Bond will return.” Speculation over the next Bond simmered ever since. Yet for five years, Bond has been MIA while his corporate handlers went to battle.

In 2022, Amazon paid more than $8.56 billion for Bond’s parent company, MGM, and thus the rights to distribute the 007 movies, but tensions soon emerged. Barbara Broccoli — who maintained creative control of the character thanks to a deal her late father, Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, had made with novelist Ian Fleming, the inventor of Bond — was reportedly highly distrustful of the data-driven Amazon, resulting in a standoff, according to a 2024 report in the Wall Street Journal.

The impasse was broken a year later when a new deal was announced to finally hand creative control of the character to Amazon MGM Studios for an undisclosed sum, ending the Broccoli family’s control over 007 after more than 60 years.

Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor were all reportedly in the running for 007. Getty Images

After that, the hunt for the next Bond began gathering steam. Casting officially began in May of this year, while second-round auditions were said to have been held in August.

Some of the biggest young stars in film were soon rumored to be in contention — although none were officially confirmed as potentials. Names floated in the press included Harris Dickinson, Callum Turner, Paul Mescal, Tom Holland, Jack Lowden, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Theo James and Jacob Elordi.

One major question long hung over the next Bond: was it time for 007 to be played by a man of color?

For years, fans of Idris Elba had championed him to play the next iteration of Bond, although as time went on the now-54-year-old actor seemed to age out of the role, especially given it would likely require stunt-heavy sequels.

James Bond has been a cornerstone of classic Hollywood for decades. Everett Collection

Still, the names of other younger actors were floated, including Dev Patel, Henry Golding, Regé-John Page and Daniel Kaluuya.

As casting continued, Elba seemed to shut down the idea of a non-white Bond as unrealistic and said the rumors around him were never based in truth. “James Bond was written how he was written for a reason,” Elba told GQ in June.

“In realistic terms, some markets just don’t go for that,” Elba said of a Black man playing 007. “Bond is big all over the world,” he said. “That’s not what they like in their culture. Period.”

No plot details or other casting for the next movie, based on a script from “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight, have been announced. It’s also not yet known if any actors from the previous films may return for what is widely expected to be a reboot of the series.

World.title: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
World.content:
Vienna, Austria Reuters —

Five European countries unveiled plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.

Under the planned scheme — which is still being negotiated with Rwanda — Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands would send people to a center where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said.

“I think it will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges of illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told a press conference in Vienna with her Austrian counterpart and ministers from the countries involved.

The five countries have been working towards a deal for a so-called return hub for several months, officials have said — part of a broader push inside the European Union to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.

With elections approaching in several EU countries, centrist governments have been toughening immigration policies to try to counter growing public support for far-right parties.

‘The risk of violations’

In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.

The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.

Migrants who were rescued off Greek islands of Crete and Gavdos, arrive at the port of Lavrio in Lavreotiki, Greece, on July 10, 2025. Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty Images/File

Although officials say such a hub would only handle about 100 people at a time, the countries championing it say it would send an important signal that they hope will discourage would-be migrants from making the often perilous journey to Europe.

The project follows the approval of the EU’s new Return Regulation, designed to speed up deportations.

The scheme differs from Britain’s abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.

Rwanda a willing host

Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record.

“Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries,” Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said on Monday.

Rwanda was not looking to be paid for the arrangement, but partner countries would meet the cost of relocation and the integration of any who chose to stay in Rwanda, he added.

Veteran President Paul Kagame won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda’s 1994 genocide and rebuilding the East African country into a destination for investment.

Rwanda’s President Paul Kagame attends the 20th Francophonie Summit, in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on Monday. Soveit Yarn/Reuters

However, critics accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting rebels alleged to have committed killings, rapes and other abuse in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo. Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.

Freedom House rates it “Not Free” and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.

“There is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Amnesty International said in a statement on Monday.

The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.

Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023. Kigali sought a £50 million ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.

During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain’s abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.

World.title: Trump says US will catch China on rare earths in 10 months. Data suggests it’s far behind
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday claimed that production of rare-earth minerals in the US will pull even with China within the next year, saying that the country is “making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before.”

“We’re gonna catch (China) within 10 months,” Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with Quad leaders in the Philippines. “Everything that we need, we’ll have in 10 months.”

CNN has reached out the Department of Interior for more information on Trump’s claim.

As China has imposed export controls on rare earths in recent years, the US has ramped up production of these critical minerals – but data suggests the US is still well behind.

In 2025, China produced 270,000 metric tons of rare earths and the US produced 50,000 metric tons, according to the US Geological Survey’s Mineral Commodity Summaries.

China has historically dominated rare earth production. As of last year, China accounted for 61% of global mined rare earth production and its control over the processing stage was 92% of the global output, according to the International Energy Agency.

The US possesses ample rare earths, but it processes an insignificant amount of them — the majority are refined in China. Processing rare earths is expensive, and US production facilities weren’t turning profits, and most have closed over the past couple decades.

Some industry experts believe the United States could reduce its reliance on Chinese rare earths this decade through sustained investment in US processing capabilities. The Trump administration has announced billions of dollars in rare earth investments. But those facilities haven’t begun meaningful production to compete with China — and some aren’t expected to open until next decade.

Rare earths are ubiquitous in everyday technologies and have been a major point of contention in the US-China trade relationship.

China agreed to roll back certain restrictions on rare earth exports after Trump met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping Ping at last year’s APEC summit. The two men are set to meet again later this week.

This post has been updated with additional information. CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

World.title: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
World.content:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.

In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.

But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia, the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.

At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.

Also known as Huang Le, the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.

But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.

“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”

But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.

On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.

“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.

In a new statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said that Huang left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there.

“Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” the statement said.

The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026. Taryn NG/AFP/Getty Images

A billion-dollar business

In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.

US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.

Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.

Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.

“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”

The orange Alibaba logo is displayed on the sunlit glass facade of the Shenzhen Alibaba Center on November 11, in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. Cheng Xin/Getty Images

Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.

In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.

Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.

“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.

“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.

Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.

In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.

Closing the loopholes

The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.

A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.

Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.

Eric and Lara Trump, SpaceX, Twitter and electric car maker Tesla CEO Elon Musk (C), Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth and Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang walk off Air Force One upon arriving at Beijing Capital Airport in Beijing on May 13, 2026. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/ Getty Images

However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.

They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”

Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.

Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.

Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.

Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

A growing number of chip smuggling cases has fueled calls for harsher legal enforcement outside the US as well. The Taiwanese government is seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong.

“There’s going to have to be new standards that are going to have to be enforced around traceability and transparency,” Capri said. “This is really going to be the beginning of a major crackdown, and actually moving on to the next phase of export control enforcement.”

World.title: Egypt, China seek to expand investment cooperation at the 2nd Egyptian-Chinese Investment Forum
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Hussein Eissa attended the opening of the second Egyptian-Chinese Investment Forum in Cairo, in the presence of Xiao Jie, Vice Chairman of the Standing Committee of China’s National People’s Congress and President of the China Association for the Promotion of International People-to-People Exchange; Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh; Chinese Ambassador to Egypt Liao Liqiang; and representatives of Chinese companies and institutions, as well as members of the Egyptian business community.

In his address, Eissa said the forum provides an important platform for strengthening the economic partnership between Egypt and China, opening new avenues for cooperation and translating the longstanding friendship between the two countries into development and investment projects that serve the mutual interests of their peoples.

He referred to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic visit to Egypt last September, which coincided with the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1956. Egypt was the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic ties with the People’s Republic of China, he noted.

Eissa said the joint presidential statement issued during the visit reflected the political will to advance the comprehensive strategic partnership and expand cooperation in investment, manufacturing, technology transfer, energy and infrastructure, opening broader prospects for economic cooperation in the coming period.

Egypt is moving ahead with a comprehensive economic reform program aimed at strengthening economic stability, improving the investment climate, increasing private-sector participation, expanding the productive base, deepening local manufacturing and boosting exports, he said.

He added that Egypt enjoys key competitive advantages, foremost among them its strategic geographic location and preferential access to broad regional and international markets.

In this context, Eissa described the Suez Canal Economic Zone as one of the main platforms for investment cooperation between the two countries and a strategic gateway for Chinese investment in the Middle East and Africa, particularly given the expansion of Chinese investments there, including the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone.

The government attaches particular importance to attracting Chinese investment in several priority sectors, especially industry, including engineering, electronics and automotive manufacturing, with a focus on technology transfer, deeper local manufacturing and higher exports, he said.

Other priority areas include infrastructure and transport, covering ports, railways, logistics zones and public utilities; education and technical training, through stronger partnerships among universities, educational institutions and research centers; and energy and the green economy, particularly solar and wind power projects and technologies and industries linked to the green transition.

Eissa also highlighted financial and banking cooperation as a key pillar of economic and investment relations between the two countries. He praised cooperation between the Central Bank of Egypt and the People’s Bank of China, including a currency swap agreement whose value has risen to 30 billion yuan, saying it strengthens monetary and financial cooperation and creates wider scope for using local currencies to settle trade and investment transactions.

He also pointed to Egypt’s issuance of panda bonds in the Chinese market worth USD 500 million, expressing hope that future issuances would increase, strengthening Egypt’s presence in China’s capital market and diversifying its external financing sources.

Eissa further stressed the importance of maximizing Egypt’s benefits from its membership in the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and expanding cooperation with the institution to finance infrastructure, sustainable development and energy projects.

The Egyptian government is keen to maintain direct communication with investors, address the challenges they face and provide the necessary support and coordination to facilitate the implementation of their projects, he said.

He expressed hope that the forum would help move beyond presenting investment opportunities to developing specific projects and practical partnerships that deepen economic integration between the two countries.

Eissa expressed Egypt’s aspiration to work with its Chinese partners to launch a new phase of investment cooperation centered on manufacturing, technology transfer, innovation, financing and sustainable development.

World.title: From Monrovia To Madrid: The Bility File- Interpol Contacted LNP As Police Probe CMC Leader’s Fuel Debt Dispute; Political Influence Allegations Fly
World.content:
MONROVIA – Weeks before rumours of his arrest in Spain spread across Liberian social media, opposition leader Musa Hassan Bility had already been called in by the country’s police chief. The subject was a complaint he believed had been settled nearly a decade ago.

By: Rodney D. Sieh

In a three-page letter dated September 30, 2026, obtained by FrontPageAfrica, Bility wrote to Inspector General of Police Gregory O. W. Coleman to challenge a central piece of evidence against him. That evidence is a bank’s written confirmation that a cheque issued by his company, Srimex Oil & Gas Company, was presented for payment and returned unpaid.



The letter is the clearest public sign yet that the dispute with his former Nigerian business partners is an active matter before Liberian law enforcement. It is more than a social media rumour.

The case has also drawn international attention. “Interpol reached out to the LNP to say that they were looking into the case,” a source familiar with the investigation told FrontPageAfrica on Tuesday. The source said a report on the matter is being sent to Justice Minister Bettie Lamin-Blamo but has not been made public. The source spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorised to comment publicly.

Interpol, the international police organisation, helps police forces in its 196 member countries share information and track suspects across borders. It does not make arrests itself. It is not clear what Interpol has asked of Liberian police.

A 2017 Complaint Revived

In the letter, written on Srimex letterhead and signed as chairman of the company, Bility says the complaint was “originally made against me in 2017 by my former Nigerian business associates.” It concerns a cheque “allegedly issued by Srimex Oil & Gas Company and said to have been returned unpaid.”

Bility writes that after the police handled the complaint in 2017, he “understood that the matter had been appropriately addressed.”

That changed in July 2026. According to the letter, Coleman invited Bility for “further discussions.” The police chief told him that the complainants planned to travel to Liberia, which had led police to look at the case again.

At that meeting, Bility says, he repeated the position he had taken in 2017. To the best of his knowledge, he wrote, the cheque “was never presented” to Guaranty Trust Bank (GTBank) for payment. It therefore “was never dishonoured or returned unpaid.”

He goes further. He writes that he “understood that the underlying obligation had already been satisfied and that my former business associates were aware of that fact.”

That sentence matters. In it, Bility does not deny that he owed his former partners money. His position is that the money was paid.

The Bank’s Confirmation

The heart of the dispute is a document Bility says he has never seen.

According to the letter, Coleman told him that the Liberia National Police had received written confirmation from Global Bank Liberia Limited, which has since been renamed Bloom Bank Africa Liberia Limited. The bank said the cheque had been presented to GTBank and returned unpaid.

Bility wrote that this “materially conflicts with my understanding of the transaction.” He asked the police for certified copies of four sets of records:

• the bank’s letter or other communication confirming that the cheque was returned unpaid, with all attachments;

• a complete copy of the cheque, showing its number, date, amount, payee, stamps and any return markings;

• any GTBank clearing record, return advice or other document showing when the cheque was presented, when it was returned and why it was not paid;

• all correspondence between the police, Global Bank/Bloom Bank and GTBank about checking the cheque.

He also asked the police to preserve all documents, bank records and investigative material in the case. If any record was never received or cannot be found, he asked the police to confirm that in writing.

The letter does not state the amount of the cheque.

‘Serious Harm’ to His Reputation

Bility wrote that the allegations “have caused serious harm to my personal and business reputation.” He said his lawyers needed the documents to assess the bank’s claim and advise him on “the protection of my legal rights and reputation.” That suggests he may take legal action against those he believes misrepresented the transaction.

He was careful to protect his legal position. The request, he wrote, “shall not be construed as an admission that the cheque was ever presented, dishonoured, or returned unpaid, nor as an admission that any amount remains due or owing.” He reserved “all rights, claims, objections, and defenses.”

It is not known whether the police have responded to the letter.

The Nigerian Document

Bility’s letter does not name the complainants. But a separate document now circulating online appears to describe the same dispute. It appears to come from Nigeria’s Attorney General, and FrontPageAfrica has seen two pages of it. The document carries the watermark of the online outlet Verity News, and FrontPageAfrica has not independently confirmed that it is authentic.

The document names the complainant as Kunle Roberts, managing director of Drake Alliance Oil Trading FZE. It names Bility as the suspect and identifies him as managing director of Nexis Enterprise Inc. and Srimex Oil and Gas Company, the same company whose cheque is in dispute.

According to the document, Roberts’ company sold Nexis Enterprise two shipments of petrol worth US$12 million in March and April 2012, aboard the vessels MT Althea and MT Liquid Fortune. Roberts alleges that US$2,450,000 remains unpaid.

The document says the suspect promised to pay US$50,000 a month from January 2015. It also says he asked Roberts to open a bank account in Liberia to receive the payments. Roberts then set up Drake Liberia Corporation and opened an account at Global Bank Liberia. That is the same bank that, according to Bility’s letter, later told police the Srimex cheque had bounced.

The document also says Roberts was introduced to Bility by his close friend Uzoma Okoro, then managing director of Global Bank Liberia.

FrontPageAfrica could not confirm whether the cheque in Bility’s letter was one of the promised payments, or how much it was for.

‘I’m Not in Jail’

The police investigation came to public attention this week, when reports spread that Bility had been arrested in Madrid. Smart News Liberia reported that Bility told Spoon TV host Stanton Witherspoon he was appearing before a court in Spain. It reported that he did not say what the case was about.

On Tuesday, Bility posted a video denying he had been detained.

“I’m not in jail, as you can see. I’m not being arrested. Don’t listen to these people,” he said. “I’ve been traveling, and now you want to turn my travels into something else.”

He mocked those who still doubted him. He suggested they each contribute US$100 to the CMC headquarters “to free me from jail.”

In the video, Bility did not address the court appearance, the police investigation or the debt allegations.

A Political Heavyweight Under Scrutiny

Bility, 59, represents Nimba County District #7 in the House of Representatives. He is the political leader of the Citizens Movement for Change (CMC), a new opposition party positioning itself for Liberia’s 2029 elections. He built his fortune in fuel imports through Srimex, once Liberia’s largest oil importer. He is also a former president of the Liberia Football Association.

He has long accused officials of President Joseph Boakai’s Unity Party government of trying to brand him a criminal without evidence. He has challenged them to prosecute him if they have a case.

With a police report now reportedly headed to the justice minister and Interpol showing interest, that challenge may soon be tested. So may Bility’s claim that the cheque at the centre of the case never bounced.

Every contribution strengthens our ability to investigate, inform, and hold power accountable while keeping quality journalism accessible to our readers.
