World.title: Senate Hearing On Port Crisis: Paying For A Scanner That Isn’t There
World.content:
MONROVIA – For weeks, Liberian traders have been paying fees to have their cargo scanned at the country’s main seaport. On Monday, the head of the country’s tax agency told senators that the port has no scanner.

By Obediah Johnson

“Right now, the facility is under construction, so there is no cargo scanning that goes on at the Freeport at the moment because it does not have a scanner in place,” Dorbor Jallah, Commissioner General of the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), told the Liberian Senate. “The scanner will come in once we dedicate the facility.”



The admission came at a Senate hearing called to address weeks of complaints from small and medium-sized importers. They say delays and high charges at the Freeport of Monrovia are driving them into debt and pushing up prices for ordinary Liberians.

The Freeport handles most of the goods that enter Liberia, a West African country of about 5.5 million people that imports much of its food, fuel and consumer goods. When containers sit at the port, the cost shows up quickly in the price of rice, cooking oil and other basics in Monrovia’s markets.

‘We Are Paying Interest Every Day’

Business owners say they are charged high fees by the terminal operator APM Terminals, by MEDTECH and under the CTN/GTMS cargo-tracking system, both before their goods arrive and before they are released. Many import on bank credit. Each day a container stays stuck at the port adds interest to their loans.

Importers have also complained of being charged for scanning that, as Jallah’s testimony made clear, does not take place.

A Scanner From China

Jallah told senators that a new facility for handling and inspecting cargo, which he called a “destination expansion facility,” is under construction at the port. A scanner will be installed once it is complete. The government is buying a custom-built machine from a manufacturer in China.

The scanner will be able to check about 40 containers an hour, Jallah said. It will let customs and security officers see what is inside containers without opening them. That should speed up clearance and tighten control over what enters the country.

Jallah said demand for imports keeps rising, and cargo bound for Liberia is piling up at transshipment hubs elsewhere in the region. Some shipping lines have taken steps to reduce delays, he said.

Banks, Customs Software and a 24-Hour Port

Jallah said many importers have been unable to pay release fees for days because banks keep short hours. The LRA is working with the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and commercial banks to allow payments around the clock. He said the CBL is expected to launch a payment switch to link the systems later this year.

The LRA is also upgrading its customs software, which Jallah said was outdated and could not connect smoothly with the banks.

“We are upgrading now to the latest version, which will allow for integration with the commercial banks and Central Bank,” he said.

After a recent meeting with importers, shipping lines and customs brokers, he said, the government has committed to turning the Freeport into a 24-hour port.

“One of the commitments that was made is that we are going to now make the port to be a 24-hour port, so that customs would be 24/7,” Jallah said. “We intend to do that, and hopefully this will help to decongest the port.”

He urged importers and brokers to prepare to work around the clock as well. He also pointed to a port expansion investment plan and the need to dredge the harbour so it can handle growing traffic.

‘The World Bank Warned Us’

Sekou Dukuly, Managing Director of the National Port Authority (NPA), told senators that the port is under severe strain and that the problem has been building for years.

“The congestion we are talking about today didn’t start last month or last year,” Dukuly said. “In 2017, the World Bank warned us and every country, not only in the Mano River Union basin but the sub-region, that every economy in West Africa was growing astronomically. They warned and advised us that we should improve and look at our infrastructure.”

Unlike Liberia, he said, many of its neighbours heeded that advice and expanded their ports. He called the past six years “a complete catastrophe” for Liberia’s port infrastructure. That period largely covers the previous administration of former President George Weah, which left office in January 2024.

Dukuly said the costs of delay to importers and shipping lines are passed directly on to Liberian consumers. He urged lawmakers to “take politics and propaganda” out of the debate, saying the port needs investment because the economy has outgrown it.

Why It Matters

A port without a scanner is a security risk as well as an economic one. Liberia has made several large cocaine seizures this year. Without scanners, customs officers must rely on physical searches or paperwork, which makes it harder to detect drugs, weapons and other contraband.

For businesses, every day of delay adds costs that end up on the price tag. Until the new facility opens and the 24-hour promises are kept, those costs are likely to keep landing on Liberian households.

World.title: Liberia: Eight Months, No Answers: Court Clears Sam Jackson to Travel to U.S. for Cancer Treatment
World.content:
MONROVIA – Samuel P. Jackson walked into court facing manslaughter charges over his wife’s death. On Tuesday, he walked out with permission to leave the country, not to escape the case, the court stressed, but to fight a cancer his doctors call high-risk.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Judge Serena F. Garlawolu of Criminal Court “B” for Montserrado County gave Jackson, one of Liberia’s best-known economists and political commentators, 90 days in the United States for further tests and possible specialist treatment. A urologist has diagnosed him with High-Risk Prostate Adenocarcinoma.



The ruling weighs two things against each other: a sick man’s right to medical care, and the unanswered questions about how his wife, South African lawyer Toni Khumalo Jackson, came to die from head injuries in their Sinkor home in March.

Conditions Attached

The court did not simply let him go. Judge Garlawolu ordered Jackson to produce two qualified human sureties, execute a bond and sign a written undertaking to return to Liberia by February 17, 2027.

The State, represented by Cllr. Isaac Williams, did not oppose the medical request at the November 11 hearing. But prosecutors asked for strict conditions so the trip could not become a way out of Liberia’s jurisdiction. They asked that the court investigate the sureties, approve them, and hold them accountable if Jackson does not return.

The judge agreed. She told the Clerk of Criminal Court “B” to make sure every requirement is met before Jackson boards a plane. Any extension past February 17 will need credible medical evidence and the court’s express approval. If he fails to return without one, the sureties could face legal consequences.

Who Was Toni Khumalo?

Born Ntombikayise Innocentia Khumalo in Gauteng, South Africa, Toni was an attorney and the founder of NK Attorneys. Friends knew her as warm and family-minded, and Jackson called her his “Zulu Queen.”

On March 13, 2026, she died at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Medical Center in Monrovia. By Jackson’s account, she was found semi-conscious in the couple’s bedroom with a deep cut to her head. She was taken first to St. Joseph’s Catholic Hospital and then transferred to JFK.

She would have turned 44 on June 23, which was also the couple’s third wedding anniversary. Months after her death, her body was still in a Monrovia morgue, and her family in South Africa, including her elderly mother, Eliza, was still waiting to bring her home.

From Person of Interest to Defendant

The Liberia National Police first treated Jackson as a person of interest. On March 16, Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman announced that he was a suspect.

On April 2, police charged him with manslaughter, negligent homicide, aggravated assault and recklessly endangering another person. Investigators cited witness accounts, photographs and communications that they said pointed to a history of physical abuse in the marriage. They also questioned Jackson’s conduct in the hours before his wife was taken to hospital.

None of these allegations have been proven in court. Jackson is presumed innocent.

Four Nights in Prison, a US$20,000 Bond

After the Special Grand Jury for Montserrado County returned an indictment, Jackson was arrested and held at the Monrovia Central Prison. He spent four nights behind bars. On April 6, Resident Circuit Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie released him on a US$20,000 criminal appearance bond.

On April 13, prosecutors challenged the property valuation bond, arguing the documents did not meet legal requirements, and sought to send him back to custody. On April 22, Judge Willie dismissed the challenge, upheld the bond, and ordered seized property returned to Jackson, including his electronic devices.

The State’s worry then, that Jackson stay within the court’s reach, is the same worry behind this week’s demand for two extra sureties.

The Autopsy That Didn’t Count

The defense’s biggest setback concerned the forensic evidence. Criminal Court “A” had authorized forensic investigator Dr. Rockefeller F. Cooper II to work on the case for the defense. Prosecutors argued that his registration as a Forensic Medico-Legal Death Investigator did not make him a licensed pathologist.

On May 26, Judge Willie agreed. He declared Dr. Cooper’s autopsy null and void and inadmissible. He let stand the rest of Dr. Cooper’s work, including crime-scene documentation, evidence collection, materials analysis, and witness interviews.

The ruling did not settle the main question. The prosecution still has to prove, with admissible evidence, what caused Toni’s injuries and whether anything Jackson did legally contributed to her death.

Waiting for the Reports

The State has also been criticized for delays. On June 23, the day that would have been Toni’s birthday and their anniversary, Jackson publicly demanded the official autopsy and toxicology reports. He said the families could not repatriate her remains without them.

On July 24, prosecutors reportedly asked Criminal Court “A” for more time, saying the reports were not yet in their case file. The delay raised questions about how ready the State was to prosecute such a serious case.

For Toni’s family, the need is simple: to know how she died, and to bury her.

Jackson’s Defense

Jackson has consistently denied causing his wife’s death. He has suggested that some of her injuries may have come from cardiopulmonary resuscitation by medical staff. He has questioned the credibility of the investigation and said authorities are targeting him because he criticizes the government.

Those are defense claims. They do not resolve the charges. The burden remains on the prosecution to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

A Test for the State

The 90-day leave is a test for the prosecution and for the courts. By demanding enforceable guarantees, the State has shown it takes the risk of Jackson not returning seriously. The court has made clear the trip is not a way out of the criminal process.

The larger task falls to prosecutors: keeping the case moving, securing the forensic evidence and making sure Toni’s family is not lost among the procedural fights.

Access to medical care is a fundamental right. So is the public’s right to a credible justice process, in which a woman’s violent death is fully investigated and decided on the evidence.

Jackson is due back by February 17, 2027. Until then, Republic of Liberia, by and through the Ministry of Justice, versus Samuel P. Jackson remains pending before Criminal Court “B.” The allegations are unproven, and Toni Khumalo Jackson’s family is still waiting for answers.

World.title: COP31 Cover Draft Raises Climate Finance Questions as Liberia Seeks Support for Implementation
World.content:
Delegates gather for negotiations at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, where countries are discussing climate finance, adaptation and the transition away from fossil fuels. Photo: UNFCCC

Summary

A draft COP31 political agreement proposes raising annual adaptation finance to US$120 billion by 2035, while countries remain divided over funding and fossil fuel commitments.

African negotiators are pressing for climate finance promises to be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms.

Liberia faces questions over implementation, with about US$360 million in climate finance commitments under its previous climate plan still undisbursed as of December 2024.

By Aria Deemie

A draft political agreement at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference proposes that developed countries keep their promise to increase annual adaptation finance for developing countries to US$120 billion by 2035, accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels and expanding electricity’s share of global energy use.



The document , known as a cover decision, is intended to capture the conference’s broad political priorities. Its first draft, released by the COP31 presidency on November 16, also proposes a global target for electricity to account for 35 percent of final energy use by 2035. However, the text contains competing formulations on fossil fuels and other issues, and the presidency has stressed that it does not represent an agreed position.

“Africa is not here to renegotiate promises; we are here to ensure they are delivered. Every climate finance commitment must be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms,” Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, said in a statement published on the group’s official Facebook page .

Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, has called for climate finance commitments to be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms. Photo: AGN

The remarks come as the African Group of Negotiators continues to push for stronger climate finance commitments at COP31. Amoah had been scheduled to brief journalists on November 14 on the first week’s negotiations and Africa’s expectations for the second week, but the planned press conference was cancelled.

As negotiations enter their second week in Antalya, Türkiye, Liberia is pressing for predictable climate finance and adaptation support. Civil society groups are questioning whether the proposed cover decision will help secure those commitments or distract from the detailed negotiations needed to deliver them. For Liberia, the issue is especially urgent because much of its climate target depends on international support, while funding for existing commitments remains undelivered.

The US$120 billion adaptation finance proposal is among the most significant parts of the draft. It seeks to give a specific annual amount and a 2035 deadline to the previously agreed goal of tripling adaptation finance. The draft also proposes a time-bound pathway for delivering the target and a method that accounts for the grant value of climate finance, rather than treating loans as equivalent to grants.

The scale of the need is much greater. The draft cites an estimated US$305 billion in annual adaptation needs for developing countries by 2035. International public adaptation finance stood at between US$28 billion and US$32 billion in 2024. Even reaching US$120 billion would therefore cover less than a third of the estimated requirement.

The draft also calls for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, including an immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. It welcomes roadmaps developed under Brazil’s COP30 presidency for the transition away from fossil fuels and ending deforestation. But it also includes language reaffirming the earlier commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, leaving room for disagreement over how strongly the final decision should address the issue.

The proposals are not final decisions. In an accompanying note, the presidency said the draft was intended to reflect the range of views expressed by countries, not consensus. It added that every element remained open for discussion, including whether it should appear in the final document.

The disagreement is not only about what the document says, but whether attention to a broad political declaration is taking negotiators away from the formal discussions where countries are expected to resolve outstanding issues.

“We think that this cover decision is directing us, and the parties more importantly, towards the wrong place instead of the decision-making rooms, or instead of the negotiation rooms,” said Jacobo Ocharan, speaking at a media briefing organized by Climate Action Network International , a global network of civil society organizations working on climate change.

The network warned that the focus on the cover decision could divert attention from negotiations on climate finance, adaptation and a just transition. It also raised concerns that announcements presented as climate finance during the first week had brought very little new public funding.

Rebecca Thissen, who spoke on climate finance at the briefing, said developed countries were expected to present new climate finance plans after the previous funding period ended in 2025. She questioned whether the Climate Finance Work Programme would focus on developed countries’ obligations under the Paris Agreement or broaden into discussions about private investment and contributions from other countries.

The African Group of Negotiators has also been pushing for climate finance to remain central to the conference outcome. In a November 12 interview with the group’s chair, Amoah said the group wanted progress on the finance work program and the goal of tripling adaptation finance. He said countries had already established plans and processes for climate action, but implementation depended on finance, technology and capacity.

The group had submitted three proposals for separate agenda items at COP31, including one on tripling adaptation finance, one on trade-related climate measures and another on financing arrangements under the Green Climate Fund. None was adopted as a standalone agenda item, although the presidency indicated that some issues would be considered through other negotiating tracks.

Amoah also questioned the proposed 35-by-35 electrification target, saying a global target should account for countries’ different starting points. He said the African group was not opposed to electrification but wanted access to electricity to be prioritized alongside the transition to cleaner energy.

“For us in Africa, access to energy is the most important thing and then clean energy under this goal,” he told African Arguments.

For Liberia, the debate over finance is not abstract. The country’s updated climate plan targets a 64 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035. But 54 percentage points of that target depend on international support, making external finance and technical assistance essential to delivering much of the commitment.

About US$360 million in climate finance commitments under Liberia’s previous climate plan remained undisbursed as of December 2024. The outstanding amount raises questions about whether new commitments made at COP31 will translate into projects and support on the ground.

“COP31 for Liberia is more about implementation,” said Benjamin S. Karmorh Jr., the Environmental Protection Agency’s Chief Technical Advisor, at a meeting at the Liberia Pavilion on Monday, November 16.

Members of Liberia’s delegation brief journalists on the week’s developments and Liberia’s participation at COP31 during a meeting at the Liberia Pavilion on Monday. Photo: Aria Deemie

Arthur Becker, the agency’s Director for Multilateral Environmental Agreements, said Liberia was seeking predictable funding to support adaptation and accelerate preparation of its National Adaptation Plan, which sets out how the country will prepare for climate risks.

Becker said Liberia had been informed during a side event involving the United Nations Development Programme, the National Adaptation Plan Global Network and Brazil’s COP30 presidency that it was among countries included in a three-year funding window for adaptation planning, supported by Ireland, Germany and Canada. Details on the amount available to Liberia and when the funding would be disbursed were not provided.

But planning is only part of the challenge. Liberia has also faced delays in projects intended to strengthen its response to climate impacts, including the Climate Information System and the Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project, which includes coastal protection work for vulnerable communities.The effects of inadequate adaptation support are already visible among communities exposed to flooding and unpredictable rainfall. Farmers who depend on rainfall need timely weather information to make decisions about when to plant and how to protect their crops. At COP31, an Environmental Protection Agency official announced plans for about 10 new automated weather stations in agriculture-producing counties over the next 12 months.

Becker said Liberia had been informed during a side event involving the United Nations Development Programme, the National Adaptation Plan Global Network and Brazil’s COP30 presidency that it was among countries included in a three-year funding window for adaptation planning, supported by Ireland, Germany and Canada. Details on the amount available to Liberia and when the funding would be disbursed were not provided.

Farmers who depend on rainfall need timely weather information to make decisions about when to plant and how to protect their crops. At COP31, an Environmental Protection Agency official announced plans for about 10 new automated weather stations in agriculture-producing counties over the next 12 months.

Farmers in Liberia depend heavily on rainfall for agricultural activities, making access to reliable weather forecasts important for decisions about planting and protecting crops. Photo: World Bank

Adaptation finance was also a major concern at the civil society briefing.

“We will not let adaptation finance be traded off again,” said Daniel Rossell of the Talanoa Institute, referring to the commitment made at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, to triple adaptation finance.

Rossell questioned how countries could implement indicators under the Global Goal on Adaptation, an international framework for measuring progress in preparing for climate impacts, without the financial resources to act.

“How are developing countries supposed to implement indicators with a hundred metadata sheets of indicators and no means of implementation?” he asked.

The proposed Belém-Antalya Mechanism, intended to advance discussions on a just transition, is another area of disagreement. A just transition means moving towards a low-carbon economy while protecting workers and communities whose jobs and livelihoods may be affected.

“This is basically like being offered a seat at the table with no food, no plates, no cutlery, and very bad wine,” said Kuda Manjonjo of Power Shift Africa, criticizing the draft negotiating text for not providing enough practical support for meaningful participation. He warned that without resources and clear commitments, the proposed mechanism could become “an empty shell.”

Liberia is also following negotiations on carbon markets and climate finance. “Don’t tie adaptation around the sale of credit,” said Elijah Whapoe, who presented the country’s negotiating updates, warning against making adaptation support dependent on carbon-credit trading.

Whapoe outlined Liberia’s engagement with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement , which sets out ways countries can cooperate on climate action, including through the trading of emissions reductions and approaches that do not involve carbon credits. He said Liberia had not registered a non-market approach under Article 6.8, the provision that allows countries to cooperate on climate action without relying on carbon markets or trading carbon credits.

On the Climate Finance Work Programme , a two-year process for discussing how developed countries should provide climate finance to developing countries, he said Liberia was engaging through the Group of 77 and China, a coalition of developing countries, the African Group of Negotiators, which represents African countries, and the Least Developed Countries group, which represents the world’s poorest countries. Liberia wants the program to move forward without new language that could weaken its focus on developed countries’ financial obligations, he said.

As negotiations continue, Liberia and other climate-vulnerable countries are seeking an outcome that moves beyond political declarations and provides the resources needed to implement their climate plans.

“The conference is responsible to finance adaptation,” Whapoe said.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership ,a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia: Despite US$50 Million Disbursement, IMF Warns Boakai Administration over ‘Macro-Critical’ Corruption, Weak Governance
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s economic recovery is increasingly presenting a complicated picture of progress and institutional vulnerability. On one hand, the administration of President Joseph Boakai has secured fresh financial support from the International Monetary Fund, recorded improvements in domestic revenue collection and maintained economic growth despite mounting international economic pressures.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

On the other hand, the same international institution providing the country with millions of dollars in additional financing has raised serious concerns about corruption, weak governance, inadequate institutional capacity and delays in implementing reforms intended to strengthen public accountability.



The contradiction is significant. While the latest IMF assessment has opened the door for approximately US$50 million in additional disbursements to Liberia, its accompanying country report delivers a sobering message about the country’s governance environment that economic growth alone cannot guarantee sustainable development when public institutions remain vulnerable to corruption, transparency is limited and accountability mechanisms struggle to perform their statutory responsibilities.

At the center of the assessment is the IMF’s characterization of systemic corruption and weak rule of law as “macro-critical” problems. The terminology is particularly important because it places corruption beyond the traditional understanding of an ethical or administrative failure. It identifies corruption as a direct threat to Liberia’s economic stability, investment environment, government revenue generation and the country’s ability to deliver inclusive development.

In practical terms, the Fund is warning that Liberia’s economic gains could remain fragile if the government fails to address institutional weaknesses that undermine confidence in public administration.

The IMF Executive Board completed the fourth review of Liberia’s Extended Credit Facility arrangement and the first review of its Resilience and Sustainability Facility on September 28, 2026. The decision unlocked SDR19.3 million, approximately US$26.2 million, under the ECF arrangement and SDR17.62 million, approximately US$23.96 million, under the RSF arrangement.

Combined, the two disbursements amount to approximately US$50.16 million.

The financial support is important for a country facing declining donor assistance, high infrastructure demands, external financing pressures and a narrow export base. It also demonstrates that Liberia has maintained sufficient progress in several areas of its economic programme to continue receiving support from the Fund.

However, the accompanying assessment makes clear that satisfying selected economic programme requirements is not the same as resolving the governance problems that have historically weakened Liberia’s public institutions.

The IMF’s concerns are particularly troubling because they come at a time when the Boakai administration has repeatedly presented governance reform, public-sector accountability and the fight against corruption as central pillars of its development agenda.

The government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development is intended to address longstanding challenges in infrastructure, agriculture, roads, education, sanitation and economic transformation. Yet, the success of those ambitions depends heavily on whether public resources are protected from misuse, government institutions operate transparently and officials entrusted with public responsibilities are held accountable. Without those conditions, increased revenue and international financial assistance could fail to produce the development outcomes expected by ordinary Liberians.

Corruption Becomes an Economic Threat

One of the most consequential findings in the IMF report concerns the country’s anti-corruption framework, particularly the declining compliance with asset-declaration requirements among public officials. According to the Fund, compliance declined by 19 percentage points compared with the previous year. The development represents a setback for a mechanism designed to help identify potential conflicts of interest, unexplained wealth and possible abuse of public office.

Asset declaration is one of the principal instruments through which governments establish accountability among officials entrusted with public resources. It allows the relevant authorities to examine whether the wealth and financial interests of public officials are consistent with their legitimate sources of income.

However, Liberia’s system continues to face legal and institutional obstacles. Under the existing arrangement, publication of public officials’ asset declarations requires court authorization. Proposed amendments intended to remove this requirement have been submitted to the Legislature but remain unapproved.

The IMF has urged the authorities to remove those legal barriers, strengthen verification procedures and establish effective enforcement mechanisms. The recommendation places responsibility on both the executive and legislative branches. Although the administration may express its commitment to transparency, meaningful reform requires the passage of legislation that gives accountability institutions the necessary authority to operate effectively.

The issue is particularly important because the LACC remains one of the principal institutions expected to investigate corruption and promote integrity in public service. Yet the IMF says the commission continues to operate under significant resource constraints, despite increased allocations to integrity institutions in the 2026 fiscal budget.

The Fund’s position is that the LACC must be fully operationalized, adequately funded and equipped to enforce accountability. This means providing the institution with sufficient financial resources, investigative personnel, technical equipment and operational independence to pursue allegations of corruption without unnecessary institutional obstacles. The concern raises a difficult question for the Boakai administration: how can the government expect an anti-corruption institution to deliver meaningful results when the international financial institution assessing its performance says it lacks the resources necessary to execute its mandate effectively?

The effectiveness of an anti-graft commission cannot be measured simply by the existence of its headquarters, the appointment of commissioners or the number of public statements issued against corruption. Its real performance must be reflected in credible investigations, verification of asset declarations, prosecution of substantiated cases and the recovery of public resources lost through corrupt practices. The IMF’s findings suggest that Liberia still has considerable work to do in this regard.

The commission’s own third-quarter 2026 report also provides an indication of the challenges confronting its operations. It recorded 237 officials as non-compliant with asset-declaration requirements at the end of the quarter and identified investigative and prosecutorial capacity as continuing institutional constraints.

Audit Findings and Unanswered Questions About Public Money

Beyond asset declarations, the IMF has identified weaknesses in the management and reconciliation of government revenue, raising additional questions about the transparency of public financial transactions. The report says recent audits identified discrepancies between revenues recorded in the Tax Administration System and amounts actually credited to consolidated revenue accounts.

The finding is significant because government revenue is expected to pass through transparent accounting and reconciliation procedures that allow authorities, auditors and citizens to determine how much money has been collected and where it has been deposited.

Any discrepancy between recorded collections and actual credits to government accounts requires prompt investigation and clarification. The IMF has consequently emphasized stronger reconciliation procedures and called for the publication of outstanding special audit reports, including the audit of historical domestic debt covering the period 1980 to 2024 and the audit of the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation.

The publication of these reports would allow the public to understand the findings, assess whether irregularities occurred and determine what corrective actions government institutions have taken. For Liberia, where public confidence in the management of national resources has repeatedly been undermined by allegations of corruption and financial mismanagement, the timely publication of audit findings is essential.

An audit that identifies irregularities but is never followed by corrective action risks becoming another administrative document with little practical impact. The IMF’s concerns extend to the Central Bank of Liberia, where implementation of recommendations arising from the General Auditing Commission’s compliance audit and the Kroll forensic audit has progressed more slowly than anticipated.

Although the Central Bank has started reconciling suspense accounts and strengthening oversight of financial guarantees, the Fund says outstanding safeguards recommendations must be accelerated. The objective is to bring the institution’s governance and internal-control framework fully into conformity with the Central Bank Act.

These recommendations are important because the Central Bank occupies a critical position in the country’s financial system. Its credibility influences monetary stability, confidence in the Liberian dollar, banking-sector performance and the country’s capacity to manage external economic pressures. Weak internal controls at such an institution could expose public resources to unnecessary risks and undermine confidence in the wider financial system.

The IMF’s assessment therefore suggests that governance reform must extend beyond ministries and agencies to include institutions responsible for monetary policy and financial regulation.

The US State Department Adds to Liberia’s Governance Concerns

The IMF’s warning is not the only recent international assessment drawing attention to corruption and institutional weaknesses in Liberia. A November 2026 assessment by the United States Department of State, contained in its 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia, has similarly highlighted corruption, judicial inefficiencies, weak institutional capacity and limited transparency as significant obstacles to the country’s investment environment.

The report presents a mixed picture of Liberia’s economic prospects. It recognizes opportunities in mining, agriculture, energy, infrastructure and other sectors, but warns that persistent governance problems continue to undermine the country’s attractiveness to foreign investors.

Of particular concern is the State Department’s assessment that corruption remains one of the most significant obstacles confronting businesses operating in Liberia. The report says investors have raised concerns about unofficial payments, charges outside investment agreements and alleged extortion involving public officials. It also identifies weaknesses in public procurement, the legal and regulatory framework and the enforcement of existing laws.

The assessment further raises concerns about the judicial environment, including lengthy commercial disputes, difficulties enforcing court decisions and allegations of bribery involving court officials. The State Department’s report describes corruption as a

major impediment to democratic consolidation and economic growth, while identifying judicial delays and weak institutional capacity as continuing investment risks. The implications are particularly serious for a country seeking to attract foreign investment to finance infrastructure development, create employment and diversify its economy.

Investors generally require predictable regulations, transparent procurement procedures, reliable judicial protection and confidence that government agreements will be respected. When businesses believe that public contracts may be influenced by political connections, that unofficial payments are necessary to obtain government services or that commercial disputes may remain unresolved for years, investment decisions become more difficult.

Such conditions can increase the cost of doing business, discourage new investors and reduce the potential for employment creation. The State Department’s assessment therefore complements the IMF’s warning. While the IMF focuses on the relationship between corruption and macroeconomic stability, the American assessment highlights how similar institutional weaknesses affect the country’s ability to attract and retain investment.

The two assessments point toward a common conclusion that the country’s economic potential is substantial, but the credibility of its institutions remains a major obstacle to realizing that potential. It is also important to recognize that the State Department report acknowledges opportunities and reforms rather than portraying Liberia as an economy without prospects. Its concerns are directed at the institutional conditions under which those opportunities must be pursued.

For the Boakai administration, however, the timing of the assessment is uncomfortable. The government has repeatedly promised to restore public confidence, improve the investment climate and demonstrate that public officials will be held accountable for their actions.

The IMF’s latest assessment has therefore placed an important responsibility before the Boakai administration to ensure that the financial support Liberia continues to receive is matched by equally strong commitment to institutional reform. The US$50 million may strengthen the government’s immediate financial position, but it cannot independently resolve the governance weaknesses identified by the Fund.

The ultimate measure of the administration’s success will not be how much international financing it secures, but whether it can demonstrate that public money is protected, corruption is confronted, institutions are strengthened and economic growth produces visible benefits for ordinary Liberians.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Orders Gender Minister to Settle Rape Survivor’s School Fees by Nov. 30
World.content:
MONROVIA – More than two years after a 14-year-old girl was raped and made pregnant by a man who lived in her yard, the Liberian government has received an unusual warning from the bench: pay the survivor’s school fees, or face contempt of court.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr., the assigned circuit judge of Criminal Court “E”, has rejected a request by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection to put off paying the survivor’s school costs until the 2027 budget year. He gave the ministry until November 30 to pay the fees and file the receipts with the court. Criminal Court “E” is Liberia’s special court for sexual and gender-based violence.



The ruling puts new pressure on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s government to show that it protects vulnerable children. It also raises a hard question: how can the state convict a man of abusing a child and then fail to help that child rebuild her life?

The Court Rejects the Budget Excuse

The court sent its directive on November 17 through Clerk of Court Abraham Richards. It came after a conference between the judge and government officials about what the state still owes the survivor and her baby.

The meeting followed a November 11 summons, also signed by Richards, that ordered two officials to appear on November 16 at 10:00 a.m.: Acting Minister of Justice and Attorney General Betty M. Lamin-Blamo and Gender Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie. They were told to explain how the government was supporting the survivor and her child.

At the conference, representatives of the Gender Ministry reportedly said the government’s 2026 budget year was nearly over. Liberia’s budget year now follows the calendar year. They asked for time to meet the court’s order through the 2027 national budget.

Judge Wesseh refused. According to accounts of the meeting, he said the girl’s education could not wait because the government’s budget year was ending. He reportedly called the matter personal and serious, and asked the officials whether they would accept the same treatment if the girl were their own daughter or relative.

The written directive says the ministry must file payment receipts with the clerk of Criminal Court “E” to prove it has paid. If it misses the deadline, it may be held in contempt. Minister Horace-Kollie could then face further proceedings, subject to due process.

The receipt requirement matters. It means the court will judge compliance by proof of payment, not by promises or administrative explanations. The contempt warning also turns a routine dispute over government spending into a possible clash between the judiciary and the executive.

A Girl, a Knife and a Life Interrupted

The case began in October 2024 in Jallah’s Town, a community in Montserrado County, which includes the capital, Monrovia.

According to the indictment, Victor Eze, then 35, sexually assaulted a 14-year-old girl who lived in the same yard. Prosecutors said he entered the room where she was sleeping, threatened her with a knife and raped her. She was injured and taken to JDJ Memorial Hospital for examination and treatment.

Eze was arrested on December 9, 2024, and charged with statutory rape under Section 14.70 of Liberia’s New Penal Law. Under Liberia’s 2005 rape law, rape of a child under 18 is a first-degree felony that can carry up to life in prison.

On June 11, 2025, Eze pleaded guilty. When the court questioned him about the plea, he admitted that the girl had given birth to a child as a result of the abuse. He said he was willing to support the mother and child. The court found that his plea was voluntary and that he understood the charge, and convicted him.

Gender Minister Gbeme Horace Kollie

On October 7, 2025, Judge Wesseh sentenced Eze to five years in prison, including the nine months he had already spent in pretrial detention. He must serve the remaining four years and three months in a Liberian prison.

The conviction held the offender to account. But the survivor’s ordeal did not end with the sentence. She is now a teenage mother, raising a child while trying to recover from the crime. She is reportedly still out of school, even though schools across Liberia have reopened.

Help That Fell Short

The question of support for the survivor and her child came up during the original trial. Court records mention US$50 paid through the Ministry of Justice’s Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit. The court also noted help from the Gender Ministry, including seed money for a small business and support through a program involving SOS Children’s Villages, an international child-welfare charity.

The new court order shows that this help has not covered her schooling. The issue is not whether the government did anything. It is whether what it did was enough, lasted long enough and met the court’s expectations and the child’s needs.

A small cash payment cannot replace an education. A small-business grant cannot replace schooling, counselling, healthcare and protection for a teenage mother and her baby. For a girl who was only 14 when she was attacked, school is more than a government benefit. It is her best chance to regain some normal life, become independent and avoid being trapped in poverty.

A Promise Put to the Test

The case is a test for the Boakai administration, which took office in January 2024. Boakai promised a government that would put human dignity, social protection and accountability first, and his administration has pledged to fight violence against women and children.

Sexual violence is a long-standing problem in Liberia, a West African nation of about 5.5 million people that is still rebuilding after civil wars that ended in 2003. Rape is among the most commonly reported serious crimes in the country, and many of the victims are children. In 2020, then-President George Manneh Weah declared rape a national emergency after a surge in reported cases.

The question now goes beyond whether Liberia can arrest, prosecute and jail offenders. It is whether the state keeps protecting the child after the sentence is handed down and public attention moves on.

Cllr. Betty Lamie Blamo

The Gender Ministry’s legal mandate is to protect and promote the welfare of women, children and vulnerable people. Yet here it has had to explain to a court why a rape survivor’s school fees have not been paid. The ministry says the budget year is almost over, and that may describe a real administrative problem. But it does not meet the girl’s immediate needs. The school calendar does not wait for the next budget, and neither does the state’s duty to a child whose life has been upended by sexual violence.

The Ministry of Justice, which took part in the earlier proceedings and was also summoned, is under scrutiny too. By summoning both ministries, Judge Wesseh signalled that he sees the survivor’s welfare as a shared government responsibility, not one that agencies can pass back and forth.

When the Executive Must Answer to the Judiciary

The order also raises a wider governance issue. Under Liberia’s constitution, the courts exercise judicial power, and the executive must obey lawful court orders. A ministry cannot treat a court directive as optional advice.

That gives the judge’s warning significance beyond this one case. It shows that the courts are willing to hold government agencies to account when their actions, or failure to act, harm vulnerable citizens. Contempt proceedings against a sitting cabinet minister would be a serious step, and any such case would have to follow proper legal procedure and give the minister due process.

November 30: A Deadline for the Government

The immediate obligation is clear: the fees must be paid by November 30, 2026, and the receipts filed with Criminal Court “E”.

But the government’s commitment to the survivor and her child must go further than a single court order. A five-year sentence may punish the offender, but it cannot send the survivor back to school or provide for her child. The state’s duty should be measured not only by how long the offender spends in prison, but by whether the survivor can return to class, get counselling and healthcare, and raise her child safely. That requires sustained government support.

For a girl whose childhood was cut short by sexual violence, justice cannot end with the conviction of the man who attacked her. A government that promises to protect its children cannot abandon them once the courtroom doors close.

World.title: Editorial: Stop Charging Liberians for a Scanner That Doesn’t Exist
World.content:
The gap costs traders and consumers money and leaves Liberia’s main seaport open to drug and arms smugglers. FPA urges the NPA, the LRA and the government to suspend scanning charges, publish a timeline, find a stopgap and make 24-hour operations real.

ON MONDAY, LIBERIA Revenue Authority Commissioner General Dorbor Jallah told the Senate there is “no cargo scanning that goes on at the Freeport at the moment” because the port “does not have a scanner in place.”

THAT SHOULD ALARM every Liberian who buys a bag of rice, a gallon of oil, or a tin of milk.



THE FREEPORT OF Monrovia is the country’s front door. Nearly everything Liberians eat, wear and build with passes through it. Yet the front door has no lock and no window. Customs officers cannot see inside the containers arriving every day. Meanwhile, importers say they are being billed for scanning that, by the government’s own account, is not happening.

A Fee for a Service That Isn’t Delivered

LIBERIA’S SMALL AND medium-sized importers are already stretched. Many bring in goods on bank loans. Every day a container sits at the port, interest piles up. On top of that come fees from the terminal operator, from MEDTECH and under the CTN/GTMS cargo-tracking system, charged before their goods arrive and before they are released.

IF ANY PART of those charges is for scanning, it is money paid for nothing. That is unfair to the trader, and the cost does not stop with the trader. It is passed on to the market woman, the taxi driver and the family in Paynesville or Ganta who pay more for the same goods. In a country where food inflation stands at 11.1 per cent, according to the Central Bank of Liberia, ordinary people cannot afford to subsidise a broken system.

A Security Gap We Cannot Ignore

THIS IS NOT only about money. A port without a scanner is an invitation. Liberia has made major cocaine seizures this year, and the country is struggling to shake the reputation that it is a transit point for international drug traffickers. Without scanners, customs and security officers must rely on paperwork, tip-offs and manual searches. That is slow for honest businesses and easy for smugglers to get around.

A COUNTRY SERIOUS about fighting drugs, arms trafficking and smuggling does not leave its main seaport blind.

The Warnings Were There

NATIONAL PORT AUTHORITY Managing Director Sekou Dukuly told senators that the World Bank warned Liberia in 2017 to expand its port infrastructure. Neighbouring countries listened, he said, and Liberia did not. He called the past six years “a complete catastrophe.”

WE AGREE THAT the crisis did not begin last month. But the public is not interested in assigning blame between administrations. Liberians want to know when it will be fixed. Dukuly urged lawmakers to take “politics and propaganda” out of the matter. The best way to do that is with clear facts and firm dates.

What Must Happen Now

WE URGE THE National Port Authority, the Liberia Revenue Authority and the Boakai administration to act on six points:

1. SUSPEND AND AUDIT scanning charges. Any fee linked to scanning should be suspended at once until a scanner is working. The LRA and NPA should publish what has been collected under that heading and say whether it will be refunded or credited to importers.

2. PUBLISH A TIMELINE. When will the new cargo facility be finished? When will the scanner from China arrive, be installed and be running? Liberians deserve dates, not “once we dedicate the facility.”

3. BE OPEN ABOUT the procurement. The public should know the cost of the scanner, the supplier and how the contract was awarded, in line with Liberia’s procurement law.

4. FIND A STOPGAP. Waiting months for a permanent facility is not acceptable. The government should explore leasing mobile scanners or seeking help from partners, as other ports in the region have done, to cover the gap.

5. MAKE 24-HOUR OPERATIONS real. Promises of round-the-clock customs and banking have been made before. The government should name a start date and get banks, customs, shipping lines and brokers working the same hours.

6. LEGISLATIVE FOLLOW-THROUGH. The Senate deserves credit for calling this hearing. It must now follow up with regular progress reports, so that this testimony does not end up as one more forgotten promise.

Restore Sanity at the Port

THE FREEPORT SHOULD be an engine of commerce. Today, for too many businesses, it is a place where money and time disappear. Traders are not asking for favours. They are asking for a port that works, fees that are fair, and a government that keeps its word.

THE SCANNER GAP was admitted in public, before the Senate. Now it must be fixed in public, with deadlines that Liberians can hold their leaders to. Until then, every day of delay is a tax on the poorest Liberians, and they have paid enough

World.title: Liberia: Gbarpolu Awaits Answers as Supt. Zinnah and Others Finally Face Court Over Controversial Yellow Machines Procurement
World.content:
Gbarpolu County Superintendent, Mr. Sam K. Zinnah and

BOPOLU CITY, Gbarpolu County – After approximately 14 months of indictment and several months of legal and procedural delays, Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah and other defendants have finally appeared before the 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Bopolu in connection with the controversial US$425,000 Yellow Machines Case.

By Augustus D.R [email protected]

The court appearance on Monday, November 16 marks an important development in a case that has attracted public attentions and raised questions about the management of public resources in Gbarpolu County.



However, the anticipated trial did not commence following the absence of two co-defendants: Omoru Sheriff, Chief Executive Officer of City Lion Inc. and former Project Management Committee Chairman Robert Benda.

The matter was consequently reassigned for Monday, November 23, 2026. According to Clerk of Court Emmanuel Worlabah, the presence or appropriate legal representation of all defendants is necessary for proceedings to continue.

Superintendent Zinnah, former Superintendent J. Keyah Saah, former Fiscal Affairs Superintendent Anthony Yorkor and prosecutors from the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC) were present.

ZINNAH: “I AM OUTSIDE AND READY”

Following the court appearance, Superintendent Zinnah took to his official Facebook page to express his readiness to face the allegations. “My long silence has been misconstrued. Now I am outside and ready to face my accusers… Enough is enough,” he stated.

Mr. Robert Benda – Former Chairman of the Gbarpolu Project Management Committee

His declaration comes after months of public debate surrounding the case and his role in the handling of the three machines.

BACKGROUND OF THE US$425,000 CONTROVERSY

The case involves US$425,000 in County Social Development Funds reportedly approved on June 4, 2023 for the acquisition of three heavy-duty machines:

* One bulldozer;

* One excavator; and

* One motor grader.

The procurement process reportedly began on September 21, 2022 during the administration of former President George Manneh Weah.

View of the Controversial Yellow Machines

Following its investigation, the LACC secured a True Bill of Indictment during the August 2025 Term of Court. On September 8, 2025, the Commission announced the indictment of five individuals:

1. Sam K. Zinnah – Current Gbarpolu County Superintendent.

2. Omoru Sheriff – Chief Executive Officer of City Lion Inc.

3. J. Keyah Saah – Former County Superintendent.

4. Anthony Yorkor – Former Fiscal Affairs Superintendent.

5. Robert Benda – Former Project Management Committee Chairman.

The indictment includes allegations relating to corruption, abuse of public resources and procurement irregularities. All allegations remain subject to proof in court.

Mr. J. Keyah Saah – Former Superintendent of Gbarpolu County

WHY ZINNAH’S INVOLVEMENT MATTERS

One major issue surrounding the case is Superintendent Zinnah’s involvement, considering that the procurement process reportedly started under the previous administration.

According to the reported background of the indictment, his alleged involvement relates to his subsequent administrative role, particularly facilitating the transportation of the machines from the Freeport of Monrovia to Bopolu.

Mr. Anthony Yorkor – Former Fiscal Affairs Superintendent

The court will ultimately determine the specific responsibilities of each defendant and whether the prosecution can establish the allegations.

GBARPOLU RESIDENTS WANT ANSWERS

Beyond the courtroom proceedings, residents want answers about the procurement, condition, management and intended use of the three machines.

The equipment was acquired to support road construction and improve connectivity across Gbarpolu County, where several communities continue to face serious transportation challenges.

The people deserve to know whether the US$425,000 investment delivered its intended public value and who should be held responsible if wrongdoing is established.

NOVEMBER 23: ANOTHER OPPORTUNITY FOR JUSTICE

The case has been reassigned for Monday, November 23 when full trial proceedings are expected to commence. The LACC will have the opportunity to present its evidence, while the defendants must be afforded the opportunity to challenge the allegations and defend themselves.

After more than a year of legal proceedings, the people of Gbarpolu are looking forward to a transparent judicial process that establishes the facts, determines individual responsibility and protects public resources.

The central question remains: What happened to the US$425,000 intended to provide Gbarpolu with three essential development machines?

World.title: Government reiterates importance of PPPs in Zambia’s infrastructure development
World.content:
Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Collins Nzovu, has reiterated the importance of Public Private partnerships (PPPs) in attaining Zambia’s infrastructure development agenda.

Speaking when he inspected works on the 321 kilometre Lusaka-Ndola dual carriage way today, Mr Nzovu said the progress made so far is a testament to partnerships between the government and the private sector.

The Minister noted that the country is coming from a situation where the economy was shrinking, with debt piling up and infrastructure projects halting, to a time where President Hakainde Hichilema has successfully necessitated PPP models to develop the country.

Mr Nzovu said the road is a model in Africa, stating that nothing of this scale has happened before under the public-private-partnership arrangement.

And the Minister expressed satisfaction on the quality of construction works noting that the concessionaire is working according to the agreed specifications.

Mr Nzovu explained that even when private partners are working, the government through the Road Development Agency (RDA) has engaged a consultant to ensure the construction works meet the Zambian standards.

“In places where we noticed that the quality of works were not of standard, we made the contractor redo those works. Remember also that the concessionaire has the obligation to repair these roads for a very long time, so it is also in their interest to ensure that the quality of work is okay,” he said.

Mr Nzovu said with the expansion of the Lusaka-Ndola road, motorists are elated as transportation business has become more attractive ,noting that the wheels of the economy are also moving at a faster rate.

Moic -LN Consortium Limited Assistant Project Manager, Jane Kang, a Concessionaire of Lusaka-Ndola Dual Carriageway disclosed that works are at over 80 percent and targets to complete the project by first quarter of 2027.

And Mr Nzovu highlighted that more dual carriageway projects are in the process including the Lusaka-Livingstone, Mongu and Chipata.

He added that aside from the construction of the main roads, township roads will also be done under the PPP model.

At Kapiri by-pass, the Minister warned of encroachment to the road reserve, stressing that no private structure should be built within 50 meters of the road reserve.

And RDA Director and Chief Executive Officer, Nelson Chuma, said the agency does not condone any encroachment of the road reserve as such acts deter road expansion in future.

Some places such as Liteta in Chibombo District will house economic activities such as a modern market and service areas through the PPP arrangement.

Meanwhile, Headman Liteta and traders in Chibombo have hailed the government through President Hichilema for transforming the district through road expansion as this will spur economic activities.

The 321 kilometer Lusaka-Ndola dual carriageway project is being constructed under the public -private- partnership model at a cost of about US$650 million.

Mr Nzovu, accompanied by officers from the Road Development Agency (RDA) and Journalists are on the tour of road infrastructure on the Copperbelt and North Western Provinces.

World.title: Government determined to position Zambia as a leading global copper producer-Tambatamba
World.content:
Minister of Mines and Minerals Development, Brenda Tambatamba, says the government is determined to position Zambia as a leading global copper producer while ensuring that increased mining activity translates into economic growth, employment opportunities and improved livelihoods for citizens.

Speaking during a breakfast meeting at Wils Hotel, in Lusaka, Ms Tambatamba said Government was committed to increasing annual copper production to three million metric tonnes by 2031, a target she said would require coordinated efforts among Government, mining companies and other stakeholders.

She said the mining sector remained critical to Zambia’s economic development through its contribution to gross domestic product, job creation and export earnings.

Ms Tambatamba pointed out that the Government would prioritise regulatory clarity and policy reforms to make the sector more attractive to investors while safeguarding national interests.

She also emphasised the need to strengthen local content policies and promote mineral processing and value addition within the country to create jobs and support industrialisation.

The Minister said the Government was equally committed to improving environmental management and ensuring mining companies observed strict environmental standards and social responsibilities throughout the life cycle of their operations.

She said corporate social responsibility should be integrated into mining operations from the commencement of projects to their eventual closure.

On small-scale mining, Ms Tambatamba acknowledged that operators continued to face challenges, particularly in accessing finance, training and markets.

She called for greater support for small-scale miners, saying the sector had the potential to contribute to livelihoods and economic opportunities for many Zambians.

Ms Tambatamba further identified geological mapping and mineral exploration as key priorities, stressing the need to discover new mineral deposits to sustain the country’s mining industry into the future.

She said transparency and accountability would remain central to the Ministry’s operations, adding that access to information and clear decision-making processes were necessary to build investor confidence.

Ms Tambatamba warned that corruption would not be tolerated in the mining sector, describing anti-corruption measures and good governance as non-negotiable.

Speaking earlier, Ministry of Mines and Mineral Development Permanent secretary, Hapenga Kabeta, said the Government was committed to developing a mining sector that was competitive, inclusive, innovative and sustainable, with opportunities for both large-scale and small-scale mining companies, mineral exploration firms, service providers and other industry players.

Dr Kabeta said the engagement provided an important platform for the Government and the mining industry to strengthen their relationship and develop a shared understanding of the sector’s priorities, opportunities and challenges.

He urged stakeholders to embrace constructive dialogue and work together towards addressing challenges and unlocking the full potential of Zambia’s mining industry.

Meanwhile, Mine Suppliers and Contractors Association, Coster Mwaba, welcomed the Ministry’s leadership and expressed optimism about improved engagement on issues affecting industry players.

World.title: Four people have died in a boat accident on Lake Kariba
World.content:
Four people are feared dead after a boat capsized on Lake Kariba in Gwembe district.

The accident occurred on Monday, November 16, 2026, between 19:00 and 20:00 hours near Chipepo Harbour Breeding Area in Chipepo Chiefdom, after strong winds triggered heavy waves on the lake.

Southern Province Police Commanding Officer, Moono Namalongo, told ZANIS that the boat carried five people and only one person survived.

Mr Namalongo also confirmed that one body has so far been retrieved, while a search operation for the three other missing persons is underway.

He has identified the deceased as 23-year-old Nyondo Zalimba Mulambia of Kafue district, who was operating the boat.

And Mr Namalongo has named the three missing persons as 44-year-old Bern Miyaba, 29-year-old Mwala Siamutale and 27-year-old Tension Manyepa.

He noted that the sole survivor, 25-year-old Nchimunya Siamutale, managed to swim ashore before alerting Harbour Aquaculture Limited Assistant Manager Chimuka Sinazugwe, who subsequently reported the incident to police.

He explains that the five had knocked off from work around 18:00 hours and decided to cross the lake aboard a banana boat fitted with an outboard engine.

Mr Namalongo says the boat encountered strong winds and heavy waves while crossing the lake, prompting the coxswain to change course towards the harbour in an attempt to reach safety.

“The coxswain attempted to steer the boat towards the harbour after encountering strong winds and heavy waves. Unfortunately, about 1.5 kilometers from the shore, the boat was struck by a massive wave, causing it to capsize and sink,” he explained.

The Police Commanding Officer has further disclosed that none of the five occupants was wearing safety gear at the time of the accident.

“All five occupants were thrown into the water when the boat capsized. Unfortunately, none of them was wearing safety gear, and only one person managed to swim to safety,” Mr Namalongo said.

He says following the incident, Mr Sinazugwe immediately mobilised a larger boat in an attempt to rescue the victims, but the initial search proved unsuccessful.

Mr Namalongo stated that a joint search operation involving officers from the Zambia Police Marine Unit, Zambia National Service Marine Unit and the Department of National Parks and Wildlife was subsequently launched.

He has confirmed that the search team recovered the body of the coxswain, Mr Mulambia, which has since been deposited at Chabbobboma Mission Hospital mortuary awaiting a postmortem examination.

“A joint search operation involving the Zambia Police Marine Unit, Zambia National Service Marine Unit and the Department of National Parks and Wildlife was launched. So far, one body has been retrieved, while efforts to locate the remaining three missing persons are continuing,” he said.

Mr Namalongo further stated that the search operation remains underway as authorities work to establish the whereabouts of the three missing persons

World.title: Tusekelele Women ‘s Club receives processing equipment
World.content:
Tusekelele Women’s Club in Hamatuba Zone, Kkota Kkota Ward, Gwembe District, has received two sets of processing equipment under the Women Economic Empowerment Programme following the successful approval and funding of its application.

The equipment comprises a ZA10 hammer mill complete with a two piston engine and a maize and rice dehuller.

The machinery is expected to improve access to maize and rice processing services in the area while creating an income generating opportunity for women in the community.

The equipment will enable the club to produce roller meal, maize bran and breakfast meal, among other products, thereby providing residents of Hamatuba with convenient access to milling services.

In a Facebook post on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Kkota Kkota Ward Councilor Edward Gama, described the development as a major milestone for women in the area, noting that an initiative which initially started as a joke had eventually become a reality.

Mr Gama said the project was aimed at promoting women’s economic independence, improving household incomes and creating sustainable livelihoods.

He said the initiative would operate as a community based business with the potential to create employment opportunities, reduce poverty and stimulate economic activity within Hamatuba.

Mr Gama further said the project would equip club members with skills in business management, bookkeeping, leadership and teamwork, which would contribute to the overall development of the ward.

He urged the women to remain united, uphold transparency in managing the project and ensure that all members benefited fairly from the proceeds generated.

Mr Gama also thanked Gwembe Constituency Member of Parliament Tyson Simuzingili, for lobbying for the initiative.

He urged the club to ensure proper management and maintenance of the equipment, expressing confidence that responsible operation and accountability would guarantee the project’s sustainability and deliver lasting economic benefits to women and the wider Hamatuba community.
