World.title: Police Reject Term Limit Marches
World.content:
Police have declined to clear two planned processions in Lusaka, one supporting the removal of presidential term limits and another opposing the proposed constitutional changes.

The two groups had planned to hold their processions and public assemblies on November 25, 2026.

Zambia Youth Organisation Consortium Vice Chairperson Boas Kanyama said 63,151 youths from all 10 provinces had confirmed their participation in a march supporting the removal of presidential term limits.

The youths had planned to march from Northmead Bus Station to Parliament Buildings.

Mr Kanyama said the consortium had formally notified the police of its intention to hold the procession and expected approximately 500 police officers to provide security.

However, in a statement, Zambia Police Service Public Relations Officer Chipo Kaitisha said the decision followed a review of notifications submitted by the two consortiums, intelligence gathered regarding the planned activities and the prevailing national security situation.

Ms Kaitisha said police had consequently advised both consortiums not to proceed with their planned processions and public assemblies.

She said the police had acknowledged receiving notifications of the intended peaceful demonstrations scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

Meanwhile, the proposed removal of presidential term limits has generated mixed reactions, with some stakeholders supporting the changes while others have raised concerns about their implications for Zambia’s constitutional democracy.

Opposition leader Given Lubinda has called for the matter to be subjected to a referendum, arguing that Zambians should have the final say on the proposed constitutional changes.

Government has maintained that it will not prevent citizens from exercising their constitutional rights, including expressing their views on the debate.

Government has also stated that President Hakainde Hichilema is not part of the discussions surrounding the proposed removal of presidential term limits.

World.title: Amnesty International Tells President Hichilema to Free Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 Other Treason Detainees
World.content:
Amnesty International called on President Hakainde Hichilema to release 18 opposition members held on treason charges straight away, among them NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu. The organisation said the group is being targeted by the Government for taking part in public affairs and holding opposing political views.

The demand came in an Urgent Action appeal dated 17 November 2026, written as a letter to the President at State House. Beyond seeking the release of the 18 and an end to their prosecution, the appeal asks the Head of State to ensure that criminal justice and national security laws are not misused to intimidate, punish or silence political opponents.

Those held are Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu, Bishop Trevor Mwamba, George Kangwa Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Francis Mulenga, Brazil Soko, Bernard Chanda Chewe, Davies Chisopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Jackson Mutyoka, Richard Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga, Darius Mwila, Simon Phiri, Harry Valden Findlay and Ezra Tolopa.

The rights body identified them as members of the Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance. It described their detention as arbitrary and placed responsibility squarely on the State.

“The Zambian authorities must immediately release all eighteen individuals as they are being targeted by the government and detained simply for exercising their rights through participating in public affairs and expressing opposing political views,” the organisation said.

The appeal says the detainees were held without charge at different stages, denied timely access to courts, lawyers and relatives, and allegedly subjected to torture and other ill-treatment. It then sets out how the arrests unfolded, beginning before the national vote.

On 1 August, Mr Tolopa, Mr Tembo and Mr Muzyamba were arrested at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport and taken to undisclosed locations. There, the organisation said, the three men were allegedly waterboarded, beaten while handcuffed and suspended from a metal bar.

Mr Findlay was arrested at his home three days later and detained at Ibex Hill Police Station. On 9 August, all four men were charged with a “terrorism related offence” and transferred to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility, where they were held incommunicado and denied access to their families and legal counsel.

Mr Findlay was also denied medication for a chronic health condition. A court order concerning him was granted on 12 August, yet the State failed to bring him to court on 18 August. He was eventually brought before the court two days later.

The largest round of arrests came the day after the polls. On 14 August, security forces raided a property linked to Mr Mundubile, then the leading opposition presidential candidate, and arrested him alongside ten others.

Those picked up with him were Mr Chisanga, Mr Mwansa, Bishop Mwamba, Francis Mulenga, Mr Soko, Mr Mutyoka, Mr Chewe, Mr Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga and Mr Mwila. Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was at the property, was fatally shot the same day.

The detainees from the raid were allegedly taken to military and police facilities and kept from their families and lawyers. They spent 16 days in custody without any charge being brought.

On 29 August, all 18 were charged with treason. A day later, they were transferred to Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility.

The organisation measured those events against the standards Zambia has signed up to. Under international human rights law, it said, anyone arrested must be told the reasons at the time of arrest, given immediate access to lawyers and family, brought promptly before an independent and impartial court, and informed of any charges.

The rights body acknowledged that the authorities may investigate and, where there is enough evidence, prosecute genuine criminal offences, including those touching on national security. That power, it said, must be exercised in line with Zambia’s international obligations, and it drew a firm line on how far it can stretch.

“National security cannot be used as a justification for arbitrary detention or for restricting the legitimate exercise of human rights, including the rights to freedom of expression and association,” Amnesty International said.

The organisation placed the 18 cases within a wider pattern since the general election. It described an escalating crackdown on opposition figures, supporters and government critics, marked by allegations of arbitrary arrests, torture and prolonged detention without charge.

The letter closes with a direct appeal to President Hichilema to act on the detainees by name.

“I urge you to immediately release Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Harry Valden Findlay, Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and the other 12 opposition members, and end their prosecution,” it reads.

The appeal, reference AFR 63/1686/2026, invites supporters to write to State House in English or their own language until 17 May 2027. The 18 remain in detention on treason charges.

FULL VERSION

First UA: 121/26 Index: AFR 63/1686/2026 Zambia

Date: 17 November 2026

URGENT ACTION

18 POLITICAL OPPOSITION MEMBERS JAILED

Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Harry Valden Findlay, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, together with 12 other opposition figures, have been detained following a series of arrests during and after Zambia’s elections in August 2026. The individuals were, at different stages, held without charge, denied timely access to court, lawyers and family members and allegedly subjected to torture and other ill-treatment. The Zambian authorities must immediately release all eighteen individuals as they are being targeted by the government and detained simply for exercising their rights through participating in public affairs and expressing opposing political views.

His Excellency, Mr Hakainde Hichilema

President of the Republic of Zambia

State House, Independence Avenue,

Lusaka, Zambia, 10101

Email: [email protected]

Dear His Excellency Mr Hakainde Hichilema,

I am writing to express my concern about the arbitrary detention of 18 opposition party members – including Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Harry Valden Findlay, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, all belonging to the Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance parties.

On 1 August, Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo and Victor Muzyamba were arrested at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport and detained at undisclosed locations, where they were allegedly subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including waterboarding and beatings while handcuffed and being suspended from a metal bar. On 4 August, Harry Valden Findlay was arrested at his home and detained at Ibex Hill Police Station. On 9 August, all four were charged with ‘terrorism related offence’ and transferred to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility, where they are being held incommunicado, denied access to family and legal counsel. Harry Valden Findlay was also denied medication for a chronic health condition.

Under international human rights law, anyone who is arrested must be informed at the time of arrest, of the reasons for his arrest, have immediate access to lawyers and their families, promptly brought before an independent and impartial court, and informed of any recognizable criminal charges against them. The Zambian authorities’ powers to investigate and, where there is sufficient evidence, prosecute genuine criminal offences, including offences relating to national security, must be exercised consistently with Zambia’s obligations under international human rights law. National security cannot be used as a justification for arbitrary detention or for restricting the legitimate exercise of human rights, including the rights to freedom of expression and association.

I urge you to immediately release Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Harry Valden Findlay, Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and the other 12 opposition members, and end their prosecution. I further urge you to ensure that criminal justice and national security laws are not misused to intimidate, punish or silence political opponents and other people simply exercising their human rights.

Yours sincerely,

World.title: ECZ holds general election review meetings in Mwinilunga
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Mwinilunga district of North-western Province has commenced a series of meetings with its district structures to review activities of the 2026 August 13th General Elections.

The meetings commenced with the District Voter Education Committee (DVEC) sitting including Voter Education Facilitators (VEFs), Voter Education Trainers (DVETs), school voter education club’s matrons and patrons and the DVEC coordinator.

Speaking when he opened the review meeting today, District Electoral Officer Joseph Kanyemba, said the meetings are necessary for the Commission to understand and appreciate challenges and successes experienced before, during and after the elections.

Mr Kanyemba said the conflict management committee and the delimitation committee include structures which will sit to review activities of the just ended election while other internal administrative reviews will equally be done to come up with a comprehensive review and report how the general elections were managed in the district.

He explained that preparation for an election is a continuous process hence periodic reviews of every activity done is critical in informing decisions on how best the Commission can implement subsequent programmes.

“Preparation for an election such as the 2031 general elections actually is in progress, it starts now, the moment one election is concluded preparations for the next one begins, so this review meeting is just one of those preparatory activities for future elections” he said.

Mr Kanyemba urged participants to make objective submissions based on their experiences during the last elections noting that their submissions as active players in the electoral process are key in helping the Commission to prepare adequately for successive elections.

And speaking in his closing remarks, District Voter Education Committee Chairperson, Jackson Kuleya, said the activities around Voter Education in the 2026 General Elections in the district were generally successful adding that the district did not experience serious challenges that can compromise the integrity of the election.

Mr Kuleya said as DVEC members they considered the opportunity to work for the Commission as a privilege to serve the community and the nation observing that the team embraced discipline, objectivity and patience which contributed to the success of the electoral activities done.

“We actually consider this as a privilege, because we also not just served our communities but we learnt a lot such as coordination, objectivity and appreciated how transparent and well-coordinated the Electoral Commission is when it comes to conducting elections” he said.

Among issues reviewed during the meeting included, recruitment process of DVETs, VEFs and reconstitution of the DVEC committee, field deployment of VEFs, voter education in the wards, correction facilities, remuneration of field staff, transport logistics and Publicity campaigns.

World.title: Alliance Against Corruption oppose merging of ACC and DEC
World.content:
The Alliance Against Corruption (AAC) has opposed recent public calls to merge the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC), stating that the two bodies have distinct roles and responsibilities essential to the country’s fight against crime.

Speaking to the media Kabwe, AAC Executive Director, Noel Chisebe, emphasized that merging the two agencies would be based on a “misunderstanding” of their mandates.

“The two institutions do not do the same job and cannot be merged,” Dr Chisebe observed.

The ACC, established in 1980 and now operating under the Anti-Corruption Act No. 3 of 2012, is tasked with preventing, investigating, and prosecuting corruption in both public and private sectors.

To the contrary, DEC, governed by the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act No. 35 of 2021 and the Money Laundering Act, is responsible for combating drug-related crimes and money laundering.

While acknowledging that both agencies sometimes cross paths in money laundering investigations, Dr Chisebe argued that such overlap requires coordination rather than a merger.

“Money laundering is the bridge where corruption and drug crime meet, and the correct response to that bridge is coordination, not merger,” he said.

Dr Chisebe warned that merging the Commissions would dilute expertise, creating officers who are “half-trained in both and experts in neither, and ultimately weakening the fight against both corruption and drug crime.

He added that most corruption cases in Zambia have no link to drugs and could be neglected if the ACC and DEC were merged.

Dr Chisebe highlighted concerns about accountability and independence, noting that two separate institutions, each with its own leadership, budget, and parliamentary reporting structure, provide stronger checks and balances.

“One mega-agency is easier to capture, to politicize, and to silence,” Dr Chisebe warned.

He urged the government, parliament, and stakeholders to safeguard the independence, mandate, and funding of both institutions.

Dr Chisebe also called for enhanced coordination through joint investigations and intelligence sharing, rather than structural consolidation.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 18, 2026
World.content:
press review

South Africa Reprimands Nigerian Envoy Femi Fani-Kayode Over Broadcast Dispute

South Africa has formally reprimanded Nigeria's new High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, following a public dispute with the Presidency over the broadcasting of his credentials ceremony. The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) summoned him, with Director-General Zane Dangor reminding him to raise diplomatic concerns through the relevant foreign ministries rather than directly with the president. Fani-Kayode had accused the Presidency of deliberately excluding his introduction and speech from an SABC livestream, a claim disputed by President Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya. The Presidency maintained that Ramaphosa had simply directed the commissioner to raise his concerns with the appropriate SABC official. DIRCO said diplomats are required under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations to conduct official business through foreign ministries. The incident comes amid already strained relations between the two countries over allegations of xenophobic attacks and deaths of Nigerian nationals in South Africa.

Ugandan Politician Besigye's Wife Renews Calls for His Release Over Health Fears

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The wife of detained Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye, Winnie Byanyima, has renewed calls for his release, citing serious concerns about his deteriorating health and need for specialised medical treatment. Besigye was arrested in Kenya's capital, Nairobi. He was abducted and taken to Uganda, where he was first charged with treason before his case was transferred to the civilian justice system. Byanyima said that he is experiencing difficulties walking, speaking, and using his hands. His family remains concerned about inadequate medical care under military surveillance. She said that soldiers remain stationed inside and around the hospital room where he is being held, raising further concerns about his welfare. His defence team has also questioned his fitness to stand trial. They argued that his communication difficulties prevent him from properly participating in his defence. Four bail applications have reportedly been rejected, while another is awaiting a hearing date. His next court hearing is scheduled for 25 November.

UN Says Over 2,230 Civilians Killed in Sudan Conflict Since January

At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 in drone strikes, according to the UN Human Rights Office. Its latest report highlights the growing use of drones by warring parties, with attacks targeting markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities and other essential infrastructure. The Kordofan region recorded more than two-thirds of verified civilian deaths. Attacks on electricity and fuel infrastructure have disrupted healthcare, water supplies and food production. During the first half of the year, the UN documented at least 39 drone strikes on markets, 20 attacks on civilian vehicles and 16 strikes on healthcare facilities. It warned that the actual death toll is likely considerably higher because its figures include only verified cases. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said the violations could amount to war crimes and called for accountability and greater protection of civilians.

Guinea Jails 224 Over Illegal Gold Mining

A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people, including 22 former regional administrators and 202 alleged illegal gold miners, over unauthorised mining activities in the northeastern Siguiri region. The former officials received two-year prison sentences. The miners were sentenced to three years for offences including environmental destruction, water pollution and illegal mining. Foreign nationals among those convicted were also banned from Guinea for 10 years. The sentences form part of a wider government crackdown aimed at protecting farmland, rivers and the environment from damage caused by illegal mining. The operation has triggered violent clashes between protesters and security forces, leaving 10 people dead and 13 injured. More than 1,200 artisanal miners have been arrested in November. Thousands have fled across the border into Mali, with many awaiting transportation back to their home countries, including Burkina Faso.

Ethiopia-Eritrea Fighting Reignites, Raising Fears of Wider War

Fighting has resumed along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, raising fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa as relations between the neighbours continue to deteriorate. Ethiopian government forces have pushed Tigrayan fighters to the Eritrean border, with reports of skirmishes and artillery fire near the contested town of Badme. Tensions have also been heightened by Ethiopia's repeated demands for access to the Red Sea, including references to Eritrea's Assab port. The town of Badme remains a sensitive territorial issue between the two countries, even with a peace agreement that awarded the town to Eritrea after their war from 1998-2000. Relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have deteriorated at the same time amid accusations of interference in each other's conflicts, including claims by Sudan that Ethiopia is backing Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, which Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates deny. Analysts warn that proxy involvement could intensify, although direct military confrontation between Ethiopia and Sudan is considered less likely for now.

Close 

Mozambican Opposition Leader Venâncio Mondlane Goes on Trial Over Post-Election Unrest

Mozambican opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial at the Supreme Court over charges including terrorism-related offences, incitement and civil disobedience linked to deadly protests following the disputed 2024 elections. Mondlane, who denies wrongdoing, maintains that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency after he challenged the victory of ruling Frelimo party candidate Daniel Chapo. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging unrest that resulted in deaths, property damage and disruption of public services. He faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge. The trial has prompted tight security in Maputo, with police urging citizens to remain calm and avoid actions that could threaten public order. Access to the proceedings has been restricted to selected media organisations, while live broadcasts have been banned over concerns about possible unrest. The case is widely viewed as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after the disputed elections triggered one of the country's deadliest post-election crises.

World.title: South Africa: ANC Postpones Media Briefing on Coalition Talks - South African News Briefs - November 18, 2026
World.content:
press review

ANC Postpones Media Briefing on Coalition Talks

The African National Congress (ANC) has postponed its scheduled media briefing on coalition negotiations, citing ongoing and extensive discussions, reports EWN. Party Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula is set to brief the media on progress at a revised date. The postponement comes after the ANC suffered major losses in the recent municipal elections. It lost its position as the largest party in Gauteng's three metros to the Democratic Alliance (DA).

Two Killed in Suspected Gang Shooting on Cape Flats



Two people have been killed and three others wounded in a suspected gang-related shooting in Seawinds, Lavender Hill, on Cape Town's Cape Flats, reports SABC News. The victims, two men in their thirties, were declared dead at the scene. A 53-year-old woman was among those injured. Police said that occupants of a vehicle drove up to the group and opened fire before fleeing. Police visibility has been increased in the area. Operation Prosper deployments are conducting crime prevention operations to restore calm.

Sport Minister Urges Athletes to Secure Own Sponsorships

Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie has urged athletes to secure individual sponsorships, reports EWN. He said that the government cannot afford to fully fund all sporting federations and their athletes. His comments follow Olympic swimmer Tatjana Smith's decision to withdraw from representing South Africa amid a sponsorship dispute with Swimming South Africa (SSA) over competing in national team sponsor Arena's apparel despite her personal Speedo sponsorship. McKenzie said federations should support athletes in securing individual deals rather than penalising them. He has demanded clarity on the sponsorship agreement while apologising to Arena for being caught up in the controversy.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Clashes Raise Fears of Regional War
World.content:
As Ethiopian troops push Tigrayan forces toward the Eritrean border, fears of a new regional war are growing. With tensions rising between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, the Horn of Africa faces uncertain times ahead.

After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.

Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.

While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.

The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement, in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.

"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.

He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.

The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea

"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.

Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.

Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.

"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.

However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."

Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.

Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads

At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.

Sudan and Egypt, both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD). The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt.

Close 

Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) , led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti . In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts.

Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now.

"The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said.

Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation.

"The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved."

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

World.title: Mozambique: Media Outlets Should Have Adopted Legal Measures to Defend Their Rights - Mondlane
World.content:
Maputo — Venâncio Mondlane, former presidential candidate and leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), believes that media outlets should have adopted legal measures to defend their rights after the country's Supreme Court has limited the number of media companies authorized to cover his trial, which started this Tuesday.

"It was the national press's obligation to take concerted action to assert its own rights. The responsibility for the lack of a legal challenge should not be attributed to the court, but to the journalists themselves", Mondlane said, minutes after arriving at Supreme Court premises in Maputo.

Upon his arrival, Mondlane had a vehicle surrounded by journalists from both domestic and international media outlets, all eager to capture his statements, marking the first day of his trial.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Mondlane added that media outlets should not limit themselves to producing reports and opinion pieces, but should instead "adopt measures with legal standing to defend their rights."

The Supreme Court spokesperson, Pedro Nhatitima, had announced the availability of only 45 special seats for media companies, adding that "other national media outlets will have to compete for four rotating spots by registering via an electronic platform." However, Nhatitima did not reveal the criteria for the appointment of companies in question, most of which are state-owned.

Mozambique's Network of Human Rights Defenders (RMDDH) also condemned restrictions on press coverage of Mondlane's trial and advocated "for equal access for media outlets."

"The Supreme Court should review its criteria regarding the allocation of seats, ensuring equal access for the coverage of the trial. It should also provide transparent criteria for the accreditation and selection of journalists, and consider moving the trial to a larger venue to accommodate media coverage. Furthermore, the Court should adopt additional measures to guarantee public access to information about the progress of the trial. Security measures must respect the principles of legality and proportionality", reads the RMDDH statement.

Mondlane is accused of five criminal charges related to post-election mass demonstrations. The mass demonstration he called to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections held in October 2024 started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

He is accused of having committed the following crimes: public apology for a crime; incitement to collective disobedience; public instigation to crime; instigation and incitement to terrorism.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Five Zimbabweans Return to South African Court Over Alleged Plans to Join Russia-Ukraine War
World.content:
Five Zimbabwean nationals are expected to appear before a South African court on Tuesday for formal bail proceedings after being arrested over allegations that they were attempting to travel to Russia to participate in the ongoing war against Ukraine.

The five men are expected back at the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court in Gauteng, where they will make their applications for release on bail.

The accused, identified as Weight Mudhanyane, Javangwe Munyaradzi, Wesley Sothole, Abel Muchenje and Knowledge Ndunduma, face charges of contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act of 1998.

They were arrested at OR Tambo International Airport on November 8 following an intelligence-driven operation involving South African law enforcement agencies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The five are part of a group of nine Zimbabweans arrested in two separate operations in Johannesburg.

While the five were intercepted at OR Tambo International Airport, the remaining four were arrested at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg, as they allegedly prepared to travel to participate in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) previously indicated that the group intended to use South Africa as a transit country before travelling to the conflict zone.

The five accused were initially expected to proceed with their bail applications on November 10, but the proceedings were postponed to November 17 after the state prosecutor failed to appear in court.

The four other suspects are being dealt with separately at the Johannesburg Magistrates' Court.

The arrests come amid growing concern over the recruitment of African nationals into the Russia-Ukraine war, with reports of individuals being lured by promises of lucrative employment and security training before allegedly finding themselves on the frontline.

In March this year, Zimbabwean authorities disclosed that at least 15 citizens had been killed in the conflict, while efforts were underway to secure the return of dozens of others reportedly trapped in the war.

South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act regulates military assistance provided to foreign states and prohibits certain mercenary activities and recruitment arrangements without the required authorisation.

The accused remain presumed innocent until proven guilty.

World.title: South Africa: SA Govt Démarches New Nigerian High Commissioner Over Social Media Comments
World.content:
Nigeriaâs new High Commissioner Femi Fani Kayode presents his credentials to President Ramaphosa at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria on 13 November.

Nigerian High Commissioner Fani-Kayode has been rebuked over a spat with the Presidency.

The South African government démarched the new Nigerian high commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, after a public spat between him and the Presidency.

The director-general of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (Dirco), Zane Dangor, called Fani-Kayode into his office on Tuesday, 17 November, to reprimand him about his behaviour on Friday, 13 November, after he presented his credentials to President Cyril Ramaphosa, "as well as subsequent remarks made on social media".

Dirco later officially confirmed that the summoning of Fani-Kayode had been a démarche, which usually expresses a diplomatic rebuke.

Fani-Kayode was one of 15 new ambassadors and high commissioners who presented their "letters of credence" to Ramaphosa at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria. This is a formal ceremonial duty all ambassadors perform when they take up a new post.

But Fani-Kayode claimed he had been discriminated against, alleging in a post on X that the SA Presidency had refused to include his introduction to Ramaphosa or his speech in the SABC livestream of the event.

"Of all the 15 introductions and speeches that were made and delivered this morning, only Nigeria's was cut out. I raised the issue with President Ramaphosa directly...

World.title: Uganda: Two Years After Arrest of Uganda Opponent Besigye, Family Raises Health Concerns
World.content:
On 16 November, 2024, Ugandan opposition figure Kizza Besigye was arrested in Nairobi, Kenya. Two years on, his wife Winnie Byanyima is calling for his release so that he can receive specialised medical care.

"Two years have been taken from him and his family. And during those two years, he has suffered," Byanyima told RFI, adding that she has serious concerns for her husband's health.

Besigye was in Nairobi for a book launch when he was abducted in the Kenyan capital, sent back to Uganda and brought before a military court. His trial on treason charges is now proceeding within the civilian justice system.

His family has been worried about his health since he became ill during a court hearing in July 2026.



Byanyima described her husband's persistent difficulties with walking, speaking and using his hands. According to her, medical examinations necessary to fully understand his condition and determine the appropriate care are yet to be carried out.

"The most important thing for me and for his family is that he be released, so that he can receive the best possible care and recover," she said.

Ugandan opposition leader Besigye unconscious in ICU after collapsing in court

Fitness to stand trial

Byanyima also told RFI that her husband remains under close military surveillance.

She said that while his personal physician is permitted to visit him and collect medical samples, the doctor has no control over the facility where he is being held.

"A soldier sleeps in his hospital room. Others sleep near the door, some in front of the building and still others at the gate," she said. "His jailers' priority is keeping him there - certainly not his health."

Byanyima is also calling for medical access for Erias Lukwago, Besigye's lawyer, who is himself in detention and in ill health.

Besigye's ability to participate in his trial is a central point of contention for his defence team.

A psychiatric report dated 17 August and shared with RFI by lawyer Eron Kiiza indicates that while his cognitive understanding appears intact, he is unable to speak or write.

Medical professionals suggest these communication difficulties could significantly hinder his ability to participate in his own defence and have recommended a specialised evaluation.

Ugandan opposition MP abducted and tortured ahead of elections

According to Kiiza, four applications for bail have been rejected and a new request is still awaiting a hearing date.

Close 

Speaking to RFI, Kiiza denounced the proceedings as "political persecution disguised as a trial" and called for Besigye's release so that he may seek medical treatment.

The next hearing is scheduled for 25 November.

"Give him to us. Let us place him where he can receive all the care he needs," Byanyima urged.

This article has been adapted from the original version in French by Christina Okello.

World.title: Sudan: 2,230 Civilian Deaths in Sudan in 10 Months, Most From Drone Strikes - UN
World.content:
A woman searches through the burnt remains of her shelter at a displacement camp in Darfur, Sudan.

Amsterdam / Geneva — At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 in drone strikes, according to the UN Human Rights Office. Its latest findings point to the growing role of drones in the war, with attacks increasingly reaching beyond the front lines to strike markets, hospitals, schools, and infrastructure essential to civilian survival.

The UN Human Rights Office has confirmed that at least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes.

A report released today says more than 1,390 civilians were killed during the first six months of 2026 in the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and allied armed movements. More than 80 per cent of these deaths resulted from drone strikes, which have become a defining feature of the war.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In the following four months, a further 840 civilians were killed, including approximately 520 in drone attacks.

The UN says these figures cover only cases it has been able to verify, and that the actual civilian death toll is likely to be considerably higher.

The report concludes that the continued disregard for the obligation to protect civilians is inflicting an "unbearable toll" on the Sudanese people.

Civilians and civilian infrastructure under attack

The report, which covers the first half of 2026, documents patterns that have persisted throughout the conflict. These include attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, indiscriminate strikes, reprisals against people accused of "collaborating" with opposing forces, and the continued use of sexual violence as a weapon of war.

It also raises concerns about unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, and the shrinking of civic space.

"Battle lines shifted and military tactics - particularly the use of drones - evolved, but the unbearable toll of the war on the Sudanese people has remained as consistent as ever, amid blatant disregard for the protection of civilians," the report says.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said: "The facts speak for themselves. The findings in our report provide more evidence, if any were needed, of the ceaselessly unbearable civilian suffering of the war in Sudan and the warring parties' continued and brazen disregard for the laws of war."

He added: "Amid pervasive impunity, the report documents, once again, serious violations of international humanitarian law. Such violations may amount to war crimes."

Civilians in Kordofan were the worst affected, accounting for more than two-thirds of the verified deaths. Darfur recorded most of the remaining casualties.

Eastern and central Sudan were also affected by drone attacks, particularly White Nile state, where at least 41 civilians were killed during the reporting period.

Markets, hospitals, schools, fuel supply facilities, water sources, displacement sites, and civilian vehicles were among the targets. Some locations were struck repeatedly.

39 drone strikes on markets

During the first half of 2026, the UN Human Rights Office documented at least 39 drone strikes on markets, 20 attacks on civilian vehicles, 17 on fuel tankers and depots, and 16 on healthcare facilities.

These attacks raise serious questions about compliance with the laws of war, which protect civilians and civilian objects, including facilities indispensable to the survival of the civilian population. They also raise concerns about the protection of healthcare workers and medical facilities, particularly in areas already desperately short of humanitarian and medical assistance.

The report says drone attacks on markets, combined with looting and restrictions on movement, have severely disrupted access to food.

In October, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) warned that conflict, displacement, and drought were increasing the risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Kordofan, as acute food insecurity and malnutrition continued to rise.

October also saw a high number of civilian casualties, alongside an escalation in drone attacks on civilian infrastructure, with devastating consequences for the population.

Close 

Attacks on power and fuel infrastructure

Among the most concerning developments is the recent escalation in drone attacks targeting power generation facilities and fuel supplies.

In just over two weeks, between 20 October and 4 November, 29 drone strikes attributed to the RSF targeted electricity infrastructure and fuel depots in 11 states. The attacks caused widespread power cuts and worsened fuel shortages, affecting millions of people far from the front lines.

The consequences for civilians and essential services have been severe. Power cuts have disrupted healthcare, including kidney dialysis and surgical procedures, while also restricting access to clean water and food production.

The report stresses that accountability, regardless of the perpetrators' affiliation, is essential to breaking cycles of violence and preventing further violations and abuses.

Türk called on all parties to the conflict to protect civilians and fulfil their obligations under international law.

"The world is watching," he said.

World.title: RFK Jr. faces fierce backlash after US loses measles-free status for first time in 26 years
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing mounting criticism from Democrats after the United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years.

The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination designation amid a resurgence of the highly contagious virus, with more than 5,400 confirmed cases reported this year — the highest annual total in more than three decades.

The virus has spread largely among unvaccinated populations, prompting criticism from Democrats who have previously scrutinized Kennedy's stance on vaccines.

On Tuesday, Kennedy vowed to stop measles outbreaks and restore the country's measles elimination status, while continuing to recommend vaccination against the disease.

CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES

"We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status," Kennedy said in a statement.

He added, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."

Several Democrats sharply criticized Kennedy following the announcement.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state has reported its first measles-associated death in more than three decades, involving a child, accused Kennedy of contributing to declining vaccination rates through years of vaccine skepticism.

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

"RFK Jr. promised to 'Make America Healthy Again.' Now America has lost its measles-free status for the first time in 26 years," Hochul said.

"A disgraceful display of incompetence from the nation's highest public health office," she added.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also blamed Kennedy, arguing that the loss of elimination status reflected the consequences of vaccine misinformation and skepticism.

"There is a clear line from the misinformation, vaccine skepticism, and incompetence of RFK Jr. to this devastating news and very real consequences," Shapiro said.

"Measles is preventable. We eliminated it in this country once, and we can do it again."

MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

Another Democratic governor called for Kennedy's removal from office.

"This dangerous setback was 100% avoidable and is the result of one person: RFK Jr.," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said. "Remove him now."

The U.S., which had maintained the measles designation since 2000, is experiencing its worst measles outbreak since 1991 and has reported more than twice as many cases as in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Measles elimination means there has been no continuous local transmission of the virus for at least 12 months. The U.S. reached the status in 2000 after years of coordinated immunization campaigns.

NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz defended the agency's response to the ongoing outbreak, emphasizing that vaccination remains the most important tool for protecting Americans.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said.

She added that the CDC had invested approximately $100 million in state and local health departments to strengthen outbreak prevention and response.

The agency also noted that MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.7% in 2023–2024.

In his statement, Kennedy cited COVID-19-era disruptions as a factor in declining routine childhood vaccination coverage, noting that several other countries, including Canada, Mexico and the United Kingdom, had also lost their measles elimination status.

World.title: Alaska Dem Peltola defeats Sullivan, flipping 9th GOP Senate seat after 'decoy Dan' uproar
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democrats flipped a ninth GOP-held Senate seat in the 2026 midterm elections, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.

Peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate.

The contest emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Republicans defending a seat in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, and Democrats eyeing a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory.

The controversy deepened just days before Election Day when The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had participated in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name.

According to the Times, text messages and interviews revealed a broader operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," aimed at recruiting candidates who could siphon votes from Sullivan. The effort reportedly involved the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and included discussions about establishing a new right-wing political party.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign, while the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) also rejected allegations of participation. The revelations prompted Republican Gov. Michael Dunleavy to order an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law.

The Cook Political Report rated the contest a toss-up, reflecting the unusually competitive environment in a state that has generally favored Republicans in federal elections.

Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election to succeed the late Republican Rep. Don Young.

GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING

She defeated former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin in that contest before winning a full term later that year. Peltola subsequently lost her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III, setting the stage for her Senate campaign.

Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, first won his Senate seat in 2014 by defeating Democratic incumbent Mark Begich, Nick's uncle. He secured reelection in 2020 and sought a third term emphasizing his experience, national security and Alaska's energy interests.

The 2026 race also featured an unusual ballot controversy involving Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who shared nearly the same name as the Republican incumbent.

Alaska election officials initially moved to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot amid allegations that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon support from the senator. The candidate denied wrongdoing, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot. The DOJ sued in October to mitigate any "misleading" impact of the newcomer Sullivan.

COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’

The controversy added another complication to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.

Under the system, a candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes wins outright. Otherwise, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated, and ballots are redistributed according to voters' next available preferences until a winner emerges.

Peltola had previously benefited from the system during her 2022 congressional victories, when ranked-choice tabulation helped determine the outcomes of races featuring multiple Republican opponents.

World.title: Mamdani's luxury second home tax hits $500M milestone despite thousands of exemptions
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York City has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million under Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial pied-à-terre tax, even as the number of homeowners receiving bills fell far below initial estimates.

"We've billed more than $500 million to owners of second homes worth more than $5 million," Mamdani wrote Tuesday on X.

"That's half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers," he continued.

According to information provided by city officials, the New York City Department of Finance mailed approximately 7,500 tax bills — a sizable drop from the roughly 17,000 initial notices sent to property owners over the summer.

APPEALS COURT HANDS MAMDANI LEGAL WIN ON NYC LUXURY SECOND-HOME TAX

Officials also said roughly 8,900 exemption applications were granted, while approximately 1,600 extension applications were denied.

The surcharge is a key part of the mayor's agenda to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and help close the city's budget gap.

Despite the smaller number of bills, the city said the total amount billed exceeded the $500 million target previously outlined by Gov. Kathy Hochul earlier this year.

However, officials did not immediately provide a breakdown showing how the total was calculated across the approximately 7,500 properties.

"As Mayor Mamdani has said before, owning a second home worth over 5 million dollars should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable," Julia Agos, a spokesperson for the Department of Finance, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.



"The Department of Finance will continue to implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone," Agos added.

The tax is assessed on a sliding scale based on property values, meaning owners of more expensive homes can face higher charges.

JIM GAFFIGAN, NEW YORK LAWMAKERS PUSH GOV HOCHUL TO AXE 'UNNECESSARY TAX' HITTING COMEDY CLUBS

In an April report, the New York City comptroller's office estimated that a version of the tax could generate approximately $500 million from more than 11,200 properties before accounting for exemptions and changes in homeowner behavior.

After accounting for those factors, however, the report projected that revenue could fall to between roughly $340 million and $380 million.

Still, Mamdani has continued to express confidence in the surcharge's revenue potential, telling reporters last week, "We continue to be confident in its ability to raise half a billion dollars per year."

The surcharge, approved by the New York state Legislature in May, applies to qualifying luxury second homes in New York City, including certain one- to three-family properties valued at $5 million or more and condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more.

MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'

Property owners who qualify for exemptions are not subject to the surcharge.

Tuesday's announcement comes after a state appeals court handed Mamdani a legal victory earlier this month, unanimously dismissing a lawsuit challenging the rollout of the surcharge.

The court found that the homeowners who brought the lawsuit lacked legal standing, overturning a lower court ruling that had ordered the city to restart implementation.

However, the tax continues to face separate legal challenges, including questions about its constitutionality.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for comment.

World.title: Ken Griffin, target of Zohran Mamdani, has officially sold his $58 million apartment to NY Jets owner

You gotta hand it to Zohran Mamdani. He may not be smart, competent or honest, but he is extremely capable of pushing people out of New York City.

"And then the second time you’re like, you know what this is? Actually, this has gone from creepy to actually not really creepy, this has gone frightening."

NBA STAR RIPS SOCIALIST NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI AS 'MAYOR PLAYING PRESIDENT' AFTER NETANYAHU VIDEO

It's unclear whether Griffin found Mamdani's videos or his fake smile more creepy.

World.title: White House drops Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination after Republicans raise concerns
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The White House is dropping Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed Tuesday.

The decision comes a day before the Senate Health Committee was scheduled to vote on whether to advance her nomination to the full Senate for confirmation.

Axios first reported the White House’s decision.

The move follows weeks of doubts from key Republicans on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. To advance to the full Senate, Overton would have needed 11 votes in the 21-member committee, meaning she couldn’t afford to lose a single Republican if all Democrats opposed her.

Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the committee’s chairman, had questioned whether Overton — a preventive medicine doctor who serves as a domestic policy official in the White House — had enough experience to lead the agency.

Prior to joining the White House, Overton worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute.

Before Overton’s confirmation hearing in September, Cassidy wrote on X that he had “strong concerns” about her nomination, saying her lack of managerial experience left her poorly prepared to lead the agency. In a post last week, Cassidy said he remained undecided.

On Tuesday night, Cassidy criticized the White House for pulling Overton’s nomination.

“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. “My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.”

“The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues. The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” said Cassidy, who is leaving Congress in early January. “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, told NBC News last week that she was undecided and had “not taken a position,” saying she needed “to get some answers on various things.”

Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska declined last week to say how she’d vote. During the confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked Overton about political pressure surrounding access to mifepristone, and criticized Overton for not taking a clear position on the subject.

Overton has praised the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion.

The FDA is set to finish its safety review of mifepristone in March, one of the most consequential decisions the agency faces.

Overton’s nomination was already working against a tight window. Democrats take control of the Senate in early January, when she would have had to be renominated if she weren’t confirmed in this Congress. Her chances of being confirmed under a Democratic-controlled Senate would be slim.

The FDA has been without a permanent commissioner since Dr. Marty Makary resigned in May, in part because of the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vaping products.

The vacancy adds to a long period of upheaval at the nation’s top health agencies.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention went nearly a year without a permanent director after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed Susan Monarez just 29 days into the job last year. Trump’s first pick for that role, former congressman Dave Weldon, couldn’t secure enough Republican support, and the agency cycled through a series of acting leaders before the Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz in August.
