Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, NBC News projects, pushing her party’s Senate majority to 56 seats after a stunning wave election.

Her party ultimately flipped nine seats in this year’s midterm elections, all but one in states President Donald Trump carried in 2024.

Peltola, a former House member, had previously been elected statewide twice before losing her seat two years ago. Now, her Senate victory bolsters a Democratic caucus that will also include members from the likes of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, forming the largest Senate majority either party has had in 16 years.

In a statement Tuesday night, Peltola said she will fight for Alaskans in the Senate.

“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said. “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.”

“As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families,” she said.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., celebrated Peltola’s projected victory and the wider margin it brings.

“With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people,” he wrote on X. “We must earn back trust by passing bills that lower costs and improve lives — and dare Donald Trump to veto them at his own peril. We will be relentless. This is just the beginning.”

Democrats’ 56-seat Senate total will include two independents who caucus with the party: Sens. Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Peltola’s win comes after the Alaska race was roiled in the final days by investigations into allegations of ballot stacking, with a legal battle over a potential spoiler candidate intensifying ahead of Election Day.

NBC News reported in July that state and federal prosecutors were investigating the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and political newcomer who Republicans suspected had been recruited by Democrats to siphon votes from the incumbent, listed as Dan S. Sullivan on Alaska’s ranked choice ballot.

Alaska utilizes a voting system in which the top four candidates from the all-party primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives an initial majority, the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted. If none of the remaining candidates has more than 50% after that, the same process will repeat for the third-place finisher.

Since Peltola won a majority on the first ballot, the race did not go to ranked choice tabulation, which means any confusion over the two Sullivans did not affect the result.

A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said in a statement Monday that Alaskans “deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.”

“We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime,” campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said. “The campaign will have more to say by the end of this week.”

In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit aimed at blocking Alaska from certifying the results if the GOP senator lost, a move that Trump told reporters he had ordered.

Several days later, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the other Sullivan to run. Peltola has denied involvement in Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign, and he has also said it was his own decision to run.

In the wake of the report, Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and the Justice Department said it would redouble its efforts to investigate whether any federal laws were broken. The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan.

GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered a state investigation into Peltola’s campaign.

Alaska has not voted for a Democrat for president since 1964, before both Sullivan, 61, and Peltola, 53, were born, and its other Senate seat has been held by a member of the Republican Murkowski dynasty since 1981.

But Peltola had won statewide before, having taken Alaska’s at-large House seat in a special election in 2022 and winning one full term that same year. She lapped Sullivan in direct fundraising — $37 million to $14 million through mid-October — which was a constant reminder throughout each quarterly reporting period that she was a formidable challenger.

Peltola ran the same playbook as Democrats across the country, yoking Sen. Sullivan to Trump. Though Trump won Alaska three times by double-digit margins, he never reached 55% of the vote. And his second-term policies proved as unpopular in the Last Frontier State as they did with voters in the Lower 48, giving Peltola plenty of room to hammer Sullivan on overall inflation, the Iran war and fuel costs.

“Dan’s part of a rigged system where politicians get wealthy and you get hurt,” she said in one ad. “They make cash while our diesel prices go up, our healthcare prices keep rising, and we have fewer fish in our rivers.”

Sullivan portrayed Peltola as a tool of Washington Democrats and as a lawmaker in name only. If she made a campaign commercial listing her accomplishments, he said, “that would be the shortest ad in American history.” None of her bills became law, and only one, which would have created a food-security office in the Department of Veterans Affairs, passed in the House.

Trump’s efforts to bolster Sullivan included a mid-October campaign visit. But the national wind blew straight across the country to Alaska, and Peltola emerged victorious.

World.title: Nvidia enters the post-Jensen Huang era with a bang
World.content:
Nvidia delivered a message with its first earnings report under new leadership: The sky isn’t falling.

With a new CEO and board chair just days after the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang, the company reported results Tuesday that beat analysts’ expectations for AI chip sales. Nvidia’s new leaders also appeared to calm some investors’ nerves about the immediate future of a company at the heart of the AI economy.

Colette Kress, the interim CEO and Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, and Harvey Jones, the newly elected board chair, used the quarterly earnings call to answer many — but not all — of the biggest questions hanging over Nvidia, including who will be running things in the near term.

Just hours before the earnings release, Huang had injected fresh uncertainty into precisely that question when announced that he would be “honored” to return to the job of CEO, if the company’s board decided to bring him back.

At the top of Tuesday’s call, Jones shot down that idea.

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” he said.

“While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners and shareholders.”

Following the earnings call, Kress poured even more cold water on the idea of Huang’s return.

“Jensen resigned from his position with Nvidia, and the board accepted his resignation,” she said in an interview with CNBC. “The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do.”

Huang resigned Thursday after reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a woman believed to be spying for China and another with an executive who reported to him. On Tuesday morning, Huang said he had made “serious mistakes in my personal life.”

Jones said the board would consider both internal and external candidates for CEO and had hired an executive search firm, Heidrick & Struggles, to help with the process.

He also endorsed Kress as interim CEO, saying that she had been “instrumental in executing strategy” and possessed a “deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position.”

Investors responded positively to the earnings report and the call, sending Nvidia’s share price higher by 5% in after-hours trading. Nonetheless, the stock is still trading about 30% below the all-time high it reached last month.

The bullishness on Wall Street was driven in part by the company’s financial results. Revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25 was $115.8 billion — more than double the revenue for the same period a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, also more than double a year earlier.

Kress also announced that Nvidia was raising its forecast for future sales from the previous estimate of 70% revenue growth over the next year, up to 75%.

“We are addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers,” she said.

Kress singled out demand coming from the frontier AI companies that are developing new models — such as Anthropic and OpenAI — and said they’d been demanding more chips, “even in the last week.”

This is all despite the headwinds confronting AI chip sales right now, such as China-related export controls, public pushback against data centers and the radioactive politics of AI.

Nvidia’s optimistic guidance was “the most important line in the release,” wrote veteran tech analyst Dan Ives, a managing director at Yorkville Ives consultancy.

“There was a real chance a board five days into an interim CEO would hold back a formal outlook, and instead Kress put a number above the Street,” he wrote in a note to clients, referring to her forecast that exceeded what Wall Street analysts had been expecting. Kress’ guidance “speaks volumes about the backlog she inherited” of demand for Nvidia’s chips.

A few of Kress’ answers to analysts’ questions were less specific, or convincing, than others.

Asked whether incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would slow down AI development next year, she said the industry would need to work together with individual communities and the government.

“We’re always going to be engaged with the government, making sure that we are all aligned in terms of what we see in terms of the future.”

AI and data center companies, she said, will need to ensure that “communities understand the jobs that are going to be newly available.”

But it’s not clear that the promise of future jobs will be enough to turn the tide of public opinion in favor of data centers. Earlier this month, 40 out of the 41 data center ballot initiatives put to voters were rejected.

At another point, Kress was asked about new rules from the Commerce Department restricting the sale of advanced AI chips to several countries that have been major sources of revenue for Nvidia in recent years.

The company would “spend some time studying” the new rules, she said, but she did not believe they would affect overall sales because demand from other customers was so strong.

How long this AI euphoria will last, though, is unclear.

Several large companies have recently announced plans to limit their spending on AI services and tokens, questioning whether the technology is delivering the huge returns it promised.

Meanwhile, the number of individuals who use chatbots is growing but the lion’s share of those users don’t pay for advanced computing power. And polls consistently show that more Americans believe AI’s impact on society will be negative, than think it will be positive.

World.title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
World.content:
NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.

An artist's impression of NASA's Voyager spacecraft. NASA

Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.

Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.

As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.

Voyager 1 was launched atop a Titan rocket on Aug. 2, 1977. NASA will mark the spacecraft's 50th anniversary next year. NASA

And what an achievement it is: No other space agency in the world has matched or even attempted a mission rivaling Voyager, one that many believe ranks with the Apollo moon landings as one of the greatest feats of American space flight.

"It's difficult to describe, difficult to put into words," said Voyager Interstellar Mission Manager Kareem Badaruddin, one of just three full-time team members keeping the aging Voyagers healthy and their antennas aimed at Earth. "I feel like this mission is one of the great things that people have ever done, that humans have ever done.

"All of us, every person, whether they've worked on this mission or not, can take some pride in it and can feel like this is a part of what our civilization has accomplished."

It's not known how long the Voyagers will continue to function as the plutonium in their nuclear power packs steadily decays. With luck and clever management, engineers hope to keep the data flowing for several more years before the signals finally stop.

The two Voyager spacecraft were launched with a variety of then state-of-the-art instruments to study Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune during close flybys and to characterize the nature of the space environment. Their nuclear generators have steadily lost power as their supply of plutonium-238 has decayed, leaving Voyager 1 with just enough power to operate two instruments while three remain functional aboard Voyager 2. NASA

Voyager 1 started out with about 470 watts of power. That's down to a little more than 210 watts now, enough to run just two of its 10 instruments while keeping the spacecraft properly oriented so it can beam magnetometer and plasma wave data back to Earth. Voyager 2 has a slightly more powerful generator and is operating on a bit more than 230 watts, enough to keep three instruments running.

But even after the power is exhausted, both Voyagers will continue on their way, expected to remain roughly intact, if powerless, for a billion years or more, almost certainly outlasting human civilization.

On the remote chance any aliens might one day stumble upon a Voyager in the cold reaches between the stars, both spacecraft are carrying what amount to messages in a bottle, gold phonograph records encoded with the sights and sounds of planet Earth.

The records include greetings in 55 languages, 115 photos of Earth's people, wildlife and technology, representative natural sounds and carefully selected art and music from multiple cultures, everything from J.S. Bach to Navajo chants to Chuck Berry singing "Johnny B. Goode."

"If Voyager should, sometime in its distant future, encounter beings from some other civilization in space, it bears a message, a phonograph record ... with instructions for use," Carl Sagan, the late astronomer who led the golden record project, said in the 1980 "Cosmos" television series.

"And on this record are a sampling of pictures, sounds, greetings and an hour and a half of exquisite music, the Earth's greatest hits, a gift across the cosmic ocean from one island of civilization to another."

Identical golden records were attached to Voyager 1 and 2, along with instructions for playing them, that include photographs, art, music and greetings in 55 languages that serve as a sort of message in a bottle on the remote chance that alien intelligences might one day find one and wonder who sent them into interstellar space. NASA

Now beyond the confines of Earth's solar system, the stream of ones and zeros describing the interstellar environment leaves Voyager 1's 12-foot-wide dish antenna with less than half the power used by a typical 40-watt refrigerator bulb.

By the time the signal reaches Earth 24 hours later, its strength is a tiny fraction of a trillionth of a watt, vastly less than the power needed to run a wristwatch — a signal so weak that giant 230-foot-wide antennas in NASA's globe-spanning Deep Space Network are needed to pull in the faint whispers.

Commands from flight controllers at JPL now take a full day to reach the spacecraft with another 24 hours required to find out if the commands were received and acted upon. Fixing a problem is a glacial, nail-biting affair.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a web posting.

Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are powered by electricity generated through the decay of radioactive plutonium 238 in compact nuclear power plants known as radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs.

Both spacecraft have slowly but steadily lost power as the plutonium in their RTGs has decayed. Flight controllers closely manage the available power and the resulting heat needed to keep fuel lines from freezing so thrusters can fire when needed to keep the spacecraft — and their dish antennas — locked onto Earth.

Badaruddin said the small flight control team feels the weight of responsibility for keeping the Voyagers alive.

"If ever you get that sense that oh, I made a mistake, I'm the one who caused a problem for the spacecraft, that's crushing," he said. "Every one of the team members feels they're committed to doing everything in our power to do our best for these spacecraft. We're doing everything we can to keep them going for as long as we can."

Only three of the 13 Voyager team members are full-time JPL employees. Two are retirees who worked on the project at launch and came back to help during the interstellar voyage while the rest split their time between Voyager and other projects.

"I've been at JPL for 32 years, and everybody loves their spacecraft, and everybody feels like it's a family member and gives everything they've got for it," said Badaruddin. "And Voyager is no different in that regard. And these two retirees have come back and given a tremendous amount of effort and time."

The Voyager program was approved in the early 1970s when the outer planets were lined up in a way that would permit a so-called "Grand Tour" of them, enabling spacecraft to make velocity-boosting flybys to jump from one planet to the next, shaving years off the time needed to explore them all.

But to reduce costs, the project was only funded for flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 was launched first, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 followed on Sept. 5.

A Voyager close-up of Jupiter's Great Red Spot, a titanic storm churning in the planet's turbulent atmosphere that has been continuously observed since the early 1800s and was possibly seen as far back as 1664. NASA

Voyager 1 was on a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter first as planned, flying past the giant planet in 1979, sending back spectacular images of its Great Red Spot — a storm that has been churning for centuries, the planet's turbulent atmosphere and its major moons, including detailed looks at Europa, where an icy crust is thought to shield a global ocean, and Io, found to be the most volcanic world in the solar system.

It then flew on to Saturn, wowing astronomers with fantastically detailed photos of the solar system's most spectacular planet, sending back never-before-seen views of its rings, small moons that shepherd the ring particles along, the planet's atmosphere and, as it departed, cloud-shrouded Titan.

A Voyager image of Saturn. NASA

With the successful Titan flyby and the completion of the mission's major objectives, NASA approved sending Voyager 2 on a gravitational slingshot past Saturn and on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively.

On Valentine's Day 1990, Voyager 1's cameras were used a final time to take a family portrait of the six largest planets — Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — from a distance of 3.7 billion miles. Earth appeared as little more than a blue dot in the pinkish glow of reflected light within the camera.

"Consider again that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us," Sagan said of the photo. "On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives ... on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam."

Voyager's view of Earth, what astronomer Carl Sagan famously called "the pale blue dot," from a distance of 4 billion miles. The planet appears suspended in a reflection inside Voyager's camera. NASA

He concluded by saying "there is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known."

Voyager 1's cameras have been powered down ever since.

In 2012, Voyager 1 flew through the outer edge of the bubble around the solar system defined by the solar wind and the sun's magnetic field, sailing out into interstellar space. It is now in what Carolyn Porco, a well-known planetary scientist and member of the Voyager imaging team, calls "the realm of deep time."

In about 18,000 years, she writes on her Substack page, Voyager 1 will reach another major milestone: passing through a distance of one light-year from Earth, roughly 5.8 trillion miles, only a quarter of the way to the nearest star and "still well within the zone where the sun is the dominant gravitational influence."

But in a million years, the silent spacecraft will have passed well beyond the confines of the solar system, reaching a distance of 56 light-years while "remaining within the sun's local interstellar neighborhood — a low density region filled with diffuse hydrogen and helium gas and scattered stars: most are very dim, some are sun-like, and comparatively few are luminous."

In 100 million years, Voyager 1 will be about 2,000 light years from Earth as the spacecraft and the distant solar system are carried along by the galaxy's rotation. "Still not very far," Porco writes. "But at this time, it will find itself among cold, dense molecular clouds, star-forming regions and nebulae and supernova remnants formed by the deaths of stars."

Finally, 1 billion years from now, the spacecraft will have sailed about 20,000 light-years from home, making four trips around the galactic core in the process. "By then, the sun's growing luminosity will have sufficiently heated the Earth to destroy atmospheric carbon dioxide, halt oxygen production and exterminate plant life and the complex lifeforms that depend on it."

"By that time, both robot and maker will be extinct."

The cosmic travelogue concludes with a personal observation: "The foretelling of Voyager's galactic wanderings leaves one to contemplate the impermanence of all existence and the preciousness of life. And that just might be Voyager's greatest gift of all."

World.title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible meeting with Kim Jong Un
World.content:
President Trump is en route to China after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit later this week, and may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Mr. Trump visited the Malacañang Presidential Palace on Wednesday to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., before his flight to China. In a public bilateral meeting, the two leaders lauded the U.S.-Philippine relationship, which Mr. Trump called "one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific." The U.S. president suggested the two countries could cooperate further on technology, energy and defense.

Marcos said his staff dropped off a "late-night snack" for the U.S. delegation on the eve of the meeting — food from the popular Philippine fried chicken chain Jollibee. Marcos argued Jollibee has now surpassed hometown favorite KFC in the United States in terms of popularity, which Mr. Trump called "fantastic."

During the meeting, which followed a tour of part of the presidential palace, Mr. Trump said: "Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes."

"I love what you've done here," he said.

In a banquet luncheon before departing for China, Mr. Trump announced that he and Marcos "just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that. And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly, and it's a magnificent deal for both."

A day earlier, after landing in the Philippine capital of Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region. The president described the relationship with the Quad — made up of the U.S., Australia, India and Japan — as "very special."

Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korea's Kim in China. After arriving in the Philippines, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

President Trump waves American and Philippine flags after he arrived at Ninoy Aquino International Airport on Nov. 17, 2026, to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila. Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.

President Trump and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines during a welcome ceremony at the Malacanang Palace in Manila on Nov. 18, 2026. Mandel NGAN /AFP via Getty Images

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.

Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."

Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president.

Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

World.title: Democrats have flipped 46 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
World.content:
Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.

Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.

So far, 46 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:

Upsets

In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana speaks at the Capitol on April 26, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Rematches

A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria of Virginia speaks at a hearing on the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Dec. 19, 2022. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Northeastern battlegrounds

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania, speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on March 6, 2024. Tierney L. Cross / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Tight Midwestern districts

A few Midwestern states will have dramatically different congressional delegations starting next year.

Michigan Democrat William Lawrence greets supporters at an election night event in Lansing on Nov. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Kristen Norman

Western states

Some Western cities and states elected their first Democrats to the House in years.

Sam Forstag Courtesy of Sam for Montana campaign

Texas

Republicans in the Lone Star State redrew their House maps last year with the goal of picking up as many as five seats that were held by Democrats. Ultimately, one seat flipped to the GOP, and two red districts were captured by Democrats. The shifts coincided with a slate of statewide Democratic wins in Texas, which elected its first Democratic senator and governor in decades.

Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for Texas' 15th Congressional District, at a campaign event in Weslaco, Texas, on Oct. 25, 2026. Gabriel V. Cardenas /AFP via Getty Images

California

Voters in California approved their own redistricting plan after Texas redrew its maps, aiming at moving several California seats to the left. Democrats have picked up all five of the seats they had hoped to flip.

Republican Rep. David Valadao of California on May 12, 2022. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

North Carolina

A large number of House seats in North Carolina changed hands, including some upsets in places that were tilted to the GOP in redistricting a few years ago, part of a wave in the Tar Heel State as Roy Cooper decisively won the state's Senate race.

North Carolina Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager greets a supporter in Asheville on Oct. 31, 2026. Allison Joyce / Getty Images

World.title: Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, flipping seat for Dems
World.content:
Washington — Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeated GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in the Alaska Senate race, CBS News projects, adding to the new Democratic majority in the Senate two weeks after Election Day.

With the Alaska race now decided, Democrats will control 56 Senate seats to Republicans' 44.

Peltola, 53, was the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in 50 years in 2022. She is now set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate, and the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the state since 2008.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said in a statement Tuesday night. " As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

"Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work," she added.

Sullivan, a second-term senator and a Marine veteran, was fighting to hold on to the seat. Peltola successfully portrayed herself as an independent voice for the state. She lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024 by less than 3 points, while President Trump won the state by 13 points. But the dynamics were more favorable for her this cycle, with the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hanging over Republican candidates.

The contest was decided by ranked-choice voting. In addition to Sullivan, Peltola faced off against another candidate with nearly the same name as the incumbent, Daniel J. Sullivan, and Republican Gerald Heikes.

The second Dan Sullivan, a former teacher, added a wrinkle to the race. He announced he was challenging the sitting senator in June, prompting an unsuccessful push to remove him from the ballot. But both Dan Sullivans ultimately appeared on the ballot, in a development that Republicans argued could impact the incumbent senator's chances.

About a week and a half before Election Day, the Trump administration sued to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if Sen. Sullivan were to lose to Peltola because of the other Daniel Sullivan.

But in the end, Peltola's margin was large enough that those votes wouldn't have made a difference.

Heading into election night, polls showed a dead heat between Peltola and Sen. Sullivan. Republicans sent their biggest names to stump for Sullivan, including Vice President JD Vance. And the Senate GOP's main super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, spent heavily in the race.

Republicans had hoped to retain the seat and their GOP majority in an unexpectedly competitive environment this cycle. Though Democrats initially faced steep headwinds, competitive races opened up in several states that Mr. Trump had won in 2024 by double digits, including Alaska.

World.title: White House drops its nomination for FDA commissioner
World.content:
The White House has dropped the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick for Food and Drug Administration commissioner, according to a senior administration official and other people familiar with the decision.

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination Wednesday.

Axios was first to report that Overton was dropped.

Overton had struggled to shore up support among Senate Republicans, CBS News had previously reported. Some lawmakers and administration allies had expressed skepticism of Overton, partly due to her testimony regarding the FDA-approved abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of Mr. Trump's pro-vape policies.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the outgoing chair of the Senate HELP Committee, argued late Tuesday the issue was not that Overton lacked the votes to get confirmed. He said the "White House abandoned a viable confirmation path."

Cassidy wrote in a statement that "pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration's commitment to life issues," but the Trump administration withdrew Overton instead.

"I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans' health at risk," he said.

Two sources familiar with the matter said the White House shared its decision to withdraw Overton's nomination Tuesday evening. At the time, whip efforts were still underway to garner enough Republican votes to advance Overton.

Mr. Trump nominated Overton — a physician and White House domestic policy staffer — to the FDA role over the summer. The agency, which regulates products that account for about 20% of U.S. consumer spending, has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since Dr. Marty Makary was forced out in May.

Overton was seen as close to former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who departed her role earlier this month.

Prior to the decision to withdraw Overton, the White House had begun talking to other potential candidates for FDA chief, including some who could serve in an acting capacity and thus forgo Senate confirmation, a source told CBS News earlier Tuesday. The agency is currently run by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas.

Two sources indicated Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, a doctor, is making a play for the FDA post. He lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton earlier this month.

Any Senate-confirmed FDA commissioner would need to be confirmed during a narrow window before Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Cassidy told CBS News on Tuesday that "with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats."

In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Cassidy expressed concern that an acting FDA administer would have less independence than a Senate-confirmed leader.

"The question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody's mind, but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence?" he said.

World.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO agrees to testify to Congress amid affair probe
World.content:
Washington — Jensen Huang, who resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia, has agreed to answer questions from House and Senate lawmakers under the threat of a subpoena, amid an investigation into his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Huang will testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee, though the hearing's date has not been determined, according to a spokesperson for the committee's chairman, GOP Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina. He will also sit for a closed-door transcribed interview with three House committees on Dec. 1.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said in a joint statement announcing the date of the hearing. Mast issued the statement with GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chair of the House China Committee, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas.

Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the House committees on Dec. 2, the lawmakers said.

"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the lawmakers added.

A representative for Huang declined to comment.

The chairmen had given Huang until 8 p.m. Nov. 13 to respond to their request for a closed-door, transcribed interview after Thanksgiving. Negotiations for the interview continued past the deadline into this week.

In a Nov. 12 letter, the lawmakers warned that "failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing."

"Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony," they wrote.

Moolenaar and Crawford signed the letter with Mast.

In an initial letter to Huang on Nov. 4, the lawmakers sought a briefing on Nvidia's security protocols against espionage from foreign adversaries and on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is not related to him.

The Singapore-based data center company gained access to Nvidia's highly prized chips that are banned from export to China under U.S. law. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers wrote in their initial letter to Jensen Huang.

World.title: Rubio says there's "zero evidence" recent tech outages are related
World.content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there's "zero evidence" that recent tech outages in U.S. air travel, banking and other systems are connected.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said Wednesday morning local time during a news conference in the Philippines.

Rubio acknowledged that people are fearful and uncertain, saying he wanted to be clear that the United States is not under systemic attack.

"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.

Rubio, who is traveling with President Trump ahead of a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, added that the administration is "always on the lookout" for any potential attacks and reiterated multiple times that reports of technical issues are not interconnected.

"Each of them are distinct, and they're different in their causation," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks to the media at the Solaire Hotel on Nov. 18, 2026, in Manila. Win McNamee / Getty Images

On Thursday, Microsoft said it experienced a worldwide outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams, impacting users, companies and government operations worldwide. The company said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity.

The following day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights for several hours, throwing the aviation industry into turmoil. Federal officials identified a contractor performing maintenance updates as the cause of Friday's disruption, but key questions remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

Other recent outages that have since been resolved include disruptions to major banks like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank, and issues with Apple's services. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline, multiple U.S. officials familiar told CBS News.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there's no indication these incidents are the result of an attack, but noted that artificial intelligence is creating pressure for companies to deal with vulnerabilities.

"AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change," Warner said in a post on X. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences. This is exactly why I've been pushing for commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections."

When asked Wednesday about the role of AI in recent incidents, Rubio said he didn't want to speculate because every incident is unique and referred to individual companies.

World.title: Airline schedules returning to normal after ground stop, FAA says
World.content:
Operations were slowly returning to normal or close to it at most major airlines Monday after a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, causing chaos in the nation's airports with thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that travelers should expect delays to continue but "we should be running at full capacity" heading into Monday.

"What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way," he said.

Still, more than 2,300 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were canceled Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 10,400 were delayed, though not necessarily as a result of ripple effects from the ground stop.

FlightAware said more than 250 Monday flights had been canceled and 850 delayed as of 6:30 a.m. EST.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

How did the FAA ground stop happen?

The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. ET Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.

"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.

It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday.

This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.

Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.

"It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new," Duffy said on "Face the Nation" on Sunday.

Duffy told reporters on Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that a contractor for L3Harris, a technology and defense company, was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

Visitors watch an airplane as it prepares to land at Washington Dulles International Airport after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted nationwide ground stops in Chantilly, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Cliff Owen/ AP Photo

It took L3Harris, which owns the network that runs the nation's air traffic control system, several hours to pinpoint the source of the frequency outage, delaying the lifting of Friday's nationwide ground stop, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service."

L3Harris said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the company said in a statement, adding that it takes the nationwide ground stop and "its impact" seriously.

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Saturday that updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.

"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.

Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.

Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."

Request for more FAA funding

Duffy said in a social media post on Friday that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH."

"I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money. I've asked for a lot of money," he said Saturday. "Now, the Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me 12 and a half billion dollars. And one of the problems that we had was they weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money."

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $30 billion late Friday.

President Trump, who broke his silence Sunday on the ground stop, said in a new post on Truth Social that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs."

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Mr. Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing the Biden administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rep. Andre Carson, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a joint statement Saturday that FAA and DOT staff will brief the committees on Monday about the additional $30 billion requested by the Trump administration.

"This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share," the two Democrats said. "The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."

The pair said the Trump administration has only used $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress.

"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money," they said.

Can Americans still travel safely?

Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said Friday.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.

Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

An American Airlines flight takes off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.

"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.

American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."

Southwest said Saturday the airline instituted a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty.

"We are working to get our Customers to their destinations as quickly as possible," Southwest said.

World.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat into Democrats' column
World.content:
Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat into Democrats' column

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Stay connected: The NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has won Alaska's U.S. Senate contest, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Peltola bested Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in one of the country's most closely watched Senate campaigns. With her victory, Democrats will have 56 Senators in the upcoming Congress.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola won a majority of Alaskans' first-place votes, meaning no ranked-choice calculation was needed.

Peltola's victory flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections. Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

The race was roiled in its final days by new allegations, reported by The New York Times, that Peltola's team was involved in efforts to recruit another candidate to the race, Dan J. Sullivan, to try to siphon votes from the incumbent.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement in the second Sullivan's candidacy. NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting.

A federal judge rejected a lawsuit by the Trump administration to block certification of the results if the incumbent Sullivan lost.

Peltola boosted by hostile political environment for Republicans

Peltola is from Bethel, a western Alaska hub city of about 7,000 that's not connected to the state's limited road system. She is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since 2008 and will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Peltola campaigned mostly on the themes that Democrats around the United States focused on: affordability, healthcare costs and accusing Republicans of flagrant corruption. The cost-of-living argument has special salience in rural Alaska, where groceries and gas can be double or triple the cost elsewhere.

With a campaign motto of "fish, family, freedom," she also spoke of the salmon crisis on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, an issue that propelled her to statewide prominence in her first U.S. House race in 2022. In this campaign, she pitched herself as the candidate who would crack down on industrial-scale pollock fishing in the Bering Sea. Alaskans increasingly blame that industry for catching and wasting salmon, halibut and other species.

Sponsor Message

Sullivan is a Marine Corps veteran elected to the Senate in 2014 who previously served as Alaska's attorney general. He is a strong advocate for augmenting the military and Coast Guard's presence in Alaska.

Sullivan has also been a steadfast ally of Trump. The president flew to Wasilla last month and held a rally to boost Sullivan's candidacy. But Trump's approval ratings in Alaska and nationally have plunged since 2024, driven largely by opposition to the Iran war and angst over high prices.

The election results suggest that unpopularity was a drag on Republican incumbents.

Justice Department appealing court ruling

The U.S. Justice Department plans to appeal the dismissal of its lawsuit, which sought to block the certification of Alaska's Senate race if Sullivan lost.

The department asked the judge to stop state officials from certifying election results to allow for an investigation into whether voters were confused by having two candidates named Dan Sullivan appear on Alaska's ranked-choice ballot.

The judge in that case concluded that such a court order would "clearly violate" Alaskan voters' right to a secret ballot. Alaska's governor has also ordered an investigation into the race.

Ballot stacking and promoting spoilers are generally legal in Alaska and have been relatively common.

Super PACs aligned with Republicans and Democrats spent more than $2 million on "ballot composition" efforts in Alaska this year, sometimes to elevate people who don't live in Alaska, including a federal inmate in New York.

But the Trump administration, the incumbent Sullivan and other Republicans claim that the goal of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was to trick voters.

The Justice Department said in a statement that "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."

Preliminary race results suggest other candidates did not act as spoilers. Peltola, as of Sunday, had more votes than the other three candidates combined.

World.title: Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
World.content:
Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet

toggle caption i Vahid Salemi/AP

CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.

The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.

Sponsor Message

Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.

Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.

A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.

The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.

toggle caption i AP

Iran may be shifting its strategy amid economic pain

Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.

Sponsor Message

U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.

Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.

Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.

Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.

"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."

U.S. expands its Middle East naval presence

With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.

Sponsor Message

The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.

Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks

Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.

The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.

"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.

Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.

Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.

Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on

The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

Sponsor Message

"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."

Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.

Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.

Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."

Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

World.title: Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
World.content:
Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO

toggle caption i Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

Nvidia said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, amid a push by the former CEO's allies to return him to lead the chipmaker he cofounded.

Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.

Sponsor Message

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang wrote in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments came as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."

"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

Sponsor Message

Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.

Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

Nvidia sought to reassure investors about the company's future during its third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday.

"Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change," said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer who is serving as interim CEO while the board finds a permanent leader.

Quarterly sales doubled to a record $115.8 billion and profit also doubled to $65.3 billion from a year ago. The company said it was raising its forecast for sales growth next year.

Sponsor Message

Nvidia shares were up 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday. The company's stock price has dropped more than 16% since Huang admitting having an extramarital affair earlier this month.

World.title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
World.content:
Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images North America

🎧 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the FAA will reevaluate future maintenance procedures, NPR's Joe Hernandez tells Up First. Mike McCormick, a former FAA senior executive and air traffic manager, told Hernandez that he thinks another nationwide ground stop is unlikely. McCormick says that in cases like this, the FAA sometimes imposes a maintenance moratorium, temporarily halting such work. The ground stop happened while L3Harris workers converted copper wires to a fiber optic system and installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.

President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.



Sponsor Message

🎧 When leaving the White House yesterday, Trump said they would discuss his "favorite subject": Ukraine, NPR's Deepa Shivaram says. The White House had previously announced that Ukraine would not be on the agenda for the trilateral meeting. Shivaram says that Europe and Ukraine are concerned about how Ukraine may be discussed at the meeting, and what might come out of it, because President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not be at APEC and Trump has recently been more lenient toward Putin and Russia.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.



🎧 Many prominent AI and venture capital figures have recognized Huang as a visionary whose company played a significant role in the AI boom, NPR's Shannon Bond says. An online petition supporting his reinstatement has garnered more than 160,000 signatures, but Bond says some of them may not be real. Elon Musk says he signed it. Brad Gerstner from Altimeter Capital, a key Nvidia investor, has urged the board to thoroughly investigate and keep all options open. Bond says the interim CEO and CFO will address the public for the first time following today's earnings report.

Sponsor Message

Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027. Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Deep dive

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative.



👶 Almost half of U.S. children aged 5 and under live in licensed childcare deserts, where demand exceeds availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.

👶 New Mexico's program has an operating budget of nearly $600 million, but some lawmakers are concerned it could be $50 million over budget this year.

👶 New Mexico state Sen. Steve Lanier tells NPR that the steep cost of the program is why he only supports universal childcare for some people, since someone earning around $450,000 or $600,000 might not need assistance. Lanier has previously sued to end the initiative, but the lawsuit was unsuccessful.

👶 Since the enactment of free, universal childcare in New Mexico, lower-income mothers have experienced significant gains. Their full-time employment has risen by 23%, according to a new paper from Arizona State University.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Europe

British actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh James Bond, taking his place among an iconic lineup of stars that started with Sean Connery and most recently featured Daniel Craig. The 69th annual Grammy Awards nominations were announced yesterday. British singer-songwriter RAYE leads with 11 nominations, followed by Spanish artist Rosalía with nine nods.
