World.title: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years. What It Means for Costa Rica Travel
World.content:
The United States is no longer considered measles-free. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced today that the virus has circulated continuously in the country for more than 12 months, ending a status the US had held since 2000. If you fly between the US and Costa Rica, this is not a travel ban. It means measles now spreads inside the US on its own, rather than arriving mainly with travelers from abroad, so your chance of running into it on a trip north is higher than it has been in a generation.

The US has recorded more than 5,000 confirmed cases so far in 2026, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is more than double the 2,289 cases in all of 2025 and the highest count since 1991. PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa said vaccination remains the main way to protect yourself. He said the US is taking steps to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response.

Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles-free status, and Guatemala could follow when its 12-month review period ends on Dec. 23. Daniel Salas, a former Costa Rican health minister who now leads PAHO’s immunization program, said Mexico’s measures have sharply cut cases but warned that as long as transmission continues, so does the risk.

Costa Rica is in a different position, it has had no endemic measles transmission since 1999, and as of September health authorities had investigated about 190 suspected cases this year and confirmed five, all imported or linked to an imported case. None was fatal.

Christian Valverde, the Health Ministry’s director general, has said national vaccination coverage against measles is above 94%. PAHO considers 95% the level needed to keep the virus from taking hold, which is why every imported case gets a fast response. If you are heading to the US, Mexico or another country with an active outbreak, you can get a measles booster before you go.

The Health Ministry opened the traveler booster to anyone 15 and older, and Health Minister Mary Munive said doses are available at Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) health centers and at private clinics. Get the shot at least two weeks before you leave. The vaccine needs that time to build protection, and it is the timing the Health Ministry recommends. More than 24,000 travelers had received a booster by September.

Not sure you are covered? Costa Rica’s routine schedule gives two doses, at 15 months and at four years. Adults who have lost their vaccination card, or who were vaccinated before records went digital, are the people doctors most often advise to get another dose. Watch for symptoms for up to three weeks after you get back. Measles usually starts with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed a few days later by a rash that spreads from the face downward. Early on it is easy to confuse with other fevers circulating in Costa Rica, such as dengue.

If you think you have measles, call your EBAIS or clinic before you go in, so staff can keep you away from other patients. It is one of the most contagious diseases known, and a person can spread it for several days before the rash appears. The Americas as a whole lost its measles-free status in November 2025, after Canada passed 12 months of continuous transmission. A country can win the status back once it shows 12 consecutive months without endemic spread.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Rent-to-Own Homes With Up to 100% Financing
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Housing and Human Settlements (MIVAH) is drafting a rent-to-own model for families who can afford a monthly payment but lack the savings for a down payment or cannot prove to a bank that they can repay a loan. Housing Minister Guillermo Carazo said the model, known in Spanish as leasing habitacional, would add a rental stage of about five years before a mortgage is formalized.

Under the proposal, a trust or real estate fund would buy the property. When the home is a new apartment, the developer would be paid and exit the deal. The future buyer would then sign a lease with a purchase option, with the sale price fixed from the start, and pay monthly rent comparable to a regular lease. Part of that rent could be set aside as savings toward the down payment, although Carazo said whether that happens, and how much, would depend on each institution’s product.

At the end of the rental period, the tenant could exercise the option and take out a mortgage, subject to the lender’s approval. Carazo said the payment record built during those years would show the lender that the household can sustain a loan payment, lowering the bank’s perceived risk.

That record could also raise the share of the price a lender is willing to finance. In the minister’s example, a borrower initially offered 80% of the appraised value could reach 95% or even 100% after four to five years of proven payments, shrinking or eliminating the down payment.

Ideally, Carazo said, the rent would be close to the future mortgage payment so lenders can confirm affordability. The rental period would not be rigid and could be extended if a family’s circumstances change, for example if one partner loses a job and the household needs to delay the purchase or drop the plan.

Public and private banks, mutual housing associations, cooperatives and the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (SUGEF) are involved in the discussions. Each authorized institution would design its own product under a common legal framework set by a new law. MIVAH expects to have a draft bill early next year, which it will discuss with the Executive Branch before sending it to the Legislative Assembly. Carazo stressed that all conditions would need to be clear to buyers from the outset.

Carazo said developers believe the model would boost home and apartment sales. He offered a preliminary estimate of a 20% to 30% increase, while acknowledging the figure is difficult to calculate. The proposal targets a wide gap. A study by the University of Costa Rica’s Graduate Program in Architecture, the Federated College of Engineers and Architects (CFIA) and the organization Gestionando Hábitat found that 81.4% of renter households, about 279,890 families, face total exclusion or significant restrictions when seeking formal home financing.

Costa Rica has no specific legal framework for rent-to-own housing, although some lease-with-purchase-option arrangements already exist. A previous bill to regulate the model did not become law. Key details remain open, including interest rates, eligibility requirements and what would happen to savings built into the rent if a family walks away before buying. Those terms will depend on the products lenders design and on the final text lawmakers approve.

World.title: Horacio Zeballos and Marcel Granollers Make Winning Start at ATP Finals
World.content:
Argentina’s Horacio Zeballos and Spanish partner Marcel Granollers opened their ATP Finals campaign with a convincing victory Monday, defeating Italy’s Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori 6-4, 6-4 to take an important first step toward the season-ending doubles championship.

The third-seeded pair needed just 79 minutes to overcome their fifth-seeded opponents at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, converting all three of their break-point opportunities to begin round-robin play with a 1-0 record. The victory was particularly satisfying for Zeballos and Granollers, who had lost to the same Italian partnership during last year’s ATP Finals and again in the Rome Masters final earlier this season.

This time, the Argentine-Spanish combination controlled the decisive moments, overcoming an uneven start before establishing themselves as the stronger team. The opening set began with three consecutive service breaks. Zeballos and Granollers struck first, but Bolelli and Vavassori immediately responded to level the score.

The experienced pair broke again in the third game and protected that advantage throughout the remainder of the set. Their serving improved as the match progressed, allowing them to keep the Italian partnership under pressure without giving away further opportunities.

The second set followed a similar pattern, although both teams held serve through the opening four games. Zeballos and Granollers made their move in the fifth game, securing the only break of the set before closing out the match 6-4. The statistics reflected their efficiency. They finished with five aces, committed no double faults and landed 74% of their first serves.

They also won 79% of the points played behind their second serve, an important advantage against opponents known for their aggressive returning and strong net play. Most significantly, Zeballos and Granollers converted all three break points they created, while saving three of the four opportunities they faced.

The result evened their career head-to-head record against Bolelli and Vavassori at four victories apiece. For Zeballos, the win represents another encouraging chapter in a remarkable doubles career. The 41-year-old Argentine and 40-year-old Granollers are competing together at the ATP Finals for the seventh consecutive season, a testament to the consistency of one of the longest-standing partnerships in professional tennis.

They have been among the world’s leading doubles teams since joining forces in 2019, reaching the top of the ATP doubles rankings and winning three Grand Slam titles together. Their most recent major triumph came at the 2026 French Open, where they successfully defended their Roland Garros doubles championship.

They also reached the finals in Dallas and Rome this season, although their campaign was interrupted by physical problems following the US Open. The pair returned to competition at the Paris Masters before arriving in Turin with renewed confidence. Despite their success elsewhere, the ATP Finals title remains unfinished business.

Zeballos and Granollers reached the championship match in 2023, losing to Rajeev Ram and Joe Salisbury. They also advanced to the semifinals in 2020 and 2021. However, their last two appearances ended during the group stage, making Monday’s opening victory especially important.

Granollers previously won the ATP Finals doubles championship in 2012 alongside fellow Spaniard Marc López, but he has yet to capture the title with Zeballos. For the Argentine, winning in Turin would carry additional historical significance. Zeballos became the first Argentine to reach the tournament’s doubles final in 2023 and is now seeking to become the first South American to win the championship.

The ATP Finals bring together the eight leading doubles teams of the season, divided into two groups of four. Each partnership plays three round-robin matches, with the top two teams from each group advancing to the semifinals. Zeballos and Granollers compete in the Mark Woodforde Group, alongside Bolelli and Vavassori, American Christian Harrison and Britain’s Neal Skupski, and Germany’s Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.

The Germans, who won the ATP Finals title in 2024, also began their campaign with a victory Monday, defeating Harrison and Skupski 6-1, 6-3. That sets up an important second-round meeting between the two unbeaten teams. Zeballos and Granollers are scheduled to face Krawietz and Puetz on Wednesday, November 18, at 6 p.m. local time in Turin.

A second consecutive victory would put the Argentine-Spanish partnership in a strong position to advance to the semifinals. For Zeballos, who has already established himself among Argentina’s most accomplished doubles players, the opportunity to add the season-ending championship to his Grand Slam success remains a powerful motivation.

Monday’s victory was only the beginning, but it was precisely the start he and Granollers needed as they pursue one of the few major titles still missing from their partnership.

World.title: Killers of Costa Rica Journalist May Have Had Help Tracking Him, OIJ Says
World.content:
Investigators believe the two gunmen who killed journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri on Route 32 may have had help following him, said Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). Muñoz said today that the attackers knew which vehicle the journalist was driving.

Investigators are examining whether a second motorcycle or another vehicle trailed Rodríguez and whether the gunmen received instructions before the attack. Agents are collecting security camera footage to reconstruct the routes the suspects used to reach the scene near San Miguel de Santo Domingo, in Heredia, and to flee.

According to the OIJ’s account, the attackers knew Rodríguez was alone in a red pickup. They pulled alongside, confirmed he was their target and opened fire, then circled the vehicle and fired again from a second angle. Muñoz said the men checked that Rodríguez was dead before fleeing toward San José. Based on how they acted, he said, they apparently set out to make sure he would not survive.

Agents have also searched Rodríguez’s home in Santo Domingo with authorization from prosecutors and the Heredia Criminal Court. Muñoz said they seized electronic devices, equipment and documents that will undergo forensic analysis as investigators try to establish a motive and identify those responsible.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said prosecutors will review the allegations Rodríguez published on social media, including the people he named, along with anyone else who may have had a reason to attack him. No arrests had been announced as of Tuesday afternoon, and the OIJ has not publicly identified any suspects.

Rodríguez, 50, had spent three days with his parents in Guápiles and set out for San José around 1 p.m. yesterday, according to his brother, Andrés Rodríguez. The Costa Rican Red Cross received the alert about the shooting at 3:21 p.m., about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) from his home.

The journalist had filed about 10 complaints over threats in the past two years, according to the OIJ. Laura Lara, one of his lawyers, said he had worn a bulletproof vest for roughly three weeks as the threats mounted and had it on when he was shot. Lara said Rodríguez turned down the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program because he believed it would restrict his work. Díaz had said yesterday that the journalist declined that protection despite the threats.

International press freedom groups added their voices on today Reporters Without Borders called the killing an alarm signal for press freedom in a country long regarded as a regional benchmark. The group urged authorities to determine whether the killing was linked to his publications and the threats against him.

José Zamora, Americas director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, said authorities should thoroughly examine any link to Rodríguez’s journalism and prosecute both the gunmen and whoever ordered the killing. The Inter American Press Association demanded an exhaustive and independent investigation.

His wake was scheduled for this evening at a funeral home in central Cartago, his brother said. A funeral Mass is set for Wednesday at 2 p.m. at the San Esteban parish, known as the Iglesia del Carmen, in Cartago’s El Carmen neighborhood. The OIJ has asked anyone with information to call its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

According to the attorney general, Rodríguez is the third journalist killed in Costa Rica, after Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. Whether investigators reach anyone beyond the two gunmen is likely to define how this case is remembered.

World.title: Dollar Expected to Keep Falling in Costa Rica After Record Low of 446 Colones
World.content:
The U.S. dollar is likely to keep losing value against the Costa Rican colón for the rest of 2026, financial analysts said. Their forecast follows the exchange rate’s fall to the lowest level in the history of Costa Rica’s foreign exchange market. On Friday, Nov. 13, the weighted average rate on Monex, the Central Bank of Costa Rica’s (BCCR) foreign exchange market, closed at 446.10 colones per dollar. That was the lowest on record in Central Bank data and the eighth straight session of decline.

The close was 0.72 colones below Thursday’s 446.82 and broke the previous record of 446.80, set on Sept. 17. The Central Bank’s reference rates for Monday, Nov. 16, stood at 442.56 colones for buying dollars and 448.34 colones for selling them. By Tuesday, Nov. 17, the reference buying rate had slipped to 441.73 colones.

Traders exchanged $49.3 million in 228 transactions on Friday, at rates between 445.80 and 446.30 colones, according to BCCR data. The Central Bank bought $41.8 million of that total, or 84.8% of the day’s volume. Of those purchases, $32.3 million were stabilization operations and $9.5 million covered the needs of the non-bank public sector.

The bank uses stabilization purchases to absorb part of the dollar supply and moderate swings in the rate. Friday’s operations did not prevent a new low. Luis Alvarado, an analyst at Acobo Puesto de Bolsa, said the downward pressure could continue over the coming weeks, practically until the end of the year. He described the colón’s appreciation as a trend that has marked much of the past three years.

Pablo González, an economist at Mercado de Valores, called the recent lows small moves within an established trend. As long as the market has an excess of foreign currency, he said, a significant change in the short term is unlikely. Neither analyst forecast a specific floor for the rate.

The analysts pointed to a steady supply of dollars from foreign-currency-earning sectors, against weak demand. Seasonal factors add to the pressure in November and December, when companies convert dollars to colones to pay taxes and the aguinaldo, the mandatory year-end bonus.

The dollar opened 2026 at 497.07 colones on Jan. 2, according to BCCR records. At Friday’s close, it had lost 10.3% this year and stood more than a third below its 2022 peak. A weaker dollar lowers the colón cost of imported goods and of debts held in dollars. It also reduces the colón value of income earned in dollars, including salaries, pensions, remittances and tourism revenue.

The Central Bank publishes the Monex result after each daily session.

World.title: JetBlue Goes Daily From New York to Both Costa Rica Airports This Week
World.content:
JetBlue is scheduled to fly every day between New York and both of Costa Rica’s international airports starting Thursday, Nov. 19, up from Saturdays only. The daily nonstops from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) go to Juan Santamaría International Airport (SJO) near San José and to Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport (LIR) in Liberia, Guanacaste.

The flights appear in the Costa Rican Tourism Board’s (ICT) official timetable for November 2026, and airline schedule listings back up the change. The expansion comes as the winter high season gets underway, and it goes against the broader trend.

International aviation consultancies project roughly 14% fewer scheduled seats from the United States to Costa Rica between August 2026 and March 2027. Juan Santamaría is projected to lose the most, about 20%, while Liberia is expected to lose around 3%. JetBlue has made cuts of its own in Costa Rica. In July, the airline ended its route between Orlando and San José.

Its New York service is going the other way. With seven flights a week to each airport instead of one, you no longer have to plan a trip around Saturdays, which matters most for short stays and last-minute winter bookings. The first daily flights leave a week before U.S. Thanksgiving.

Daily service to both airports also lets you choose your arrival point by where you’re going. Liberia is closer to the beaches of Guanacaste and the Nicoya Peninsula, while San José is the better starting point for the Central Valley, the Caribbean coast and the southern Pacific.

JetBlue is the only airline flying nonstop between JFK and San José. The New York–Liberia route has more competition, and Delta is scheduled to add Saturday flights from JFK to Liberia starting Dec. 19, using 194-seat Airbus A321neo aircraft. JetBlue is also bringing its new first-class cabin, BlueFirst, to Costa Rica this winter. It starts on Fort Lauderdale–Liberia flights on Dec. 26 and reaches the JFK–Liberia and Fort Lauderdale–San José routes on Jan. 5, 2027, with introductory fares from $299 one way between New York and Liberia.

ICT’s timetable covers November only, and it is not yet clear how long the daily schedule will last into the new year. Airline schedules can change close to departure, so anyone with a booking should check flight times directly with JetBlue.

World.title: Costa Rica Wildlife Cameras Catch Heron Catfish Hunts and an Ocelot Latrine
World.content:
My camera traps continue to provide me with brief glimpses into the hidden lives of Costa Rica’s wild animals. Today we look at a new discovery and revisit one that has been providing me with interesting videos for years now.

Armored Catfish for Lunch

I found my first armored catfish something like five years ago on the banks of the Río Cañas while doing a camera trap study for a sugarcane plantation. It was a smallish, classically catfish-looking fish with armored plates. I poked at it and thought, ‘I wonder what eats a rock-hard fish like this?’

Fast-forward to 2026 and I’m implementing a camera trap project on a large property that used to be a sugarcane plantation and still has some of the canals that plantations use to move water round to irrigate the sugarcane. Water always attracts life, so I stuck some cameras on the banks of the canals, as well as a small lake on the property. While installing the cameras, I couldn’t help but notice that some species of fish was constantly shooting up to the surface of the water to gulp oxygen and disappearing to the bottom. They were moving some quickly, I could never see what they were.

After a few camera revisions, I’ve come to realize that they’re one and the same as my old crusty friend that I found on Río Cañas, the armored catfish. This realization came quite easily because I kept recording videos of large herons, mostly great blue herons and bare-throated tiger herons, with catfish in their beaks. Which of course answers the question, ‘What eats these rock-hard fish?’

Unisex Cat Bathroom

I’ve had a camera trap pointed at a hole in the base of huge Guanacaste tree every day since sometime in January 2023. Generally, a tree cavity is a good location for a camera trap. Lots of different species like to visit, hunt, and sleep in tree cavities. What makes this one extra special is this particular tree cavity happens to act as a communal unisex bathroom for ocelots.

Over the years, I’ve recorded 223 videos of ocelots with this camera. Sometimes they’re just passing by, sometimes they’re taking naps, but most of the time they’re pooping or smelling one another’s poop. Ocelots are known to use communal latrines to leave scent messages to the individuals whose ranges overlap in a given area. I just reviewed the bathroom camera yesterday, and I continue to record ocelots sending stinky messages back and forth.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Slain Costa Rica Journalist Filed 10 Threat Complaints Before His Killing
World.content:
Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri, the journalist shot dead yesterday afternoon on Route 32 in Heredia, had filed about 10 complaints over threats to his safety in the past two years, according to Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). Investigators are now examining whether those threats are connected to his killing.

Rodríguez, 50, was driving a red pickup toward San José near San Miguel de Santo Domingo when, according to the OIJ’s preliminary account, two men dressed in black on a white motorcycle pulled alongside and opened fire. Muñoz said the attackers first shot at the driver’s side, then circled the vehicle and fired through the passenger window before fleeing toward the capital.

Muñoz said agents recovered nine to 10 shell casings outside the vehicle and that the number of shots could prove higher. An earlier account attributed to the OIJ on Monday evening cited seven to eight casings. Agents are reviewing security camera footage to trace the escape route and are checking whether the suspects had been following Rodríguez before the attack.

The case has been assigned to an interdisciplinary team from the OIJ’s San José Homicide Section, which is looking to identify both the gunmen and anyone who may have ordered the attack. No arrests had been announced as of this morning, and authorities have not established a motive.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Monday that the scene resembled a contract killing, according to international wire reports. Díaz also said Rodríguez had declined to enter the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program despite the threats, a point the OIJ confirmed, meaning he had no police protection. The public complaints Rodríguez made on social media, in which he named alleged drug traffickers, are one line of inquiry, which Muñoz described as broad. Further details are in our first report on the Route 32 shooting.

President Laura Fernández condemned the killing late last night, calling it a cowardly murder and a stain on freedom of expression regardless of the content of his statements. She said she had instructed all police forces to support the investigation so that those responsible are punished. Fernández had sued Rodríguez for defamation during the 2025 campaign over a video in which he alleged her home was built with money from a drug trafficker, according to wire reports. The shooting came on the same day the president said jailed gang members had ordered her own killing.

Former president Luis Guillermo Solís condemned the crime and called for a thorough investigation with no impunity for the gunmen or whoever planned the attack. In the Legislative Assembly, the 47 lawmakers present unanimously approved a motion for a minute of silence and a call for investigation, according to legislative reports.

National Liberation Party caucus leader Álvaro Ramírez said insecurity in the country had spiraled out of control, while Social Christian Unity Party lawmaker Abril Gordienko called the attack an alarming sign of the level of insecurity. Broad Front lawmaker José María Villalta said Rodríguez was killed for practicing journalism and urged investigators to pursue whoever ordered the crime.

Press organizations both here and around the world joined the condemnation. Yanancy Noguera, president of the Costa Rican Association of Journalists (Colper), said that the evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice, and the association demanded a swift investigation.

The Press and Freedom of Expression Institute (IPLEX) called for a prompt, independent, rigorous and exhaustive inquiry into both the perpetrators and anyone who ordered or financed the killing, while cautioning against drawing early conclusions about the motive. The Central American Journalists Network also condemned the attack and urged prosecutors and the OIJ to act quickly.

Rodríguez worked in radio, print and television before turning to social media, where he posted allegations about drug trafficking and alleged links between criminal groups and political and business figures. He said he had shared information on those links with the US Drug Enforcement Administration, a claim that has not been independently verified. He also sought public office, pursuing the Costa Rican Renewal Party’s presidential nomination in 2022 and heading the Aquí Costa Rica Manda party’s San José legislative list for the 2026 elections.

According to the attorney general, Rodríguez is the third journalist murdered in Costa Rica, after radio host Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. The case lands as Costa Rica posts drug seizures the US Embassy calls historic, in a country that ranked first in the Americas in this year’s World Press Freedom Index.

Costa Rica has long counted press freedom among its democratic strengths, yet a recent survey found that four in ten Costa Ricans hold back their opinions on social media out of fear. How quickly investigators identify those responsible, and whether they reach anyone who ordered the attack, is likely to shape how safe people feel speaking out.

World.title: Belize City bartender denied bail after waitress alleges he choked her and threatened to kill her at bar where they work
World.content:
Belize City bartender denied bail after waitress alleges he choked her and threatened to kill her at bar where they work

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 44-year-old Belize City bartender was denied bail Monday after a 22-year-old waitress told police he punched her in the face and choked her, then threatened to kill her the following day.

Jose Mario Aguillar Alfaro pleaded not guilty to one count of burglary and one count of threat of death in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court. The prosecutor intended to oppose bail, but before he could lay out his objections, the magistrate exercised her discretion and denied bail. Alfaro was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until January 19, 2027.

The woman told police she was trying to rest in a room at the establishment where they both work at about 2 a.m. on Saturday, November 14, when Alfaro opened the door and entered without permission. She said he told her to stop working, punched her in the face and began choking her. Chirinos said she managed to push him away.

The woman reported that Alfaro approached her again at the same establishment at about 1:30 p.m. Sunday and told her, “I wah kill yuh and put yuh remains in a plastic bag.” She said he was standing about 20 feet away and holding what appeared to be a knife.

The woman told police she had known Alfaro for three years through work. She reported both incidents at the King Street Police Station on Sunday afternoon and gave police a recorded statement.

World.title: Murder charge against Robert Lamb dropped in 2023 killing of Gabriel Tillett; Kevin Lanza, Samuel Trapp still face trial
World.content:
Murder charge against Robert Lamb dropped in 2023 killing of Gabriel Tillett; Kevin Lanza, Samuel Trapp still face trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Robert Emmanuel Lamb, 26, is no longer facing trial for the murder of 18-year-old Gabriel Tillett, but he was escorted back to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday because he remains on remand in a separate attempted murder case.

The Crown entered a nolle prosequi before High Court Justice Candace Nanton, formally discontinuing the murder prosecution against Lamb. Breaking Belize News understands the decision was made because there was insufficient evidence to proceed against him.

The Crown is still proceeding to trial against Lamb’s two former co-accused, brothers Kevin Lanza, 29, and Samuel Trapp, 31. Both appeared by video from prison, while Lamb appeared in person with attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. Justice Nanton granted an adjournment requested by Bryan Neal, who represents Lanza, and Orson “OJ” Elrington, who represents Trapp. The trial is expected to begin in early January 2027.

Tillett was found with multiple facial injuries inside Belize City’s Lord Ridge Cemetery on the morning of July 4, 2023. His brother identified him at the scene. As BBN previously reported, police said footage from a surveillance camera at Pitter Street and Antelope Street Extension, behind the cemetery, helped lead investigators to the three men.

Lamb has not been granted bail in the separate attempted murder case, which stems from an alleged attack and robbery involving businessman Deepak Rupuchand Katariya in Belize City on January 28, 2023. Lamb was arraigned three days later on charges of attempted murder, use of deadly means of harm, dangerous harm and robbery.

World.title: Caye Caulker Village and village councils across Belize to issue Trade Licenses under new act
World.content:
Caye Caulker Village and village councils across Belize to issue Trade Licenses under new act

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government issued a statement to clarify misinformation being spread by the Guardian newspaper.

The Ministry says that there has been no revocation of Caye Caulker Village Council’s authority to collect trade licenses.

On the contrary, this is the first time that Caye Caulker and many other rural communities will be able to issue trade licenses.

“The fees collected will be reinvested directly into our rural communities for the benefit of all residents and local businesses.

The revocation published in the Gazette was to allow for corrections on the tenure of the Boards. Subsequent Statutory Instruments (S.I. Nos. 105 and 106 of 2026) were published in the Gazette,” the Ministry explained.

In addition, the Ministry reminds that the Trade License Act, No. 19 of 2024, is now fully in effect for the new trade licensing year starting January 1, 2027.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture equips farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture equips farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Agriculture is equipping farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills.

The Ministry noted that 16 coconut producers participated in an intensive one-day Coconut Tree Management Training held today at the Agriculture Department Office.

The workshop was organized by the Corozal District Extension Service in collaboration with the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project Officer, Uziel Vasquez (CRESAP).

Facilitated by the National Fruit Tree Program Coordinator, Enrique Rivas and Israel Pech from the Research Unit at Central Farm, the training aimed to equip local farmers with modern, sustainable practices to optimize yields and build resilience in coconut farming.

Sessions covered industry insights, sustainable soil and plant nutrition, crop selection and cultivation, environmental factors and disease control and organic soil and plant nutrition.

In addition, farmers received coconut seedlings Brazilian Green Dwarf Coconuts.

World.title: Antonio Copo faces six charges after crash kills motorcyclist Dariel Perez in Guinea Grass
World.content:
Antonio Copo faces six charges after crash kills motorcyclist Dariel Perez in Guinea Grass

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Dariel Perez, 24, was on his way home from work Friday evening when his motorcycle collided with a vehicle in Guinea Grass Village, Orange Walk District. Perez was killed and his passenger, 25-year-old Ray Ramirez, was injured. Police have arrested and charged the other driver, 39-year-old Antonio Copo, with six offences.

Police Staff Officer ASP Stacy Smith said Perez and Ramirez were travelling toward Guinea Grass around 6:30 p.m. on November 13. According to the preliminary investigation, Copo was approaching from the opposite direction when he allegedly made a sudden left turn into the motorcycle’s lane. Perez and Copo are both residents of Guinea Grass Village.

Smith said Copo was charged with manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, negligent wounding, driving without due care and attention, driving under the influence, and failing to give way when changing direction.

World.title: Colorful lights and Christmas ornaments to brighten Belize City for Holiday Season
World.content:
Colorful lights and Christmas ornaments to brighten Belize City for Holiday Season

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council, in partnership with Coca-Cola, will host its 9th Annual Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony on Friday, November 27, 2026, at Battlefield Park and Mule Park in downtown Belize City.

The event begins at 6:00 p.m. and will feature festive displays, live entertainment and the Christmas edition of the Francis Reneau Concert Series.

The public is invited to bring family and friends to enjoy the holiday celebration.

See you there!

World.title: International News: More than 140,000 take part in nationwide cost-of-living protests across France
World.content:
International News: More than 140,000 take part in nationwide cost-of-living protests across France

By Zoila Palma: Today, more than 140,000 people took to the streets across France as public sector workers, students and private sector employees joined nationwide demonstrations demanding higher wages and improved public services.

The French Interior Ministry estimated participation at 146,000, including 28,000 in Paris, while trade unions put the turnout significantly higher at approximately 550,000 nationwide and 175,000 in the capital.

The demonstrations marked the third nationwide public sector strike since September, following failed discussions with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Friday.

Unions are demanding salary increases after the government ruled out a general pay rise for public employees for the fourth consecutive year. They estimate that public servants have lost 16 percent of their purchasing power since 2017, arguing that declining wages and worsening conditions are affecting essential services, including schools and hospitals.

Students also joined the demonstrations, with many expressing concerns about education, university access and the country’s economic future.

In Paris, nurse Aurelane Thos said deteriorating conditions in schools and hospitals and staff shortages were among the issues motivating workers to protest. University professor Nicolas Prevot also called for the protection of human rights and public services, while warning against the far right gaining political power ahead of next year’s presidential elections.

Although most demonstrations remained peaceful, authorities deployed security forces and temporarily prohibited the sale of firecrackers amid concerns about possible violence.

World.title: International News: Series of US outages raises cybersecurity concerns as FBI warns of AI-powered hacking tool
World.content:
International News: Series of US outages raises cybersecurity concerns as FBI warns of AI-powered hacking tool

By Zoila Palma: A series of major technical disruptions affecting U.S. transportation, banking and online services over the past several days has raised concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure, particularly as the FBI warns that cybercriminals are using an advanced hacking tool powered by artificial intelligence.

The disruptions included a nationwide flight ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday after an air traffic communications network became unstable, alongside outages affecting Microsoft 365 and payroll provider Workday.

CNN reports that the FBI had issued an urgent warning to private-sector cybersecurity officials earlier that Friday, identifying a tool known as ARTEX that was originally developed to help organizations detect weaknesses in their own computer systems.

However, the agency warned that malicious actors had gained access to the tool and were using it to target organizations globally across sectors including finance, government, technology, defense, energy, healthcare and telecommunications.

According to the FBI, some attacks using ARTEX have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

The warning comes as additional disruptions were reported on Monday, when United Airlines experienced a technical shutdown that grounded flights, while JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo customers reported difficulties accessing their accounts online.

Although none of the incidents had been classified as the work of foreign adversaries or cybercriminals, cybersecurity experts noted the unusual concentration of major disruptions within a short period.

Experts also cautioned that AI-powered hacking tools could allow individuals with limited technical expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks at a much faster pace.

World.title: Reggae Boyz edged by Mexico in Nations League quarter-final
World.content:
Jamaica's defender #02 Miguel Freckleton reacts at the end of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final second leg football match between Mexico and Jamaica at the BBVA stadium in Guadalupe, Nuevo Leon state, Mexico on November 17, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz were edged by Mexico on away goals after losing 1-0 to El Tri in the quarterfinal return leg at the BBVA stadium in Monterey, Mexico on Tuesday.

A first half goal from Jesus Corona was the difference on the night, levelling the scores at 3-3 on aggregate, but the Mexicans won based on the two away goals they scored in Saturday’s first leg 3-2 loss.

Jamaica, ranked 66th in the world, spectacularly led the first leg tie 3-0 before Mexico rallied late at the National Stadium in Kingston to reduce the deficit.

In addition to being eliminated from the Concacaf Nations League, Jamaica will now have to attempt to qualify for the Gold Cup though the play-offs.

Tuesday’s win was the first for Mexico’s newly appointed coach Rafa Marquez in six games.

Jamaica had several chances in a frenetic first half, the best in the 25th minute when they caught Mexico on a break with goalkeeper Raul Rangel caught outside the 18-yard box. But, despite getting past the defender, Renaldo Cephas tripped up and was overtaken by a fast recovering defender.

At the other end, Jamaica managed to keep out Mexico which had made several changes to the team that started in Kingston. Goalkeeper Jahmali Waite made a brilliant save in the 13th minute, parrying a header from Roberto Alvarado for a corner.

However, the Boyz had no answer for a well struck left footer from Corona, starting for El Tri for the first time since 2022, from just on the edge of the 18-yard box into the low left hand corner of Waite’s goal in the 35th minute.

The second half failed to rise to the intensity of the first 45 minutes and, despite throwing a number of attacking players into the fray, Jamaica failed to get the goal that would have seen them create one of the biggest upsets in Concacaf football.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: SYGNUS COURTS LENDERS TO HIT US$1-BILLION TARGET
World.content:
(Photo: Dacx Productions)

SYGNUS Credit Investments Limited (SCI) expects to announce a second multilateral financing partnership within weeks and is in talks with two other development lenders, as it looks to secure a larger bank credit line to fund private-credit deals across the Caribbean.

Jason Morris, co-founder and chief investment officer of Sygnus Capital, told investors and analysts on SCI’s November 16 earnings call that the forthcoming partner would finance SCI directly. The company is still working towards term sheets with the two other institutions. Morris did not name the incoming lender or disclose the size and terms of the facility.

“We’ve cracked the glass ceiling, so to speak, by getting a partnership with IBD Invest, and as you’ll see, in hopefully days or weeks’ time, we have a second multilateral financing partner that will finance SCI directly,” Morris said.

SCI’s first multilateral partnership dates to June, when it agreed to guarantee an uncommitted revolving working capital facility of up to US$10 million from IDB Invest for Sygnus Investment Bahamas. SCI is also an anchor investor in the Bahamas vehicle, which provides financing against businesses’ receivables.

Morris said backing from several development lenders would expand the pool of capital SCI can invest and strengthen its case when it approaches banks.

“Once we have two, three, four multilaterals, which will increase SCI’s ability, our pool of capital, it will also increase SCI’s ability to perhaps, soon enough, get access to a credit line from a bank that wants to do business in the Caribbean,” Morris explained during the question and answer segment.

SCI wants to build up US$100 million in capital available for investment, preferably with a large share in revolving credit lines. That would give it room to draw funds as deals close and borrow again as it repays the lines. At September 30, the company held US$11.16 million in cash and short-term instruments available for investment, with about US$2.45 million in undrawn revolving credit lines. It received the equivalent of US$13 million from its Class J and Class K perpetual preference-share offer during the quarter and said it expected the remaining proceeds after quarter-end.

The continuous drive for funding comes as SCI aims to lift cumulative private-credit deployment across its platform to US$1 billion by June 2030. Morris said SCI and its Puerto Rico business, Acrecent Financial, had deployed more than US$683 million to date and that he would like to reach the target about a year early. He said the platform would need to originate and deploy at least US$100 million annually. At the time of the call, he put the platform’s portfolio at about US$332 million.

SCI financed US$4.11 million in new investment commitments in the September quarter, roughly in line with US$4.10 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, Acrecent deployed US$26.44 million over the same period, including deals originated in the previous quarter.

Morris noted that several SCI transactions had reached final documentation, with deployment likely to pick up later in the financial year.

Net profit attributable to SCI shareholders rose 14 per cent to US$3.62 million for the quarter, helped by higher net interest income, lower fair-value losses and stronger foreign exchange gains. Total investment income of the firm slipped 1.1 per cent to US$5.19 million, while net investment income fell 9.7 per cent as operating expenses rose.

World.title: Fired up!
World.content:
There are more than 1,500 Church’s Texas Chicken locations in over 20 countries.

CHURCH’S Texas Chicken says it remains on track to open 10 restaurants in Jamaica in five years after its first two Kingston locations beat sales projections.

This was the update provided by Anthony Sabga-Aboud, director at Global Brands Limited, during the official opening of its second location at Parade Square, in downtown Kingston. Global Brands Group of Companies is the franchise holder for the Church’s brand in Trinidad & Tobago, St Lucia, St Kitts and Jamaica.

“So, we are on track to hit our goal of 10 locations in five years. This is our second location, and we are actively looking at other sites,” Sabga-Aboud explained on Monday.

The new downtown location saw the company invest more than US$1 million to transform the property at the corner of King Street and South Parade. The company then hired 70 new employees, while creating a space that meets the Church’s brand and improves disability access.

With the company securing two locations in under two years, the Trinidadian businessman noted that his team is in active discussion with several property owners about opening new stores next year.

“We’re very excited about this [Parade] location and we think it’s going to be an iconic location for us,” he said.

The Church’s brand returned to Jamaica in December 2025, nearly two decades after it last operated on the island. Global Brands made a similar investment in its first Jamaican location, at Mall Plaza on Constant Spring Road, where it hired 60 employees.

The re-entry to the Jamaican market broke several global records according to Watson George, the Global Brands executive responsible for the Church’s Texas Chicken brand. That Mall Plaza store broke metrics such as customer count, transaction count and even sales for the first-day opening of a new Church’s location. There are more than 1,500 Church’s locations in over 20 countries.

“In fact, that [Mall Plaza] opening in that market was the best opening globally,” George added.

The Parade Square location also broke a regional record as it’s now the largest Church’s restaurant in Latin America and the Caribbean. The available space on the property also gives the team more room to expand the operations as it adjusts to the downtown environment.

Although the company intends to expand across the island, focus will be placed on Kingston and St Andrew; Portmore and Spanish Town, St Catherine. Deandra Jones is the country manager for Church’s in Jamaica while Dane Swaby is the restaurant general manager for Mall Plaza location.

“We are proud to be part of downtown Kingston, proud to be creating jobs for Jamaicans and proud to bring that great taste. This is only the beginning of our Jamaican journey, and we think that the future is extremely bright,” George added in his remarks.

Aside from the new jobs created, George also pointed to the various suppliers and contractors who are benefiting from the continued expansion of the brand in Jamaica. Jamaica Broilers Group Limited, Wisynco Group Limited and Massy Gas Products Limited all supply each Church’s brand with various inputs needed to serve their customers. Massy Gas Products is a subsidiary of Trinidadian conglomerate Massy Holdings Limited.

The success of Church’s in Jamaica continues to reinforce Global Brands’ confidence in the Jamaican economy which was significantly impacted by Hurricane Melissa in October 2025. The positive reception from customers and speed to launch the second Church’s location reinforces the demand from the Jamaican public for different quick-service brands.

Global Brands currently operates several food brands such as Pizza Boys, Wok ‘n Roll, Rituals Sushi and Rituals Coffee House across the Caribbean. Rituals Coffee House operates at Village Plaza, adjacent to Mall Plaza.

“It’s been very, very positive. It’s a great country. A great economy. You know, we want to keep growing and keep being part of the community,” Sabga-Aboud reiterated.

Church’s Texas Chicken is currently owned by private equity firm High Bluff Capital, with the brand receiving an injection of capital by Golub Capital in July 2026. The company signed an agreement in April 2026 to open 600 or more restaurants in China over several years. Church’s Texas Chicken was founded in April 1952 by George W Church Sr.

World.title: Fiscal watchdog backs another year of relief from Jamaica’s budget rules
World.content:
The town of Black River, the capital of St Elizabeth, is seen decimated by Hurricane Melissa last October.

Jamaica’s fiscal watchdog has backed a plan to keep the country’s budget rules suspended for another year, saying the cost of rebuilding after Hurricane Melissa is putting continued pressure on government finances.

The Independent Fiscal Commission said the government faces higher recovery costs while collecting less revenue than expected. Requiring it to meet the rules in 2027/28 could disrupt reconstruction, the commission warned.

The proposed extension still needs Parliament’s approval.

The rules are intended to keep the government’s finances and debt under control. Extending the suspension would give it more room to meet recovery costs while the economy recovers.

The government also plans to seek parliamentary approval for a separate change: moving the deadline for bringing public debt down to 60 per cent of the size of the economy, or less, from 2027/28 to 2031/32.

That would give it four more years to meet the debt target. The one-year extension of the suspension would not automatically change that deadline.

Fiscal Commissioner Courtney Williams validated the request for the additional year on November 13, following a review of the finance ministry’s submission and other economic data.

The commission found that Jamaica was still dealing with significant financial and economic damage from Melissa, which struck as a Category 5 hurricane on October 28, 2025.

Updated assessments by the Inter-American Development Bank and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean put damage and losses at about US$12.2 billion, the commission said.

That is almost 40 per cent higher than the initial estimate and equivalent to more than half the value of everything Jamaica’s economy produced in 2024.

The larger damage estimate points to a more expensive rebuilding effort that will take longer to complete. Central government spending on infrastructure and other capital projects is projected to increase by J$21.8 billion in 2027/28.

At the same time, government income has fallen short of expectations.

Revenue and grants were J$27.8 billion below budget between April and September 2026. Most of that gap came from tax collections, which were J$22.6 billion below target.

The commission said some of the shortfall reflected when payments were received. However, it also linked weaker collections to continuing disruption from the hurricane and expects those pressures to last into 2027/28.

The economy is also expected to grow more slowly than previously forecast, limiting growth in tax revenue and making it harder to reduce debt relative to the size of the economy.

Public debt is projected to stand at 65.5 per cent of gross domestic product — the total value of goods and services produced — at the end of 2026/27. It is forecast to decline to 58.8 per cent by 2031/32.

The commission’s assessment clears a required step towards extending the suspension. The finance minister must now make an order and secure Parliament’s approval before it takes effect.

Changing the debt deadline would require a separate amendment to the Financial Administration and Audit Act.

The commission said the additional flexibility would leave financial scrutiny in place. The government would still have to report on its finances, Parliament would retain oversight, and the commission would continue monitoring public debt and other fiscal risks.

World.title: WATCH: Church’s Chicken expands Jamaica presence with second location
World.content:
Buoyed by strong sales at its Mall Plaza outlet, Church’s Texas Chicken is expanding its footprint in Kingston with the opening of a second location, signalling confidence in the Jamaican market and growing consumer demand for the international fast-food brand.

Supervisor Kevin Wilson said the outlet at Mall Plaza has done “exceptionally well”, fueling the move to launch the second location at the corner of King Street and Parade Square in downtown Kingston.

“We [Church’s Mall Plaza] were one of the best Church’s regionally and internationally so therefore … we are looking forward to maximizing on the [performance] of the first store, and doing even better,” Wilson said at the launch on Monday.

(Video: Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: CORRECTION AND APOLOGY
World.content:
On October 16 2026, the Jamaica Observer on its online edition published an article entitled “Update: Two men killed after gun battle with police in Sligoville” which contained a photograph and several allegations and statements concerning Lamond Sutherland.

The information contained in the article was published based on information received from law enforcement authorities at the time. It has since been established that Mr Lamond Sutherland was incorrectly identified, that the allegations and statements were false and that he was not in any way a party to the incident.

Jamaica Observer unreservedly retracts the article and sincerely apologises to Mr Lamond, Sutherland who is still very much alive, for any distress, embarrassment or damage to his personal and professional reputation which may have been caused by the publication.

World.title: ‘I will not be intimidated’ says House Speaker Juliet Holness
World.content:
House Speaker Juliet Holness speaking in Parliament on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. (Photo: Karl McLarty)

Embattled Speaker of the House of Representatives Juliet Holness has declared that she will not be intimidated by any member while carrying out her duties in the nation’s Parliament.

Holness made the remark in a statement at the start of Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives, the first since the near brawl that came at the end of the last sitting on November 3.

WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

She told her fellow lawmakers that disagreement with the chair does not render its statements improper and it should not become a demand by any member for silence.

“Let me be equally clear, I will not be intimidated into silence or pressured into abandoning my responsibilities,” she stated while promising to continue to discharge her duties as speaker “with firmness, fairness and impartiality while respecting the rights of every member while upholding the authority of the chair”.

During the November 3 sitting of the House, Opposition Member of Parliament Mikael Phillips and Government member Desmond McKenzie had to be physically separated. Opposition members have alleged that the way the speaker conducted herself during the sitting led to the standoff. Even so, the relationship between Holness and Opposition members has been both testy and antagonistic.

During her statement on Tuesday, Holness emphasised that her role as speaker is separate and apart from her marriage to Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness. She also said the strength of Parliament rests not merely in the authority that it exercises, but in the principles it upholds and the standards it maintains.

She said while robust debate and principled disagreements are essential to democracy, “neither protest nor disagreement justifies disorder, obstruction or defiance of the chair”.

Holness said the standing orders governing the function of the Parliament are not merely guidelines made pursuant to the authority of the constitution of Jamaica. She said they govern parliamentary proceedings, protect members’ rights and establish the responsibility of the chair to maintain order.

She insisted that:“No member stands above these rules and their application cannot depend on whether a ruling meets with individual approval”.

Holness also noted that questions have been raised about her independence because of her marriage to the prime minister. She said while she has generally allowed her service to speak for itself, the constitutional position should be made clear.

She pointed out that she is the duly-elected three-term Member of Parliament for St Andrew East Rural and said it was her duty in terms of representing her constituents in the House.

“The mandate is mine in own right, neither conferred nor diminished by my marriage,” she remarked.

Holness pointed to section 43 of the Constitution which provides for the election of the speaker and the circumstances in which the office becomes vacant.

“I was duly elected to this chair and my marriage is neither a constitutional disqualification nor a measure of my independence or judgment,” she declared.

She told the House that any disagreement concerning her rulings are matters for parliamentary procedure to be assessed against the standing orders rather than her personal relationship.

“I stand by the rulings I have made and procedures grounded upon which they were given,” she said. She also told members that they are entitled to challenge decisions through the appropriate parliamentary processes but insisted that there is a clear distinction between legitimate scrutiny and personal attacks or intimidation intended to undermine her authority.

-Lynford Simpson

World.title: Deadly drug-resistant infections are surging in European hospitals
World.content:
The findings on treatment-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae were “the biggest concern” among all the data collected on superbugs in Europe over the past year, Christian Giske, who leads this work at ECDC, told a press briefing.

It’s one example of the dangers posed by antimicrobial resistance — the ability of bacteria and fungi to evolve to be resistant to drugs designed to destroy them — which is estimated to kill 35,000 people in the EU, Iceland and Norway every year. For Europe, this is a “major public health threat,” Giske said.

Despite progress in some areas, the latest reports show the EU is still far from reaching its 2030 targets to reduce rates of drug-resistant infections. Among the challenges is the limited number of new drugs available to treat such infections.

The news comes as Europe's new pharmaceutical legislation is set to be signed into law in December and includes measures to boost the discovery and development of new antibiotics — through a market monopoly perk for industry and a push for steady payment models for countries to buy them.

Harder to tackle

Given that it spreads between patients, tackling the surging rates of Klebsiella requires stronger infection prevention and control measures in hospitals, the ECDC warns. This includes strengthening hand hygiene, ensuring correct use of personal protective equipment like gloves, and effective environmental cleaning and disinfection.

And while similar measures have helped to significantly cut EU rates of the better-known hospital-acquired superbug, MRSA, for Klebsiella, missing even the tiniest surface can lead to the bacteria spreading.

World.title: When EU foreign policy jobs collide
World.content:
Kaja Kallas may be the EU’s top diplomat, but her role in key diplomatic discussions —whether on Ukraine or Israel — remains murky.

Today on the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart examine the increasingly overlapping job descriptions of Kaja Kallas and the EU’s Commissioner for the Mediterranean, Dubravka Šuica, and unpack what that says about EU diplomacy.

Also on the podcast: Is Russian President Vladimir Putin serious about peace? Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys doesn’t think so.

And finally, nobody seems to want to live in Luxembourg — which is problematic for the institutions based there looking to recruit more people.

World.title: Procès “femmeblancherie” : quand l’idéologie masculiniste devient une menace sécuritaire
World.content:
En face, les associations de lutte contre la haine en ligne, comme Point de contact, StopFisha, Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement et la Fondation des femmes, se sont constituées parties civiles au procès. Leur objectif : l’ériger en exemple des dangers du masculinisme pour la sécurité nationale.

“Ce qui n’est pas assez identifié, c’est le lien entre les masculinistes et le passage à l’acte violent”, explique à POLITICO Alejandra Mariscal, directrice de Point de contact. “Telegram est la partie émergée de l’iceberg, il faut évoquer la porosité avec les autres services numériques et le continuum entre les violences en ligne et hors ligne.”

Il faut dire que les affaires du genre se multiplient. Questionné par POLITICO, le Parquet national antiterroriste (Pnat) pointe l’essor, en 2025, des enquêtes sur “ce champ idéologique protéiforme” — qui reste toutefois marginal par rapport à d’autres menaces, comme les courants djihadistes.

La toute première enquête a ainsi été ouverte en juin 2025, soit quelques mois avant le début des investigations sur le réseau “femmeblancherie”. Elle concernait un jeune homme de 18 ans se revendiquant de la mouvance Incel, rappelle le Pnat à POLITICO.

L’épineux problème des “zones grises”

L’administrateur du groupe “femmeblancherie” postait quotidiennement des publications sur la thématique du “problème femme”, largement commentées par ses abonnés. L’enquête a aussi mis en avant l’attrait des membres pour les mouvances d’extrême droite radicales. L’exploitation des téléphones des prévenus a ainsi révélé une appétence des abonnés du canal pour les sites des négationnistes Alain Soral et de Vincent Reynouard, “eux-mêmes fréquemment condamnés pour des incitations à la haine”, souligne le parquet de Paris, qui précise que Telegram a répondu à toutes les réquisitions et permis d’identifier un certain nombre de prévenus.

Ces derniers ont reconnu pour la plupart les messages, mais se défendent en invoquant “un ‘humour noir’ ou ‘humour beauf’, ou avoir écrit sous l’effet de l’alcool ou de l’agacement”, relate le parquet.

World.title: Trump trifft Putin und Xi: Was bedeutet das für den Ukraine-Gipfel in Berlin?
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share via email

Während der Kanzler die Koalition der Willigen morgen zur Ukraine-Unterstützung in Berlin versammelt, inszeniert sich Donald Trump heute schon am anderen Ende der Welt. Beim Gipfel im chinesischen Shenzhen trifft er auf Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin, während seine Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner im Kanzleramt weitgehend schweigen müssen. Was dieses geopolitische Schattenspiel für den Westen bedeutet, analysiert Vize-Chefredakteurin Annett Meiritz zusammen mit Rixa Fürsen.

Wie blickt Europa auf dieses Dreiertreffen der Weltmächte, bei dem die EU nicht dabei ist? Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, Vorsitzende des EU-Verteidigungsausschusses, erklärt im 200-Sekunden-Interview, warum es paradoxerweise ein gutes Zeichen ist, dass in China nicht über die Ukraine gesprochen wird und welche Rolle der Iran in Trumps globalem Machtpoker spielt.

Nach elf Jahren hat die Bundeswehr ihren Einsatz im Irak beendet, auch die US-Truppen sind abgezogen. Nun reist Entwicklungsministerin Reem Alabali Radovan nach Erbil, um den Fokus auf wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit zu lenken. POLITICO-Reporterin Carlotta Diederich berichtet vor Ort, wie fragil die Sicherheitslage im irakischen Machtvakuum zwischen IS-Überresten und pro-iranischen Milizen tatsächlich ist.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: Europe fears Putin is stringing Trump along on Ukraine
World.content:
Some European observers fear that if it does fall apart, Trump could simply cut a deal with Putin and walk away from Europe and Ukraine — and that’s one reason why they’re sticking with the talks.

“Putin is not interested in a ceasefire or peace now,” said Fredrik Wesslau, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “He believes he has more to gain from continuing the war than having a ceasefire. This is the fundamental problem.”

European officials’ doubts show that despite intensive efforts to revive the peace process — and time-consuming internal debates about who would represent Europe — the fate of the talks is still likely out of their hands.

Moscow’s hard line

Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, bombing two major bridges in Kyiv, as well as continuing attacks on energy and water networks. Ukraine has kept retaliating with strikes deep inside Russia that have damaged oil facilities, much to the U.S.’s ire.

Teams from Ukraine and Russia gathered with Trump’s two senior peace envoys — his son-in-law Jared Kushner and fellow real estate developer Steve Witkoff — in Abu Dhabi for two days of negotiations last week, the first since February.

The talks yielded a promise of a prisoner swap between Ukraine and Russia although the details have still not been finalized. But beyond that, there wasn’t much to write home about. European officials involved in Abu Dhabi reported that the Russian side had been reluctant to give ground.

World.title: The ‘bad boys of Brexit’ are getting a boost from Burnham’s EU reset
World.content:
Their pro-EU counterparts have proved slower out the traps, but they are discussing their next steps and watching nervously as Burnham appears to already be tempering expectations of what he can achieve.

One thing EU Rejoiners are clear on is that they won’t be dusting off the berets and gold star flags of 2016. They are using a familiar progressive playbook, and emphasizing how closer ties could ease cost-of-living pressures on Brits.

Where the campaigns go next rests largely with Burnham, and on just how far he decides to go in his rekindling of the European flame after Friday’s upcoming EU-U.K. summit in Brussels.

Old kids on the bloc

Eurosceptic campaigners — like in 2016, both competing and complementary — are already getting to work trying to convince Britons they don’t want to be back in the EU.

A new look “Vote Leave” outfit was the first to fire up, with former Brexit negotiator Oliver Lewis launching “Stay Out” — with the backing of Conservative former Cabinet minister Michael Gove.

The Leave.EU campaign co-founded by Nigel Farage ally Arron Banks — who once branded his allies the “bad boys of Brexit” — is re-emerging as “Enough Official.” Its opening offer is a hardline video on immigration.

World.title: Commission takes EU’s Middle East spotlight as Kallas’ Israel channel stays frozen
World.content:
“By allowing the high representative to be frozen out by Israel and not working together on the Middle East in line with the Treaties and international law, President von der Leyen is helping undermine the EU as a credible global actor,” Barry Andrews, a liberal EU lawmaker and chair of the European Parliament’s Development Committee, said.

Šuica has become a regular point of contact for Israel and the U.S. She attended the inaugural meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace in Washington in February and has met or spoken with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar at least four times this year.

“Without Israel, you can’t do anything,” Šuica previously told POLITICO, referring to efforts to get aid into Gaza. “We need the approval of Israeli authorities. And this is why we have to keep channels open … They are there, and we need to work with them.” Her Middle East missions are coordinated “around a table” with Kallas, she said.

Kallas’ channel to Sa’ar has been closed since a public falling out in June. The rupture came after reports that she had compared Israel’s treatment of Palestinians to apartheid-era South Africa. Sa’ar said he would “sever all contact” with her until she retracted what he called a “blood libel” against Israel.

Kallas has not addressed the reported apartheid comment, and her allies have declined to say whether she used the analogy.

The decision to cut off contact remains in place, Sa’ar’s spokesperson Michal Maayan said, adding that the choice “relates solely” to the chief diplomat. “Israel continues to engage constructively with EU institutions and Member States, and Minister Sa’ar maintains strong and close ties with the foreign ministers of EU Member States and other EU officials.”

World.title: Same purchase, different protection
World.content:
On November 20, the revised Consumer Credit Directive (CCD2) will start to apply. Among a number of updates, it will give shoppers across the EU who split purchases into interest-free instalments through buy now, pay later (BNPL) products, regardless of provider, the same core protections: a creditworthiness check, clear pre-contract information and a right of withdrawal. Yet many member states have not yet written the directive into national law, so those protections are not yet consistent across the bloc.

According to the European Commission’s infringement procedures published on October 1, 16 of 27 member states failed to meet the November 20, 2025 deadline to write the directive into national law. This means that, one year on, consumers face a patchwork of protections, with BNPL remaining unregulated in some markets.

We have called for BNPL to be regulated for years, and we welcome CCD2. We have held a Swedish banking license since 2017 and already assess credit on every purchase, so the directive changes less for us than for many competitors. That is why we care about consistent application across Europe. Uneven implementation works against the directive’s aim.

One year on, consumers face a patchwork of protections, with BNPL remaining unregulated in some markets.

Slow transposition is not the only concern. In some countries, national rules go beyond the proportionate framework set out in Brussels. Each addition may be well-intentioned, but together they cut against CCD2’s aim of modernizing credit. Belgium offers a telling example: its rules require Belgian consumers to give signed confirmation of delivery before a credit agreement takes effect. This obligation was designed in the 1990s, when e-commerce was just starting, and is impractical in today’s e-commerce world, in which consumers want payment and credit products embedded in their online shopping experience. In the Netherlands, where national implementation is still being discussed, credit providers may be required to create a dedicated register of merchants to be held by the financial regulator. Yet it is not clear how this register would concretely benefit consumers. Taken together, these market-by-market differences mean a provider serving consumers across the EU must build and maintain several versions of the same product, which runs against the spirit of the single market.

We are not suggesting CCD2 needs to be revised, nor are we seeking a delay to implementation. We are ready for CCD2 and believe it will bring great improvements to the market for consumers and providers. But late transposition and unnecessary gold-plating result in poor outcomes. To return to the Belgian example, the final rules containing the outdated delivery-signature requirement were only published in July 2026. This has meant providers have had only a few weeks, rather than the 12 months intended by the directive, to get everything in place to be compliant by November 2026. Such a short transition period affects the whole ecosystem, not just credit providers. Retailers that advertise or offer BNPL credit at checkout must adapt too, just as the busiest shopping season of the year begins.

The goal is not to remove national protections but to apply one high standard everywhere. A consumer should not receive weaker protection because their government was late, or different protection because of a national quirk.

CCD2 is also a useful cautionary tale for Europe’s competitiveness agenda. A directive sets an objective and leaves each country to write its own rules, which, exactly as we have seen with CCD2, can lead to delay, divergence and gold-plating. A regulation applies directly, everywhere, at the same time. Moving more of Brussels’ rulemaking to regulations would, as a former Italian prime minister, Enrico Letta, argues in his report on the future of the single market, do wonders for the overall cohesiveness of the EU. Another former Italian prime minister, Mario Draghi, agrees, and recommended in his report on European competitiveness that directives be phased out in favor of more regulations. For its part, the European Commission appears, at the very least, to recognize the problem, and in its recent communication on the competitiveness of the banking sector committed to look more closely at national implementation of CCD2 and other directives. We welcome that scrutiny.

The goal is not to remove national protections but to apply one high standard everywhere. A consumer should not receive weaker protection because their government was late, or different protection because of a national quirk. Fragmentation does not protect consumers. It leaves gaps and makes products harder to compare.

So what should happen now? The immediate priority is to close the open infringement cases, which should encourage member states to finish transposition.

More broadly, EU co-legislators should learn from this rollout for the next round of consumer law. As debates begin on the Digital Fairness Act, policymakers have an opportunity to choose a regulation from the start, rather than repeating the patchwork of CCD2.

A shopper in Madrid should receive the same protection, on the same day, as a shopper in Berlin, Paris or Amsterdam, whoever they borrow from — November 20, 2026 was meant to be that day. In too many countries, it will not be. Europe has these principles. What it still has to show is that it can apply them evenly.

World.title: 007 set-jetting: Iconic James Bond filming locations around Europe you can visit
World.content:
Five years after Daniel Craig had his last outing as the iconic British spy in No Time to Die (2021), we finally know who is stepping up as the seventh James Bond: Robert Pattinson.

 

Whether you agree with the casting or not – Euronews Culture’s David Mouriquand says it’s “simultaneously an inspired choice, a frustrating one, and a very safe bet” – the news has us feeling nostalgic.

Over the course of 25 official movies, the shaken-not-stirred martini drinker served Her Majesty’s Secret Service in countries across the globe, inspiring travellers to visit far-flung locations long before “set-jetting” had entered the lexicon.

Filming location pilgrimages will no doubt include Khao Phing Kan in Thailand, aka Scaramanga's Island in The Man with the Golden Gun (1974), and Udaipur’s Taj Lake Palace, which served as Octopussy’s floating palace lair. Mexico City’s Day of the Dead parade – which was actually reverse engineered from scenes in Spectre (2015) – is on the bucket list, too.

But what about Bond locations closer to home? Ahead of Pattinson’s turn serving His Majesty’s Secret Service (the first time ever for 007!) in 2028, we’ve rounded up some of the most iconic James Bond filming locations in Europe.

Scene-stealing Bond landscapes

Glen Etive Road features in Skyfall as the secret agent and M make their way to Bond's family home, Skyfall Lodge Cara Anna/AP

Glencoe and Glen Etive, Scotland: Skyfall (2012)

Scotland has long been a popular choice for moviemakers for its dramatic scenery, with several James Bond films featuring scenes shot here, including The World Is Not Enough (1999), The Spy Who Loved Me (1977), and From Russia With Love (1963).

The most memorable, however, might just be Skyfall, when the double-oh agent and M make their way to the Bond family home, Skyfall Lodge, along Glen Etive road.

With the brooding hero and his Aston Martin DB5 set against the Buachaille Etive Mòr mountain, this iconic shot has been recreated plenty of times over the years.

Furka Pass was the scene of the car chase in Goldfinger Maud Bocquillod/Unsplash

Furka Pass, Switzerland: Goldfinger (1964)

Another recognisable road, this time in Switzerland, the Furka Pass had its starring role in Goldfinger.

The movie series is known for its car chases, and Sean Connery’s Bond sets after the eponymous villain along the winding roads here.

Today, drivers passing through can stop at “James Bond Strasse” which has a view over all the twists and turns.

You can bungee jump from Verzasca Dam like Pierce Brosnan did in GoldenEye AP Photo

Verzasca Dam, Switzerland: GoldenEye (1995)

Bond sure knows how to make an entrance, but the opening scenes of GoldenEye were particularly of note.

Marking Pierce Brosnan’s debut as Ian Fleming’s world-famous character in spectacular style, Bond bungee jumps off the Verzasca Dam to make his way into the secret base below.

The 220-metre-high dam is open to the public, and, if you’re feeling Bond levels of brave, you can even bungee jump off it.

In Quantum of Solace, Bond chases after Quantum mole Mitchell across the rooftops of Siena Harry Robinson/Unsplash

Siena, Italy: Quantum of Solace (2008)

Like Scotland, Italy features in numerous Bond movies, including Craig’s second outing as the sartorial secret agent in Quantum of Solace.
