While the Day of the Dead parade from Spectre is (or at least, was) fictional, the horse race that serves as the backdrop for a high intensity chase in the 2008 flick is very much real, and has been going on for centuries.

With the Palio di Siena going on below, Craig follows Quantum mole Mitchell across the rooftops of Siena, and while we don’t recommend attempting your own recreation of the various stunts here, you can enjoy similar views over the terracotta tiled roofs from the Siena Cathedral.

Bond-approved hotels

Hotel Cala di Volpe, Sardinia, Italy: The Spy Who Loved Me (1977)

Sardinia’s Hotel Cala di Volpe has long attracted celebrity guests, including the world’s most famous spy in 1977.

Roger Moore checked in here with Bond girl Naomi in The Spy Who Loved Me, although the suite they took was actually the property’s bar, which has since been transformed into Japanese restaurant Matsuhisa.

We’re not sure if Bond would approve, but during the summer months, you can wash down chef Nobu’s famed dishes here with a Matsutini, a twist on the classic with passionfruit and yuzu.

Palácio Estoril Hotel, Portugal: On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969)

Cascais’ Palácio Estoril Hotel has not one, but two connections to the franchise.

In George Lazenby’s one-time Bond portrayal, On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, the charismatic assassin with a licence to kill stays at the property.

You can even meet one of the film’s (ahem) stars as José Diogo, then an 18-year-old bellboy, who hands over the room key to Bond, still works here as a concierge.

As for the second connection, Bond author Ian Fleming stayed here in 1941, and the register in which he checked in as a government official is framed in the hotel’s royal gallery.

Plus, a card game between enemy spooks at Casino Estoril is said to have inspired the high-stakes showdown with Le Chiffre in Casino Royale.

The exterior shots of the Hotel Spendide in Montenegro were actually Grandhotel Pupp in Czechia Grandhotel Pupp/Jan Maly

Grandhotel Pupp, Czechia: Casino Royale (2006)

Speaking of, the 2006 reboot of the franchise, Casino Royale, may be centred around the Hotel Splendide in Montenegro, but its stand-in – the Grandhotel Pupp – is in Czechia.

Nearby, you’ll also find the Kaiserbad Spa, which was used for the exterior shots of the Casino Royale.

Bond’s bites, beverages and bets

Switzerland's Schilthorn mountain featured in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service Aswathy N/Unsplash

Piz Gloria, Switzerland: On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969)

While you probably wouldn’t want to eat here in the Bond universe, given it’s where Ernst Stavro Blofeld plotted to create a biological weapon in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, in reality Piz Gloria is home to a revolving restaurant with one hell of a view.

Located at 2,970 metres above sea level, after reaching the summit via cable car you’ll be surrounded by alpine peaks which stun year-round.

Sky high views obviously come with sky high prices, but for mega fans, it’s more than worth it.

Le Jules Verne restaurant, Paris: A View to a Kill (1985)

The 14th Bond film, A View to a Kill, certainly delivered on the view and the kill part, with a French agent assassinated over lunch with Moore’s Bond at Le Jules Verne restaurant in the Eiffel Tower.

The stunt element, which sees the assassin parachute off the tower after being pursued by the world-class operative on the stairs, was filmed on-site, although the restaurant interiors were shot on a set.

Hopefully, you won’t suffer the same fate if you choose to dine at the Michelin two-starred eatery yourself…

Pierce Brosnan's Bond played baccarat with femme fatale Xenia Onatopp at the Casino de Monte-Carlo RAVI TRIPATHI/Unsplash

Casino de Monte-Carlo, Monaco: GoldenEye (1995)

Brosnan’s Bond plays the brilliantly-named Xenia Onatopp at baccarat at the Casino de Monte-Carlo in GoldenEye, with the exterior shots filmed on location in Monaco.

For a taste of Bond’s glamorous lifestyle, make a beeline for the casino’s Salle Europe Bar, which serves up both a shaken, not stirred martini as well as a Vesper, a cocktail invented by Bond in the first novel of the series featuring vodka, gin and white lillet.

Dukes Bar, London

Okay, so this spot isn’t featured in any of the James Bond movies, but as a regular hangout spot for Fleming, London’s famed Dukes Bar is well worth a visit.

Known for its martinis, which are served in frozen glasses with no ice, it’s said that the intelligence officer-turned-journalist-turned-author came up with the “shaken, not stirred” line while drinking here.

Open since 1908, the hotel the bar is in is currently under renovation but will reopen in mid-2027, so you’ll be able to wash down a few martinis steps away from your bed.

World.title: Apple outage hits App Store,  becoming the latest casualty of major cyber breakdowns
World.content:
Many of Apple’s online services went down in a major outage following an update on Tuesday by the company, which followed other major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.

 

Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

Apple’s status page now suggests that none of its services is down.

Marriott International, the largest US hotel operator, also had technology issues, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.

In an emailed statement, Marriott said it has “resolved a technical issue” that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. The company added that a company review found no sign the problem “was cybersecurity-related.”

The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.

On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travellers across the US.

Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.

Banks were also affected on Monday after thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank's systems were operating normally.

Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.

The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

World.title: Human resources: Stop buying talent, start building it
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Paul Hamilton is the founder of Halo Service Solutions, a UK software company that has built its workforce around graduates, degree apprentices and other early-career talent. Here, he argues why businesses need to stop competing for the same pool of experienced candidates and start investing in developing the next generation.

 

I didn’t start growing the business with a theory about early-career talent. Fifteen years ago, working from my mother-in-law’s spare bedroom, I needed to make my first hire and could not compete with established companies for someone with a long track record. Recruiting a graduate was initially a practical decision, but it changed my view of what good hiring looks like. I saw that ability and experience were not the same, and people could progress much faster when an employer gave them real work and clear expectations.

I saw that ability and experience were not the same, and people could progress much faster when an employer gave them real work and clear expectations. Paul Hamilton Founder of UK-based software company Halo

Businesses: more a sports team than a family

I’m a huge fan of team sports, which probably explains why I think of a business more as a sports team than a family. A strong team gives people a sense of belonging without lowering its standards or losing its competitive edge. Experienced players help prepare the next generation because they know the whole team benefits when new talent comes through, and I think the same should be true in business.

Leaders need to know when to step in, but doing something faster themselves is not always a good reason to take over. Sometimes the better investment is letting someone else learn, despite mistakes having to be accounted for as part of individual growth.

Sports clubs understand a truth that many businesses seem to have forgotten: a strong first team cannot rely solely on buying established players. You need an academy that spots potential early, gives people time to learn and creates a clear route into senior roles.

You need an academy that spots potential early, gives people time to learn and creates a clear route into senior roles. Paul Hamilton Founder of UK-based software company Halo

Viewing the development of talents as part of running the business

Yet businesses across Europe continue to complain about skills shortages while competing for the same small pool of experienced candidates. They pay a premium to move proven people from one company to another, attach years of experience to supposedly entry-level jobs and then wonder why the supply of talent never grows.

This is the thinking behind Cantera, the name I use for our graduate, scholarship, degree-apprenticeship and college-leaver programmes. In Spanish football, the cantera is the system through which a club finds, develops and promotes young players. The word literally means “quarry”: a place where something valuable is found and carefully developed.

Athletic Bilbao's fans celebrate at San Mames stadium in Bilbao, Spain Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Athletic Bilbao is a prime example of a club that puts its academy at the heart of how it competes. Its commitment to fielding players from the Basque region means it must maintain high standards throughout its youth system.

Players who come through the academy learn the club’s standards, methods and identity long before they reach the first team. For employers, the lesson is not to copy a football club’s recruitment rules. It is to treat developing talent as part of running the business, rather than something separate from it.

Younger team members need work they can grow into

Gianmarco Rubino’s career shows that this route exists. He joined our Graduate Scheme in 2020, moved from Software Consultant to Product Manager in 2022 and became a director in 2023. His experience of the product, the industry and working directly with customers was part of that journey, alongside high levels of aptitude and the right attitude.

For new starters, seeing someone take that route successfully makes the opportunity and their own growth path tangible. Paul Hamilton Founder of UK-based software company Halo

For new starters, seeing someone take that route successfully makes the opportunity and their own growth path tangible. It shows that responsibility is not reserved for people who arrive with a senior title or a decade of experience.

Too often, young employees must spend years proving themselves before doors are opened to them. Customers and colleagues may instinctively place more trust in an older voice, including in the software industry. Employers cannot remove every external assumption, but they can choose not to reinforce it.

Younger team members need a clear remit, visible backing from senior leaders and opportunities to lead meetings, answer difficult questions and own the outcome. That does not mean leaving them to sink or swim. It means giving them work they can grow into, with someone ready to help when needed and develop their confidence as well as their understanding. We see trust grow when newer employees are given meaningful responsibility early.

Funding can support recruitment; it cannot replace development.

The October 2026 UK Budget gives employers more help to build younger workforces, but it does not remove that responsibility. It confirmed £100 million (Editor’s note: approximately 120 million Euro) to extend mayoral apprenticeship brokerage across England, along with a £2,000 (Editor’s note: approximately 2,400 Euro) payment for eligible young apprentices hired by non-levy-paying employers and a £3,000 (Editor’s note: approximately 3,600 Euro) Youth Jobs Grant for businesses taking on eligible unemployed young people.

These measures should make it easier, especially for smaller firms, to open the door. What happens after someone walks through it still depends on the employer: the quality of the coaching, the usefulness of the work and whether there is a real route to progression. Funding can support recruitment; it cannot replace development.

AI changes the work through which new starters learn

The same responsibility applies as AI changes the work through which new starters learn. The answer is not to preserve every repetitive task for its own sake. It is to redesign early-career learning so that AI becomes part of the academy rather than a substitute for it. New starters should use AI, as ignoring the productivity increases it provides would be naive, but they must also learn to question its output and explain why an answer is right or wrong. Used well, AI can speed up learning, but used carelessly, it can create false confidence without depth.

Used well, AI can speed up learning, but used carelessly, it can create false confidence without depth. Paul Hamilton Founder of UK-based software company Halo

A credible academy model has to account for hires that do not work out. It also needs to give experienced colleagues time to coach and check whether people are progressing. The test is not simply how many young people are recruited, but whether they become capable of taking on greater responsibility.

Our retention continues to sit well above 90% for employees who have been with us for over two years, which we are proud of, while recognising that this approach will not work in every case. The alternative, however, carries costs of its own: repeated recruitment fees, rising salaries for scarce experience, longer vacancies and a business that remains dependent on the external market.

Start deciding how you will help build the talent you need

By the end of 2030, we will have a team of over 1,000 in the UK, all recruited as graduates, degree apprentices or through other youth schemes. People often tell me how unusual that is. I am proud of the opportunities we can offer, but I do not want this approach to remain unusual. I want other businesses to see a model they can adapt, not an exception they can admire from a distance. This is how we intend to keep building the business as we grow.

We do not have all the answers. Developing people takes patience and a willingness to let people learn, and I understand that time can be one of the commodities businesses value most. But competing for the same experienced candidates will not give Europe a larger pool of talent.

The question is not whether to value experience, it is whether we are willing to give people the chance to gain it. Paul Hamilton Founder of UK-based software company Halo

More employers must help create it and be rewarded by retaining a large percentage of the best talent from the next generation. The question is not whether to value experience, it is whether we are willing to give people the chance to gain it. Stop asking only where you can buy the talent you need. Start deciding how you will help build it.

Paul Hamilton is the founder of UK-based software company Halo. Paul has built a successful technology business without external investment, taking an unconventional approach to recruitment and talent development. His team has an average age of 24.5, with 93% of employees joining without any previous experience in the software industry.

Halo is specialising in service management software, helping organisations streamline operations, manage IT services and improve customer support. Halo works with major organisations across a range of sectors, as well as professional football clubs including Ipswich Town, where it is the headline partner and shirt sponsor.

World.title: Black Friday deals under scrutiny as Portuguese consumer group DECO warns of dubious discounts
World.content:
Black Friday officially takes place on 27 November, but promotions begin several days earlier, with different retailers announcing discounts and campaigns from the start of the month.

 

For anyone looking for a "bargain" a few weeks before the Christmas season, it may be possible to find one, but the Portuguese Consumer Protection Association (DECO) issues a warning: not everything that glitters is gold.

On 2 and 3 November, the consumer protection association analysed (source in Portuguese)products from the online shops of four major brands: Auchan, El Corte Inglés, Euronics and FNAC, detecting several infringements of the so-called promotions law, which sets the rules for commercial practices involving price reductions.

"The rules are clear and say that the same shop has to apply the discount to the lowest price of the last 30 consecutive days before the start of the price reduction", Nuno Pais de Figueiredo, DECO spokesperson, told Euronews.

The association's analysis found that in some cases this did not happen, and identified products that are now in promotion that were cheaper a few days before the supposed "sale".

One of the examples listed was a pair of headphones at FNAC, which were being sold for 249.99 euros as part of a Black Friday campaign but which, according to DECO, between 12 and 18 October were sold in the same shop for 199.99 euros, in other words, 50 euros less than at the start of the campaign.

"What often happens is that a week, 10 days before Black Friday, product prices go up", the spokesperson explained. "What actually happens is that in the final accounts the retailer is not giving any discount, it is selling at precisely the same price", he stressed.

Another infringement detected by DECO involves using the recommended sale price set by the manufacturer, producer or supplier (PVPR) as the term of comparison, thereby misleading the consumer, who thinks he or she is buying a product at a discount when in fact that is not the case. The association explains that there are many cases in which the PVPR is accompanied by a percentage or value of discount that does not correspond to a reduction actually applied, which, according to DECO, breaches the law on sales with price reductions.

In addition, even if they do not know the price history of certain products, the information provided by retailers must be clear and transparent, so that consumers can understand how prices have changed. While stating the discount percentage is optional, the new price and the lowest price previously applied must be explicit and visible.

DECO stresses that any consumer can complain when he or she detects irregular practices. "He or she can and should", Nuno Pais de Figueiredo emphasised. "In the shop itself, using the Complaints Book, or by lodging a complaint with DECO PROteste or with ASAE. There are a range of tools available to do this", he explained.

"The fine pays off"

According to DECO, irregularities during Black Friday campaigns cut across different product sectors and happen in different ways, because "the fine pays off".

"The fine is not a deterrent and this is the problem most of the time", Nuno Pais de Figueiredo explained, stressing that every year the association finds irregularities. "It is common and has not decreased, not by a long shot, because again, the amount companies have to pay is not sufficiently dissuasive".

As a result, the association recommends caution and above all preparation before starting the shopping journey.

At a time when all consumers are constantly targeted with information and stimuli to buy, the trick lies in popular wisdom and taking an old saying literally: "When the handout is too big, the poor man gets suspicious".

"Be suspicious first and look closely afterwards", the spokesperson explained. "There are situations where we look at the prices and think: 'how do these people manage to make money, they're almost giving things away'. So you need to be careful", he stressed.

"Everything depends on how people behave. By making an impulse purchase, the consumer risks falling for the trick behind those so-called 'super, mega, hyper promotions'," he said, underlining the need for consumers to know the product they intend to buy well. DECO even offers an online price comparison tool (source in Portuguese)designed to help consumers make more informed decisions.

"In this specific case of Black Friday, avoiding impulse buys and being wary of offers that seem too good to be true ends up helping people to make the best purchase", the spokesperson said who, despite everything, insisted that "there are good deals" at this time of year.

"If you know what you are going to buy, and have clearly decided what you want, you will get good deals".

Marked on the last Friday of November, the well-known Black Friday originated in the United States and marks the start of the Christmas shopping season.

Boosted by online commerce, the occasion has gained ground in European countries, particularly in Portugal, where it is no longer just one day but a month-long event: promotions start at the beginning of the month and, alongside Black Friday, you are likely to hear about Black Week, the week leading up to the main day, and Cyber Monday.

World.title: Can you survive 72 hours? The EU wants you to prepare an emergency plan
World.content:
The guidelines, presented on 3 November, aim to keep pressure off emergency services so help reaches those who need it most.

 

Brussels recommends storing food, water, medicines, a battery or wind-up radio, a phone charger, some cash, a household plan, and copies of key documents. Basic skills such as first aid are also encouraged.

The guidance is voluntary. Belgium and the Netherlands already advise at least 72 hours, Sweden a week and Germany ideally ten days.

The 72-hour goal was part of the EU’s Preparedness Union Strategy, but cyberattacks, climate-related disasters, and health crises have increased uncertainty over power, communications, and supplies.

In the latest Eurobarometer, 49% of Europeans said they feel well prepared and 48% said they do not, though that measures confidence rather than actual stockpiles. An earlier survey found almost four in ten lacked time or money to prepare.

The Commission urges “affordable and gradual” steps and covers older people and people with disabilities. However, there is no new dedicated funding or free EU-wide kit, and civil protection remains a national responsibility.

For the full story, read our in-depth explainer on Euronews.com.

World.title: Europe and Jordan: A strategic partnership for prosperity and a stable Middle East
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Sustainable investment requires more than capital. It requires trusted partners, predictable political and economic conditions and a long-term vision. European businesses looking to invest in the Middle East have a trusted partner in Jordan.

 

Jordan offers these foundations – and an opportunity for Europe to turn its longstanding partnership with the Kingdom into a new generation of regional investment that strengthens our shared prosperity and security.

New opportunities for Jordanian and European businesses

Jordan’s skilled workforce and trade relationships make it a natural base for businesses seeking regional and international markets. Its location can help European companies diversify supply chains and connect with emerging economic corridors. In the first half of 2026, Jordan’s industrial exports reached approximately €5.5 billion (USD 6.2 billion), up 8.9% year on year. Its industrial products reached 150 global markets in 2025, supported by an extensive network of free trade agreements.

European companies are already part of this story. An EU mapping study provided a snapshot of the contribution of 80 European companies operating in Jordan: approximately €2.5 billion in annual turnover, close to €230 million in corporate taxes and 22,000 direct and indirect jobs created. This presence provides a foundation for deeper economic ties, creating jobs and opening new opportunities for Jordanian and European businesses alike.

Expand productive capacity and create quality jobs

Building on these advantages requires commercially viable projects, reliable infrastructure, a predictable business environment, and access to finance. Jordan’s economic modernisation vision aims to attract investment that expands productive capacity and creates quality jobs.

The economy grew by 3% year on year in the second quarter of 2026. The dinar’s peg to the US dollar, maintained since 1995, provides a monetary anchor, while Fitch reaffirmed Jordan’s BB- sovereign rating with a Stable Outlook in May 2026. Foreign GCC-owned company registrations increased by 23% in the first half of 2026, compared with 7% growth in total registrations.

Related EU leaders vow to boost security and economic ties with Middle East to minimise effect of Iran war

The EU–Jordan Strategic and Comprehensive Partnership, launched in January 2025, provides an ambitious framework to translate political trust into economic opportunity. Its €3 billion package for 2025–2027 combines €640 million in grants, €1 billion in concessional macro-financial assistance and around €1.4 billion in additional investments to be mobilised. These funds will act as wind on the sails of growing businesses, creating jobs and leading to real returns.

Jordan’s strengths meet European expertise

European cooperation can help make this happen. Through investment grants, guarantees and partnerships with development finance institutions, the EU can help reduce investment risks, improve project viability, and mobilise fresh financing. This also means more opportunities for European businesses and the Jordanian economy.

ordan's King Abdullah II, 2nd right, Crown Prince Hussein, right, European Council President Antonio Costa, 2nd left, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Our shared priorities include renewable energy and water infrastructure, digital technologies, logistics and high-value manufacturing – sectors where Jordan’s strengths meet European expertise, and where investment can reinforce regional connectivity. This is even more important as Europe is diversifying its supply chain, making businesses more resilient to shocks while strengthening Jordan’s role as an anchor of regional stability.

The Jordan-EU Investment Conference on 19 November at the Dead Sea is an opportunity to further turn this ambition into tangible projects. The European contribution to Jordan’s National Conveyance Project, a major step towards strengthening the Kingdom’s long-term water security, will be presented at the Conference, demonstrating the scale of what we can achieve together.

Europe’s trusted gateway to the wider Middle East

The Aqaba Digital Hub, supported by the EU, is another example of how our partnership delivers concrete benefits. The Hub is expanding data-centre capacity and digital infrastructure, alongside plans for an academy to develop ICT and cybersecurity skills. The Conference will provide opportunities to build on these projects and forge new investment partnerships.

By bringing European investors together with Jordanian businesses and project promoters, we can lay the groundwork for ambitious investments across more sectors, creating lasting economic value for both sides. Jordan can be more than a stable destination for investment: it can be Europe’s trusted gateway to the wider Middle East. Investing in this partnership is an investment in our shared prosperity and security.

World.title: Thousands rally in Slovakia against PM Robert Fico perceived as too pro-Russia
World.content:
Thousands of people rallied across Slovakia late on Tuesday to demonstrate against the government of Prime Minister Robert Fico, under fire over curbing rights and his close ties with the Kremlin.

 

Tuesday's demonstrations were held to mark the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that toppled communism in the former Czechoslovakia.

The demos came a week after Slovakia's parliament rejected a key government-proposed amendment to the penal code as Fico's coalition had lost its majority, leading to calls for a snap election.

Fico, who has served as prime minister four times in the EU and NATO member over more than two decades, has faced a series of protests since he returned to power in 2023.

Around 25,000 protesters gathered in central Bratislava, the leader of the opposition Progressive Slovakia party said, holding placards with slogans such as "Run, Fico, run!".

"We're the last ones in the European Union to be negotiating with the Russians...It's a disgrace," Igor Vico, a doctor still working at age 74, told the AFP news agency.

People attend a rally titled "November 17th for Change" organised by the opposition Progressive Slovakia (PS) party in Bratislava, 17 November, 2026 AP Photo

"We're at the bottom of the world, not just in Europe, and it makes me sad," he said.

Other demonstrations were also held across the country, including in the eastern city of Košice and Banská Bystrica in the centre.

Close relations with Putin

Fico, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and maintains close relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin, has repeatedly clashed with the European Union during his current term.

Last year, parliament amended the constitution to state that national law takes precedence over EU law in the country of some 5.4 million people.

Fico has also drawn anger over moves to exert greater control over the media and culture and to curb LGBTQ+ people's rights.

Critics have also slammed his efforts to strengthen ties with the Kremlin despite Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including a visit to Moscow in October by Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár for a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission.

Slovakia's Premier Robert Fico attends a press conference in Godollo, 23 June, 2026 AP Photo

The Slovak government this week brought forward a cabinet meeting to discuss the results of Blanar's Moscow visit and deepening cooperation with Russia from Wednesday to Tuesday, further angering protesters.

Student Jan Ducho, 15, told AFP in Bratislava he did not think the government should be negotiating with Moscow.

"Russia isn't a partner we should have, after all, they attacked Ukraine," he said.

Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993.

World.title: Eurobonds are back as Brussels unveils new support loan for Ukraine
World.content:
Show of strength: The European Commission will today present its hotly anticipated proposal to issue a €45 billion support loan to Ukraine to help plug the cash-strapped country's gaping wartime deficit.

 

The announcement will be made by President Ursula von der Leyen herself, flanked by Valdis Dombrovskis, Commissioner for the Economy, and Andrius Kubilius, Commissioner for Defence, a sign of the high stakes at play.

"It's important to continue both supporting Ukraine and putting the pressure on the aggressor, Russia," Dombrovskis told us yesterday on our new show Europe Tonight. "Russia only understands a position of strength."

The money will be raised through joint debt (the arch-famous Eurobonds), which means member states will have to foot the annual interest. As in previous operations, the repayment of the principal will be made contingent on Kyiv receiving war reparations.

"What happens if Russia does not pay reparations?" Dombrovskis said. "We have explicitly foreseen in the regulation that in this case, the Union reserves the right to use immobilised Russian sovereign assets."

These assets, we must remember, are worth a whopping €210 billion on EU soil. Despite a push to use them now, Brussels think it's best to keep them for later on.

AAA graded: Though the Commission still enjoys a triple rating, the scheme won't come cheap. Borrowing costs have soared this year amid high energy prices, geopolitical volatility, investor jitters and the costly AI race. Still, the EU is determined to support Ukraine for "as long as it takes", as von der Leyen often says. The prevailing opinion is that the costs of a failed Ukrainian state would exceed any financial undertaking.

The proposal is set to be discussed by EU leaders later this month at a special summit. Also on the table will be the next EU budget. Technically, the two subjects are separate entities, but they have de facto become one single package. It's all money after all.

But wait: Didn't EU leaders approve a €90 billion support loan meant to cover Ukraine's military and financial needs for 2026 and 2027? Yes, they did.

But that loan, which is still ongoing, was designed under the (completely unfounded) assumption that Russia's war would end sometime this year. Don't ask me what prompted Commission officials to assume such a thing, because I'm as baffled as you are. The premise, of course, has fallen apart. Moscow is escalating airstrikes to make Ukraine's winter insufferable and destroy the levers of the local economy.

The non-stop attacks are disrupting business activity, hampering trade and causing widespread blackouts, all of which diminish Kyiv's ability to collect revenue and maintain public services. This makes the country even more dependent on foreign aid.

The devastation has drilled a €70 billion hole in Ukraine's 2027 budget. The bloc's new €45 billion loan is meant to cover two-thirds of this shortfall. The remaining third will fall on other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan.

According to an internal document I've seen, the 2027 gap could be reduced by up to €13 billion if all NATO allies deliver on their pledges made at the July summit. The proposal might offer some ways to maximise (or incentivise) external contributions.

Count them out: The joint debt of the €45 billion loan will not be so "joint" after all. Four member states – Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria – have all indicated they will opt out. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico seized on the resumption of the peace talks to say no to "war loans" and yes to peace.

Count her out: Marine Le Pen has confirmed that, should she become president of France next year, she would end financial support for Ukraine due to France's high public debt. Le Pen said she would still honour the existing commitments and carry "active diplomacy", our Paris correspondent Estelle Nilsson-Julien reports.

Meanwhile, the French government has rejected as "absurd" Moscow's claims that French troops had been deployed to the battlefield in Ukraine. Deputy Defence Minister Alice Rufo said the soldiers were there for "training and equipment maintenance".

What now? The €45 billion support loan comes as Europe, Ukraine and the US prepare for multilateral talks with Russia in the peace process. Moscow, however, continues to procrastinate and regurgitate old grievances to divert attention from what matters.

"If anybody's going to talk about European security order, Europe has to be there," Norway's Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told my colleague Angela Skujins.

"We're not happy about this language about architecture. We believe that we have European security architecture. There was nothing wrong with it until Russia violated it."

Brussels is already preparing a new package of economic sanctions to tighten the screws on Russia. Don't rule out the possibility that Moscow uses the loan and the sanctions as a convenient excuse to refuse the multilateral format.

How Ukrainian forces struck Putin's prized Crimean bridge

Russian President Vladimir Putin may be hoping for his own Yalta moment alongside Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the three leaders meet in China on Thursday. But the historical reference carries a particular irony.

Ukraine has dealt a major blow to the Crimean bridge, a symbol of Moscow's occupation of the very peninsula where the original Yalta Conference took place in 1945.

Kyiv's forces struck the heavily defended bridge, partially destroying the crossing in an unprecedented seven-stage operation involving eleven different weapons systems.

Inaugurated by Putin in 2018, the bridge has long been both a vital transport link for Russian forces and one of the Kremlin's most prized symbols of its control over Crimea.

The ingenious military strike complicates Putin's efforts to portray Russia as winning the war ahead of his sought-after meeting with Trump and Xi.

"There will be more of our operations – operations in response to Russian aggression," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Sasha Vakulina has the must-read story on how the bridge went down.

More from our newsrooms

Rwanda 'return hubs' spark backlash. Humanitarian organisations and progressive lawmakers have denounced the deal between five EU countries and Rwanda for building "return hubs" outside the bloc. Vincenzo Genovese breaks down the backlash.

EU delays Brazilian chicken ban. Member states postponed a vote to lift the ban on Brazilian chicken imports after several countries requested further clarification over Brazil's compliance with EU antimicrobial regulations. Peggy Corlin has the story.

Jensen Huang eyes Nvidia return. The embattled executive is preparing for a comeback after resigning as CEO amid a love affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But the Nvidia board says it has no plans to reinstate him.

We’re also keeping an eye on

European Commission holds its weekly College meeting. President Ursula von der Leyen presents a €45 billion support loan for Ukraine.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola speaks at the Schuman Security and Defence Forum in Brussels.

Chinese President Xi Jinping hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in Shenzhen.

Anthropic sets the final price of its shares before going public.

That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina and Angela Skujins contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
World.content:
The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.

The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.

Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.

The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.

Peltola promises to deliver for 'Alaska's working families'

"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.

Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.

Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.

Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.



Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Vote siphon allegations

The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.

The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.

The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.

"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.

Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.

The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

World.title: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
World.content:
Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?

The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.

Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.

Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.

Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."

A historic trilateral between Xi, Trump and Putin is scheduled for Thursday during the APEC summit Image: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.

"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.

"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."

Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.

Contentious issues may be left for later

Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.

She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.

Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."

She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.

With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.

China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas

Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.

What new alliances will reshape the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.

"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."

Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.

"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."

Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.

An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."

Trump said on Tuesday he would take a separate bilateral meeting with Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen 'if it's available' Image: Dmitry Azarov/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance

The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.

He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."

He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.

"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.

"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."

Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation

W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.

The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."

Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.

"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

World.title: Pakistani man gets 27 years for foiled plot to kill Trump, Biden
World.content:
A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison for his role in plotting to kill US politicians, including President Donald Trump.

A US court sentenced a Pakistani man to more than 27 years in jail for plotting to kill US President Donald Trump and other prominent politicians at the behest of Iran, authorities said on Tuesday.

"Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a US president or other senior government official," said US District Judge Eric Komitee while reading out the sentence.

The 48-year-old man was handed 330 months in prison for "attempting to commit an act of ​terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire," the US Department of Justice said in a ​statement. That's 27 years and six months.

A US jury had already convicted the man in March of traveling to the US to arrange political assassinations on American soil.

The trial had begun in late February, days before the Trump administration ordered strikes on Iran that it carried out with Israel. The war has killed thousands, mostly in Iran, Lebanon and Yemen, but also in countries around the Persian Gulf.

It is still ongoing.

A plot to kill Trump: What prompted it?

Prosecutors said the convict tried to recruit people in the US for a plan to kill Trump and other US politicians in retaliation for Washington's killing of Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani in January 2020.

Trump was in his first term as US president at the time.

Other targets in the 2024 plot included then-US President Joe Biden and Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump for the Republican presidential nominination, prosecutors said.

What else do we know about foiled plot to kill US politicians?

During his trial, the man testified that he had joined the plot with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps but did so unwillingly to protect his family in Tehran.

Tehran has denied targeting Trump or other US officials or plotting attacks against them.

The Pakistani man bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump's rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally to an acquaintance. He then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he had borrowed from a relative.

The man also said that he assumed that US authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward.

The DOJ said that a person contacted the man in April 2024 to help with the plot, only to report his activities and become a confidential informant.

The convicted man was arrested in Texas in July 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump's life in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

World.title: Slovakia: Thousands protest against pro-Kremlin leader Robert Fico
World.content:
Prime Minister Robert Fico has been under fire over his ties to Russia. The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that toppled communism in Czechoslovakia.

Thousands of people protested across Slovakia on Tuesday to demonstrate against Prime Minister Robert Fico and his pro-Russian government.

The demonstration was organized by opposition parties and non-governmental organizations (NGOs).

The largest protest was on SNP Square, which was the site of the main anti-Communist protests during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, in the capital, Bratislava.

Organizers said 25,000 people had gathered there.

Other rallies were also held across the country, which is an EU and NATO member​​​​​​, including in the cities of Kosice and Banska Bystrica.

Robert Fico was the only serving EU leader to visit Moscow for the annual Victory Day parade this year Image: Ramil Sitdikov/AP Photo/picture alliance

Why are people protesting in Slovakia?

The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended decades of communist rule in what was then called Czechoslovakia.

Protesters commemorated the fall of the communist dictatorship, which ruled Czechoslovakia for 41 years. They also called for more support for Ukraine.

The demonstrators mostly focused on Slovakia's prime minister, however, chanting slogans such as "We've had enough of Fico!"

One banner told the prime minister to "Go to hell."

Slovakia amid deepening political and social strains To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are Slovaks angry with Fico?

Since Hungary's Viktor Orban was removed from power in April, Fico stands as Europe's most pro-Russian leader.

He opposed military aid for Ukraine and has maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite European Union sanctions against Russia.

Fico, who has served as prime minister four times in over two decades, has faced numerous protests since returning to power in 2023.

Fico has also repeatedly clashed with the EU. Last year, Slovakia's constitution was amended to state that national law takes precedence over EU law.

He has also been criticized for trying to exert greater control over the media and culture, and curbing LGBTQ+ rights.

"We're the last ones in the European Union to be negotiating with the Russians... It's a disgrace," Igor Vico, a 74-year-old doctor, told AFP.

"We're at the bottom of the world, not just in Europe, and it makes me sad," he said.

World.title: Nvidia beats Q3 expectations in first report post-Jensen Huang
World.content:
The AI chipmaker said it doubled its third-quarter revenue and confirmed that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated as CEO after a Chinese spy scandal.

US AI chip giant Nvidia doubled its third-quarter revenue to more than $115 billion (about €104.59 billion), the company said Tuesday.

Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones also confirmed that the board of directors has no plans to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang resigned on Thursday after a string of extramarital affairs came to light, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

What did Nvidia say about the results and Huang?

In a statement on Tuesday, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" as the firm tries to move on from the Huang affair.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since she was appointed last week.

Colette Kress is Nvidia's interim CEO Image: Nvidia/Handout/REUTERS

She did not address Huang's resignation or the uncertainty surrounding his successor as Nvidia's CEO.

During an earnings call with Nvidia investors on Tuesday, Chairman Jones said the board had "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Huang pitches return after 'outpouring' of support

The results, which exceeded expectations, were announced hours after Huang said he would be willing to return to the company if the board agreed.

After Huang's resignation, tech industry figures such as Elon Musk, as well as US President Donald Trump, called for Huang to be reinstated as part of a campaign called "Bring Jensen Back."

In a post on X — his first public statement since the scandal plunged the company and AI sector into crisis — Huang acknowledged that he had made "serious mistakes in his personal life" and had failed to "live up to the standards expected of everyone at" the company.

Huang also said he had received an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers" for him to return.

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips driving advanced AI models.

Under his leadership, Nvidia grew into one of the world's biggest — and most strategically important — companies.

Nvidia has been at the center of the AI boom that has pushed markets to record levels and spurred economic growth around the world.

Nvidia's chips are critical for training and operating advanced AI systems, making them crucial to governments, the military and the tech industry.

World.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
World.content:
Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

The conviction in September of Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders was greeted with shock, disappointment and anger in Kosovo Image: Ermal Meta/Matrix Images/IMAGO

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Speaking of Thaci's September conviction of war crimes in September, Prime Minister Albin Kurti has said that the government of Kosovo 'is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers' Image: Liam McBurney/PA Images/picture alliance

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

Parliament considers amending law

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute stresses that there is a fundamental difference between criticism of courts based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts Image: Bekim Shehu/DW

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

World.title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
World.content:
Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM , the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Saudi police forces reacted to peaceful protests by opening fire at the demonstrators in Quatif in 2011 Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Major sports events in Saudi Arabia are either postponed or canceled due to the ongoing attacks from Yemen's Houthis and Iran Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST , echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

World.title: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
World.content:
The United States lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization has said. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status.

The ​United States is experiencing its highest number ​of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.

As ​of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus this year.

Pennsylvania has been the worst-hit state, reporting seven measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases.

Why are measles caseloads rising despite readily available vaccines?

Tuesday's declaration by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but is the latest sign of measles' avoidable resurgence.

"Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.

Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.

Vaccine hesitancy and disinformation has risen in recent years in the US, seemingly fueled at least in part by the COVID pandemic.

The rising influence of renowned vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now the US Health Secretary — who dropped out of the 2024 presidential election campaign to form an alliance with Donald Trump — was one of the clearest indicators of this.

"This is a serious warning for our region, but it is not an irreversible setback," PAHO Director Barbosa said. "We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again."

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bolivia, Mexico, US and Canada no longer designated measles-free

As of November 13, PAHO said that the Americas region had reported 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year.

The organization considers endemic transmission to be re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.

Canada had reached this status in November 2025, with Bolivia, Mexico and the US now deemed to have joined it.

The PAHO said that Canda had "interrupted the chain of transmission" that led to its designation and was working to regain elimination status.

Meanwhile, it said the other three countries "are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response."

World.title: El mapa del voto táctico para que el último escaño por provincia se lo lleve la derecha o la izquierda: ¿qué dicen las encuestas?
World.content:
El modelo de EL PAÍS dice que hay 42 escaños en el aire. Consulta a qué partido le sirve más tu voto

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima el voto y los escaños en cada provincia, y les asigna probabilidades. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos en cada territorio, con las encuestas publicadas hasta el 16 de noviembre.

En el interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 168 seguros, 140 probables y 89 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Las provincias con más escaños en juego son las más grandes, Madrid (con 10) y Barcelona (con nueve). Pero hay pulsos muy reñidos en algunas provincias pequeñas. En Lleida, que reparte cuatro diputados, cinco partidos se disputan los dos últimos: Junts, PP, PSOE, ERC y Vox.

El voto táctico: ¿qué voto ayuda a tu bloque?

Muchas personas votan para maximizar las opciones de un gobierno de izquierdas o de derechas. Quizás tienen un partido favorito, pero se hacen otra pregunta: ¿a qué partido de su bloque le sirve más su voto? Es lo que se llama voto táctico o estratégico. La respuesta cambia en cada provincia: por el método D’Hondt, un voto al PP y otro a Vox no valen lo mismo en escaños, porque uno de los dos suele estar más cerca de ganar el último diputado. Y lo mismo pasa con PSOE, Frente Amplio o BNG.

¿Cuál es el voto táctico en tu provincia? Puedes verlo en el mapa. Primero elige un bloque. Entonces el mapa mostrará, para cada provincia, el partido de ese espectro que tiene más probabilidades de ganar (o salvar) un escaño para su bloque.

Para un votante de derecha, existe voto táctico en 38 provincias. Hay 21 donde le conviene votar al PP (probablemente) y 17 donde le conviene hacerlo por Vox. A veces la diferencia es grande: en Gipuzkoa, Lugo y Ourense, un voto a Vox casi nunca decide un escaño, mientras que el PP se disputa el último con Bildu o el BNG. En Álava o Melilla, un voto al PP vale más de cinco veces lo que uno a Vox. Pero hay territorios donde un votante indiferente entre PP y Vox maximiza sus opciones eligiendo al partido de extrema derecha. Es lo que pasa en La Rioja, por ejemplo.

En la izquierda, el voto táctico favorece casi siempre el PSOE. En 23 provincias es el único del bloque que mueve escaños en nuestras simulaciones, porque los Frentes y Podemos tienen números débiles en los sondeos. Hay excepciones en territorios con fuerzas locales: por ejemplo, en Lugo y Ourense parece que un voto al BNG es mejor para los intereses del bloque. Y ocurre algo parecido con Adelante Andalucía en Córdoba y con la Unidad del Pueblo Canario en Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

En las provincias grandes, en cambio, el voto táctico apenas existe. En Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla da casi igual votar a un partido u otro del bloque: las fuerzas principales tienen todas opciones de lograr representación.

Nuestra simulación también muestra otra cosa: mover un escaño es mucho más barato en las provincias más pequeñas. La probabilidad de que justo tu papeleta sea la decisiva es siempre minúscula (un voto cualquiera tiene una posibilidad entre 116.000 de decidir un escaño). Pero no es siempre igual de minúscula. En Lleida un voto al PP pesa casi seis veces más que la media: una posibilidad entre 20.000. Y en Ávila o La Rioja, uno al PSOE pesa unas cinco veces más.
