World.title: Ukraine blames Russia for graffiti glorifying WWII Ukrainian nationalists on Polish monuments
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around a dozen public monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two nationalist partisan group that was responsible for the massacre of Poles and Jews. Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia, which has previously been accused by the Polish authorities of orchestrating provocative graffiti on monuments. W sobotę, 14 listopada, w Warszawie doszło do kolejnych dwóch dewastacji pomników. Napisy „Slava UPA” pojawiły się na Pomniku Bohaterów Getta przed Muzeum Historii Żydów Polskich POLIN oraz na Pomniku Żołnierzy 1 Armii Wojska Polskiego przy ulicy Andersa 13. To kolejna odsłona… pic.twitter.com/Y7NDsfpjxn — Miejski Reporter (@MiejskiReporter) November 14, 2026 The latest spate of vandalism was first reported in early November in the western city of Poznań, where three World War two memorials were painted with graffiti saying “Glory to the UPA” (Slawa UPA). While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him. Similar graffiti was subsequently reported on seven monuments, including ones dedicated to Polish World War Two heroes and anti-communist protests that took place in 1970, in Gdańsk and Gdynia, neighbouring cities on Poland’s northern Baltic coast. On Friday, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian on suspicion of “painting offensive slogans propagating hatred”. They shared blurred-out images of the suspect as well as cans of spray paint. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. If convicted, he could face up to three years in prison. Previously, on Tuesday this week, MOST, a Polish-based Belarusian independent media outlet, published findings that an anonymous person on messaging service Telegram, which is popular among Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians, had been offering $500 plus travel expenses for a job in Poznań. When an undercover MOST journalist responded to the advert, he was told that the job would involve spray painting “Glory to the UPA” on monuments. The recruiter confirmed that the job was illegal, “but if you cover your face and do everything quickly, they won’t find you”. They also revealed that similar jobs were available in other Polish cities, including Warsaw, Wrocław and Lublin. Subsequently, similar inscriptions appeared in Warsaw on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which honours the Jews who rose up against their German-Nazi oppressors in 1943; a monument commemorating the Polish First Army, which fought in World War Two; and a monument to sappers who served in the war. The vandalism was condemned by Poland’s Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH), which called it a “disgraceful attack on the memory of the victims of the Holocaust and the heroes of Jewish resistance”. Noting MOST’s findings and the vandalism of other monuments, ŻIH said that “this points to the possibility of an organised provocation intended to incite hatred and divide society”. Warsaw police told PAP that they are investigating and seeking to identify the perpetrator. An unnamed police source also told Gazeta Wyborcza they see the incidents in all four cities as related to one another, pointing to the similar style of the inscriptions. On Sunday afternoon, Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, condemned the vandalism and shared images of the municipal authorities cleaning the graffiti off the Ghetto Heroes Monument. “Given the scale of similar incidents in other cities, we must consider the possibility that this is a planned provocation,” added the mayor. “Let us not let ourselves be divided – the authorities are working to identify both those who carried out these acts and those who ordered them.” Nie ma zgody na wandalizm w Warszawie. Minionej nocy służby miejskie wyczyściły pomniki oszpecone przez wandali – między innymi Pomnik Bohaterów Getta. Sprawców szuka policja. Patrząc na skalę podobnych incydentów w innych miastach, musimy brać pod uwagę, że mamy do czynienia… pic.twitter.com/5xMgPhnHf8 — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) November 15, 2026 A day earlier, on Saturday, the Ukrainian embassy had also condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation”. “In our view, these unlawful acts are a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states, and in Poland in particular,” wrote the embassy. “The objective is clear: to incite hostility between Poles and Ukrainians, undermine mutual trust, and weaken support for Ukraine.” Writing in both Polish and Ukrainian, the embassy appealed to Ukrainians “not to be tempted by offers of ‘easy money’ in exchange for painting graffiti, damaging property, or carrying out other illegal tasks” and to report any such offers to the Polish police. “Let us respect the laws of the country in which we reside, as well as historical memory and each other’s dignity,” they added. “Polish-Ukrainian solidarity is our shared strength. Let us not allow the enemy to destroy it.” Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence. The issue has recently flared up again this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. World.title: Polish president vetoes law on removing harmful online content, warning of “censorship”
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill creating new powers to block harmful online content. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the measures were too far-reaching and could be abused to introduce “censorship”. Government figures have strongly criticised the president’s decision, arguing that it will leave young people in particular more exposed to dangerous content. It also means that Poland still has not fully implemented the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA). ❌ Nie dla cenzury Internetu! pic.twitter.com/WusnK7LImD — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Previously, in January this year, Nawrocki had vetoed an earlier bill intended to implement the DSA, describing the measures as “Owellian”. That prompted the government to split the legislation in two. In September, Nawrocki agreed to sign one of those bills, which appointed the president of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) as Poland’s digital services coordinator, responsible for overseeing enforcement of the DSA. A second bill was then needed to introduce the actual powers to block harmful online content. In October, it was approved in parliament by the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The right-wing and far-right opposition either voted against it or abstained. Among the new powers included in the legislation were authorisation for the heads of UKE and the National Broadcasting Council (KRRiT) to order the blocking of online content containing violence or threats based on race, nationality, ethnicity, religion or political affiliation. It also allowed the immediate blocking, at the request of a prosecutor or the police, of content involving the acceptance of a contract to commit murder or inciting or assisting in suicide or self-harm. “Perpetrators of serious crimes should not be allowed to use the internet to spread violence and threats,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. “The state must have effective tools to quickly respond to such threats. The safety of internet users must transcend political divisions.” The government also argued that last month’s series of stabbings in schools and this month’s deadly terrorist attack in Kraków – which have raised concern about the online radicalisation of young people – have emphasised the importance of tough controls over digital content. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 However, on Friday, the final day by which the president had to make a decision on the bill, Nawrocki announced that he was vetoing it. He argued that “the government has clearly mixed up European obligations with its own political interests”. The measures in the bill threaten to create a “censorship official” and “essentially give the government arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish, said the president. Decisions on whether content is permitted or not should be “the exclusive competence of the justice system and independent judges”, he argued. Nawrocki also said that the powers in the vetoed bill were “disproportionate”, allowing an entire domain to be blocked due to a single example of illegal content. “The security of citizens cannot be a pretext for weakening their freedoms,” said Nawrocki. “We must not create a false choice: either the security or the freedom of its citizens. A responsible state must ensure and balance both.” Dlaczego Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o DSA? ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/1BUJVFEftl — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski, however, said that the president was “not defending free speech” but instead “once again siding with global [digital] platforms and allowing them to decide what users see”. “The vetoed provisions concerned illegal content, not opinions or views expressed online,” added the ministry, which also noted that all decisions on blocking content were subject to appeals and judicial review. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, accused Nawrocki of “waging war on the government at the expense of Polish children and Polish security”, which would both be threatened by the absence of the vetoed measures. Z prezydenckiego weta zadowoleni są hejterzy, rosyjskie farmy trolli, pedofile, ekstremalni nihiliści i lobbyści. Ofiarami tego weta są polskie dzieci, rodzice, bezpieczeństwo wszystkich obywateli. Tego nie da się w żaden sposób usprawiedliwić. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 14, 2026 Aleksandra Wójtowicz, an analyst on new technologies at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), told the Fakt newspaper that the measures do “not in any way relate to alleged censorship”. They are intended to force digital platforms to remove illegal content, she explained. Wójtowicz added that the measures would actually have protected free speech by giving Polish users whose accounts were unjustly deleted by social media platforms the right to appeal against those decisions outside of the platform itself. However, Nawrocki’s veto was praised by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party. Czarnek told TV Trwam that the proposed measures had been intended to “fight the opposition” rather than actual hate speech. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops. The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture. We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Huge thanks to: 🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk 🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC — Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026 “The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.” The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH). “The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general. “We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.” The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year. All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums. The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community. 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim. W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53 — Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026 The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending. “Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.” The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch. The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology. A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for. The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state. ❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees. Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised. Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026 On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed. Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury. “The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry. In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”. “It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.” Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters. World.title: West Ham Star Tomáš Souček Launches English Autobiography in Prague
World.content:
Tomáš Souček has presented the English edition of his autobiography at the British Embassy in Prague, with the book set to reach UK readers ahead of Christmas.

British Ambassador Matt Field welcomed the West Ham United midfielder to Thunovský Palace on Monday, November 16, for the launch. The event marked the next step for the autobiography, which was first published in the Czech Republic a year ago.

The English edition will be titled Tomáš Souček – My Story and will initially be available through West Ham’s official fan shop. Souček said the decision to translate the book had been made from the beginning, with the aim of making it accessible to supporters in England.



“I’m living a second life in England. My children are growing up there, and I feel right at home. That’s why I’m so happy we can bring this book to West Ham fans. I have an incredible connection with them, and they deserve it,” Souček said to Prague Morning.

The launch also featured an unusual alternative to the traditional champagne toast. Instead of pouring sparkling wine over the book, Souček and Field blew bubbles above its cover, referencing West Ham’s pre-match tradition and the club anthem I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles.

“In England, seeing a bubble blower means seeing West Ham. Besides, I’m not really a fan of being doused in alcohol. Bubbles are a much better fit for this book,” Souček said.

Field, meanwhile, recalled watching the Czech midfielder lift the UEFA Europa Conference League trophy in Prague in 2023.

“I’ve been a fan ever since. I know he’s scored more goals in the Premier League than any other Czech footballer. But apparently, that wasn’t enough for him, so he decided to write a book, too. As a diplomat, I can only hope he doesn’t decide to try his hand at my job as well. That would start to look like a hat-trick,” the ambassador joked.

The autobiography was written by Souček together with football journalists David Čermák and Jan Palička. It covers both his professional career and personal life, including his struggles with insomnia and depression at different stages of his football journey.

The English edition includes an additional chapter covering West Ham’s relegation season, the disappointing World Cup campaign in the United States and Souček’s return to football after a serious ankle injury.

World.title: Furiant Is Back: Prague’s Czech Sweets Pop-Up Reopens November 27
World.content:
Furiant, the Czech pastry pop-up that attracted long queues and sold out daily during its first run, will reopen on November 27 at its original location inside the Parnas restaurant.

The project brings together Jiří Matějka, former head pastry chef at Karlín’s Eska and Café Slavia, and Jozef Onderka, owner of Café Slavia, SmetanaQ and the Forbína cocktail bar.



Their idea was to create a modern Czech confectionery focused on traditional sweet dishes rather than the croissants and French-style pastries found in many of Prague’s newer bakeries.

When Furiant first opened in October 2025, the response exceeded expectations. Operating from Thursday to Sunday, the pop-up sold out every day, sometimes closing earlier than scheduled.

The team initially struggled to keep up with demand, choosing not to increase production at the expense of quality.

Matějka developed the concept after several years working in Berlin, where he began to miss traditional Czech sweets. His experience at Eska and abroad helped shape an approach that combines familiar dishes with contemporary pastry techniques and carefully selected ingredients.

The menu puts the spotlight on Czech sweet meals, including semolina porridge, rice pudding, plum dumplings, pancakes and buchtičky se šodó (small sweet yeast buns served with vanilla custard).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Furiant (@furiant_prague)

One of Furiant’s defining characteristics is its deliberately limited menu, which changes regularly according to the season and availability of ingredients.

The kitchen works with Czech flour, dairy products from the Struhy farm, chocolate from the Herůfek family and locally sourced poppy seeds, which are ground on-site.

The reopening will give Prague residents another opportunity to visit the pop-up at Parnas, overlooking the Vltava River and Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Unveils New 70-Metre Velvet Bridge on Kampa Island
World.content:
Prague has unveiled a new public artwork on Kampa Island, marking the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution.

Created by Czech-born artist and illustrator Petr Sís, the 70-metre-long ceramic mural traces key moments in the country’s history from the founding of Czechoslovakia in 1918 to the fall of communist rule in 1989.

The installation, known as the Velvet Bridge, was originally conceived as a gift to Prague for the 30th anniversary of the Velvet Revolution in 2019.



Its completion was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and administrative obstacles, but the project finally reached its conclusion on November 17, 2026, exactly 37 years after the demonstrations on Národní Street that helped bring down the communist regime.

Sís, who emigrated from Czechoslovakia and has lived in the United States for decades, returned to Prague for the unveiling ceremony.

The artwork occupies a previously unused wall along the Vltava River, facing Střelecký Island. The same location hosted the project’s original presentation in 2019.

Twelve scenes from Czech history

The design takes inspiration from Charles Bridge, with 12 symbolic images set beneath its arches. Together, they portray important moments and figures associated with Czech democracy, independence and the struggle for freedom.

Portraits of two former presidents replace the traditional bridge towers. Václav Havel appears at one end, while Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, the first president of Czechoslovakia, stands at the other. Both figures also appear in individual scenes along the structure.

The images draw heavily on Sís’s own books, including The Three Golden Keys, in which the artist revisits Prague through the perspective of someone living in exile, uncertain whether he would ever return, and The Wall: Growing Up Behind the Iron Curtain, his account of childhood in communist Czechoslovakia.

The theme of freedom runs throughout Sís’s work. During the unveiling, music from the 1960s played from the artist’s personal vinyl collection, including the Beatles’ Yellow Submarine, which also features in the mural.

The Velvet Bridge cost approximately CZK 5 million to create. Its construction involved hand-painted ceramic tiles produced by a workshop in Portugal.

The project was financed by 16 donors. The finished artwork has been donated to the City of Prague, with its future maintenance entrusted to the Technical Administration of Communications.

World.title: First Ski Slopes Open in the Czech Republic for 2026/2027 Season
World.content:
The 2026/2027 ski season is underway in the Czech Republic.

Monínec, a resort near Sedlec-Prčice in the Central Bohemian Region, opened its slopes on Sunday, November 15, becoming the first ski resort in the country to welcome visitors this winter.

Around 400 to 500 people turned up on opening day, taking advantage of sunny, cold weather and up to one meter of snow on the prepared section of the slope.



For now, only the upper 600 meters of the resort’s main 1,200-meter run are open. The lower section is expected to follow by November 27, with its opening delayed by renovation work on a building at the resort.

The resort operates nine Snowfactory units, which can produce snow even when temperatures are above freezing. It also uses snow stored under special insulating covers during the warmer months.

Two storage areas were established at the resort this year, allowing it to preserve almost half of the snow accumulated last winter. Around 8,000 cubic meters remained in the upper storage area, with additional reserves kept in the lower part of the complex.

The resort has also kept online ski-pass prices unchanged from last season. Tickets purchased directly at the ticket office, however, have become more expensive.

The resort has regularly launched the Czech ski season around the middle of November since 2016.

Last year, it opened its entire 1,200-meter main slope on November 15, 2025. According to the resort’s management, this was the earliest opening of a fully operational ski slope in the history of the Czech Republic.

World.title: Now in English! Experience 17 November 1989 in Prague With a Free Audio Walk
World.content:
As Prague marks the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution on November 17, visitors and international residents can follow the route of the 1989 student demonstration through a free English-language audio walk.

Created by SmartGuide in cooperation with Korzo Národní, the walk follows the students’ journey from Albertov, through Vyšehrad and along the Vltava River to Národní třída, where the demonstration was violently suppressed by communist police on November 17, 1989.



The newly released English edition allows those who do not speak Czech to explore one of the defining moments in modern Czech history through eyewitness accounts, historical recordings and stories connected to the locations along the route.

The audio walk uses the original recordings made during the events, including accounts from people who witnessed the demonstrations.

Its English version also includes dubbed radio communications between agents of StB, the communist secret police, giving listeners an insight into how security forces monitored and prepared for the student demonstration.

Unlike a traditional guided tour, the walk can be completed independently, at any time and at the participant’s own pace. It requires no booking or app download. Visitors only need a smartphone and headphones to follow the route and listen to the recordings at the relevant locations.

The starting point is Albertov, where students gathered on November 17, 1989, for a demonstration commemorating the 1939 Nazi crackdown on Czech universities and marking International Students’ Day. What began as a permitted march later developed into a turning point in the country’s history.

After the demonstration was blocked by police on Národní třída, news of the crackdown spread across the country, helping trigger a wave of protests that eventually brought down the communist regime. Within weeks, Czechoslovakia had begun its transition to democracy, in what became known as the Velvet Revolution.

World.title: INTERVIEW: “We Chose the Riskier Option”: From Nashville to Prague, With No Regrets
World.content:
Seven years ago, Joshua Hayden swapped a secure career in Nashville for Prague, drawn by his research on Václav Havel and Charter 77.

Today he teaches leadership at Anglo-American University, where Václav Havel, poetry and the spirit of 1989 are part of the curriculum.



Joshua Hayden, EdD, holds a doctorate in leadership from Vanderbilt University and taught at three universities around Nashville, Tennessee, before moving his family to Prague. At Anglo-American University (AAU), the country’s oldest private university founded in 1990, he is the Department Chair of Social Sciences, teaches the psychology of leadership, ethics and leadership, and a summer course on the Czech dissident tradition.

Ahead of November 17, we talked to him about teaching far from home, why small classes matter more than ever in the age of AI, and why Havel’s words still resonate with students today.

You built your career in Nashville. Why did you leave it for Prague?

Before my family and I moved to Prague, I worked at three universities in and just outside Nashville, Tennessee. I earned my doctoral degree in leadership at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, and my wife and I really loved the city. After a lot of discernment and prayer, we decided to live a bigger story for our family and move to Prague, partly because of my research on Václav Havel and Charter 77.

During that year of transition, I was offered a job running a leadership program at a liberal arts college. It was in a small town in the US, so we had a choice between the risk of moving internationally in the hope of teaching leadership and the “sure thing” of running a program in the US. We chose the riskier option. What I remember most about that time is the assurance that we were making the right decision, come what may.

Teaching Far From Home

What’s it like to teach in a country that isn’t your own, to students who are often far from home too?

It’s just the kind of challenge I was looking for. I’ve learned so much in dialogue with students, and in many classes we end up talking about cross-cultural differences. The adjustment for me meant trading many of my American examples for international ones. I often ask students to share their cultural perspectives and interpretations of the research and data I share in class. On the other hand, for all the cultural differences, I am struck by the commonalities between cultures and the connections that can be made if we are open to them.

For example, I include poems in my class on the psychology of leadership. Poems and leadership? Yes! Poems have a way of expressing the human condition and the dynamics of change, power, resistance and critical engagement that are really at the heart of leadership. I include poems from different cultures around the world, and one day we used a Polish poem. A Polish student looked it up in her own language after reading it in English and showed us how the author used political and subversive terms. Our class had a great discussion about how language shapes our own and other people’s reality. She brought a cultural perspective that I did not anticipate, and it added so much to our class.

Small Classes, Big Difference

What happens in a small class that you’d never see in a big lecture hall?

Students learn at a much deeper and more active level. There are experimental studies showing that students in active-learning classes learn more than those in traditional lectures, even if they don’t feel they learned more. I’ve found that when I get students into groups working on problems and applying the course materials, they correct each other’s misunderstandings and get immediate feedback.

Written and verbal feedback is another thing that sets small classes apart from large ones, and the more frequent feedback students get on how they explain, apply and synthesize information, the more higher-order learning takes place. I think one misconception old-school professors tend to have is that if students enjoy discussing and working actively in the classroom, there must be less learning going on, because you aren’t covering as much material. But the evidence does not support this.

Especially in the AI-saturated world we all live in, practicing social and argumentative skills, problem-solving and critical thinking in the classroom is more important than ever. In my classes we have case studies, role plays, simulations and hands-on experiments, we go on field trips, and we have small-group discussions. Students are rarely distracted by technology if they are immersed in a problem, a group task or a deep discussion. I have the same challenges all professors do in the classroom, but the small, diverse classes we have are great environments for deeper learning.

If you could take one AAU class as a student, which would it be and why?

Take a colleague’s class? I would take Professor Ondřej Pilný’s course Theatre and Politics or Pavla Jonssonová’s Czech Culture in Film and Literature. They are both great teachers!

Do you stay in touch with former students? Is there one whose story surprised you?

Yes, I do stay in touch with former students, and I love to follow their lives and careers. One of my thesis advisees had a profound experience taking a course in South Africa, went on to write a great thesis, graduated and then pursued her passion for pottery. I gave her a copy of one of my favorite books, Let Your Life Speak by Parker Palmer, and she read it while working in a pottery studio in California. She wrote to me about it, and later she came to Prague and told me she was in the process of opening her own pottery studio.

Some of us take the necessary path of getting a job that works for the lifestyle we want, but I love it when former students take risks and go for something they are passionate about that also serves others.

Havel in the Classroom

You’ve spent years studying Václav Havel. How does he show up in your classes?

I teach a summer leadership course on the Czech dissident tradition. It starts with Jan Hus and ends with Václav Havel: his early life and absurdist theatre – we see his plays performed – and the context of communist Czechoslovakia in the 1950s and 1960s, his emergence as a “dissident” in the 1970s and 1980s, and finally his presidency. I am much more interested in taking a critical approach, discussing Havel in his social, economic and political context and in relation to artists, writers, former communists, rock bands and philosophers.

Havel also shows up in my Ethics and Leadership course, where we use ethical theories to examine the leadership of various historical and contemporary figures. I use Gabriel Marcel’s ethics of hope to look at Havel and others and their collaboration in starting Charter 77, VONS (the Committee for the Defense of the Unjustly Prosecuted) and other human rights groups. We read his Letter to Husák, The Power of the Powerless and the speech he gave as president when he received the Sonning Prize.

I’ve found Havel’s 1990 New Year’s Address helpful in other leadership courses I teach, such as Leadership and the Self. We look at the context of the speech and how he called on his listeners to take responsibility for their society after communism fell, instead of seeing themselves only as victims.

The Spirit of 1989

AAU was founded in 1990, right after the Velvet Revolution. Does that history still feel present at the university today?

It does, thanks to the initiative of our faculty and their desire for students to catch the spirit of the revolution: a love of freedom, democracy and dialogue – all great outcomes of a university education. My colleague Monika MacDonagh-Pajerová was literally one of the student leaders of ’89. She teaches a very popular course and weaves her experience and relationships into it.

About six years ago, I created a walking tour of the Velvet Revolution for our students and staff, which takes place every November 17. Colleagues who remember the communist days usually join us, and some of them were actually there on Národní třída on November 17, 1989. Other colleagues teach courses that involve Havel and other Czech artists and dissidents.

We regularly have events and special guests that bring that history alive. A few colleagues and I are “screening” a radio play Havel wrote, Guardian Angel, and then discussing it with our students and faculty. This play captures so many themes highly relevant to us today: technology and humanity, the nature of trust, listening, and how the powerful understand the needs of others. Of course, it was written under communism in the 1960s – it’s history – but it also has a timeless quality to it.

Why Prague?

If a student were choosing whether to study in Prague, what would you tell them?

I hope that a student would choose Prague to get immersed in its culture and history, not to live in a bubble. The Czech Republic has so much to offer. It is rich in history and beautiful, in and outside of Prague. It is also in the heart of Europe, so you can jump on a train and visit so many cultures and people. The city is safe and walkable, and it has a nice pace of life. After seven years, I never get tired of the sights, the streets to roam and the places to get good beer.

I think many students find it refreshing, especially those coming from large schools, that AAU is small and a close community. It is quite an intellectual place, so I see many students having deeper conversations in groups than I had ever seen in the places I’ve worked before. If you are coming from far away, it is a transformative experience to be a foreigner and live in such a different culture. You’ll never be the same. In a good way.

About Anglo-American University

Founded in 1990, Anglo-American University (AAU) is the oldest private university in the Czech Republic and offers bachelor’s and master’s programs taught entirely in English. It holds both Czech and US (WSCUC) accreditation, and its campus is located in the Thurn-Taxis Palace just below Prague Castle. More information at aauni.edu.

World.title: Love Sausages? Prague Has a New Bistro Serving Berlin-Style Currywurst
World.content:
Prague has a new fast-food spot dedicated to one of Germany’s best-known street dishes.

Currywurst11 opened on Palackého Street on November 11, serving German sausages with a selection of traditional and locally inspired sauces.

The project took nine months to prepare. Its menu features several types of German sausage, including traditional grilled bratwurst, Bauernwurst with herbs and steamed Bockwurst.

A vegetarian option made from peas is also available.

The sausages are served with tomato-based curry sauce, but customers can choose from several alternatives. These include an American-style version made with Coca-Cola, a Czech-inspired sauce combining plum butter, caraway seeds and beer, and a honey-mustard option.

Side dishes include French fries, bread, sauerkraut, pickled vegetables and kimchi.

The drinks menu features German bottled beers, homemade lemonades and Spezi, a popular German mix of cola and orange soda. Seasonal specials are also planned, with Pizza-Fleischkäse, a meatloaf-style sausage with cheese and red peppers, among the current offerings.

A currywurst with sauce costs CZK 150, with side dishes available for an additional CZK 20.

Currywurst11 is the latest venture from Ondřej Bednář, Tomáš Huml and Martin Červenka, the three entrepreneurs behind Dim Sum Spot.

They opened their first restaurant in Prague’s Letná district in 2019 and have since expanded to several locations in Prague and one in Liberec.

The partners initially considered opening an Asian noodle shop in the space next to their existing restaurant on Palackého Street. They eventually opted for German street food instead.

World.title: Documents reveal former FM Szijjártó’s ministry sought special treatment for Orbán’s brother’s companies in Vietnam
World.content:
Hungary’s former foreign ministry under Péter Szijjártó asked Hungarian consulates in Vietnam to give preferential treatment to companies linked to Áron Orbán, the younger brother of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, according to documents published by a government official. The instructions reportedly included arranging appointments outside normal procedures to speed up the processing of paperwork needed to bring Vietnamese workers to Hungary.

György László Velkey, a state secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, shared a document on Facebook on Tuesday, claiming it showed how the ministry intervened on behalf of the companies in September 2023.

According to the document, Hungarian consulates in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi were instructed to continue giving special attention and priority treatment to HR Capital Kft. and Multi Shoot Zrt., both linked to Áron Orbán. The consulates were also told to provide appointments outside regular opening hours for administrative procedures required to bring the companies’ employees to Hungary.

The ministry reportedly justified the request by referring to the “expectations of the ministry’s senior management”.

Velkey accuses former ministry of serving private interests

In his post, Velkey criticised the former foreign minister, Péter Szijjártó, arguing that the ministry had prioritised family business interests over representing Hungary’s interests abroad.

“This was Szijjártó’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs: instead of representing Hungarian interests, its priority was serving family business interests,” Velkey wrote.

The document follows another disclosure by Velkey last week. He then published correspondence from autumn 2023 in which Áron Orbán offered cooperation to Szijjártó, who was foreign minister at the time.

The latest revelations raise further questions about the relationship between the former foreign ministry and companies associated with the former prime minister’s family.

Áron Orbán arrested over suspected people smuggling

The documents have emerged amid a criminal investigation into the recruitment and movement of Vietnamese nationals. Áron Orbán was arrested last Wednesday on suspicion of people smuggling.

According to reports by Hungarian media, the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) is investigating suspected people smuggling committed as part of a criminal organisation. Investigators suspect that foreign nationals were helped to obtain Schengen visas through Hungarian diplomatic missions in Vietnam in exchange for recruitment fees.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) is also investigating suspected influence peddling. According to the allegations, individuals demanded an unlawful advantage from a recruitment company while referring to their political connections.

Investigators suspect that many of the Vietnamese nationals involved officially applied for visas to attend short vocational training courses in Hungary. However, they allegedly did not attend the courses and instead intended to travel onwards to Western Europe after obtaining their visas.

Áron Orbán and his partner were reportedly placed in pre-trial detention due to concerns that they might flee, go into hiding or interfere with the investigation.

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán previously responded to the case by claiming that he himself was the real target and that his brother was merely being used as a tool.

The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations against those involved have not yet been established by a court.

World.title: EU’s Russian gas imports plunge to near-historic low – But one route remains unchanged
World.content:
Europe appears to be gradually preparing for a future without Russian gas, as imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) have fallen sharply in recent months. The decline has pushed the share of Russian gas in the EU’s total imports close to a historic low, although pipeline deliveries through Hungary have remained largely unchanged.

According to an analysis by Hungarian business outlet G7, based on data from energy think tank Bruegel, EU countries imported 17.4 billion cubic metres of Russian LNG between January and October 2026. This was 1.1 billion cubic metres more than during the same period last year. However, the increase was concentrated in the first half of the year, with a clear reversal emerging in recent months.

Russian LNG imports fall sharply

In August, the EU received just around 700 million cubic metres of Russian LNG, the lowest monthly volume in almost five years. Imports remained below one billion cubic metres in October, despite being more than twice that level at the beginning of the year.

The decline in LNG deliveries has also reduced Russia’s share of the EU’s overall gas imports. In the third quarter of 2026, Russian gas accounted for around 10.6% of total imports, according to the G7 analysis. This is close to a historic low: in some months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the figure exceeded 50%.

The reduction in Russian LNG imports has been particularly significant because Hungary remains the only route through which Russian pipeline gas enters the EU from the south. As a result, the decline in shipments by sea has had a substantial impact on Russia’s overall share of the European gas market.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Hungary’s pipeline route remains largely unchanged

Despite the sharp fall in LNG imports, there has been no comparable decline in the volume of Russian gas arriving through pipelines via Hungary.

Around two-thirds of the natural gas delivered to Hungary still comes through the southern route, which carries Russian-origin gas. This means that while the EU’s overall reliance on Russian supplies has decreased, Hungary remains an important transit route for Russian gas entering the bloc.

EU ban on Russian gas imports approaching

The decline comes as the EU prepares to phase out Russian energy imports. Earlier this year, the European Council approved a timetable for ending purchases of Russian energy in several stages from 2027.

Under the current schedule, EU countries will be prohibited from purchasing Russian-produced LNG from 1 January 2027. The ban on Russian pipeline gas is due to take effect in autumn 2027.

Although the EU eased some restrictions on Russian oil amid the war involving Iran, the planned phase-out of Russian gas has remained in place.

The figures suggest that European countries have already begun reducing their reliance on Russian LNG ahead of the deadline. However, the continued flow of pipeline gas through Hungary highlights how uneven the transition away from Russian energy is.

World.title: Hungary aims to reach net zero emissions by 2050: Here’s how much it would cost
World.content:
How much would it cost Hungary to reach net-zero emissions by 2050? A new analysis shows the exact numbers and tells how Hungary’s efforts alone would impact global temperatures.

Hungary aims to reach net zero emissions by 2050

Reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 could cost Hungary an estimated HUF 17,600 billion (approximately EUR 48.28 billion) in total between 2027 and 2100, while generating only HUF 2,500 billion (currently EUR 6.86 billion) in climate-related benefits, according to calculations published on a new website examining the costs and benefits of climate policies.

The figures, presented on NetZeroCostBenefit.com, suggest that Hungary would receive just HUF 14 (EUR 0.038) in estimated benefits for every HUF 100 (EUR 0.27) spent on achieving the target. The calculations are based on international climate and economic models, although their conclusions reflect the assumptions and scenarios selected by the website’s author.

According to the analysis, the annual cost of reaching net zero would already amount to HUF 1,790 billion (EUR 4.91 billion) in 2045. All the long-term figures are expressed in present-day monetary value, reports Portfolio.

Limited global impact from Hungary alone

The website’s calculations also examine how much Hungary’s efforts would contribute to reducing global warming. If the country achieved net zero by 2050 and maintained it thereafter, while the rest of the world continued its current climate policies, global average temperatures in 2100 would be just 0.000346 degrees Celsius lower than otherwise expected.

The analysis argues that this would be virtually imperceptible, despite the substantial economic burden on Hungary. Its author says the calculations draw on the MAGICC climate model, which is also used in United Nations climate assessments, and economic estimates from research by climate economists Richard Tol and Nobel laureate William Nordhaus.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Global net zero also questioned

The analysis also challenges the economic case for achieving net-zero emissions worldwide by 2050. Based on three models identified in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s assessments as reaching that target from current emissions levels, the global economic cost could range from 3 to 19 per cent of GDP. The website uses the middle estimate, putting the economic loss at 7.2 per cent of global GDP in 2050 under the scenario examined.

By comparison, estimates from Tol and Nordhaus suggest that climate change could reduce global GDP by between 1.8 and 2.8 per cent by 2100 under current policy trajectories. The author argues that these projected damages are considerably smaller than the estimated costs of reaching net zero, and that emissions reductions would prevent only part of them.

In case you missed it: Péter Magyar announces EUR 160 million green overhaul: Millions of trees and cooler cities planned

How much would the whole world need to reach net zero emissions?

On a global scale, the website estimates that achieving net zero by 2050 would cost around USD 255 trillion in present-day value, while avoiding approximately USD 24 trillion in climate-related damage over the century. That amounts to a return of just nine cents for every dollar spent.

The author does not argue that climate change causes no damage, but questions whether net-zero policies represent an economically effective way to address it. The analysis suggests that investments in early-warning systems, more resilient infrastructure and poverty reduction could protect vulnerable communities more directly and at lower cost.

The figures are not an official Hungarian government estimate, but an assessment based on selected modelling scenarios. They nevertheless raise questions about the economic trade-offs involved in pursuing the 2050 target.

World.title: EU forecasts economic growth for Hungary, but can one problem overshadow future progress?
World.content:
Hungary’s economy is expected to regain momentum after a prolonged period of stagnation, with growth approaching 3 per cent in both 2027 and 2028, according to the European Commission’s Autumn 2026 Economic Forecast.

European Union forecasts growth, but there is one problem

However, the improved outlook comes with a warning: the country’s budget deficit is likely to remain above 5 per cent of GDP, while public debt is set to increase. The Commission expects Hungary’s gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by 1.8 per cent in 2026, before accelerating to 2.8 per cent next year and 2.9 per cent in 2028.

Household consumption is expected to remain the main driver this year, while recovering investment and exports should contribute more substantially over the following two years. The forecast is more optimistic about Hungary’s growth prospects than the broader outlook for the EU, where GDP is projected to rise by 1.4 per cent in both 2026 and 2027, and by 1.5 per cent in 2028.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Investment and exports to support recovery

Hungarian investment is expected to contract in 2026, partly because of reduced public development spending. However, the Commission anticipates a recovery as business confidence improves, the country’s risk premium declines and access to EU funding becomes available again following rule-of-law reforms.

New automotive assembly plants are expected to support export growth, although profits repatriated by foreign-owned companies are likely to keep the current account balance in deficit.

The labour market is also expected to remain tight. Employment is forecast to increase by 0.4 per cent this year, while unemployment could fall from around 4.6 per cent currently to 4 per cent by 2028. Wage growth, estimated at approximately 10 per cent in 2026, is expected to slow to 6.8 per cent next year.

As Portfolio reports, inflation is forecast to average 2.2 per cent this year, helped by a stronger forint and temporary price controls. It could rise to 3.4 per cent in 2027 as energy and food prices increase, before easing to 3 per cent in 2028.

Stay up-to-date: Tisza government promises new era with 2027 budget, opposition calls it austerity

Deficit remains the main concern

The Commission expects Hungary’s budget deficit to rise from 4.7 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 7.3 per cent this year. Higher spending, including pension payments, housing support and one-off payments to members of the armed forces, is contributing to the increase. Tax exemptions and expanded family tax benefits have also reduced government revenue.

Fiscal policy is expected to tighten considerably in 2027, with spending cuts across ministries and higher taxes, including a planned wealth tax and increases to corporate and excise taxes. The measures are projected to bring the deficit down to 5.2 per cent of GDP.

However, the Commission expects the shortfall to edge up again to 5.3 per cent in 2028, partly because sector-specific taxes are due to be phased out. This could complicate the government’s longer-term fiscal plans. Public debt is also forecast to rise, from 74.4 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 78.2 per cent by 2028, reflecting persistent deficits and borrowing under the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility.

World.title: Hungary’s energy minister dismisses head of Paks nuclear power plant with immediate effect, announces new leader
World.content:
Hungary’s economy and energy minister, István Kapitány, has dismissed the chief executive of the country’s Paks I nuclear power plant with immediate effect, appointing a long-serving member of the plant’s management team as his successor.

Kapitány announced on Tuesday that Péter János Horváth’s appointment as chief executive of MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant Plc had ended. He subsequently confirmed that Károly Vigh, the facility’s operations director, would take over the position. The minister made both announcements on Facebook, without giving a reason for Horváth’s departure.

New chief executive has spent more than 22 years at Paks

Vigh has worked at the nuclear power plant for more than 22 years, progressing through its operational ranks. He began his career as a reactor operator and later served as a unit duty manager before moving into senior management. Since 2024, he has been the plant’s operations director, overseeing the work of more than 800 employees, according to Kapitány.

The minister highlighted improvements in operational efficiency achieved under Vigh’s leadership, as well as the completion of major maintenance work on schedule and a reduction in delays associated with restarting reactor units. Kapitány also described the incoming chief executive as a team-oriented manager who values cooperation, his colleagues’ expertise and their professional development.

Vigh holds qualifications in mechanical engineering and nuclear power plant operations, as well as a degree in economics. He has also expanded his professional experience through international programmes run by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO), the minister said.

Horváth’s previous energy-sector roles

Horváth was appointed chief executive of MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant Plc in January 2023. Before taking up the role, he had twice headed the Hungarian Energy and Public Utility Regulatory Authority, serving between 2010 and 2013 and again from 2020 to 2023.

The company operates Paks I, Hungary’s existing nuclear power station, which plays a significant role in the country’s electricity supply. It is separate from Paks II, the new nuclear plant project currently under development.

Kapitány also dismissed the chief executive of Paks II, Gergely Jákli, in July, appointing Attila Ságodi as his replacement a few hours later. At the time, the minister cited Ságodi’s more than 25 years of strategic and energy-sector experience, alongside his nuclear expertise.

In announcing Vigh’s appointment, Kapitány stressed the importance of the existing Paks plant’s safe, reliable and economical operation for Hungary’s energy security. He said Vigh would continue the work he had pursued for more than two decades, now as chief executive.

World.title: US extends Hungary’s exemption from Russian energy sanctions: MOL and MVM can keep buying oil and gas
World.content:
Hungary will be able to continue purchasing Russian crude oil and natural gas without facing US sanctions, after Washington extended the country’s exemption until March 2027. The decision allows energy companies MOL and MVM to maintain transactions linked to Russian supplies through key pipelines.

The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) informed Hungary’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs that it had extended the relevant authorisations, the ministry announced on Facebook on Tuesday. Hungary’s previous exemption was due to expire on 21 November.

MOL can continue buying Russian oil through the Druzhba pipeline

The extension covers transactions necessary for MOL to purchase Russian crude oil from Lukoil and Litasco, either through immediate market purchases or to fulfil existing contracts.

The oil is delivered through the Druzhba pipeline, which remains an important supply route for Hungary. OFAC’s guidance allows the transactions to continue until 19 March 2027.

The US authority has also extended its guidance for MVM, Hungary’s state-owned energy company. This covers financial transactions related to Russian natural gas deliveries through the TurkStream pipeline.

The ministry said the guidance could be renewed after the March deadline. The decision means both companies can continue purchasing Russian energy without the transactions covered by the exemption exposing them to US sanctions.

Hungary and Slovakia secure extensions

The decision follows months of diplomatic efforts to maintain Hungary’s access to Russian energy. Former prime minister Viktor Orbán previously claimed that he had secured an exemption from US sanctions during a meeting with President Donald Trump in autumn 2025. According to Orbán’s account at the time, the arrangement would remain in force for as long as both leaders held office.

However, the issue remained on the agenda after the change of government in Hungary. In September 2026, Márton Hajdu, the Tisza Party chairman of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, travelled to Washington to lobby US lawmakers against sanctions on Hungary over its continued purchases of Russian crude oil.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán also visited the United States in late October, where she reached agreements with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on regional natural gas and oil industry developments, as well as law enforcement cooperation.

Slovakia has secured a similar extension. On Tuesday, Slovak Economy Minister Denisa Saková announced that Washington had extended the country’s exemption by 120 days beyond its original expiry date of 21 November. This will allow Slovakia to continue buying and paying for Russian crude oil without the risk of US sanctions during the extended period.

The decisions mean that both Hungary and Slovakia can maintain at least some of their Russian energy purchases for the coming months, despite the international efforts to reduce reliance on Russian supplies.

World.title: Index: Figures reveal how much money actually arrived from Brussels since the elections
World.content:
Despite the government’s repeated claims that it has unlocked around HUF 6,000 billion (EUR 15 billion) in previously frozen EU funding, only HUF 162 billion actually reached Hungary’s central Treasury account between April and September 2026, according to data obtained by Index. Most of the money arrived before the new government’s agreement with Brussels.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has repeatedly presented the release of EU funding as a major achievement since taking office. In June, he declared that the government had brought Hungarian taxpayers’ money home after reaching an agreement with the European Commission. Government communications have since described the deal as a historic breakthrough, claiming that around HUF 6,000 billion in EU funds had become accessible.

However, there is an important distinction between reaching an agreement to unlock funding and actually receiving the money. The HUF 6,000 billion figure covers several EU funding programmes, each with its own conditions and payment schedule.

To establish how much money had genuinely arrived, Index submitted a public information request to the Hungarian State Treasury.

Most of the money arrived before the Brussels agreement

The Treasury’s figures show that a total of HUF 162.2 billion in EU funding reached its central account between 1 April and 30 September.

Of this amount, HUF 116.4 billion arrived between April and 28 May, the day before the agreement between Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Only HUF 45.8 billion came in between 29 May and the end of September.

The total is also relatively modest compared with Hungary’s budget deficit. For context, the central budget recorded a deficit of HUF 200.6 billion in October alone. The first ten months of 2026 saw a cash-flow deficit of almost HUF 5,500 billion.

The largest individual payment during the period was HUF 70 billion in agricultural support, received on 7 May.

Agricultural support and international cooperation dominate

The breakdown of the Treasury’s accounts shows that the largest share – HUF 77.3 billion – was linked to the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF), which primarily finances direct payments to farmers.

A further HUF 55 billion came through accounts linked to Hungary’s 2021–2027 EU operational programmes. These funds support projects in areas including economic development, transport, education, healthcare and environmental protection.

Other payments included HUF 16.6 billion for the Danube Region Programme, HUF 6.7 billion for Hungarian-Slovak cross-border cooperation and HUF 6.5 billion for the Hungarian-Serbian programme.

These international initiatives finance joint projects involving universities, research institutions, local authorities and other organisations across several countries. Their funding does not necessarily remain in Hungary, even when it is initially transferred to a Hungarian Treasury account.
