World.title: Qatar Airways Cuts 24,500 Seats on Zagreb-Doha Route
World.content:
November the 17th, 2026 – Qatar Airways is set to cut 24,500 seats on the Zagreb-Doha route, abandoning its previous plans for 7 weekly flights between the two cities.

Qatar’s national airline Qatar Airways has reduced the planned number of flights between Doha and Zagreb for the summer 2027 timetable. Index reports that instead of the originally planned daily flights, according to the latest changes the company will operate four times a week. This is the second unfavourable announcement for Zagreb Airport for next year, after Austrian Airlines decided to withdraw from the route between Zagreb and Vienna, reports the portal Croatian Aviation.

Qatar Airways will thus retain the number of flights it operates on this route during the current winter timetable, as well as in the recently completed summer one. That frequency was introduced after the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East and the consequent disruptions in the company’s operations.

93 total cancelled rotations

Airbus A320 aircraft with 132 seats have been announced on the route between Doha and Zagreb. This means that each return rotation offers 264 seats. By reducing from seven to four flights a week, Qatar Airways is cancelling three weekly rotations, i.e. six individual flights. The summer timetable lasts 31 weeks, from the end of March to the end of October 2027, so this amounts to a total of 93 cancelled rotations. When the capacity of the announced aircraft is taken into account, with this decision Qatar Airways is withdrawing a total of 24,552 seats from sale on the route between the two cities.

a blow to zagreb’s connectivity with asia and australia

This is a significant reduction in capacity on one of the key routes from Zagreb. Through its hub in Doha, Qatar Airways enables passengers from Croatia to fly to numerous destinations in Asia, Australia, Africa and other parts of the world. The reduction in frequencies therefore does not only affect the direct link between Zagreb and Doha, but also the possibilities for onward travel.

In recent months the company has been adjusting its operations due to the security situation in the Middle East. Although it has gradually been restoring some capacity, limitations compared to the original plans still exist on certain markets. Zagreb will thus remain connected to Doha four times a week during the summer 2027 timetable as well, without a return to the daily operations that were on sale until a few days ago. Any increase in the number of flights will depend on the development of the situation in the region, the availability of the fleet and the strategy of the Qatari carrier.

World.title: Estonia unsure why number of people with disabilities falling rapidly
World.content:
The number of people with disabilities has fallen by more than 60,000 or nearly 40 percent over the past eight years. Neither the Ministry of Social Affairs nor the Social Insurance Board can pinpoint the exact reason.

Almost every day, the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People (EPIKoda) is contacted by someone whose officially recognized disability has been downgraded or whose disability status has been removed altogether, said the organization's lawyer, Kristi Rekand.

"For example, a person has repeatedly been assessed as having no capacity for work and a severe disability. They submit a new application and are once again found to have no capacity for work, but the Social Insurance Board determines that they have only a moderate disability or does not recognize any degree of disability at all. Naturally, this raises questions for the person about what has changed when they themselves feel their condition has remained the same," Rekand said.

According to the Social Insurance Board (SKA), there are currently 97,490 people with disabilities living in Estonia. About one-tenth have profound disabilities, while the remainder are divided equally between those with severe and moderate disabilities. In 2018, Estonia had 158,474 people with disabilities. Over eight years, that number has fallen by 38.5 percent.

"Considering improvements in diagnosis, the rise in chronic illnesses, the aging population and the number of young people experiencing mental health problems, such a decline is difficult to explain," Rekand said.

According to Rekand, reassessments show that the SKA's approach and practices have changed and this has become a pattern.

"We are not seeing any signs of stabilization and that is extremely concerning. We certainly have no reason to believe there is some kind of agenda behind this or that the state has a policy of reducing the number of people with disabilities. But at the same time, we look at the statistics and have no answers as to why the number is falling," Rekand said.

Possible effects wide-ranging

Government officials themselves cannot say exactly what has caused the decline in the number of people with disabilities. Kalev Härk, head of the Social Insurance Board's disability assessment department, said one major, clearly observable factor is that fewer people are applying for disability status. Comparing 2022 with 2025, the number of applications submitted last year was 15,000 lower.

When working-age people apply for a work capacity assessment, they can also request a disability assessment on the same application. To do so, they must check a separate box on the work capacity application. According to Härk, the number of these combined applications has also fallen by about 10 percent over the past three years.

Aids for elderly people and people with disabilities. Source: Raigo Pajula

Kristi Rekand noted that if the number of applications has declined, it is important to examine why fewer people are applying. One possible explanation, she said, is a growing perception that it is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain official disability status, discouraging people from applying in the first place.

"If that is the case, it is certainly unacceptable for a country that should put people first and be there to support them. In that case, we need to address this perception so that people still submit applications, receive the benefits they are entitled to and can access other support measures linked to their officially recognized degree of disability," Rekand said.

Härk also believes misinformation circulating online has played a role, including claims that the government is limiting the number of people granted disability status to save money.

"That is categorically false. First, no one has imposed an annual limit on the number of disability assessments the Social Insurance Board can approve or the amount of social benefits it can pay out. Not once have we received any indication that we are spending too much," Härk said.

He also acknowledged that people who do not receive the assessment results they had hoped for sometimes spread claims that the SKA is deliberately stripping people of their disability status.

But how can a person's disability disappear in the first place? According to Härk, this can happen in cases involving temporary health problems, such as injuries, strokes or serious sudden illnesses, which may leave someone in a very severe condition for a period of time. However, if they recover following a long and successful course of treatment, their degree of disability may be reduced.

"The illness itself may not have gone away, but we are not assessing the illness. Our job is to assess whether a person can independently manage activities involving vision, hearing, language, speech and cognitive functioning. If we find that they can perform the activities necessary for everyday life and do not have limitations that meet the criteria for an officially recognized degree of disability, then we simply cannot grant that status," Härk explained.

Combined applications sowing confusion

Kadri Mets, head of disability rights policy at the Ministry of Social Affairs, said there is no single explanation for the declining number of people with disabilities. She also confirmed that the ministry has issued no instructions to reduce the number of people granted disability status.

"Social benefits for people with disabilities are classified as an expenditure determined by eligibility in the state budget. This means benefits are paid to everyone who qualifies, regardless of whether the actual annual expenditure ends up exceeding the original forecast," Mets explained.

However, she noted that the combined applications mentioned earlier are causing confusion because, in these cases, the Social Insurance Board determines the degree of disability based on data from the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund, without involving an external expert.

"Once the Unemployment Insurance Fund has assessed a person's work capacity, the Social Insurance Board calculates their degree of disability based on the scores assigned in the different assessment categories. In about 90 percent of cases, this is simply a mathematical calculation. What we are seeing is that people find it difficult to understand how a decision on their work capacity assessment translates into a decision on their degree of disability," Mets said.

According to Mets, the Ministry of Social Affairs wants to introduce a single assessment process for working-age people next year, making the system easier to understand.

Kristi Rekand said it is precisely through these combined applications that many people have seen their officially recognized degree of disability reduced.

Mets confirmed that the ministry is concerned about the decline in applications and the accompanying perception that obtaining official disability status is either impossible or extremely difficult.

"Having a degree of disability officially recognized is certainly very important for people, perhaps most of all because it allows them to receive social benefits intended to partially cover additional expenses. At the same time, in recent years we have been moving toward a system in which people can receive the assistance they need even if they are not officially recognized as having a disability," Mets said.

Designated area for passengers with disabilities or a baby stroller on a bus. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Courts can overturn decisions

People can challenge decisions made by the Social Insurance Board in court free of charge, with the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People offering advice and assistance. According to Kristi Rekand, the organization received around 20 such requests for help last year and the number is increasing this year.

"Going to court is by no means easy for people. Even when there are no court fees, it is emotionally very difficult to have to turn to a court for help and guidance on an issue like this."

According to Rekand, court cases often end in a favorable outcome, meaning the Social Insurance Board must review its decision.

Kalev Härk of the SKA acknowledged that some of the agency's decisions have not been sufficiently justified or that expert opinions have been too brief. However, this does not necessarily mean the decisions themselves were incorrect.

"We have provided additional training to our medical experts and explained how to write their assessments in a way that makes them clearer and more legally sound. Considering that we have around 45,000 applications to review each year, I would say we have not done a particularly bad job," Härk said.

"A few cases have also ended up in court. When that happens, we take a very critical look at the matter and if we find that we have made a mistake, we acknowledge it and correct it," the SKA official added.

World.title: Estonian homeowners call for right to leave expensive district heating networks
World.content:
The Estonian Homeowners' Association has criticized the government for delaying district heating reform, arguing that addressing the root causes of high heating costs would be more effective than subsidizing winter heating bills.

The Estonian Homeowners' Association has sent a letter to the Ministry of Climate, pointing out that while the state is prepared to spend more than €6 million on compensating households for winter heating bills, it is simultaneously delaying reform of the heating sector that would address the root causes of high prices.

Andry Krass, head of the association, said many residents could heat their homes much more cheaply, for example, using an air-source heat pump. However, if their heating comes from a renewable source, they are not legally entitled to disconnect from the district heating network.

"By establishing district heating zones, the state has prohibited residents from buying heat from anyone other than the monopoly heating provider," Krass said.

Another problem is that allowing consumers to disconnect from expensive district heating networks would drive up heating prices even further for residents who remain connected. According to Krass, this happened in the village of Tarbja, five kilometers from Paide, where heating costs twice as much as in Paide.

"Many district heating zones in Estonia are not sustainable and the primary goal of this reform must be to find a solution for these areas — how to phase out these district heating networks while ensuring that consumers continue to have heating and can make a reasonable transition to a new heating system," he said.

The Estonian Homeowners' Association has also proposed a concrete solution.

"We believe the issue of district heating zones should be addressed alongside building energy efficiency. Renovation subsidies should be directed toward areas where heating prices are high and district heating networks are unsustainable in the long term. Support should be provided both for renovating buildings in these areas and for switching to independent heating systems," Krass said.

Krass said the Ministry of Climate had actually presented some ideas for district heating reform a year ago.

"There was just one problem: No solution was offered for consumers who would remain connected to the district heating network and could not afford to switch to an independent heating system. We pointed this out and the ministry lost interest in pursuing the reform after that," Krass said.

According to Krass, the Estonian Homeowners' Association has also presented the government with the idea of directing renovation subsidies toward areas with unsustainable district heating networks and has received feedback from the ministry.

"They look down at the floor. That's their reaction. Or they say they have to protect the investments made by heating monopolies. The Competition Authority has told us that its job is to ensure the profitability of heating monopolies. Those are the responses we've received," Krass explained.

Rein Vaks, head of the Ministry of Climate's energy department, said that if the entire problem could be solved with a single legislative amendment, the state would already have done so. He said cities and municipalities have the primary responsibility for addressing the issue, while the state mainly provides advice and support.

"Each area needs to be assessed individually. It is extremely difficult to simply turn to the ministry and say, 'Please amend the law and everything will be fine.' It just doesn't work that way," he said.

The state cannot introduce new subsidies at present because it lacks the funds. Vaks said the ministry is currently in talks with the European Commission about securing financial assistance for communities like Tarbja during the next EU budget period.

"We want to ask the European Commission whether replacing unsustainable district heating networks with local heating solutions would be eligible for funding and whether any money could be allocated for this purpose. These discussions with the commission will begin in December and continue until next spring," Vaks said.

World.title: Minister rejects Ryanair's criticism of Estonia's aviation market
World.content:
Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis has rejected claims by budget airline Ryanair that Tallinn Airport's fees are uncompetitive for the region, pointing to record growth this year and discounts for opening new routes.

Ryanair has claimed the Baltic states' airport fees are too high, and a year ago the low-cost airline cut five routes from Tallinn in its winter schedule, citing a 70 percent increase in airport fees.

In October, Ryanair Chief Commercial Officer Jason McGuinness called on Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to reduce their fees. He said the airline had expansion plans in the Baltic states that depended entirely on whether the governments and airports here became more competitive.

Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis (Reform) replied to the Ryanair executive this week. He said the company's concerns had been carefully considered and that the pressures facing airlines this winter were understandable, but that the factors affecting Estonia's air connections should be viewed in a broader context.

Leis noted that challenges related to Estonia's air connections remain.

"Nevertheless, we cannot agree with the assessment that Estonia is one of Europe's least recovered aviation markets," he wrote, noting that in 2024 Tallinn Airport exceeded its pre-pandemic passenger numbers, serving approximately 3.5 million passengers compared with 3.27 million in 2019.

Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis (Reform). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

The minister said passenger numbers reached 3.49 million last year, nearly 7 percent above pre-pandemic levels, adding that this shows Tallinn Airport's recovery has been favorable compared with the European average.

"Growth has continued in 2026. During the first 10 months, Tallinn Airport served 3.27 million passengers, representing an 11 percent increase compared with the same period last year," he pointed out.

Leis said 19 new routes were opened at Tallinn Airport in 2025–2026 and new airlines entered the market.

"Although reductions in services by individual airlines are regrettable, the overall development reflects the continued interest of airlines and passengers in Estonia," he said.

Tallinn Airport last increased its fees in April 2025 and will not do so this year.

"We therefore believe that this year's capacity adjustments should be viewed in a broader business context rather than attributed solely to a fee change introduced 18 months ago," Leis said. "In our assessment, Tallinn Airport's fee structure remains competitive in the regional context. The introduction of new routes and continued growth in passenger numbers further demonstrate the attractiveness of the Estonian market."

He added that, at the same time, the airport must ensure sustainable financing for its infrastructure and services.

Discounts for new routes

Leis emphasized that a diverse network of airlines is important for connectivity and highlighted airBaltic and SAS as important partners for Tallinn Airport.

"Both direct flights and frequent connections through hub airports are important for a market the size of Estonia. A significant proportion of Tallinn Airport's passengers reach their final destination with at least one transfer. Maintaining and developing both types of service, together with a diverse selection of airlines, remains essential to meeting the needs of passengers and businesses," the minister said.

Tallinn Airport also supports the opening of new routes with discounts.

"Ryanair is also welcome to make use of these opportunities if the relevant conditions are met," Leis said, encouraging Ryanair to communicate directly with Tallinn Airport's management regarding further growth opportunities.

Eero Pärgmäe. Source: ERR

Eero Pärgmäe, a member of the management board of AS Tallinna Lennujaam, confirmed to ERR that the scheme exists and that many European airports have similar incentives.

The program reduces airlines' risks when launching new connections and supports the establishment of new routes. When opening a new route, an airline can receive a discount of up to 90 percent on airport fees.

"Ryanair can also receive support under the same conditions," Pärgmäe said.

He noted that Tallinn Airport's support program is based on the principle of equal treatment and is open to all airlines under the same conditions.

Pärgmäe sai all airlines and routes are important to Tallinn Airport, and developing new air connections and maintaining existing ones is one of the airport's most important objectives.

World.title: Closing Estonia's southern border with Latvia would cost €65 million
World.content:
Restoring border controls between Estonia and Latvia would cost approximately €65 million, which would be better directed to the Police and Border Guard Board (ISS) and the Internal Security Service (KAPO), Ministry of the Interior Secretary General Tarmo Miilits has said.

This discussion has arisen after eight Latvian residents were detained following an attempted arson at a drone maker's factory in Viimsi on Saturday morning. The incident has been attributed to Russia's military intellegence service, the GRU.

In response, Estonia is planning to close land crossing points on the eastern border with Russia from December 1. But some have asked about the situation with Latvia.

Several Latvian residents were also arrested in September after an attempted arson, also attributed to the GRU, on another defense company in Tallinn.

However, Miilits said there are no threats on the southern border.

"The Police and Border Guard Board is prepared to restore border controls with Latvia fairly quickly if this becomes necessary for security or safety reasons. Today, there is no need for this on security or safety grounds. /.../ At present, our Police and Border Guard Board and Latvian colleagues, both in the security services and border guard, are cooperating very well," Miilits told Tuesday's "Aktuaalne kaamera."

He said restoring border controls on the southern border would be expensive, and the money could be put to better use.

"It comes with quite a hefty price tag. If I had a choice – I am not a politician, but if I were to make a recommendation to politicians – it would be much more sensible to invest around €65 million in the Police and Border Guard Board, which would help double the current number of patrols, and to invest in counterintelligence at the country's security agency, the Internal Security Service. That would bring much greater benefits," he said.

The official added that if the eastern border closes, Estonia's security agencies and international partners are also prepared for the possibility that Russia may begin organizing illegal migration toward Estonia in retaliation, as it has done in Latvia, Lithuania and Poland.

Estonia's political parties are split on the issue of closing the southern border.

World.title: Estonian goshawk may have spent winters raiding Russian poultry farm
World.content:
While migrating birds in Estonia usually fly south for winter, one goshawk headed north-east to Russia, where GPS data suggest it may have found food near a poultry farm.

The unusual movements of the bird were documented in a study by Ülo Väli.

The female goshawk, tracked by researchers between 2022 and 2024, traveled approximately 280 kilometers from her breeding grounds in southeastern Estonia to the same wintering area in northwestern Russia, in two consecutive years. GPS data recorded the bird of prey near a large industrial poultry farm and on multiple occasions. So even while the planned closure of the border with Russia next month may work for humans, wildlife will perhaps pay it less heed.

The claim suggests the goshawk hunted at the poultry farm near Pervomayskoye, also known as Kivennapa, close to St Petersburg. Väli suggested that the bird may have fed on chicken carcasses or pigeons in the surrounding area.

According to the researcher, goshawks generally lead fairly sedentary lives. Males tend to remain close to their nests, while females are slightly more mobile and can expand their home ranges to an extent. However, for an adult bird to travel almost 300 kilometers from its breeding grounds is a truly exceptional thing.

There could be several explanations for this, Väli said. The bird may have originally hatched near Pervomayskoye and subsequently established its breeding territory in Estonia after dispersing south as a juvenile. Alternatively, it may have visited the area to explore it as a juvenile, a time when goshawks roam more widely, or perhaps reached it later in life while searching for food. The possibility that the Russian area was its original home is a particularly interesting one, as the availability of prey there may have encouraged the bird to return.

It is also unusual that the goshawk flew to Russia over the sea, across the Gulf of Finland, as she would likely have had to do, Väli explained. "Birds of prey generally do not like crossing open water, but there was no easier route to fly there," he said.

What makes this even more remarkable is the bird's build. Goshawks are roughly the size of ravens, with short wings and long tails. Their physical characteristics are adapted to life in forests, rather than long-distance migration across open landscapes, still less water. Nevertheless, GPS data suggest that the female crossed the Gulf of Finland during both winters, Väli said.

Ornithology is not untouched by the war in Ukraine either

The ornithologists tracked the goshawk's movements using a solar-powered GPS device attached to the bird like a backpack. The device weighed just 30 grams, approximately two per cent of the bird's body weight, and recorded its location at intervals of as little as 10 minutes.

According to Väli, fitting the device was relatively straightforward on this occasion. "A kindly farmer in Põlva County caught it in his chicken enclosure and, instead of killing it, as many people probably would have done, notified ornithologists," he said. This meant the researcher did not have to spend time catching the bird himself.

The GPS device transmitted the bird's location remotely, allowing researchers to follow its movements across national borders. Although the ornithologists tracked the bird during the first years of the full-scale war in Ukraine, Väli said he initially had no problems with this.

The situation has since changed, however, and the researcher confirmed that the war has also affected ornithologists' work. "GPS jamming [in Russia] is already quite serious; we can no longer even track birds' movements properly," Väli noted.

The device itself can also pose problems when tracking a bird. It is powered by solar panels, meaning that prolonged periods of poor weather can affect its operation. "When the weather is wintry and gray, the battery inside does not get recharged," Väli said.

The goshawk eventually died in Russia in 2024. According to the scientific study, the bird was captured in a dovecote near St Petersburg, severely injured, and transferred to a rehabilitation center. Väli said it was however challenging to obtain information about the bird's fate from a country waging a war of aggression. Here limited movement initially indicated that she had died, while a Russian ornithologist he knew also informed him of its death. There is no broader cooperation, however, he said, with Russian authorities, and universities have also ended cooperation with Russian counterparts.

An estimated 400 to 600 Eurasian Goshawks (Astur gentilis) breed in Estonia.

The article was originally published in the scientific journal Ringing & Migration.

World.title: Tallinn to increase road construction and cut officials in 2027
World.content:
Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said Tallinn will continue investing in infrastructure next year while cutting jobs in the city administration.

Major projects will include the reconstruction of Pärnu maantee and Petrooleumi tänav, the continuation of the second phase of Peterburi tee, and the reconstruction of the Hipodroomi intersection.

The second phase of Peterburi tee will involve repairing uneven sections of road made of concrete slabs near Iru, which Järvan described as a roller coaster made of concrete blocks.

At the same time, the city government will continue to reduce the size of the public sector, Järvan said.

He said approximately 100 officials were hired every year in previous years, but expansion cannot continue at this pace.

The deputy mayor highlighted that the current coalition abolished the green transition department after coming to power.

"Today, almost a year later, we can ask whether the City of Tallinn has collapsed as a result. No, but costs are lower. Some jokers might claim that if the green transition department had not been abolished, we would already have snow on the ground in November. I doubt that," he commented.

Seven positions will be cut in the city's business service next year. "We have clearly demonstrated that we can do more with less," Järvan noted.

World.title: Estonian parties take different views on restoring border control with Latvia
World.content:
According to EKRE Chairman Martin Helme, the party has repeatedly called for Estonia's eastern border to be closed. Helme suspects the government decided to close the border in the hope of boosting its approval ratings.

"It is particularly embarrassing to watch this farce over the eastern border when EKRE has repeatedly demanded since the summer that not only the eastern border but also the border with Latvia be brought under control. That is where those saboteurs and provocateurs came from who, according to the Internal Security Service, were carrying a GRU identification card and an operational plan. Not across the eastern border, but across the southern border. Just as hundreds of illegal immigrants have crossed from there unchecked whom the police are trying to apprehend every day. Yet the government is unwilling even to discuss closing the southern border, let alone bringing it under control," Helme wrote on social media.

"To the jokers in the government: Now that you've finally found your backbone and common sense, do us all a favor and bring the entire border under control. If that doesn't happen, all this huffing and puffing about closing the eastern border can only be seen as a pre-election circus. An exercise in futility. There is certainly no security dimension to it, nor can there be as long as the southern border remains open," he added.

SDE head: Closing the Estonia-Latvia border very resource-intensive

Social Democratic Party Chairman and former Interior Minister Lauri Läänemets said closing the Estonian-Latvian border would require substantial resources and that he does not consider it the most sensible solution.

"Since we don't have a border fence there either, it would mean deploying significantly more personnel. In fact, it would have the same effect on the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) as during the COVID-19 pandemic when many officers who were investigating various cases or dealing with migration issues, including foreign labor, had to take turns guarding the border. This means the PPA's other activities would have to be scaled back or put on hold," Läänemets said.

"Partial border controls could be reinstated, but they have significant gaps, especially along land borders, and mainly involve spot checks or increased inspections at border crossing points. Yes, this could be done and it has been implemented before," Läänemets said.

The SDE leader believes that instead of increasing border controls, Estonia should invest more in the counterintelligence capabilities of the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS/KAPO) and the response capabilities of the Police and Border Guard Board.

"That would be cheaper and more effective because it would be more precisely targeted. And ultimately, we wouldn't be stretching our police resources too thin," Läänemets said.

He predicted that closing the eastern border could prompt Russia to create migration pressure along Estonia's border as well.

"If we completely close the Estonian-Russian border — which is a very sensible move in this case — we may find ourselves facing increased migration pressure on that border at some point. One possible reason why Russia has not previously generated migration pressure in this way is that the border crossing points have remained open," Läänemets said.

"So we need to consider all possible future scenarios and target our measures more precisely. I think closing the Latvian border would not achieve the desired effect but would instead waste our resources unnecessarily," Läänemets added.

Center: Temporarily restoring checks on southern border worth considering

Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart said that, as with the eastern border, border controls along Estonia's southern border should not be a matter of political debate, particularly since genuine threats to Estonia have already come through Latvia.

"In my view, this is not even a political question but a matter of basic logic. If we close the eastern border because there is a threat that could cross it, then in the case of the Latvian border, we know that this threat — not a theoretical threat, but actual attacks — has already materialized. Not to mention that illegal migrants are also entering through Latvia. This is not yet a crisis, but it is always better to prevent a crisis than to deal with its consequences afterward. So I think this is an entirely objective issue: We need to discuss it with our Latvian counterparts, but also consider temporarily reinstating border controls," Kõlvart said.

"If we are currently taking preventive measures along one border, it makes sense to do the same along the other," Kõlvart added.

"As for resources, closing the eastern border would free up some of them. How border controls should be reinstated is, again, not something for politicians to decide. Whether that means restoring full border controls, conducting spot checks, increasing the number of patrols and so on — these are matters for experts in the relevant field to discuss. But when it comes to security, threats and potential crises, strengthening border controls is an entirely logical step at this point," Kõlvart said.

According to Kõlvart, closing the eastern border is not a political question either.

"If we identify an escalation in the situation and threats that could come across the border have also been identified — based on assessments by the relevant authorities, primarily the Estonian Internal Security Service — then we are dealing with an objective situation. And if this measure is necessary to ensure our security, then it must be implemented," Kõlvart said.

Isamaa leader: Border control suitable measure as migration pressure persists

Isamaa Chairman Urmas Reinsalu also said closing the eastern border would free up resources to strengthen the southern border, primarily to curb illegal migration pressure from Latvia.

"If we assume that the pressure will continue — primarily from Belarus, but also through Russia, with people being brought illegally into Latvian territory — and that this border cannot be secured, then introducing additional border control procedures within the Schengen Area would clearly be an entirely legitimate, appropriate and proportionate measure. A number of European countries, including Germany and Austria, have done this. It does not mean that such controls would be applied across the board, but rather according to the threat assessment. Isamaa is open to this option if less restrictive measures fail to stop illegal migration," Reinsalu said.

"However, we do not have a specific proposal. I think it is important for the government to prepare its own assessment of why such a large number of people have entered Estonian territory illegally, why these spot checks have failed to stem the flow of people and what the outlook is for the future," Reinsalu added.

"If this migration flow has continued since the summer, then clearly more needs to be done. One option is to introduce border controls, while another is to implement other control and surveillance measures," Reinsalu said.

Addressing reports that some Latvian citizens had entered Estonia to carry out acts of sabotage, Reinsalu said that because they are European Union citizens, they must be apprehended through means other than border controls.

Reform: Solution in cooperation with Latvia, not border checks

Mati Raidma of the Reform Party, a member of the Riigikogu National Defense Committee, said he does not see reinstating border controls between Estonia and Latvia as an option.

"Cooperation between the Estonian and Latvian security services is very effective, as can be seen in the resolution of all these cases. In reality, the key to addressing today's challenges lies in good cooperation and mutual assistance, not in closing the border," Raidma said.

"Close cooperation between the Estonian and Latvian security services is what allows us to keep the situation under control and thwart all kinds of plans at the earliest possible stage. These activities are not being orchestrated by the Latvian state, but by Russia and its intelligence services. That is where the real enemy lies," Raidma added.

Eesti 200 whip: Border control seems excessive

Toomas Uibo, chairman of the Eesti 200 parliamentary group, said that although the group has not discussed the issue, he personally believes there is currently no need for border controls.

"At the moment, it does seem like a somewhat excessive measure. Of course, we need to keep an eye on developments. If it becomes justified at some point, then naturally it should be done. Experts are better placed to make that assessment than politicians," Uibo said.

Interior minister: Government far from weighing border control

Interior Minister and Eesti 200 member Igor Taro said he does not believe any of the conditions that would warrant seriously considering the reinstatement of border controls between Estonia and Latvia have been met.

"We are nowhere near a crisis situation or anything that would require the introduction of full-scale border controls along the Latvian border," Taro told ERR.

"To actually restore border controls between Estonia and Latvia as they once existed, we would have to build infrastructure along the entire border. We would have to reinstate checkpoints on roads, but we obviously couldn't leave fields and forests unguarded. Restoring such border controls would cost around €300 million in investment alone, based on current construction costs, such as those incurred in building the Estonian-Russian border infrastructure," Taro said.

According to Taro, this would not be a practical use of resources at present.

"We have successfully dealt with illegal immigration, apprehended everyone who has attempted to travel through Estonia or enter the country illegally and, most recently, successfully thwarted an attempted act of sabotage involving individuals recruited in Latvia. This was possible thanks to very good cooperation with Latvia's security services and law enforcement agencies. Through this cooperation, we are able to keep the situation along the Latvian border well under control and mitigate risks without having to seriously consider building new border infrastructure between Estonia and Latvia," Taro said.

Addressing suggestions of introducing spot checks or more limited border controls, Taro said that compensatory measures under the Schengen framework are already in place.

"We have 50 patrols operating across Estonia, monitoring everything, including traffic coming from Latvia. There is no need for a vehicle to be stopped at a former border crossing point. We can apprehend illegal migrants attempting to pass through without obstructing the movement of ordinary law-abiding people or having to maintain a visible presence directly on the road at the Estonian-Latvian border," Taro added.

The debate follows the detention of eight Latvian citizens after an attempted arson at Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems, which Estonia's domestic intelligence service has attributed to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Estonia is weighing closing its eastern border in response.

World.title: Estonia's youth jobs paradox: Firms struggle to find workers
World.content:
Estonian employers report staff shortages despite high youth unemployment, pointing to a mismatch between the skills young people have and those companies need.

Youth unemployment reached 23.7 percent in the third quarter, as employers struggled to fill technical, healthcare and education jobs.

Estonia's overall unemployment rate rose to 7.9 percent in the third quarter as employment fell. Young people were among the hardest hit, with youth employment down 5,400 year on year.

Employers say they see the same paradox from the other side. Hando Sutter, CEO of the Estonian Employers' Confederation, said that while employment in Estonia is "quite high", so too is youth unemployment, which is among the highest rates in Europe. At the same time, companies have been complaining of staff shortages.

"There is certainly more than one reason for this," Sutter said. He noted that young people are being trained in fields and occupations where there are fewer opportunities in the labor market. These tend to be less technical fields, he said. Demand is high in manufacturing, however, where employers are looking for people in engineering, mechanics and energy.

Hando Sutter. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Sutter, a former board chair of state-owned generator Eesti Energia, added there is also strong demand for workers in healthcare, while teachers are needed too. He said work can almost always be found in these areas. "We have a slight mismatch between supply and demand," he said.

"We have also discussed the quality of young people's training, which may be lacking in at least some fields," Sutter said. He added that employers also need to do more to support young people. An increasing number of companies in Estonia are taking on interns to help young people take their first step from education into employment and make the transition smoother.

Sutter noted that work processes are becoming increasingly complex as more technology is introduced. "I don't just mean artificial intelligence, but automation in general," he explained. With work becoming more complex, fewer simple entry-level jobs are available across the board. "For this reason, we need workers to have better skills and knowledge when entering the labor market," he said.

Social skills are also important, Sutter noted, as employees increasingly need to work in teams and interact with people across different teams. "Young people are still acquiring all of these skills," he said.

Estonia's unemployment rate has fluctuated in recent quarters amid weak economic conditions and declining employment. Young people have been particularly affected, with youth unemployment reaching 23.7 percent in the third quarter, while employment among those aged 25–64 remained relatively stable. Economists have pointed to factors including AI, remote working and employers' preference for experienced staff as contributing to weaker job prospects for younger workers.
