Most current antifungal drugs work by destroying fungal cells. However, fungi can gradually develop resistance to these medicines, making infections increasingly difficult to treat. A team led by Sriram Varahan at CCMB studied ‘Candida albicans’, a fungus commonly found on human skin and in the body. While generally harmless, it can cause serious infections when it enters the bloodstream or internal organs.

The researchers focused on ‘morphogenesis’, in which the fungus changes from a round-cell form into long, filament-like structures, a transformation allowing the pathogen to evade the body’s immune defences and spread more effectively within tissues.

What did CCMB scientists target?

Earlier studies had shown that glycolysis, the process through which cells metabolise sugar, plays a key role in controlling this shape change. Building on these findings, the team screened a library of small molecules that target glycolysis and identified two compounds capable of blocking the transformation.

Although the fungus continued to grow, it remained in its harmless rounded form suggesting that the compounds could serve as “anti-infective” agents that reduce the fungus’ ability to cause disease without necessarily eliminating it.

The study also identified pyruvate kinase, an enzyme involved in sugar metabolism, as a crucial regulator of fungal morphogenesis. Researchers further found that one of the compounds reduced biofilm formation, a protective layer that helps fungi resist treatment. The compound also increased the effectiveness of widely used antifungal drugs such as fluconazole and amphotericin B.

In a mouse model of systemic Candida infection, treatment with the lead compound significantly improved survival rates, highlighting its potential for future therapeutic development. “Our findings suggest that fungal disease-associated behaviour can be targeted without necessarily stopping fungal growth,” said Dhrumi Shah, first author of the study. “We need further studies to evaluate the compounds effectiveness and safety but by blocking the fungus from becoming invasive, they could complement existing treatments,” said Sriram Varahan.

The findings, published in ACS Infectious Diseases, emerged from a collaboration between CSIR-CCMB and the BRIC-Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, said a press release on Tuesday.

World.title: Indian national missing after attacks on commercial vessel in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
An Indian national went missing and two others sustained injuries after their Panama-flagged vessel came under attack in the Strait of Hormuz this week that triggered a strong condemnation from New Delhi.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said that of the 24 Indian nationals on board MT Tara Gas, 21 have been safely evacuated.

"We condemn the attack on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT Tara Gas in the Strait of Hormuz on 16 November 16," it said in a statement.

India said the targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure must end.

"Of the 24 Indian nationals on board, 21 have been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, two injured Indian crew members have been admitted to hospital, while one Indian national remains missing," it added.

The MEA said the Embassy in Oman is closely monitoring the ongoing search and rescue operations in coordination with the Omani authorities.

"We appreciate the timely assistance and support extended by the Government of Oman in the rescue efforts," it said.

New Delhi said the "continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region are deeply worrisome and pose a serious threat to the safety of civilian seafarers."

"The targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through international waterways, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," it said in a statement.

World.title: No mandate only women personnel can ‘handle’ women in crowd-control operations, Delhi Police to SC
World.content:
The Delhi Police has told the Supreme Court there is no strict rule that only women police officers must “handle” women in crowd-control operations.

The police was responding to allegations of manhandling women protestors and journalists by male police officers during widespread protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The allegations were made in petitions by Network of Women in Media, India, represented by advocate Aarthi Rajan, and others like the Delhi Union of Journalists, Free Speech Collective and the Kerala Union of Working Journalists.

The legal requirement that only women police officers could arrest or carry out searches on women was not a mandate in crowd-control situations, the police submitted in an affidavit.

“With regards to the allegations of manhandling of women journalists, it is respectfully submitted that the requirement of women personnel handling women is not a statutory mandate in the context of crowd-control operations, in the same manner as it is expressly prescribed under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 in relation to searches and arrests,” the police said.

The police said the deployment of women personnel in a crowd-control situation was an “operational consideration” depending on various factors, including the need to maintain propriety, avoid unnecessary confrontation and defuse tensions at a protest site, particularly if there were women participants.

The mere presence or involvement of male police personnel in crowd-control operations during the CJP protest cannot, itself, be construed as misconduct.

There is no legal bar on a male police officer from acting as a first responder. Nor is he stopped from assisting a woman police officer in the discharge of her duties.

“Such decisions have to be taken at the fraction of a second,” the police affidavit said.

The affidavit said an October 11 direction of the apex court to the Delhi Police to not “hinder” journalists, lawyers and other professionals in the discharge of their professional duties did not extend to reel-makers, social media influencers or unruly elements who break the lawful directions of the police at the site of a prohibited assembly.

The police said it “fully respects the role of the press”. However, there were individuals masquerading as journalists by using a camera and a microphone. The protest site, which the police repeatedly said was “illegal”, was replete with ‘content creators’ for YouTube.

The affidavit said though the police had found it difficult to distinguish between journalists and reel-makers, the latter were neither obstructed nor hindered unless they posed a risk to public order and law.

The Delhi Police pointed out that the current laws, guidelines and rules did not consider reel-makers, creative or otherwise, or content-creators as ‘working journalists’.

The police said it was yet to be determined if “reel-makers can be elevated to the status of journalists or reporters”. The police said the lack of a clear distinction in law hampered the police in its duties to maintain law and order, especially in an unprecedented situation when thousands marched to the Parliament in July as part of an “unauthorised” protest. The July protests were against question paper leaks in the NEET-UG 2026.

The affidavit said that the police have consistently maintained restraint though people with cameras and microphones defied orders to keep a reasonable distance from “operational areas”.

The police denied any attempt on their part to obstruct or interfere with journalists engaged in their professional pursuits. Anybody apprehended on account of mistaken identity had been immediately released in verification of identity, the police said.

“The police action was directed solely towards dispersing and removing the protestors from the illegal protest sites and restoring public order, and was neither intended nor directed towards detaining, restraining or obstructing any media personnel in the lawful discharge of their professional duties,” the Delhi Police maintained.

World.title: Six months of Keralam UDF govt: is the administration lumbering or hitting the ground running?
World.content:
With the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government marking its six months in office on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), the question hovering over the polity is whether the ruling alliance’s actions have matched its soaring rhetoric about expediting a transformative vision for Keralam’s development and welfare.

The debate also remains centred on whether the UDF has hit the ground running or is still strolling, as promised by Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan.

World.title: 'He who claims equity must come with clean hands': Asif hits back at Bilawal
World.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif joined others from the ruling PML-N on Wednesday in responding to PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari following the latter’s hard-hitting speech over several issues, including new provinces and constitutional tweaks and treatment of the opposition.

“He who claims equity must come with clean hands,” Asif reminded Bilawal in a post on X, as the wrangling between coalition partners PML-N and PPP appeared to deepen.

The exchange has particularly heated up after Bilawal delivered a no-holds-barred speech the previous day that covered the question of new provinces. The Bhutto scion also expressed support for several opposition demands and questioned past decisions and actions taken by the ruling coalition.

Bilawal referred to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s recommendation of holding a referendum to decide on the creation of new administrative units and said: “In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one.”

The PPP chairperson also remarked that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse” — seemingly reacting to Naqvi’s statement in July that the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

Asif began his response to Bilawal by addressing this matter.

He said: “No system can reset without public support. If you are talking about a system collapse, then all of us, as people connected to this system, must also take stock of our responsibilities.

The defence minister also appeared to throw his weight behind the proposal for holding a referendum on new province as he said that there would surely be a debate on “system reset” in Parliament, but the public too could not be “deprived of its fundamental right”.

“The pinnacle of legitimacy would be reached if the public opinion is also taken into account along with that of Parliament.”

Seemingly reacting to Bilawal’s support for the release of incarcerated former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan and other demands by the opposition, Asif added: “Holding politicians accountable in this country is nothing new, and no politician exempt from accountability.”

He mentioned that the PPP had been in power in Sindh for 18 years.

“Sindh has turned into paradise. The world admires the condition of Karachi,” he said, seemingly taking a jibe at the PPP, which is often criticised over the lack of development in Sindh.

Asif then said Bilawal and his party had been a “partner of the PML-N in the business of government since 2022. You get the profit and the PML-N and Pakistan suffer loss”.

“He who claims equity must come with clean hands,” Asif continued. “This is a centuries-old maxim of equity. Are your hands clean? Do you have the right to lecture or threaten?”

The defence minister said, “We have just one objective: to change the lives of the people of Pakistan so that ordinary people can live with dignity. Make public participation in governance a reality … Do not confine the people’s rights to the pages of the Constitution.”

More to follow

World.title: Pakistan, Turkiye discuss expanding defence cooperation in electronic warfare, drone and aerospace technologies
World.content:
Air Chief Marshal (ACM) Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu and Turkish Air Force Commander General Rafet Dalkıran discussed opportunities to enhance bilateral defence cooperation in unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare, advanced aerospace technologies, and indigenous research, development and production.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Pakistan Air Force’s Directorate General of Public Relations (DGPR) said the air chief highlighted that the Pakistan-Turkiye partnership, founded on shared history, common values and mutual trust, had evolved into a robust strategic relationship with considerable potential for expansion in the defence and aerospace domains.

ACM Sidhu also assured the visiting dignitary of the PAF’s all-out support in the areas of pilot training, professional development and capacity-building endeavours of the Turkish Air Force, the statement added.

The DGPR said he apprised the visiting dignitary of the PAF’s ongoing transformation into a “technologically advanced, multi-domain air force”, driven by capability-centric modernisation, indigenous innovation and investment in next-generation operational concepts.

Both air chiefs identified “substantial opportunities” for enhancing bilateral defence cooperation in unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare, advanced aerospace technologies, and indigenous research, development and production.

They also stressed the importance of institutionalised professional exchanges, integrated training programmes and joint exercises to enhance interoperability and foster greater operational synergy between the two air forces, the DGPR said.

Turkish Air Force Commander General Dalkıran acknowledged the PAF’s “remarkable professional standing, operational proficiency and combat experience”.

He also appreciated the PAF’s progressive modernisation trajectory, growing indigenous aerospace capabilities and pursuit of technological self-reliance under the leadership of ACM Sidhu, the statement said.

The visiting Turkish officer also expressed his “earnest desire” to leverage the PAF’s rich combat legacy and extensive operational expertise to advance bilateral defence cooperation.

Upon arrival at Air Headquarters, the Turkish air force commander was accorded a guard of honour by a “smartly turned-out contingent” of the PAF.

The visit reflects the growing strategic depth of Pakistan-Turkiye relations and a shared resolve to move towards a more “integrated, technology-driven and forward-looking defence partnership”, the statement said further.

The Turkish air force commander also called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the General Headquarters a day earlier, where matters of mutual interest, regional security dynamics and avenues to enhance bilateral defence cooperation were discussed.

CDF Munir highlighted the “deep-rooted historical, cultural and strategic ties between the two countries” and appreciated the strong defence partnership between their armed forces.

Earlier in May, the PAF and Turkish Air Force reaffirmed their “growing strategic convergence” in defence, aerospace innovation and emerging technologies during ACM Sidhu’s official visit to Turkiye.

During the visit, discussions also focused on joint exercises, training programmes, professional exchanges and cooperation in unmanned aerial systems and emerging technologies.

Pakistan and Turkiye, meanwhile, are co-signatories to multiple defence agreements, including the Makkah Defence Pact signed in August this year with Saudi Arabia, as well as the multilateral Badr defence cooperation pact in October alongside Qatar and Indonesia.

World.title: Xi, Putin meet ahead of historic Trump trilateral summit
World.content:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin began talks in Shenzhen on Wednesday, a day ahead of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city.

Thursday’s trilateral has triggered fears that the three powerful men could decide the fate of Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv and Europe, and seek to carve up the world into 21st-century spheres of influence.

Washington had signalled that Ukraine — something Xi vehemently sees as not China’s problem — was not expected to be addressed, before Trump said that it would.

China has said only that the leaders would hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.

Chinese President Xi Jinping attends a meeting with President of Russia Vladimir Putin (not pictured) at the APEC China 2026 Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, 18 November 2026. — AFP

Also up for discussion are the Iran war and nuclear disarmament, according to Washington, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.

Beijing has long maintained that the US and Russia should reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.

In from the cold

Chinese and Russian news agencies reported at around noon on Wednesday that Xi and Putin had met for talks — the fifth time the two leaders have met this year, including once by video link.

Putin has been shunned by the West since launching Europe’s worst conflict since World War II with his 2022 attack on Ukraine.

Addressing the APEC gathering on Wednesday, he said he expected the trilateral summit with Xi and Trump to be “highly useful”.

“At a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division… and dialogue rather than ultimatums,” Putin said.

Chinese President Xi Jinping attends a meeting with President of Russia Vladimir Putin at the APEC China 2026 Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, 18 November 2026. — AFP

He said Western sanctions imposed on Russia since his 2022 invasion of Ukraine had failed, arguing that they were “not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying the economies of the competition”.

Earlier, Xi called for greater international cooperation on AI and free trade.

“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said as he opened the event.

Xi and Putin were expected to discuss energy and finance and then – in a smaller format – foreign policy including Ukraine and North Korea, Russian officials said.

Kim incoming?

Trump was on Wednesday still in the Philippines where a day earlier he met fellow leaders of the Quad — Australia, Japan and India — for the first time in his second term.

The grouping is broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence.

He said he was eyeing one-on-one talks with Putin and Kim Jong Un at his next stop in Shenzhen, saying the North Korean leader “would like” to meet in China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday stopped short of confirming the meeting with Kim.

“If we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we’re ever going to solve it is if we engage with them,” Rubio said in Manila.

Trump was in the Philippines for a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

His visit saw protests by around 2,000 people carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica” – a reference to a US supply chain initiative.

Tariffs, chips and rare earths

While ASEAN leaders grappled with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s own expanding trade with the bloc.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canada’s Mark Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the US market.

On Tuesday, a combative Trump showed no let-up in his trade war with Beijing, saying the United States would catch China in rare-earths production “within 10 months”.

Hours before Trump touched down in Manila, Washington announced new rules on the transfer of advanced AI chips, a move that could potentially rankle ASEAN members.

Companies shipping high-end chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will now require a special licence, as the countries were said to represent a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.

Singapore responded by saying it was now exploring ways to facilitate “trusted access” for firms based in the city-state.

World.title: Sri Lankan bowlers trigger Pakistan collapse in second Test
World.content:
Sri Lanka fought back strongly with the ball on the second morning of the second Test, claiming four wickets to restrict Pakistan to 221 for seven at lunch on Wednesday, although the hosts maintained a 123-run first-innings lead at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium.

Resuming their first innings at 121 for three, Pakistan appeared well placed to build on their advantage after bowling Sri Lanka out for a paltry 98 on the opening day. However, disciplined bowling from the visitors, particularly Lahiru Kumara, prevented the hosts from extending their dominance without a fight.

Pakistan added 100 runs in 31.4 overs during the morning session but lost four wickets in the process. Overnight batter Azan Awais, who was unbeaten on 47, failed to add significantly to his tally before falling for the same score as Sri Lanka found the breakthrough.

Kumara led the visitors’ fightback with an impressive spell, using pace and movement to trouble Pakistan’s middle order. Operating from round the wicket, he removed Awais before accounting for Saud Shakeel, who departed for 24.

The Sri Lankan pacer also dismissed nightwatchman Saqib Khan, who had shown considerable patience after resuming on two overnight. Saqib spent more than an hour at the crease and contributed a useful 37 before misjudging a dipping full toss from Kumara, having apparently anticipated a short delivery, and was trapped leg-before-wicket.

Salman Ali Agha offered some resistance with 21 but could not carry on, falling leg-before to Asitha Fernando late in the session.

At lunch, wicket-keeper Ghazi Ghori was unbeaten on eight, with Aamer Jamal on one, as Pakistan reached 221 for seven.

Kumara was the pick of Sri Lanka’s bowlers, claiming three wickets during the morning’s play, while Fernando provided valuable support with two.

Milan Rathnayake also maintained pressure through accurate and economical bowling, despite going wicketless.

The visitors’ response with the ball was particularly significant after a difficult opening day, when Pakistan’s pace attack had bundled them out for just 98.

The home side had capitalised on the conditions to secure a substantial advantage, but Sri Lanka’s morning effort ensured that Pakistan could not turn that position into an even more commanding one.

Pakistan, nevertheless, remain firmly in control with a 123-run lead and three wickets in hand.

World.title: Man sentenced to over 27 years in US for plot to assassinate Trump
World.content:
A US judge has sentenced a Pakistani man, found guilty of plotting to assassinate President Donald Trump and other prominent US politicians, to more than 27 years in prison, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said on Tuesday.

“Earlier today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Asif Merchant, 48, of Pakistan, was sentenced by US District Judge Eric R Komitee to 330 months in prison for attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire,” the DOJ said in a statement.

Prosecutors said Merchant tried to recruit people in the US in a plan targeting Trump and others in retaliation for Washington’s assassination of Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani in 2020, when Trump was in his first term.

Targets in the 2024 plot also included then-President Joe Biden and Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump that year for the Republican presidential nomination, federal prosecutors said.

A federal jury in March convicted Merchant of travelling to the US to arrange for political assassinations on American soil, according to the Justice Department.

That trial in the New York City borough of Brooklyn started in late February.

Merchant testified at his trial that he joined the plot with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps but did so unwillingly, to protect his family in Tehran.

Merchant said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but that his Iranian handler named three people in the course of conversations in the Iranian capital.

Law enforcement thwarted the plan before any attack occurred. A person Merchant contacted in April 2024 to help with the plot reported his activities and became a confidential informant, the DOJ said. Merchant was arrested and pleaded not guilty that year.

Tehran has denied that it targeted or plotted to attack Trump or other US officials.

US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have killed thousands and displaced millions. Many top Iranian leaders, including then-supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, have been assassinated, too.

World.title: Cricket Australia to open 'Sandpapergate' forum for players to share their versions but rules out new probe
World.content:
Cricket Australia (CA) on Wednesday ruled out reopening an investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal but will launch an independent forum for players to share their version of events as a “circuit breaker”.

Festering wounds over what happened in the third Test at Cape Town eight years ago reopened last week when former Australian cricketer Usman Khawaja released his autobiography.

In the book, he alleged that the whole team knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing, an allegation strenuously denied by current captain Pat Cummins.

A Cricket Australia probe at the time concluded only skipper Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were in the know, with all three sent home in disgrace and banned.

Warner, who has backed Khawaja’s new version of events, over the weekend accused CA of conducting “a shoddy investigation”, claiming not all players were interviewed.

CA Chief Executive Todd Greenberg said the past week had been an “incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved”.

But, speaking in Hobart ahead of Australia’s one-day clash with England on Wednesday, Greenberg was adamant that “the investigation has been completed” and ruled out making it public, citing confidentiality.

Interim chairman David Boon said instead that a forum, likely led by a former judge, would be established.

But there would be no new sanctions coming out of it.

“After careful discussion, we agreed to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and their perspectives,” he said.

“We believe it is time for a circuit breaker. This is not about litigating the past. It is about giving the opportunity to those involved to have their voices heard.

“Australian cricket is at its strongest when we’re united, and we owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together with understanding, respect and perspective.”

‘Game needs to move on’

Cricket Australia would not commit to making the contents of the forum public, which it hopes can be wrapped up within a month.

“We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward,” Greenberg said.

He denied the forum was to appease Warner, who has been vocal in support of Khawaja.

“This is not about appeasing any individual. This is about the game, it’s about the sport,” Greenberg said.

“The game needs to move on somehow from this. These events were eight years ago. They caused enormous pain and hurt for lots of people and are doing it again now.

“And at some point we have to move forward. And we can’t move forward without putting some of the steps in place.”

Warner said he agreed that there should be no new sanctions for anyone involved, but would prefer to have an open inquiry.

“I would’ve liked an open inquiry and the people that were there at the time actually can come forward and speak,” he said while commentating on the Australia-England match.

“It’s not about penalties. It’s about transparency and accountability — which Todd’s acknowledged, on CA’s behalf, about the culture at the time with the players and CA.”

Khawaja, also on commentary for the match, said he welcomed a “safe space to chat”, but voiced concern that it would be behind closed doors.

“The biggest question I have is [that] the board makes the decisions of what comes out at the end,” he said. “How is that an actual way of trying to present what people have said? I can go in there and say something but then the board can decide they’re not going to release that.”

World.title: Policeman martyred after being abducted, tortured in Bannu
World.content:
BANNU: A policeman was abducted and tortured to death by unidentified armed men near Taziri Chowk in Bannu on Wednesday, police said.

According to police, the incident took place within the jurisdiction of Basia Khel police station, where armed men abducted policeman Javed and later tortured him to death.

Police said an investigation into the incident was underway and efforts were being made to trace and arrest those responsible.

The latest killing in the area comes a day after Head Constable Zahid Khan of the Elite Force was killed by unidentified armed men near the Afghan refugee camp. He was performing duty at the Central Jail.

Several police personnel have been targeted in similar attacks in Bannu in recent months, with incidents of targeted killings and abductions reported across the district.

On June 29, unidentified armed men pulled Constable Umar Niaz Khan out of a rickshaw near Lora Pul, and shot him dead while he was travelling to work.

In September, Elite Force personnel Ahmadullah was shot dead at a shop in the Daud Shah area of Peepal Bazaar, within the jurisdiction of the Cantonment police station.

On October 15, Head Constable Raqeeb Khan of the District Security Branch (DSB) was shot dead near Muslimabad on Circular Road. A day later, five policemen were injured in an armed attack on Gambati police checkpost.

On October 31, Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) driver Constable Sadiq Zaman was shot dead by unidentified armed men at Barmarshil Chowk while he was on leave. The same day, Head Constable Ziaullah, who was posted at Bannu Police Lines, was abducted near Baran Dam in the Karam Garhi area and later killed.

Apart from targeted killings, police posts and personnel in different parts of Bannu have also come under armed and drone attacks, leaving several policemen injured and prompting security operations in affected areas.

Meanwhile, Section 144 has been in force in Bannu since November 14, imposing various restrictions as part of measures to maintain law and order.

World.title: Tech outage wave reaches US government, Trump says all is 'fine'
World.content:
Technology outages that shut down email for many companies and grounded thousands of flights over the past few days extended to the US National Security Agency (NSA) on Tuesday, as President Donald Trump’s administration downplayed concerns about a broader problem.

The NSA said its network experienced a “temporary degradation” during routine maintenance, but that “mission-critical capabilities” remained operational. The series of disruptions to critical systems, which also touched the banking system on Monday, prompted even some Trump allies to demand more information.

“If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world,” US Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, told reporters.

Trump earlier played down the incidents, which raised questions of whether the government and private sector had moved too quickly in cutting tech staff.

“It’s like when you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump told reporters in Manila, where he was attending meetings with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who doubles as national security adviser, acknowledged the incidents were “unsettling” but said they were completely unrelated.

“We are not under systemic attack,” he told reporters in Manila.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyberhackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio added.

Daily downtime

Technology-related disruptions have hit every weekday since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.

The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) called for a nationwide ground stop that lasted 4-1/2 hours, the longest halt to US air travel since the attacks of September 11, 2001.

The spate of outages included a United Airlines technology failure on Monday that delayed about 150 flights on the same day that a JP Morgan Chase software problem disrupted some banking services.

On Tuesday, Apple said it was working to restore its systems after an internal update caused an outage that affected customer services including iCloud and Apple Pay. The issue was not caused by a cyberattack, Apple said.

Insurance provider Marsh also said on Tuesday its clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October more than double the 48 recorded in the final two weeks of May.

Experts worry that AI tools are feeding a surge of cyber activity, with cybersecurity companies regularly turning up examples of hackers using AI to launch scores of intrusions at once.

“The recent string of major disruptions across industries highlights how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems,” said Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior FBI cyber official and current senior vice president of cybersecurity firm Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Centre.

The string of tech outages is likely due to issues emerging from system upgrades, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in an interview with Fox Business on Tuesday.

“We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack … And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here. And we can be fairly confident in that,” Clayton said.

He attributed the NSA outage to patches deployed for a PHP vulnerability discovered using AI last month a bug that could let hackers remotely take control of servers.

“Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” Clayton told the ‘Claman Countdown’ programme on Fox Business.

Outages follow layoffs, warnings

At many organisations both private and government the outages follow layoffs and, in some cases, explicit warnings about potential disruptions.

At the FAA, which was hit by Elon Musk-driven job cuts after Trump took office last year, Congress warned the agency’s sped-up modernisation effort was poorly organised and could trigger service outages. United Airlines said last year that AI advances had helped it cut management headcount by four per cent and that it planned to cut by an additional four per cent this year.

At Microsoft, the email outage came a month after the company said it was offering buyouts to a quarter of its global workforce, a move that follows previous headcount reductions.

While there is no evidence job losses at any of these places led to the disruptions, one tech labour organiser said cuts tended to make safety margins thinner.

“Part of the resilience of a system comes from people who are experienced with a system,” said Liz Fong-Jones, who has worked for 20 years on software resilience issues.

Democratic US Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island joined in calls for more information from the White House.

“Just the last few days, America has seen tech glitches all across the board,” Reed told reporters. “The president has to get on top of it, explain to the American people what’s going on, and do it quickly, and that is a mission that he is not doing at this moment.”

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
