World.title: Regime Minister Turns to Migrant Workers in Malaysia to Plug Foreign Currency Gap
World.content:
Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint, admitted while talking to Myanmar workers in Malaysia last week that the junta is increasingly relying on migrant workers to bring in foreign currency as sanctions and declining export earnings squeeze its finances.

“The world sanctions us,” Maung Myint said during his visit to the country. He also claimed that one of the reasons for the decline in Myanmar’s international revenue was that the regime had deliberately “reduced” exports of natural resources.

Following the 2021 coup, Western countries and blocs including the U.S., the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada imposed targeted economic sanctions on senior Myanmar regime officials, including coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, as well as state enterprises and military-controlled banks.

The sanctions remain in place, leaving some foreign development assistance programs suspended and interrupting international banking transfers, fueling the country’s foreign currency shortage and exacerbating an economic crisis caused by the regime’s mismanagement.

While Maung Myint claimed the regime had deliberately reduced natural-resource exports for environmental reasons, a World Bank report suggests that natural gas exports to Thailand and China—one of Myanmar’s major sources of foreign income—dropped by US$200 million in 2025-26 due to “reduced output” from existing offshore operations.

As international sanctions began to bite, the regime imposed remittance rules and enforced tax laws targeting overseas workers in 2023, aiming to extract funds from them. Foreign remittance value reached US$5.6 billion in 2025, and Maung Myint is hoping to match that figure this year.

“We’re trying to cover the shrinking income with remittances from workers,” he said in a video posted on his TikTok channel on Sunday.

He added that the rules and restrictions targeting migrant workers would be only temporary, claiming that potential increases in revenue from rare earths and a major deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea would eliminate the need for them.

However, he cautioned that rare earth sites “are not under the government’s control,” and are a “prospect” for foreign revenue once the regime gains control of them.

The majority of Myanmar’s approximately 600 rare-earth mining sites are concentrated on the China-Myanmar border in Kachin State under the control of the Kachin Independence Army. The rest also lie beyond the Myanmar regime’s control in eastern Shan State, in territory run by armed groups over which China exerts a great influence, including the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Its lack of control over these deposits deprives the regime of billions of dollars in potential revenue, as global powers like the U.S. and India court it for access to the critical minerals.

He said the deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea’s Block M-15 could earn $400-500 billion. According to the World Bank report, the project could produce up to 94.6 trillion cubic feet of usable gas “if confirmed”, but its output “is not expected soon.”

Maung Myint last week turned his focus to Malaysia, which hosts the second-largest population of Myanmar migrant workers, after his efforts to extract more foreign currency met with resistance from migrant workers in Thailand.

Since being appointed labor minister in October, he has been pushing hard for workers to comply with the new remittance and tax rules, particularly the Certification of Identity (CI) process.

The push sparked widespread boycotts in Thailand, where only 15,000 of nearly 750,000 undocumented Myanmar workers applied for the CI. Workers refused to apply for fear of funding the military’s war on civilians and exposing themselves to military conscription.

In Malaysia, he used flattery, calling workers national “heroes” and comparing them to soldiers who “sacrifice their time with families to serve the country.”

World.title: All Quiet in Northern Shan—and for Good Reason
World.content:
For several months, speculation has swirled over whether northern Shan State could see a return of resistance offensives on the scale of Operation 1027. But what is the likelihood of a resurgence of fighting?

The speculation appears to stem from signs of friction between Beijing and Myanmar’s military regime over how the ethnic armed organizations are to be managed, as well as the regime’s recent efforts to restore ties with the U.S. and Japan.

Yet the differences between China and the military regime are not fundamental—they do not amount to a strategic or ideological split.

China has not abandoned its long-held view that the military is a central pillar in maintaining stability in Myanmar. What has changed is Beijing’s growing recognition that the crisis cannot be managed through the military alone.

The fact that Beijing now acknowledges other forces has become a source of discomfort for the regime. But that is not a policy shift, only a tactical adjustment in how China seeks to implement its existing policy.

Beijing’s position on border stability remains unchanged. China does not want to see a return of armed conflicts to northern Shan, which shares a 200-km stretch of border with Yunnan.

All the rare-earth mines and other major investments operating in areas controlled by Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan involve Chinese capital. Given the technical requirements involved in rare-earth extraction, the companies operating these projects are more likely to be state-linked Chinese enterprises than private firms. The Chinese government is unlikely to allow such investments to be jeopardized.

One point of frustration for China has been the regime’s handling of border trade. Naypyitaw frequently claims that cross-border trade was disrupted by ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) that now control the major border trade routes. Yet Beijing is well aware that the military has also restricted border trade with Thailand, even though it fully controls the trade corridor there. From China’s perspective, regime policy puts up more barriers to trade than the MNDAA or TNLA.

Estimated at US$6 billion annually, that business is relatively small compared with the scale of the Chinese economy. The more pressing concern for Beijing has been online scam operations. Since the MNDAA and TNLA established control over large parts of the border, scam syndicates targeting Chinese citizens have been brought under much tighter control. The central military regime, by contrast, failed for years to address the problem.

Chinese policymakers may therefore calculate that restoring central military control across northern Shan could revive the criminal networks Beijing has made considerable effort suppressing. The financial and political costs of that scenario would surely outweigh the benefits of expanded border trade.

The EAOs themselves have little incentive to launch new offensives. The MNDAA and TNLA now control substantially more territory than before Operation 1027, and arguably more than they had dared to dream of. Having achieved those objectives, neither group has a pressing need to expend additional force.

Beijing may have a similar view and is therefore likely to restrain them from fighting the regime again. That means there is virtually no prospect of the MNDAA or TNLA initiating hostilities. The only realistic scenario under which fighting might resume would be if the military regime attacks first.

For its part, Naypyitaw expects China to pressure EAOs to return all the territories in northern Shan State to it. That is how the regime recovered the northern Shan capital of Lashio. Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun’s recent proposal of “high-level autonomy” for ethnic forces was therefore a bitter pill for the regime to swallow. And soon after Deng made the proposal, the regime dispatched reconnaissance planes to northern Shan.

Having survived the military disasters of 2023 and 2024 in large part because of Chinese intervention, the military’s top brass is now dreaming of eventually reclaiming all lost territory by force. Such thinking is hardly surprising for an institution that seized power by forced and continues to view military means as the answer to political problems.

But here dreams and reality collide. Before Operation 1027, the Northeastern Command was backed by roughly 20 infantry and light infantry battalions, in addition to artillery, logistics and support units. It was further reinforced by as many as seven or eight division-sized formations rotated through the theater.

That force no longer exists. Now only about 10 infantry and light infantry battalions remain under Northeastern Command, dispersed across Muse, Tangyan and Mongyai. The military now fields only a single major combat formation across the region, spread among Nantlan, Kyaukme, Hsipaw and Nawnghkio, while smaller units are deployed in Mongmit and Mogoke.

Indeed, since the ceasefire with the MNDAA and TNLA, the regime has moved an estimated seven division-sized formations out of northern Shan State to active fronts in Rakhine, Chin, Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay.

That mean it simply does not have the strength to maintain more than a presence in northern Shan and hold existing positions. The convoys that are regularly observed traveling between Taunggyi, Kho Lam, Mong Nawng, Mongyai and Tangyan do not represent substantial reinforcements: they mainly transport batches of new recruits to and from military training facilities.

The military’s ability to sustain operations elsewhere, then, depends heavily on the fact that northern Shan remains relatively quiet. To reopen that front, it would first have to withdraw troops from other battlefields, which would risk repeating the overstretch that contributed to the military’s earlier defeats.

In essence, the regime would be creating a new battlefield at a time when it can barely manage the existing ones.

No matter how much it resents the loss of northern Shan’s borders, there is nothing it can do about it. In addition, any attempt to violate the Beijing-brokered ceasefire could invite retaliation from China itself. Unlike Thailand, which has repeatedly shown restraint when fighting spills across its border, Beijing is unlikely to tolerate renewed instability along a frontier it regards as strategically vital.

In other words, the regime would be digging its own grave.

Moe Set Nyein Chan is a military analyst

World.title: Dozens of Civilians Killed in Myanmar Regime Strikes as ASEAN Leaders Meet
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has continued bombing civilian targets nationwide after its leaders were barred from attending the ongoing 49th ASEAN Summit for rejecting the bloc’s peace plan.

Rakhine State has borne the brunt of attacks, which have killed over a dozen civilians in the past week as the ethnic Arkan Army (AA) pushes to seize the state capital, Sittwe, and Kyaukphyu, home to China-backed mega projects.

Junta warplanes pounded residential areas in the AA-held town of Kyauktaw on Monday night, but casualty figures were unclear as of press time. The strike followed an Oct. 28 attack on the town’s busy market that killed 50 civilians including children and wounded 60, drawing international condemnation.

The AA also reported another deadly strike on a displacement camp in Ponnagyun Township on Friday evening. Twelve people were killed and 18 injured as blasts ripped through the Byar La shelter for war-displaced civilians. The attack came just weeks after two regime fighter jets bombed the same IDP camp, killing eight civilians and destroying homes and shops on October 4.

The airstrikes continued Sunday as ASEAN leaders gathered for their summit in Manila, with Myanmar’s crisis topping the agenda.

Blasts destroyed bridges in the Rakhine townships of Minbya and Ramree, according to the AA. The attacks followed a Nov. 1 airstrike on a Kyauktaw bridge that killed seven commuters and injured seven others.

Meanwhile, the regime’s Taung Maw Oo naval base used drones and artillery to destroy around 60 homes Kyaukphyu’s Sane town at the weekend, months after it was abandoned by civilians.

Former army captain Zin Yaw, who defected following the 2021 coup, said the regime is targeting bridges to cut supply lines of the AA, which is pushing to seize the regime’s last remaining toeholds in Rakhine.

“The regime has failed to meet its military objectives, so it is now attempting to destroy the enemy’s administrative and supply chains,” he said.

Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and relief worker, said regime forces are destroying bridges to slow the AA’s advance.

The AA has seized 14 out of Rakhine’s 17 townships plus Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State since launching a major offensive in November 2023.

The ethnic army has also expanded offensives across the border into Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady regions.

World.title: UN Chief Backs Engagement With Myanmar But ‘Violence Needs to Stop’
World.content:
MANILA—UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed support Monday for fresh diplomatic efforts to engage with Myanmar’s post-coup government, but said that “violence needs to stop.”

Guterres made the remarks in Manila, where leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) agreed Sunday to pursue a “calibrated engagement” with the war-torn country.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021, but the regional bloc is seeking a path towards normalizing diplomatic relations.

“We have never opposed the idea that it is always necessary to engage with whoever is involved in a conflict,” Guterres told a press conference on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

While “engagement is not appeasement,” Guterres said the “intolerable violations of human rights in Myanmar” must end.

“Violence needs to stop, humanitarian access needs to be granted, and all those arbitrarily detained must be immediately released,” Guterres said.

“And these are the conditions that could allow for what everybody should will [to happen], which is that Myanmar will find a way to move… to a true democratic situation.”

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” in an effort to implement ASEAN’s long-languishing five-point plan to end the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders adopted that language on Sunday in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach,” according to the joint statement.

Guterres’s remarks came as the UN’s International Court of Justice prepares to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalized Muslim Rohingya minority.

World.title: Yangon Condo Raid Reveals Myanmar’s Cyber Scam Sector Thriving in Commercial Capital
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has arrested 106 suspected online scammers in Yangon, signaling the country’s cyber-fraud epidemic has spread from the lawless borderlands to its largest city.

The regime announced Saturday that its forces raided Golden River Residence Condo in Yangon’s Thaketa Township on November 12, arresting 52 Chinese naionals, eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar citizens from multiple apartments.

The arrests come as Naypyitaw and Beijing trumpet crackdowns on cyber-fraud syndicates in notorious border scam hubs.

Those reportedly detained included a high-profile target of China’s Public Security Ministry — the first arrest of a warranted Chinese scammer in Myanmar in months. Also seized from the condo were over 120 computers and laptops and nearly 200 mobile phones.

Authorities said the gang ran online investment fraud schemes targeting Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian citizens, while separate Telegram-based operations targeted victims in Brazil and Colombia through fake e-commerce platforms.

The raid came shortly after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi pressed Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe to intensify efforts to combat scams and prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Karen State’s Myawaddy crime hub on the Thai border.

Analysts say the Yangon bust signals a growing shift of Myanmar’s online scam industry from border enclaves to urban centers.

After the 2024 collapse of notorious fraud compounds in northern Shan State’s Laukkai and crackdowns along the Chinese and Thai borders, many scam syndicates dispersed in small, mobile operations through remote eastern and southern Shan, according to regime arrest reports and independent monitors.

However, many that had fled to Myawaddy have since moved deeper into the country under the protection of regime-aligned militias and other armed groups.

In September, 28 foreign and Myanmar nationals were arrested in Mandalay — the country’s second city — over an online gemstone scam involving Chinese, Indonesian and Malaysian suspects. The gang was charged with selling fake jade products via livestream and transferring the profits to accounts in Indonesia and Malaysia.

While the Nov. 12 raid was the first of its kind reported in Yangon, former fraudsters told The Irrawaddy that scam operations have long established a foothold in the commercial capital, targeting overseas victims through operations based in condominiums, housing estates and companies registered as legitimate businesses.

Analysts say enforcement efforts target low-level operators while overlooking the networks and militias behind the multibillion-dollar industry. Among them is the regime-aligned Karen Border Guard Force, whose Western-sanctioned leaders remain untouched even as the regime hails the demolition of scam compounds in Myawaddy.

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Kazakh FM Tileuberdi Discusses Transport Links, Economic Cooperation in Brussels
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi held a series of bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Germany, Romania, Latvia, Estonia, Ukraine, France, Croatia and Bulgaria on the sidelines of the Second Ministerial Meeting on Cross-Regional Connectivity and Security on Nov. 16.

The talks focused on bilateral relations, international developments and opportunities to expand trade, economic and investment cooperation.

Tileuberdi highlighted Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen the country’s transit and transport potential and attract European companies to projects aimed at modernizing social, transport and engineering infrastructure across the regions.

Talks with Germany and Romania

During a meeting with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, the sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027.

They discussed implementing agreements reached during Tokayev’s official visit to Germany in September 2026, as well as the joint statement by the two heads of state and the 2026–2028 Roadmap for Industrial, Technological and Raw Materials Cooperation.

Wadephul welcomed the positive momentum in political dialogue, noting the political consultations between the two foreign ministries held in Astana on Nov. 10 and the visit of Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev to Germany for the Alatau City investment roadshow in Berlin and Frankfurt.

The ministers also discussed promoting the German language in Kazakhstan and expanding cooperation within the Central Asia–Germany format and international organizations.

In talks with Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu, the sides expressed interest in strengthening trade and economic ties and agreed to hold the 18th meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific and Technical Cooperation in 2027. They also discussed maritime security in the Black Sea and the uninterrupted transportation of Kazakh oil through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) pipeline system.

Engagement with other European partners

In a meeting with Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže, the sides discussed prospects for cooperation and practical engagement on issues of mutual interest.

Tileuberdi and Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna reaffirmed their commitment to constructive political dialogue and implementing agreements reached following Estonian President Alar Karis’ state visit to Kazakhstan.

During talks with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the ministers discussed the work of the Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, as well as trade and logistics issues. Tileuberdi and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot reviewed bilateral relations and considered ways to intensify political dialogue through existing cooperation frameworks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Turn Landlocked Position Into Advantage Through Middle Corridor, Kazakh FM Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to turn its landlocked geography into an advantage by expanding transport connectivity and strengthening its role along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said during talks with Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot in Brussels.

“We are a landlocked country, but we are determined to turn this geographical disadvantage into an advantage and make the most of the opportunities it presents,” Tileuberdi said.

The talks focused on translating the momentum generated by high-level exchanges between the two countries into economic cooperation, particularly in transport and logistics, critical raw materials, energy, industrial development and emerging technologies.

The meeting followed President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Belgium in June and the state visit of King Philippe of the Belgians to Kazakhstan in October. The visits marked a new stage in bilateral relations and resulted in the adoption of a joint statement and the signing of 40 bilateral documents.

The agreements include 16 commercial deals, 22 agreements in science and education, a memorandum of understanding in healthcare and an interministerial roadmap for cooperation for 2027–2029.

Prévot described King Philippe’s visit as an important opportunity to strengthen ties between the two countries.

“We greatly appreciated this visit, the first in a long time. I believe it came at the right moment to strengthen our ties, not only because Kazakhstan is our strategic partner, but also because it is located in a strategically important region,” he said, reaffirming his intention to also visit the country in 2027 as part of a wider tour of Central Asia.

Belgian investment exceeds $15 billion

Economic cooperation remains a key pillar of the partnership. Belgian investment in Kazakhstan has exceeded $15 billion since 2005, with gross foreign direct investment inflows surpassing $1 billion in 2025 alone.

The ministers expressed interest in expanding Belgian companies’ presence in Kazakhstan and advancing cooperation on the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe through Kazakhstan and the Caspian Sea. They also identified industrial cooperation, critical raw materials, energy, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and scientific and technological collaboration as priority areas for further engagement.

The ministers welcomed the entry into force on Nov. 1 of a visa-free regime for holders of service passports from Kazakhstan and the Benelux countries. They also discussed mutual support for initiatives and candidatures within international organizations. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the agreements reached at the highest level and turning the growing political engagement into tangible results across the bilateral partnership.

World.title: Kyrgyz Republic’s GDP Grows 10.5% in January-October
World.content:
ASTANA – The Kyrgyz Republic’s gross domestic product (GDP) reached 1.87 trillion soms (US$21.4 billion) in January-October, up 10.5% from the same period last year, according to preliminary estimates from the National Statistical Committee published on Nov. 16.

Goods-producing industries, the services sector and net taxes on products drove growth. Output in goods-producing industries rose 16.7%, net taxes on products rose 10.7%, and services expanded 6.3%.

Services accounted for 48.9% of GDP, down 2.3 percentage points from the same period last year. The share of goods-producing industries reached 36%, up two percentage points.

World.title: CKU Railway: New Link in Eurasian Connectivity
World.content:
For shippers moving goods between China and Iran, transit time can be an important factor in choosing a transport mode. Some rail services through Central Asia advertise transit times of around 14–18 days, while sea freight can take considerably longer. However, these figures depend on the origin, destination, route, border procedures and whether the estimate covers terminal-to-terminal or door-to-door delivery. The difference can be significant for time-sensitive cargo, but it should not be treated as a guaranteed one-month saving. Transit time is particularly important for cargo that requires expedited delivery, such as manufacturing components, perishable or semi-perishable goods, and shipments subject to strict contractual deadlines. For these goods, shippers may be willing to pay a higher freight rate in exchange for faster delivery and lower inventory costs.

An existing overland rail route connects China and Iran through Central Asia. One established route passes through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran. As China–Iran trade develops, existing overland routes are attracting interest. At the same time, Central Asia’s railway network is continuing to expand. The China–the Kyrgyz Republic–Uzbekistan (CKU) railway is under construction. Once operational, it could provide a new rail connection from western China to eastern Uzbekistan. If linked to the existing Uzbek rail network and onward connections through Turkmenistan, it could create an alternative route for China–Iran freight. The viability of this route will depend on infrastructure connections, border procedures, gauge changes and commercial agreements among the countries involved.

The significance of transit time

Sea freight from East Asia to the Persian Gulf can be cost-effective, particularly for large volumes of lower-value cargo. However, door-to-door delivery may involve several stages, including port handling, transshipment and inland transport, which can extend the overall transit time. Rail transport offers a different set of advantages: potentially shorter transit times, less reliance on maritime port handling, and direct access to inland rail terminals. However, rail services remain dependent on border procedures, network capacity, operational coordination and the availability of reliable schedules.

The value of faster transit varies by cargo type. Sea freight is likely to remain competitive for low-margin bulk cargo and large shipments where cost matters more than speed. For high-value or time-sensitive cargo, shorter transit times could reduce working-capital requirements and the risk of supply shortages. These are the types of cargo for which rail corridors are most likely to be competitive.

Existing corridor: China – Kazakhstan – Uzbekistan – Turkmenistan – Iran

This corridor benefits from existing infrastructure and established operating experience. Container trains from China can travel through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran, depending on the route used. Over time, cooperation between railway administrations, customs services and logistics providers has supported the development of this corridor and its role in China–Iran overland trade.

The existing corridor benefits from established operating experience, familiarity among shippers and the development of regular services. Several structural factors could affect the competitiveness of an alternative route. The route passes through several jurisdictions and involves different track gauges, requiring coordination among railway operators and border authorities. Capacity at key interchange points, departure frequency and the predictability of border and terminal dwell times all influence the transit time experienced by shippers.

A potential new route to Iran

If the CKU railway is connected to the existing Uzbek railway network, freight could travel by rail from China through Kyrgyzstan to Uzbekistan, then continue along existing rail infrastructure through Turkmenistan and into Iran. The route would pass through Uzbekistan, whose established railway network provides connections to regional and international markets.

The wider regional significance of the project was already recognised by the GAFG Board member Vladimir Norov, then Secretary-General of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. In a lecture delivered at the Indian Council of World Affairs in January 2020, he observed that the CKU railway “may become one of the promising additional routes connecting East Asia with the Middle East, Turkey and Europe, as well as an important link in the transport network within the framework of East-West and North-South” connectivity.

The new route would not necessarily replace the existing Kazakhstan corridor. Instead, it could provide an additional option, allowing shippers to choose between routes according to origin, destination, cost, transit time and service reliability. Railway administrations and operators may seek to improve their services to attract freight traffic. For consignments originating in western China, the CKU route may offer a geographical advantage. For other origins, the existing Kazakhstan route may remain more competitive, depending on the final destination, tariffs and service frequency.

The CKU railway should also be considered within the wider architecture of Eurasian rail connectivity. Existing networks, including the Trans-Siberian Railway, the growing China–Central Asia connections and other transcontinental routes, form part of an increasingly diversified transport landscape. As Alice Ferrari (2026) argues in her discussion of Eurasian corridors, individual routes are better understood as interconnected and potentially complementary elements of a wider network. From this perspective, the CKU railway could extend connectivity through Central Asia towards the Persian Gulf, adding another option without necessarily displacing existing routes.

This broader perspective is consistent with the GAFG Connectivity Doctrine: individual corridors should be understood not as isolated infrastructure projects, but as components of wider connectivity ecosystems. Their value depends on the quality of connections between transport infrastructure, logistics hubs, institutional arrangements and the markets they serve.

The potential regional implications of the CKU railway have also been examined by Nargiza Umarova (2024), who argues that the project could strengthen Central Asian transport connectivity, increase the region’s transit attractiveness as a transit and logistics hub, boosting the existing cargo flows. She also highlights the possibility of new international trade corridors and the importance of coordination among Central Asian countries to ensure mutual benefits. This reinforces the importance of viewing the CKU railway as part of a wider and interconnected transport network rather than as an isolated infrastructure project.

The gauge question

However, there is one technical consideration that should be mentioned separately: the track gauge. China and Iran use the standard gauge of 1,435 mm, while the main railway networks in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan use the 1,520 mm gauge. The CKU project itself is planned with different gauge sections, meaning that gauge compatibility and the location of transshipment facilities will need to be considered along the route. Any China–Iran service using the CKU line would therefore need to account for gauge changes and the arrangements for transferring freight between railway systems.

Possible approaches include container transshipment at gauge-change terminals, bogie exchange where technically feasible, or specialised variable-gauge systems. Each option has different implications for infrastructure, cost, handling time and operational complexity. Container transshipment is an established solution, but its efficiency depends on terminal capacity, handling equipment, staffing and the coordination of train schedules. Bogie exchange is suitable for some wagon models. The availability and practical application of variable-gauge technology in the region would also need to be assessed.

The number, location and efficiency of gauge-change points will directly affect the corridor’s overall performance. Efficient transfer arrangements may help reduce delays and handling costs, even where the route is geographically longer. In this connection, the gauge configuration of the CKU railway route and its connections with the 1,520 mm gauge systems of Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan therefore becomes an important consideration. The location of transshipment points and the design of terminal facilities may be as important to corridor performance as the railway infrastructure itself.

Factors of competitiveness

The new corridor does not compete merely through geography. Several other factors will determine whether the route attracts sustained freight traffic.

Tariffs. Cargo owners assess the total cost of moving a container from its origin to its final destination. Through-tariff systems, which provide a single rate across several railway operators, can make the corridor easier for customers to use than a system requiring separate negotiations and payments with each national operator. Coordinated tariffs across the participating railway systems, together with competitive transit rates, could strengthen the route’s appeal.

Transit time and reliability. The predictability of delivery can be as important as speed. A corridor that consistently meets its scheduled transit time may be more attractive than a faster route with frequent delays.

Customs procedures: Requirements and documentation procedures vary across countries and can create delays at border crossings. Electronic pre-notification, recognition of compatible documentation, coordinated operating hours and joint or coordinated inspections—where feasible—could reduce border dwell times.

Container transshipment. Transshipment efficiency depends on terminal capacity, handling equipment and scheduling. Although terminal improvements may require less investment than constructing new railway lines, they can still have a substantial effect on the shipper’s experience.

Service frequency: Regular departures allow shippers to plan shipments and reduce the need to hold large inventories. However, increasing train frequency requires a sufficient cargo base. During the initial phase, operators may need to coordinate pilot services and build demand gradually.

This approach also reflects key themes of the GAFG Connectivity Doctrine, particularly connectivity, interoperability and complementarity. The value of a new railway connection lies not only in the infrastructure it creates, but also in how effectively it connects with existing transport networks, logistics facilities and regional markets. For the CKU railway, coordination between railway operators, border authorities and logistics providers will be essential to developing these connections.

What can be done today?

With the railway under construction, the pre-operational period provides an opportunity to prepare the wider corridor for commercial operations. Several measures could strengthen its operational and commercial viability from the beginning of operations. This requires looking beyond the railway itself and preparing the institutional, operational and commercial arrangements that enable infrastructure to function as part of an integrated connectivity ecosystem.

Coordinate across railway administrations: Working groups involving railway operators and relevant ministries could agree on technical standards, operating procedures and tariff arrangements before the corridor begins commercial operations.

Prepare transit nodes before operations begin: The location, capacity and equipment of transshipment facilities should be considered during the construction phase. Dry ports and logistics centres in Uzbekistan, particularly in the Fergana Valley and along major east–west and north–south routes, could help consolidate freight and improve connections between transport modes.

Improve the Uzbekistan–Turkmenistan–Iran connection: The performance of the entire corridor will depend on the capacity and efficiency of its individual sections. Assessing infrastructure conditions, capacity constraints and border-crossing procedures along the southern route could help prevent delays from undermining the time savings achieved elsewhere.

Introduce digital solutions and facilitate border procedures: Electronic data exchange, advance notification of train arrivals and harmonised border processes could reduce administrative delays. These measures can be prepared alongside railway construction rather than waiting until the line is operational.

Build commercial relationships: Shipping companies, railway operators, exporters and freight forwarders should be involved from the outset. Initial demand could be developed through pilot services, trial shipments and targeted engagement with potential customers.

Define a clear value proposition for shippers: The route should identify the markets and cargo types for which it offers a practical advantage, such as improved access from western China, reliable schedules or better connections within Central Asia.

Socio-economic perspective

The impacts of a transport corridor extend beyond trade volumes. In Kyrgyzstan, the railway could improve regional connectivity, support employment during construction and operation, and provide businesses with better access to markets. It may also improve transport options for communities that currently depend heavily on road transport. In Uzbekistan, increased freight volumes could create opportunities in logistics, warehousing and customs-related services. For Turkmenistan and Iran, an additional corridor could diversify cross-border transport and trade options.

Beyond direct employment, increased freight activity could support small and medium-sized enterprises involved in transport, storage, packaging, maintenance and other logistics services. Improved connections may also help regional producers access markets beyond their immediate surroundings. For landlocked countries such as Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, additional international rail connections could broaden trade options and strengthen their roles as transit and logistics centres. Workforce training, local supplier development and environmental considerations—particularly in mountainous areas—should therefore be incorporated into planning.

Existing rail services between China and Iran demonstrate how overland transport can offer an alternative to sea freight when transit time is important. The CKU railway could add another option by improving rail access from China to Central Asia and potentially supporting a new route for freight moving onward to Iran through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan.

The viability of this route will depend on practical factors such as tariffs, transit times, border procedures, handling arrangements, train frequency and gauge compatibility between the 1,435 mm and 1,520 mm networks. Its wider value will also depend on how effectively it complements existing Eurasian transport corridors and connects regional markets.

The key question is therefore not only when the railway will be completed, but how effectively the wider corridor will be prepared for commercial operations. Coordination among countries, railway operators and logistics providers on tariffs, border procedures, infrastructure connections and service schedules could help the route attract China–Iran freight traffic. Ultimately, the CKU railway’s value may lie not in replacing existing routes, but in contributing another interconnected and complementary option within the wider Eurasian transport network.

The author is Sheika Lubna Fathima, an Information Officer at Global Academy for Future Governance (GAFG), a platform and executive institution that focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence, robotics, geo-economics, and institutional transformation.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina Breaks Into World’s Top 10 Figure Skaters
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina has reached a career-best 10th place in the updated International Skating Union (ISU) world rankings, earning 2,881 points after improving her previous position by three places.

Her rise followed a strong performance at Skate America 2026, the fourth stage of the Grand Prix series, held in Everett, United States, on Nov. 12-15. After placing 11th in the short program with 61.03 points, Samodelkina scored 137.56 points in the free skate, setting a season best and finishing fifth overall with 198.59 points.

During the free skate, she became the first Kazakh female figure skater to perform a triple Axel, an ultra-C element, at an official international competition.

Japan’s Ami Nakai won the event with 236.81 points, followed by Russia’s Alexandra Ignatova with 213.90 and Japan’s Rino Matsuike with 211.63.

Samodelkina has earned 14 ranking points across two Grand Prix events, having also finished fifth at Skate Canada. She is preparing for the second half of the season, including the Four Continents Figure Skating Championships, scheduled for Almaty in February 2027.

Her achievement means Kazakhstan now has representatives in the top 10 of both singles world rankings. Olympic champion Mikhail Shaidorov holds second place in the men’s standings with 4,261 points.

World.title: Air Astana to Launch Direct Almaty-Tokyo Flights This November
World.content:
ASTANA – Air Astana will launch regular direct flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita Airport on Nov. 30, operating twice a week.

The route was discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and Seiichi Tajima, Assistant Vice-Minister for International Aviation at Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, on the sidelines of the Seventh ICAO Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7), the ministry reported on Nov. 17.

Lastayev said the launch of direct flights would restore air connectivity between the two countries after a long interruption and support business, tourism, investment and cultural ties.

The flights will be operated on Airbus A321LR aircraft. According to Air Astana’s schedule, the flight from Almaty to Tokyo will take approximately seven hours and 30 minutes, while the return journey will take nine hours and 25 minutes. Ticket sales opened on Oct. 2.

Lastayev and Tajima also discussed prospects for expanding air services and cooperation between their national carriers.

They also addressed cooperation within the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Lastayev congratulated the Japanese side on electing Toshiyuki Onuma as President of the ICAO Council, marking the first time a representative from the Asia-Pacific region has held the position.

The officials emphasized the importance of continued dialogue and cooperation on international aviation platforms to promote safety, sustainability and efficiency in civil aviation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins ICAO Conference to Shape Global Aviation Agenda Toward 2050
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is taking part in the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which opened in Montreal, Canada, on Nov. 16 and brought together representatives of 193 member states and international aviation organizations to discuss the future of global air transport.

The conference focuses on key priorities for the aviation industry, including air transport liberalization, stronger international connectivity, infrastructure investment, digitalization, innovation and sustainable development.

According to the ministry, the Kazakh delegation is led by Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and includes Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to ICAO Timur Tlegenov, ministry officials and representatives of the country’s aviation industry.

The opening ceremony featured remarks by ICAO Council President Toshiyuki Onuma, UN Tourism Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais and Canadian Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon. ICAO Secretary-General Juan Carlos Salazar also delivered a presentation.

Addressing participants, Onuma highlighted the aviation sector’s reliance on international cooperation, emphasizing that global air travel depends on common standards and mutual trust established under the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation.

He stressed the need for ICAO to remain responsive to technological advances, evolving markets and increasingly complex operational requirements.

ATConf/7 marks the first worldwide air transport conference in 13 years, following the sixth edition in March 2013. Its agenda reflects significant changes in the global aviation landscape and the need to adapt regulatory and economic frameworks to emerging industry challenges.

The conference agenda covers aviation’s long-term development toward 2050, investment in airport and aviation infrastructure, regulatory cooperation, emergency preparedness and consumer protection. Participants will also discuss ways to strengthen international air connectivity, improve economic and regulatory frameworks, and enhance the aviation sector’s competitiveness and resilience.

An extraordinary ICAO Assembly is also scheduled to open on Nov. 19. Its main objective is to elect four additional member states to the ICAO Council following the expansion of its membership from 36 to 40 countries. The assembly is also expected to adopt a ministerial declaration.

For Kazakhstan, participation in the conference provides an opportunity to advance its aviation priorities, exchange international expertise and strengthen cooperation with foreign governments and international organizations.

The delegation is also expected to hold bilateral meetings and discuss prospects for developing Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector.

Kazakhstan’s participation underscores its commitment to international aviation cooperation and contributes to the development of a safe, competitive and sustainable global air transport system.

World.title: Uzbekistan and Oman Advance $5 Billion Cooperation Package Across Key Sectors
World.content:
ASTANA – Uzbekistan and Oman are advancing nearly 30 agreements and contracts worth approximately $5 billion across energy, industry, transport, finance and other sectors, as part of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Oman.

During the visit, Mirziyoyev met with representatives of major Omani businesses led by Abdulsalam al-Murshidi, President of Oman’s Investment Authority, to discuss expanding investment cooperation and implementing joint projects, the President’s press service reported on Nov. 16.

The talks focused on increasing the Uzbek-Omani Investment Company’s authorized capital and developing projects in mining, electrical engineering, chemicals, renewable energy, construction, transport and logistics, infrastructure and agriculture.

The officials also discussed establishing an Uzbek-Omani Business Council to strengthen direct engagement between companies. They agreed to form a joint working group to advance the proposed initiatives and review progress quarterly.

The business meetings followed the Uzbek-Omani Business Forum held in Muscat on Nov. 16, which brought together more than 150 business representatives from both countries. The forum resulted in the signing of a package of cooperation documents covering energy, industry, transport and logistics, finance, agriculture and technology.

The two countries are also seeking to expand bilateral trade and investment. Trade reached approximately $2.3 million in 2025 and increased by more than 70% in the first nine months of 2026 to $3.3 million, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Pakistan discuss expanding transit links between Central and South Asia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Turkmenistan and Pakistan explored ways to boost trade routes, strengthen transport connectivity between Central and South Asia and improve access to regional and international markets.

The issue was discussed at a meeting of the Joint Turkmenistan-Pakistan Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, held in Islamabad under the co-chairmanship of Turkmen Foreign Minister Rashid Meredov and Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar, the Turkmen Foreign Ministry reported.

“The parties discussed the prospects for leveraging the geographical locations of the two countries to develop trade routes, strengthen ties between Central and South Asia, and expand access to regional and international markets,” the ministry noted.

Turkmenistan's geographic position makes it a potential transit link between Central Asia, the Caspian region and markets further south. The country is developing its role in both the North-South and East-West transport corridors by expanding its railway, road, seaport and logistics infrastructure. Its transport network provides opportunities to connect landlocked Central Asian countries with international trade routes, including routes through Afghanistan to Pakistani seaports such as Karachi and Gwadar.

The development of these connections could help diversify regional trade routes, improve access to external markets and create additional opportunities for freight transit between Central and South Asia. Turkmenistan also participates in regional connectivity frameworks, including the International North-South Transport Corridor and TRACECA, which are aimed at strengthening transport links between Europe, the Caspian region and Asia.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Oman's Asyad Group eye new export routes through Omani ports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Uzbekistan and Oman's national logistics group Asyad Group have discussed using Omani ports and international logistics networks to expand exports of Uzbek agricultural products and other goods to global markets at a meeting in Muscat on November 17.

According to Uzbekistan's Transport Ministry, the issue was discussed during a meeting between Uzbek Transport Minister Ilkhom Makhkamov and Asyad Group Chief Executive Officer Abdulrahman Salim Al Hatmi, held as part of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev's state visit to Oman on November 16-17.

The talks focused on strengthening transport and logistics cooperation, expanding export opportunities for Uzbek products in Oman and developing logistics and warehousing infrastructure.

In particular, the sides discussed the potential use of Oman's strategically important ports of Sohar, Duqm and Salalah to facilitate shipments of Uzbek products to African markets and other international destinations.

They also explored opportunities to deliver Uzbek goods to markets in Europe, Africa and Asia through Asyad Group's network of logistics operators and warehouses operating in multiple countries.

The meeting also addressed imports of in-demand products from international markets to Uzbekistan, the development of international transport and logistics chains, and more efficient use of existing transport corridors.

Following the discussions, the sides emphasized the importance of expanding mutually beneficial cooperation, advancing practical logistics projects and strengthening Uzbekistan's access to international trade routes.

World.title: Azerbaijan-Türkiye relations set to remain strong, FM says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Azerbaijan-Türkiye relations are strong today, and they will continue to be so in the future, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov said during a joint briefing with German Foreign Minister Johann David Wadephul on Wednesday, November 18, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

The minister noted that certain processes take place in every state, and every society has its own unique development trajectory.

"Such fraternal relations do not preclude the possibility that these societies may hold different perspectives on events occurring in other countries. In this regard, Azerbaijan’s position is clear: our country takes steps in alignment with its own development model. We believe that the fraternal relations between the two countries will remain strong and continue to flourish. The clearest evidence of this is the visit of the President of Türkiye to Azerbaijan on Victory Day, as well as the messages delivered jointly with the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev," he remarked.

World.title: Pakistan, Turkmenistan consider alternative trade routes to Central Asia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Pakistan has proposed exploring alternative trade corridors together with Turkmenistan to facilitate Pakistani exports to Central Asian markets, including marble, and address cross-border logistical challenges, the Pakistani government's press service reported.

Pakistan's Commerce Minister Jam Kamal Khan raised the proposal during a meeting with Turkmenistan's Minister of Trade and Foreign Economic Relations Dortguly Suleymanov in Islamabad.

Khan emphasized the need to facilitate cross-border movement and examine possible alternative routes for Pakistani marble and other exports to Central Asian markets.

“He emphasized the need to facilitate cross-border movement, explore alternative trade corridors and address logistical challenges affecting bilateral commerce,” the press service sited Khan as saying.

The discussions also covered logistical challenges affecting bilateral commerce and ways to improve regional trade connectivity.

As Trend previously noted in its analytical article, “Pakistan's southern gateway: How ECO could bring Central Asia closer to the Indian Ocean,” three potential transport routes could strengthen Pakistan's access to Central Asian markets: through Turkmenistan and Iran, through Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, and through China and Kyrgyzstan. Each option has different infrastructure requirements and geopolitical constraints.

The Kyrgyz route envisages transporting goods from Pakistan through Chinese territory and the Karakoram Highway. In spring 2026, Kyrgyzstan tested a road connection to Karachi via China. The route could provide an additional link between Central Asian markets and Pakistani seaports, while the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, currently under construction, could further strengthen regional connectivity. However, this option depends heavily on transit arrangements with China and the development of cross-border infrastructure.

The two other options involve Turkmenistan. The Afghan route could use existing cross-border links and further development of road and railway infrastructure to connect Turkmenistan with Pakistan. Its main advantage is geographical proximity, although political tensions between Islamabad and Kabul complicate its implementation.

Meanwhile, the Iranian route has an existing railway foundation: Pakistan's Quetta-Taftan line connects with Iran's network in Zahedan, while Iran is linked to Turkmenistan through Sarakhs. However, regional tensions and potential difficulties with financial settlements and international transit arrangements remain significant constraints.

World.title: Pakistan, Turkmenistan trade ministers discuss business ties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Pakistan and Turkmenistan have discussed measures to expand bilateral trade, improve market access and strengthen regional connectivity, with a focus on developing cooperation across several business sectors, the press service of the Pakistani government.

The issues were discussed during a meeting between Pakistan's Commerce Minister Jam Kamal Khan and Turkmenistan's Minister of Trade and Foreign Economic Relations Dovletgeldi Rejepov in Islamabad ahead of the sixth session of the Joint Intergovernmental Commission on November 17.

Khan highlighted opportunities for closer commercial cooperation in textiles, agriculture, food processing, manufacturing and logistics.

He also emphasized the importance of regular exchanges between business delegations to identify new investment opportunities and develop commercially viable trade agreements.

Addressing changes in the global economic environment, the Pakistani minister noted that rising international freight costs and disruptions to traditional trade routes had increased the importance of regional economic integration.

He said Pakistan and Turkmenistan were well positioned to benefit from emerging trade opportunities linking South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East.

“Highlighting changing global economic dynamics, the Federal Minister said rising international freight costs and disruptions to traditional trade routes had increased the importance of regional economic integration. He observed that Pakistan and Turkmenistan were well positioned to benefit from emerging trade opportunities linking South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East,” the press release quoted the Pakistani minister as saying.

World.title: German FM: Middle Corridor holds strategic importance for Europe
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. The Middle Corridor holds economic and strategic importance for Germany, German Foreign Minister Johann David Wadephul said in response to Trend’s question during a joint briefing with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov on Wednesday, November 18.

Wadephul noted that one of the primary objectives of Germany and the European Union is to identify reliable partners in both the political and economic spheres.

"For this very reason, we promote free trade agreements and work to ensure that infrastructure enables us to better establish connections with promising partners.

In this context, the Middle Corridor holds strategic importance for Europe. That is why its implementation is one of the priority projects on which the European Union and Germany are actively working.

I hope that we’ll be able to achieve positive results in the near future. I will also work to advance this objective in Armenia and urge the country to move towards concrete, practical steps on this project," he said.
