World.title: Kazakhstan completes scheduled overhauls of nine power units
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Kazakhstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Kazakhstan has completed major overhauls of all nine power units scheduled for maintenance in 2026, according to the country's Ministry of Energy.

The maintenance work covered power units No. 2, 4 and 6 at Ekibastuz GRES-1, units No. 1 and 2 at Ekibastuz GRES-2, units No. 5 and 8 at the EEC power plant in Aksu, and units No. 2 and 3 at Zhambyl GRES.

As part of preparations for the heating season, repairs have also been completed on 51 of the 55 boilers scheduled for maintenance. Work on the remaining four boilers is expected to be completed within the established timeframe.

In addition, maintenance has been completed on 17,100 kilometers of electricity networks, 444 substations and 3,408 distribution and transformer facilities. A total of 377 kilometers of heating networks have also been repaired.

On November 16, Kazakhstan's power generation reached a new instantaneous record of 17,356 megawatts at 6:20 p.m. The previous record of 17,273 MW was set in 2025.

The ministry noted that the maintenance campaign is aimed at ensuring reliable and uninterrupted energy supplies to consumers during the heating season.

Meanwhile, electricity generation in Kazakhstan increased by 2.3% year-on-year to 102.4 billion kilowatt-hours in January-October 2026.

World.title: Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race to give Democrats 56 seats
World.content:
Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Dan S Sullivan in Alaska to complete the best Senate performance in a US midterm election by the Democratic Party since 1958.

The Alaska race was the last Senate contest to be resolved and gave the Democrats a 56-44 majority after they flipped nine GOP-held seats to retake the chamber.

Due to the logistical challenges of collecting ballots from across the sparsely populated state, it took two weeks of counting to call an Alaska winner after the November 3 poll.

Alaska's 'decoy' Dan Sullivan Something fishy is going on in Alaska ahead of the midterms, but it has nothing to do with the state's famous seafood and everything to do with two men with the same name.

With 99 per cent of ballots counted, Ms Peltola had slightly more than a 50 per cent share, while Mr Sullivan trailed with less than 46 per cent.

The party also won campaigns in other conservative states, including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi.

Ms Peltola's win overcame allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the Republican incumbent's name and completes a political comeback in a state US President Donald Trump won by wide margins in 2024.

Independent Daniel J Sullivan Jr won 1.65 per cent of the vote. But even with his votes combined with those for the GOP's Mr Sullivan, Ms Peltola still eked out a narrow victory.

A spokesperson for Dan S Sullivan did not respond to a request for comment, but said on Monday that the campaign would let the process "run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified".

Dan J Sullivan has denied any contact with the Peltola campaign or running at the Democrats' behest, but the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit pending an investigation into possible voter confusion.

A jubilant Ms Peltola said voters sent a clear message that "the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

"Over the course of this campaign, I've spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table," she said.

" Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first. "

Voters responded to Mary Peltola's connection to all parts of Alaska. (Reuters: Kerry Tasker)

Ms Peltola, a 53-year-old mother of seven, including three stepchildren, played up her rural roots during the campaign.

She tapped into Alaskans' frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat, and are generally only accessible by air or water.

Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of "Alaska first".

"Alaskans who know me know that I'm not liberal or radical," Ms Peltola said.

"I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can."

Alaska is America's largest and most remote state, which delayed the final vote count. (Unsplash: Eddie Bugajewski)

The strategy resonated with voters who felt they could relate to Ms Peltola, who is Yup'ik and often spoke about growing up in western Alaska.

Winning Alaska was pivotal to Democrats' plans to retake the Senate.

The party's flip of nine Senate seats represents the most since the 1958 midterms, when they wrested away 13 Republican-held seats.

The incoming 56-seat Democratic caucus is the most Senate seats held by Democrats since January 3, 2011, at the conclusion of the 111th Congress.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Internal documents show half of David Jones job losses are casual staff
World.content:
Half of the 1,689 jobs slated to go at David Jones are permanent roles, while the rest are casuals with no entitlements to be paid out once 19 stores close, internal documents show.

A briefing document seen by ABC News shows the specific breakdown of jobs at the stores set to be shut by the end of 2026.

There are 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand closing, as last week confirmed by the receiver, FTI Consulting, acting on behalf of David Jones' secured lender, Hilco Capital.

Of the 1,689 roles encompassed in the earmarked stores, 843 are casuals while 846 are permanent workers employed on either a full-time or part-time basis.

The workforces are larger in urban stores slated for closure, including the Perth flagship store in Hay Street Mall, and Warringah and Hornsby in Sydney's north.

The briefing by FTI Consulting sent out this week noted "redeployment options".

"Although we will try and redeploy as many staff as possible, there is unfortunately no way to avoid a large amount of job losses," it said.

The retail workers' union believes only 170 jobs will be saved at this stage, with the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association (SDA) giving the ABC more detail this afternoon.

"We expect in the coming couple of days, between Thursday and Monday, that people who have got those redeployments will be informed about them," the union's NSW branch secretary Bernie Smith said.

Are you a David Jones worker or do you know more? Confidentially contact our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me

What are these workers entitled to now?

David Jones was went into voluntary administration earlier this month. (ABC News: Zahra Anwary)

This week, it was confirmed that the retailer's 6,000-strong workforce was owed $11 million at the time the 188-year-old retailer was put into voluntary administration on November 5.

It is understood that figure only includes annual and long service leave entitlements owed to staff, and does not include the extra ballooning debt to permanent workers that will now be owed severance.

The SDA said it was working to confirm information about redundancy payouts.

In an administration process, workers are paid back their entitlements before other creditors, such as suppliers. However, clawing back cash is contingent on a rescue package or successful sell-off.

This means the workers could face a drawn-out process to get what they are due.

FTI Consulting and David Jones' administrator McGrathNicol were both contacted for comment about who is responsible for paying various entitlements to workers.

There are federal government guarantees in place to help workers when no cash can be recovered; however, these exclude migrant workers.

Meanwhile, casuals do not get accrued entitlements like holiday pay, instead receiving a higher hourly rate. The casuals will now just be out of work.

Bernie Smith says the union is focused on securing employee entitlements. (ABC News)

"They don't receive redundancies, and they are very focused on trying to get alternative employment for as many workers as possible outside of David Jones," Mr Smith said.

"We think there's a bit of a missed opportunity for David Jones, but I know the cost of doing business is challenging."

Mr Smith said the union had been in talks with other retailers about taking on the haemorrhaged David Jones workforce but would not share brand names.

"Those are early discussions and [it's a] difficult time of year for hiring," he said.

"But we've been pleasantly surprised at the willingness of what could be done. It's a difficult time in retail, but there is a real interest in these experienced salespeople."

David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff.

Mr Smith said in the meantime the union was focused on securing employees' entitlements.

"There's $11.3 million of accrued entitlements to annual leave, long service leave," he said.

"But there's also the redundancy payments on top of that, that isn't available to our members until the administration comes to an end, which could be months away.

"So we want to fast-track that."

World.title: NT aged care facility set for 2028 finish as government fast-tracks project
World.content:
An aged care facility planned for Palmerston will now house up to 150 residents and begin construction next year, as the federal and Northern Territory governments seek to address the NT's overburdened aged care system.

Federal Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae was in Darwin today to announce the Commonwealth would contribute an extra $20 million to the site, which Anthony Albanese spruiked during the 2025 federal election campaign.

It takes the federal government's funding for the facility to $80 million, along with $20 million from aged care provider Ozcare and $20 million from the NT government, which also provided the land for the site.

The funding boost will support the creation of an additional 30 beds at the centre.

Sam Rae says the government is fast-tracking the project, with construction likely to begin mid next year. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The NT Country Liberal Party (CLP) government has previously criticised its federal counterpart for dragging its feet on the planned facility.

Today, Mr Rae said the Commonwealth would fast-track the project.

New Darwin aged care facility promised years ago The prime minister's promise to build a new residential aged care facility in Darwin has come too late for people like Jill.

He said construction would "hopefully" begin midway through 2027, which would allow for residents to move into the facility by the end of 2028.

"These facilities take somewhere between five and seven years usually from inception to the time that people can start moving in," he said.

"This is a project that we are collectively aiming to deliver in a much shorter period of time."

NT Treasurer Bill Yan said the NT government was proud to be partnering with the Commonwealth to deliver the project.

Questions remain around demand, workforce

There has long been heavy demand on aged care services in Darwin, leading to high numbers of senior Territorians occupying beds in local hospitals.

In a statement, NT Health Minister Steve Edgington said 77 older Territorians were currently occupying public hospital beds in the NT due to the short supply of aged care facilities.

"These are people who should be living in a suitable aged care home, not on a hospital ward," he said.

Lanna Ramsay says with 150 beds, the facility is "sitting pretty close" to the current level of demand. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Ozcare's chief operating officer for aged care, Lanna Ramsay, said while she was pleased Ozcare had been selected to run the facility, the soaring demand for residential aged care in the Top End could not be overlooked

"The more we spoke to people in preparation for that expression of interest, [we realised] the demand was sitting pretty close to what we were going to build," she said.

Mr Rae noted one of the reasons for bed blockages in public hospitals was due to the delayed discharge of patients with complex dementia-related illnesses.

He said the new facility would provide dementia care and a specialist dementia care unit to meet the needs of patients with dementia in the Top End.

The centre's backers hope it will alleviate the problem of bed block in NT hospitals. (ABC News Dane Hirst)

However, Mr Rae acknowledged more work needed to be done in relation to immigration policy to ensure demand for aged care workers was met.

"Of course there's a sensible conversation to be had across our community about what sustainable migration looks like, I'd never argue against that, but we have to recognise that we do rely largely on people that come here from overseas with a huge bank of skills," he said.

"These are highly skilled migrants that we're talking about, to come and work within our care sector, within our care economy."

World.title: Duckett makes ton, Renshaw takes wickets in ODI decider
World.content:
England opener Ben Duckett has whacked a century to help his side set Australia a target of 329 in the deciding game of their one-day international series.

Duckett made 133 off 115 balls at Hobart's Bellerive Oval today after the tourists won the toss in the third game.

England was bowled out for 328 with nine balls remaining and found it tough against the part-time spin of Matt Renshaw through the middle overs.

Renshaw picked up 3-51, including a flighted delivery to bowl Joe Root (12) in the 15th over, the scalp of Jordan Cox (12) stumped, and Duckett off a top edge in the 39th over.

Australia went into the game without a specialist spinner after Adam Zampa withdrew at the last minute because of back spasms.

Duckett had a life on 29 when Alex Carey, making a rare appearance as a specialist batter, dropped a catch at forward square off Mahli Beardman's bowling.

Beardman, who starred in game one with six wickets on debut, did not have the same success and finished with 0-54.

Matt Renshaw's impressive spin bowling brought three vital wickets for Australia against England in the final ODI in Hobart. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Will Jacks posted back-to-back half-centuries, with 59 off 48 deliveries, batting with the tail, before being the last batter out when he holed out off all-rounder Jack Edwards.

Edwards finished with 4-31 courtesy of late scalps.

England got off to a quick start, with Duckett sharing a 74-run opening stand with Tom Banton (44 off 35 deliveries), who fell to a juggling running catch by Mitch Marsh.

Harry Brook (17) failed for the third time this series, caught in the deep off Cooper Connolly's bowling.

Tailender Jofra Archer was elevated to number six as a pinch hitter but could not get going and was caught in the deep off the bowling of Travis Head for just seven.

Quick Xavier Bartlett sent a scare through the Australian camp when he limped off midway through the innings, but returned to bowl at the death.

England named an unchanged side following its comfortable win in game two, while Australia brought in Beardman and Carey for Riley Meredith and Zampa.

AAP

World.title: Family First disendorses election candidate over 'unacceptable' posts
World.content:
Family First has disendorsed its Victorian election candidate for Bendigo West over "unbecoming and unacceptable" online content and language.

On Wednesday, the ABC sent Family First questions about content that appeared linked to its candidate Christos Harisopoulos.

A Substack account under a pseudonym posted an article on November 12 with a by-line attributed to Mr Harisopoulos, titled "Put Family First For Bendigo West".

In it, Mr Harisopoulos admitted he was not a career politician, but "a bit of a larrikin".

Earlier posts on the same Substack account, however, include a 2023 music video titled "PM Adolf (F*** Off)" where Mr Harisopoulos sings lyrics appearing to reference the Voice referendum.

A screenshot from a 2023 Substack video 'PM Adolf (F*** Off)'. (Supplied: Substack)

Another article posted on the account in 2024, titled "It's Time to Kick the Duopoly Up the Arse", states it is "written, spoken and authorised by Christos Harisopoulos aka Senator Papahatziharalambrous".

It claims Labor and the Liberals had "sold 25 per cent of our land to the community party of China", and are "importing replacements" who will vote for their "traitorous politicians without question".

The Substack account description says it is: "Just News, Views and Parody: Provoke The State With Satire! Vote 1 For Senator Papahatziharalambrous to #TipOutTheRats #DrainTheBillabong #TakeBackOurStates and Let's Make Australia Grouse Again! #ForAustralia".

Content on other social media platforms and music linked to Mr Harisopoulos includes crude language in reference to former and current political leaders, which the ABC has chosen not to publish.

In one post to his X.com account, which is no longer available on Wednesday afternoon, Mr Harisopoulos said his account had been banned due to a meme he shared of former premier Daniel Andrews.

A post on X by Christos Harisopoulos saying he had been banned for posting a Daniel Andrews meme. (Supplied: X.com)

Family First national director Lyle Shelton told the ABC on Wednesday afternoon that Mr Harisopoulos had been disendorsed by the party, following the identification of online content and language he was linked to.

"We are a small party with limited resources. We regret that this material was not picked up in the vetting process," Mr Shelton said.

The ABC has contacted Mr Harisopoulos for comment.

A now-deleted page on the Family First website said Mr Harisopoulos, 57, had a "varied working life" and was currently working for an Australian company developing drones and IoT technology for farmers.

It said Mr Harisopoulos was standing for Family First, "because he believes faith, family, freedom and common sense must come first".

"For those who have followed his public commentary over recent years, he simply asks for one more chance to help put things right," the page said.

The seat of Bendigo West includes parts of Bendigo's CBD and west, as well as the towns of Castlemaine, Maldon and Harcourt.

It has been held by Labor since 1996; however, current MP Maree Edwards is not recontesting at next week's election.

The Nationals are targeting Bendigo West, alongside the neighbouring Bendigo East seat being vacated by former premier Jacinta Allan.

The Nationals' how-to-vote card for Bendigo West encourages voters to place Family First's Christos Harisopoulos at third, while One Nation has preferenced Family First second.

World.title: Royal commission quizzes bikie on $165k bill for mystery work
World.content:
Bikie Joel Leavitt has been accused of forging invoices and pocketing hundreds of thousands of dollars for non-existent work on Victorian government building sites.

The Big Build royal commission heard the Bandidos member had issued labour hire company BK Labour an invoice of $165,000.

The invoice was issued by a company of which Mr Leavitt was the sole director, JVL consulting. Two days later, the lump sum was paid into his account.

Mr Leavitt could not recall the exact details of the work he carried out or the duration of the job, but at one stage suggested to the commission it could have been just hours of work.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis highlighted that would have equated to about $20,000 an hour for his services.

"Maybe I would have [charged that]," Mr Leavitt said.

"If a client's willing to pay, why not? Everyone likes money."

The commission indicated it had evidence to suggest the money was a standover tactic and which it suggested could have been for one of two reasons: either Mr Leavitt had information on BK Labour that it would want kept quiet, which he denied; or that he stood over the labour hire company with some sort of explicit or implied violence.

Mr Leavitt sought legal advice before he told the inquiry "to the best of my recollection I've never stood over anyone at BK".

The inquiry later heard from the man who paid the bill, Bernard Kearney of BK Labour Hire.

Chris Kourakis: He didn't do any work for you did he? Bernard Kearney: No. Counsel assisting: Ever saw him in the office? Bernard Kearney: No, I've never seen him, no.

Mr Kearney told the inquiry he "decided to pay" the bill and "move on", but failed to explain why.

Bernard Kearney told the inquiry Joel Leavitt had not done any work for BK Labour Hire. (Supplied)

Bikie accused of being a 'heavy', taking advantage of union power

The inquiry was later shown another invoice for souvlakis for construction workers at the Hurstbridge rail line job, which it also suggested was fraudulent.

The catering bill came in at $9,000 but was inflated to $20,000.

Text messages accompanying the invoice suggested $5,000 was pocketed by two CFMEU health and safety representatives, one of whom was Mr Leavitt.

Mr Leavitt was questioned over text messages that appeared to show a Rebel bikie member asking Mr Leavitt if there were any other Rebels on a particular Big Build project to give someone "a talking to".

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr SC put to Mr Leavitt that he was "nothing more than a bikie heavy that the CFMEU wanted on building sites so [he] could intimidate people into doing what the union wanted" and that he "took full advantage of the CFMEU's power to get [his] bikie mates jobs".

Carr: You were prepared to act without morals and you were prepared to be a heavy to get what the union wanted. Isn't that the truth? Leavitt: Not to the best of my recollection.

At one stage, a hungover Mr Leavitt said he had consumed alcohol after the previous day's hearing, which left him "bamboozled".

On another occasion, he invited the commissioner for "a beer" to get to know him better, and revealed using cocaine had helped him complete job-related paperwork.

Evading questions a crime, commissioner warns

During Wednesday's hearing, Mr Kourakis gave Mr Leavitt several stern warnings that it was an offence to fail to answer questions put to him under examination.

"The only reason I'm saying this is to warn you that a finding could be made that you've made what some people would see as outlandish claims of … having no memory over periods of years in an attempt to avoid answering the questions," he said.

Mr Leavitt had responded that he could not recall more than 200 times to questions he was asked during Tuesday's hearing.

He told the inquiry he was seeing a psychologist to help with memory loss, which he attributed to post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and claimed that during the period of time he was being questioned on, a gang squad had had a contract on his life.

Chris Kourakis issued Joel Leavitt a warning about his apparent lack of memory. (Joe Armao: AAP)

Mr Leavitt said he was also shot, contributing to the trauma, but when asked questions about the shooting, he did not have any recollection of being shot or going to hospital with a gunshot wound.

He also did not remember where it happened but said media reporting suggested he was at a Rebels clubhouse.

"I am doing the best to my ability, commissioner, to get this thing going, I don't know what else to say. It f***ed me up," he said.

Shortly after the shooting, Mr Leavitt said, he patched over to the Bandidos, but told the commission he could not remember why he did that.

After seeking some legal advice, Mr Leavitt's memory appeared to return at times.

Mr Carr accused Mr Levitt of answering questions in a particular way to ensure he would not be caught denying something that might later be proven.

"You persist in claiming that you have no memory about anything that goes to your discredit," Mr Carr said.

Mr Leavitt denied doing so.

He was stood down from the commission but advised he could be asked to return for further questioning.

World.title: Sydney's Papley banned for three games after roadside drug test
World.content:
Sydney's Tom Papley will miss the Swans' preseason game and the first three matches of the 2027 season after being banned by the AFL over a failed roadside drug test.

The AFL banned Papley for conduct unbecoming, giving the Swans small forward a notifiable adverse finding under the league's Illicit Drugs Policy.

He was also given a suspended $5,000 fine.

NSW Police stopped Papley on November 2 for a roadside licence check.

He was issued with a court attendance notice for driving with a suspended licence, due to an unpaid parking fine.

The Swans player then completed a random drug test that gave a positive initial result. Today, the AFL said the secondary sample had confirmed the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

NSW Police has fined Papley $722, and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Swans culture issue Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich expresses "bitter disappointment" after Tom Papley's drug test result hurls the AFL club back into the spotlight.

AFL COO Tom Harley said the sanction reflected the seriousness of the breach.

"AFL players are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with illicit drug use," Harley said in a statement.

"The player is being held accountable for his actions and has acknowledged he made a grave mistake."

Papley apologised for his behaviour in a statement released by the Swans.

"I am extremely sorry for my behaviour which has caused distress for my family, everyone connected to the Club and broader industry," he said.

"I accept my actions have fallen well short of the standards that is expected of me at this football club, and I will work very hard to win the trust back of everyone in the wider community.

"Road safety is something that affects everyone in our community, and I take full accountability for my mistake.

"I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my wife, my family, my manager Winston, the Club, my teammates, the AFLPA and all those who have supported me over the last fortnight."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich said Papley understood the sanction and was taking responsibility for his mistakes.

"While we are very disappointed in his actions, he is an important member of the team, and we will work closely with him and the entire AFL program to reinstate the high standards the Club expects of everyone.

"We need to be better, and change must occur."

World.title: Albanese says Trump, Xi and Putin talks on Ukraine 'not up to Australia'
World.content:
Anthony Albanese says Moscow's illegal war must end on "Ukraine's terms" as he calls for a de-escalation of global conflicts ahead of landmark talks between the US, China and Russia.

The prime minister arrived in Shenzhen on Tuesday afternoon ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit where he reiterated Australia's opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

But Mr Albanese also indicated he would likely appear in the traditional APEC family photo alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, describing it as a matter of "respect" for China as host of the summit.

"I will bear in mind the wishes of our host," he said.

"If you are invited to an event … I respect that, but we'll also make our position very clear when it comes to Ukraine."

AI is transforming US–China relationship The ASEAN summit has become a platform for showing how economies are swept up in the newest and most potent form of US–China rivalry.

Asked whether he would follow Tony Abbott's confrontational approach to Mr Putin, Mr Albanese said he would not take lessons in diplomacy from the former prime minister.

Mr Abbott said he would "shirt front" Mr Putin if he saw him at the G20 summit in 2014.

Instead, Mr Albanese said he would use his time at APEC to make clear Australia's position on Russia's invasion, which he said was unchanged.

"This is a big power intervening in an illegal way to try and assert its will and underestimate the will and courage and conviction of the Ukrainian people to fight for their national sovereignty," he said.

PM says trilateral dialogue a 'good thing'

The annual gathering of 21 economies from around the Asia Pacific is at risk of being overshadowed by a trilateral summit between Mr Putin, US President Donald Trump and China President Xi Jinping due to take place on the same day.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against the three leaders deciding his country's future without Kyiv at the table, likening the trilateral to a modern-day Yalta conference where in 1945, allies negotiated post-war settlements in Europe.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against the three leaders deciding his country's future without Kyiv at the table. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Asked if it was appropriate for Ukraine to be discussed at the meeting between the US, China and Russia, Mr Albanese said it was "not up to Australia to determine who people have met with".

"We do say that any solution and peace, which we want to see in Ukraine, needs to be on Ukraine's terms," he said.

But Mr Albanese said "in general" it was a "good thing that dialogue happens" between countries.

"At a time when there are more conflicts than at any time since the Second World War … we want to see more dialogue, less military conflict," he said.

Albanese to sit down with Xi

Mr Albanese is due to sit down with Mr Xi on the sidelines of APEC on Friday morning but would not foreshadow the issues he planned to raise with China's leader.

Asked if Labor would be able to deliver on its election promise to return the Port of Darwin lease into Australian hands before the next election in 2028, Mr Albanese said the commitment was unchanged though he could not guarantee a timeline.

"Of course, there are processes [that] take place there, including some international processes," he said.

Mr Albanese said there might also be "legal consequences and actions".

Loading...

The port is leased to Chinese-owned company Landbridge, with the government's push to return it to Australian control a sensitive issue in the bilateral relationship.

Mr Albanese also signalled he would continue pressing China to remove barriers to Australian agricultural exports after being asked about tariffs on beef exports that exceeded an annual quota.

"We'd rather not have any quotas on Australian goods anywhere in the world," he said.

But he said strong demand for Australian beef demonstrated the appeal of local products to Chinese consumers.

Earlier, Mr Albanese visited a supermarket in Shenzhen that stocked Australian products including apples, cherries, beef and lobster.

The prime minister said trade with China was important for Australian jobs and economic growth.

World.title: Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWSelective schools Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots Christopher Harris November 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Selective school shopping will become harder for parents under a new policy that blocks private school students from being offered any last-minute vacancies which arise throughout year 7 or 8. The overhaul will prioritise entry for comprehensive public school pupils, in a bid to restore fairness to the fiercely competitive second-chance entry pathway, which last year saw 1100 pupils compete for just 10 spots in year 8. Students after sitting the selective school entry exam this year. Sitthixay Ditthavong It is the latest in a series of changes to selective school entry, which includes reserving 50 per cent of total places for girls, who are underrepresented in the academically elite institutions, and easier entry for certain disadvantaged students. Under current rules, families hoping to make a last-minute switch apply directly to the school, and the criteria can include external academic test results, school reports and extracurricular activities.



Related Article Education The winners and losers of Sydney’s new selective school gender quotas The changes in 2028 will remove direct entry for those grades entirely, with only comprehensive school students eligible and entry based on the results they received in the selective exam they sat in year 6. Students enrolled in a selective or partially selective school will be blocked from switching to another. Those entering year 7 in 2028 will be the first cohort subject to the changes, which will apply to enrolment places that open up between the second term of year 7 and the last term of year 8. A Department of Education spokesman said the new policy simplified year 8 entry and would build stronger links between gifted education in comprehensive and selective schools.



Australian Tutoring Association chief executive and UTS education lecturer, Mohan Dhall, said it was unfair and against the spirit of a public education to block prospective students because they happened to be attending a private school. “To me, that is actually discriminatory,” he said. “The public system says it caters for all. It means it is not closed to a citizen of NSW whose parents pay taxes from entering a public high school.” There are more selective high schools in NSW than in any other state. Oscar Colman He also criticised basing selection on test data dating back to year 6, which could be up to two years prior. “A kid who missed out in year 6 could, on merit, be academically stronger in year 7 and 8,” he said.



NSW has more selective high schools than any other state, with 17 fully selective, 27 partially selective and four fully selective agricultural high schools. Related Article Selective schools Ilia missed out on selective school – until he found another way in Students entering year 7 next year are the first cohort where the gender equity model will apply, which reserves 50 per cent of places for girls in co-ed schools. There will be an equal number of spots across the system in single-sex schools. Parents of boys have vented on online forums about the policy change. An online petition accused the government of undermining merit-based selection in favour of quota-based social engineering. “This policy represents direct discrimination against male students who work hard and achieve high test scores but will be denied places simply because of their gender,” the petition said. World.title: CFMEU’s former Big Build boss billed controversial labour firm $256,000
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaBig Build royal commission CFMEU’s former Big Build boss billed controversial labour firm $256,000 Clay Lucas November 18, 2026 — 7:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A controversial labour hire firm pushed onto state projects by the CFMEU has received invoices totalling $256,000 from the union’s former Big Build boss Joe Myles. BK Labour Hire, also paid a violent bikie $165,000 for consulting work that was never done, the Big Build royal commission heard on Wednesday as it probed how bikies and favoured firms won access to the multibillion-dollar taxpayer-funded infrastructure program. Witness Bernard Kearney (right) walks into the royal commission with his lawyer, construction industry barrister Jim Stavris, on Wednesday. Penny Stephens BK Labour Hire co-owner Bernard Kearney appeared before the commission and confirmed his company received a “succession” of consulting invoices from the CFMEU’s Myles – as the firm’s total profits surged past $24 million over the four years to 2025. The admissions capped a day of hearings in which royal commissioner Chris Kourakis warned Kearney, and Bandidos and former Rebels bikie Joel Leavitt, of potential legal consequences in the wake of their refusal to answer questions.



The inquiry also heard a major state contractor let Leavitt hand out taxpayer-funded jobs to his mates and paid an inflated $20,000 bill for free on-site souvlakis, from which Leavitt and another CFMEU delegate would pocket $5000 each. Leavitt, a former CFMEU health and safety representative, who arrived at Wednesday’s hearing admitting he was hungover, told the inquiry he used cocaine to “zone in” on safety paperwork, and conceded he may have skimmed thousands from the souvlaki catering rort. Bandidos and former Rebels bikie Joel Leavitt arrives at the Big Build royal commission on Wednesday. Penny Stephens Under questioning from counsel assisting Chris Carr, SC, Kearney confirmed BK Labour Hire – the firm which numerous witnesses have said was placed onto the $110 million Gap Road level crossing removal project after union pressure – received $256,000 in consulting invoices from Myles. Myles lost his senior CFMEU role in 2024 following The Age’s Building Bad investigation that year. Last week, witnesses told the inquiry that Myles demanded BK Labour Hire be appointed at Gap Road and boasted of a “direct line” to former premier Jacinta Allan’s office.





Leavitt had also earlier been warned that refusing to answer questions carried a two-year jail sentence. That warning came after Leavitt recited a memory-loss claim eight times in five minutes, and blamed trauma from being shot in the leg at a Rebels clubhouse in 2023. Loading “How do you think you would act if you’ve ever been shot?” Leavitt asked Kourakis at one point during this questioning. “Fortunately, I can’t answer that,” Kourakis said in response.



BK Labour Hire’s Kearney denied knowing of Leavitt’s outlaw motorcycle gang ties when he first employed him on a rail project in Hallam in 2021, claiming hiring deals were “done between the CFMEU and Laing O’Rourke” and saying: “I didn’t even know who he was.” The commission heard earlier this week that the union had campaigned for months to get Leavitt hired by Laing O’Rourke. Financial records tendered on Wednesday showed BK Labour Hire went from losing more than $300,000 each year in 2020 and 2021 to clearing more than $24 million in profit between 2022 and last year. By 2023, when Kearney and his business partners were considering selling their firm, accountants valued BK Labour Hire at $43.5 million.



Kourakis noted that after winning its first contract with Laing O’Rourke, in future tenders “you won every time” – a point Kearney accepted. “You’re charging more than the industry average and still winning almost every time. It’s pretty remarkable, isn’t it, Mr Kearney?” Carr said. Before Kearney took the stand, the commission heard how major contractor Acciona allowed Leavitt to hand out taxpayer-funded jobs to his associates on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade, and sought his permission before hiring workers. Text messages tendered by Carr showed Acciona site superintendent Tim Alford telling Leavitt: “I don’t care [about] bringing your mates on and putting them in spotting roles and finding homes, but they all need to do their jobs.”



In another exchange, Leavitt messaged Alford: “Hey Tim, can you send Cycon [Civil] a request for two people at Diamond Creek and one person for Alpington (sic)?” Cycon Civil is a labour hire and civil firm whose ties to the CFMEU and payments to underworld figure Mick Gatto have previously been reported by The Age. Carr also showed tendered as evidence a text message from a site superintendent seeking Leavitt’s permission to place onto a job a worker from Women in Construction – a firm run by a man convicted of domestic violence whose labour hire licence was revoked earlier this year. Other texts showed Leavitt promising work with Cycon Civil and labour hire firm OCC to a Rebels bikie named “Corbo”, and offering to have the bikie’s partner hired by Women in Construction. It prompted Carr to observe that Leavitt was running “an employment agency for Rebels and their partners”.



The commission also examined March 2023 texts between Leavitt and a fellow CFMEU safety delegate arranging a free souvlaki lunch for 600 Hurstbridge workers, with Leavitt writing: “So just make up a quote that hits 20k, and we will collect the other nine off the subbies”. Texts between bikie Joel Leavitt and Acciona’s Tim Allford. In a follow-up message, Leavitt wrote the pair would get “five each”, before sending a $20,000 invoice to Alford for a meal that a cash register receipt showed cost $9000. “Can I take it that you’re not surprised that you might have engaged in that conduct?” Kourakis asked. “I’ll accept that. I’m not surprised that I could of,” Leavitt replied.

Cameron Bancroft says the entire Australian team knew he was using sandpaper to achieve reverse swing during the 2018 tour of South Africa, backing Usman Khawaja’s account of events and saying he felt betrayed and angered by Pat Cummins’ denials last week.

Bancroft, in a 4000-word piece released in The West Australian on Wednesday evening, said he failed to provide a “complete and truthful” account of events when investigated by Cricket Australia in 2018, withholding important details about when the use of sandpaper began, how long it continued, and the awareness of the rest of the travelling party.

Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images

“It was not just the three of us – Steve Smith, David Warner and I – who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team,” he wrote.

“I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.”

World.title: ‘I couldn’t walk’: The moment Rose Byrne knew she’d gone too far for her new thriller
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a point in every crime thriller when the puzzle pieces start to click together – new evidence is unearthed, new testimony is recorded, a new suspect appears and turns the case on its head. In each episode of new thriller The Good Daughter, each assembled piece reveals only more loose ones, widening the scope of an addictive and emotional story set in the American South until just about every resident of the town of Pikeville is in the crosshairs. At the heart of the story, adapted from legendary crime writer Karin Slaughter’s 2017 book, are sisters Samantha and Charlotte “Charlie” Quinn, played by Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy. As girls, they were raised by a sharp, cerebral mother as interested in Emily Dickinson as she was in studying the science of weather patterns. Editor's pick ★★★★

Review Is there a better villain on TV right now than David Tennant? Their father, Rusty, played by Brendan Gleeson, is the town’s notorious defence attorney and has a list of enemies a mile long for taking on cases without neat moral boundaries. He’s a larger-than-life figure, a kind of funhouse-mirror version of Atticus Finch who keeps the town – and his girls – in line with a dirty mouth and sly smile. “[Slaughter] has a richness of character and a detailed place in the American South,” says Byrne. “And she’s an absolute force to work with. It was interesting having the author on set because [she’s had] these characters for decades in her head.” Loading Fahy agrees. “Karin’s pretty unflinching,” she says. “She’s really not afraid to go anywhere with a character. And there’s not really any topic of conversation that she’s not willing to put under a microscope.”



She’s an expert at surprise, at building in twists and reveals and herrings of all colours in characters you care deeply about. “You really can’t get ahead of her plot-wise.” We meet the Quinns, in episode one’s opening flashback, on the day the violent ripples of their father’s work floods their doorstep. Rose Byrne plays Samantha Quinn, who returns home to help on a court case, in The Good Daughter. Thirty years after experiencing the town’s brutality first-hand, the sisters are splintered. While Sam is practising sterile and safe patent law in New York City, Charlie has stuck around in town to follow in their father’s footsteps, hauling teenagers in front of the judge to face their petty crimes, messing around on her estranged husband and knowing the rules just well enough to break them. Related Article Australian TV Another spiky and difficult female detective? That’s just the way Anna Samson likes it “I was involved with casting and we were so lucky to get Meghann, who brings such a lightness of touch to a character that is very tightly locked up and is hard to reach for the people around her – and the audience,” says Byrne, who served as an executive producer on the series. “Charlie is the heart and soul of this story.” After witnessing a school shooting, Charlie senses there’s more to the story than what Pikeville’s corrupt cops are telling the community – but she can’t argue the case alone. When her sister returns home, the layers of their personal history unravel alongside this complex new case.



The sisters are like magnets with opposing fields; they push at and test each other, denying the fact they’re fated to face the world and their shared trauma shoulder-to-shoulder. When one stays, the other runs. One sister deals with her pain by enforcing control over every element of her life, while the other attracts chaos. Meghann Fahy and Brendan Gleeson as Charlie and Rusty Quinn in The Good Daughter. The youngest of three sisters, Slaughter wove the specificities of a sisterly bond into every line of her book, and the series’ scripts – all of which she wrote. She also served as a showrunner and an executive producer. “Karin’s dialogue is so specific. It does a lot of the heavy lifting in terms of who the characters are,” says Fahy. “There’s a very particular way that Charlie speaks and there’s a very particular way that Sam speaks. When we were in scenes that were quite snappy and going back and forth, you do start to slip into the rhythm of these people because it’s so clearly there on the page.” Related Article Streaming The 10 best Rose Byrne performances to watch after her Golden Globes win For as much as Sam tries to plaster over her past, her scars are visible on the surface. The violence in her childhood left her disabled and walking with a limp, and affected her speech. Fresh off her Golden Globe win and Oscar nomination for last year’s If I Had Legs I’d Kick You, Byrne grabbed the opportunity with both hands – but might’ve accidentally gone a little too method.



“I worked with a PT trainer who works in rehab with people with injuries to establish [Sam’s] walk, and then with another person with dysarthria [to accurately portray] how she spoke,” says Byrne. “It had quite a consequence. I was in Melbourne on a holiday with my family and all of a sudden … my back seized up and I couldn’t walk and I had to lie down for two days. “I saw this osteopath, and they said, ‘What have you been doing?’ I said, ‘Well, I was playing a person with a limp. I did it every day for eight weeks.’” Rose Byrne (left) and Meghann Fahy arrive at the premiere of The Good Daughter in New York. AP Photo/Christopher Smith Turns out that’s the precise amount of physical adjustment it takes to fundamentally change how your body operates. Alongside Byrne and Slaughter, a largely female creative team brought The Good Daughter to life with care and thoughtfulness. Oscar-nominated Steph Green directed the entire series, which was also overseen by Australian super-producer Bruna Papandrea, co-founder of Reese Witherspoon’s production company, Pacific Standard. “It was a very sensitive topic we were covering and it felt like we were just in really great hands the whole time,” says Byrne, referring to the crew as an “incredible coven”. Her character, Sam, is in many ways a literary classic – the prodigal child returning home to face their family’s demons – and in others, an entirely modern invention. “It’s something we’ve seen countless times with men, but not as much with women,” says Byrne. “It felt very fresh in that sense that it was about a woman doing that.”

Jamal Fogarty could make an immediate switch to Wests Tigers as the joint-venture club prioritises the signature of the Manly halfback above that of Josh Addo-Carr. Fogarty is contracted to the Sea Eagles until the end of 2028, but has been given permission to leave early. The Sea Eagles are looking to free up salary cap space with Fogarty, Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor among the players the club is prepared to release early. Jamal Fogarty could be heading to Concord. Getty Images The Tigers believe Fogarty’s experience could be invaluable after the departure of Jarome Luai to Parramatta. Coach Benji Marshall has several playmaking options at his disposal, including Adam Doueihi, Latu Fainu, Javon Andrews and Jock Madden. However, Fogarty has been identified as the controlling No.7 the club requires to break a finals drought stretching back to 2011.



Any move is likely to be subsidised by Manly, who are trying to reshape their roster. The Sea Eagles have a surplus of halves with Fogarty, Brooks, Joey Walsh and Onitoni Large on their books. The northern beaches outfit recently released Blake Wilson to the Perth Bears, but are for more salary cap wiggle room. Fogarty – who has made 140 NRL appearances for the Titans, Raiders and Sea Eagles – isn’t the only player of interest to the Tigers. Out-of-favour Eel Addo-Carr could also be making the move to Concord, despite a player swap with Heamasi Makasini falling through. Parramatta were keen on taking Makasini for one season in exchange for Addo-Carr, on the understanding the young centre would return to the Tigers for 2028. The deal fell over at the last minute after the Tigers decided they wouldn’t part with Makasini, but their interest in Addo-Carr remains. However, those chats will be put off until they get a definitive answer on Fogarty. In other signing news, South Sydney has shored up their coaching staff by extending Wayne Bennnett’s contract until the end of 2028. Assistant Ben Hornby has also been given a one-year extension, while Kangaroos assistant Ben Te’o has been signed for three years.



The seven-time premiership-winning coach will become the Rabbitohs’ second-longest serving coach at the end of this contract, with the scope to further extend his career beyond the 2028 season. Related Article NRL 2026 Gould receives medical attention after feeling faint at Langmack memorial “Wayne Bennett is still hungry for success and has the complete respect of everyone connected with the Rabbitohs organisation,” Rabbitohs chairman Nick Pappas said. “Wayne has proven results over an extended period of time and is able to extract the best out of his players. We are confident that he can lead the Rabbitohs to premiership success during his tenure. “Ben Hornby has done a tremendous job over the past seven seasons and has become one of the most sought-after young coaches in the game. Personally, I am delighted that Ben is extending his tenure with us as he is a key contributor to the coaching and management of our playing squad. “And last, but by no means least, I know that everyone at the club is delighted to be welcoming back Ben Te’o. Ben’s significant role in the club securing its 21st premiership in 2014 has been followed by an impressive start to his coaching career.”

Recently disendorsed Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann chased down a man he alleges defaced his corflutes in a video that shows them zigzagging across a football oval. Lindemann aggressively yells,“Is this democracy, mate?” as he chases the alleged offender across Robertson Reserve in Williamstown. Loading At numerous points the man attempts to change direction and get away from the candidate, but Lindemann follows him closely. “You’re shitting yourself, mate” Lindemann says in the video. “You’ve been caught mate. Vandalling [sic] my boards. What type of person are you?



“Did you put Nazi signs on my board? That’s a Commonwealth federal offence, mate. “Is it nice being caught … This is gonna go on everything you see, mate.” When contacted, Lindemann said he could not comment because it was a police matter. There is no specific offence for vandalising political signage, although normal laws around property damage still apply.



Lindemann is running as an independent after being disendorsed by the Liberal Party last week over comments he made about Indigenous Australians on a Facebook account named after his yacht. Police have been contacted for comment but were unable to verify the information without a specific date, which Lindemann did not provide. The date of the video is unknown, but in early November, 3AW’s Rumour File reported a frustrated candidate had chased someone defacing their signs. It has been circulating in group chats across Williamstown and surrounding areas as Lindemann has dug in and continued to campaign to unseat Labor MP Melissa Horne. Paul Lindemann has been posting on Facebook under an account called Biddy Hu Biddy Hu, named after his yacht.



The account was revealed by The Age and came a day after this masthead also reported he had been suspended for six weeks by Basketball Victoria because of his behaviour as a coach towards an under-14s female basketball player from an opposing team. Lindemann has been spotted handing out flyers at railway stations and on at early voting centres. Signs have also appeared around the electorate asking people to “Vote 1 Team Paul”. The signs don’t have the Victorian Liberal logos but are a similar shade of blue. A sign for Paul Lindemann, who is now running as an independent. On Wednesday, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson was asked about Lindemann’s decision to keep using the party’s traditional colour.



She did not say whether it was misleading or whether the party would ask for the signs to be taken down. “That’s a matter for his team. He’s not a candidate for Liberal Party,” Wilson said. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Liberals dump candidate over Indigenous slurs on secret Facebook account Williamstown is a heartland seat for Labor and was held by former premiers Joan Kirner and Steve Bracks during their time in parliament. Government minister Horne retained the seat four years ago with a two-party-preferred margin of 13.4 per cent.

World.title: ‘Ploughed into’: Driver fined after wife of top AFL executive struck on Brighton crossing
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD ‘Ploughed into’: Driver fined after wife of top AFL executive struck on Brighton crossing Fiona Byrne November 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Police have slapped a 63-year-old Beaumaris driver with a penalty infringement notice for failing to give way, after Felicity Harley, the wife of the AFL’s second in charge, Tom Harley, was left with a “head full of stitches, concussion, and lacerations” after being hit by a car while running with her two sons in bayside Melbourne. Harley, a journalist and podcaster, was hit by the four-wheel-drive driven by the man as she stepped onto a pedestrian crossing at Head Street, Brighton, about 11am on Sunday. Felicity Harley was hit by a car in Brighton on Sunday. Instagram/@felicityharley Miraculously, her children escaped serious injury as she copped the full impact. Harley revealed her ordeal on social media, describing the impact with the vehicle as being “ploughed into”.



“We stepped out on a pedestrian crossing, the green person luminescent, pinging away … when the car ploughed into my side,” she posted. “Thankfully, my body took the brunt, Hugo a little bruise, Jimmy screaming, ‘Oh Mum!’ “I have a head full of stitches, concussion, and lacerations and bruises down my legs – no broken bones or permanent injuries, thankfully. “Please stay aware when you drive. Runners, run aware.” Harley was taken by ambulance to The Alfred hospital. By Tuesday, she had returned home to continue resting and recovering.



Tom and Felicity Harley at the 2025 Brownlow Medal. AFL Photos “It is understood the pedestrian and two children were crossing Head Street when she was struck by a Jeep Grand Cherokee about 11.20am,” police told CBD in a statement. “The two children were not physically injured, while the pedestrian, a 50-year-old Brighton woman, was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. “The driver of the Jeep, a 63-year-old Beaumaris man, remained on scene. He was issued with a penalty infringement notice for failing to give way.” Harley gave a shout-out to passers-by, paramedics and the medical team who attended to her in the aftermath of the incident.



“This is a heartfelt thank you to all the people who stopped, kept me conscious, dabbed my blood – I don’t know who you are, but thank you,” she wrote. “To the two female paramedics, your calm & care is beyond. The doctors & nurses at the Alfred, thank you. And to the most special humans (my new home nurses) of them all: Tom, Jimmy, Hugo & Arabella. It could’ve been far worse. Life is precious. Humans are kind.” The Harley family put down roots in Brighton after moving from Sydney to Melbourne at the end of last year for Tom, a former captain of Geelong, take up the second-in-command gig behind Andrew Dillon at the AFL. He had previously been chief executive at the currently trouble-prone Sydney Swans for six years. Leaders meet their match



The Victorian election leaders’ debate on Tuesday bore more than a passing resemblance to the infamous Channel 9 “Jacketgate” drama, with Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson dressed in remarkably matchy-matchy outfits. Both politicians wore open-collar light-blue shirts under navy jackets. It was like a hive mind was working in their respective teams. Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson dressed in similar outfits at the televised leaders’ debate. We reached out to Toby Ralph, a marketer and market researcher who has worked on more than 50 elections globally, for his take on the sartorial choices of Carroll and Wilson and what message the looks conveyed. “Carroll dressed like he was there to reassure us, and Wilson dressed like she could replace him,” Ralph told us.



“They had both dressed for the same voter. Someone who wants a premier serious enough to run the state and patient enough to listen to them moan about a pothole. “Wilson wore Liberal blue. Carroll wore so much of it you would think he was trying to take the brand by stealth.” Just to recap, Jacketgate took place in 2017, when off-air footage of reporter Julie Snook and newsreader Amber Sherlock having an awkward conversation over them both wearing the same coloured top went viral, with one asking the other to put a jacket on. Sherlock’s concern was they would look too similar on air. Imagine, people on a televised debate dressing in similar outfits. While there was no spat over fashion on Tuesday between Wilson and Carroll, there were political barbs traded. Ex-Neighbour looks for a political role



Former Neighbours actor Nicola Charles is having another crack at politics, having thrown her hat into the ring as one of 11 candidates standing for the seat of Frankston. Former Neighbours actress Nicola Charles is standing for the seat of Frankston under her legal name Nicola Barry. Charles, who is running under her legal name of Nicola Barry (she was once married to Irish actor Jason Barry, who starred alongside Leonardo DiCaprio in the box office smash Titanic), is standing as an independent and has been fundraising on Give, Send, Go to raise money for her fliers, pamphlets and corflutes. While Charles made her name as a soap opera star on the very middle of the road Neighbours, she has in recent years taken a sharp-right detour, courted controversy online, railed against lockdown rules and vaccine mandates, and pushed wild conspiracy theories, including spreading a bizarre claim that the Voice to parliament referendum in 2023 was a plot by the UN to take control of Australia. The claim was labelled “absurd” by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.



In 2024, she flagged plans to run for the Senate under the Great Australian Party banner, which did not eventuate. In contesting the seat of Frankston this month, she is campaigning on a number of issues, including calling for “castle law” – the right for people to defend their property from attack. Nicola Charles in a scene with Alan Fletcher in the Australian soap opera Neighbours. Channel 10 Charles said her connection to Frankston went back to her Neighbours days, when she “used to do personal appearances there, often at the 21st Century Nightclub”. Her partner is also from the suburb. Harking back to her acting heyday, her campaign tag line is “When good neighbours become good MPs”.



Shuffles continue on city’s boards The changing of the guard on boards around town continues. Following on from the Victoria Racing Club and the Melbourne Cricket Club appointing new board chairs, the Melbourne Royal has announced Kate O’Sullivan’s appointment as the organisation’s president and chair. O’Sullivan, whose other board positions include the Essendon Football Club and the Moonee Valley Racing Club, as well as being chair of the Prahran Market, takes the reins after Matt Coleman stepped down at last month’s annual general meeting after 10 years in the role. Kate O’Sullivan is the new president and chair of the Melbourne Royal. Melbourne Royal is the body that runs the Royal Melbourne Show and the Melbourne showgrounds.



“I’m proud to be taking on the role of president of Melbourne Royal and look forward to continuing to work with the board, members, exhibitors and the broader agricultural community to maintain its strong legacy, whilst ensuring it continues to evolve and advance the industry and communities it serves,” O’Sullivan said. For what it is worth, O’Sullivan, who has been a member of the Melbourne Royal board since 2021, is the first woman to hold the role of president. World.title: Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWSelective schools Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots Christopher Harris November 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Selective school shopping will become harder for parents under a new policy that blocks private school students from being offered any last-minute vacancies which arise throughout year 7 or 8. The overhaul will prioritise entry for comprehensive public school pupils, in a bid to restore fairness to the fiercely competitive second-chance entry pathway, which last year saw 1100 pupils compete for just 10 spots in year 8. Students after sitting the selective school entry exam this year. Sitthixay Ditthavong It is the latest in a series of changes to selective school entry, which includes reserving 50 per cent of total places for girls, who are underrepresented in the academically elite institutions, and easier entry for certain disadvantaged students. Under current rules, families hoping to make a last-minute switch apply directly to the school, and the criteria can include external academic test results, school reports and extracurricular activities.



Related Article Education The winners and losers of Sydney’s new selective school gender quotas The changes in 2028 will remove direct entry for those grades entirely, with only comprehensive school students eligible and entry based on the results they received in the selective exam they sat in year 6. Students enrolled in a selective or partially selective school will be blocked from switching to another. Those entering year 7 in 2028 will be the first cohort subject to the changes, which will apply to enrolment places that open up between the second term of year 7 and the last term of year 8. A Department of Education spokesman said the new policy simplified year 8 entry and would build stronger links between gifted education in comprehensive and selective schools.



Australian Tutoring Association chief executive and UTS education lecturer, Mohan Dhall, said it was unfair and against the spirit of a public education to block prospective students because they happened to be attending a private school. “To me, that is actually discriminatory,” he said. “The public system says it caters for all. It means it is not closed to a citizen of NSW whose parents pay taxes from entering a public high school.” There are more selective high schools in NSW than in any other state. Oscar Colman He also criticised basing selection on test data dating back to year 6, which could be up to two years prior. “A kid who missed out in year 6 could, on merit, be academically stronger in year 7 and 8,” he said.



NSW has more selective high schools than any other state, with 17 fully selective, 27 partially selective and four fully selective agricultural high schools. Related Article Selective schools Ilia missed out on selective school – until he found another way in Students entering year 7 next year are the first cohort where the gender equity model will apply, which reserves 50 per cent of places for girls in co-ed schools. There will be an equal number of spots across the system in single-sex schools. Parents of boys have vented on online forums about the policy change. An online petition accused the government of undermining merit-based selection in favour of quota-based social engineering. “This policy represents direct discrimination against male students who work hard and achieve high test scores but will be denied places simply because of their gender,” the petition said. World.title: CFMEU’s former Big Build boss billed controversial labour firm $256,000
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaBig Build royal commission CFMEU’s former Big Build boss billed controversial labour firm $256,000 Clay Lucas November 18, 2026 — 7:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A controversial labour hire firm pushed onto state projects by the CFMEU has received invoices totalling $256,000 from the union’s former Big Build boss Joe Myles. BK Labour Hire, also paid a violent bikie $165,000 for consulting work that was never done, the Big Build royal commission heard on Wednesday as it probed how bikies and favoured firms won access to the multibillion-dollar taxpayer-funded infrastructure program. Witness Bernard Kearney (right) walks into the royal commission with his lawyer, construction industry barrister Jim Stavris, on Wednesday. Penny Stephens BK Labour Hire co-owner Bernard Kearney appeared before the commission and confirmed his company received a “succession” of consulting invoices from the CFMEU’s Myles – as the firm’s total profits surged past $24 million over the four years to 2025. The admissions capped a day of hearings in which royal commissioner Chris Kourakis warned Kearney, and Bandidos and former Rebels bikie Joel Leavitt, of potential legal consequences in the wake of their refusal to answer questions.



The inquiry also heard a major state contractor let Leavitt hand out taxpayer-funded jobs to his mates and paid an inflated $20,000 bill for free on-site souvlakis, from which Leavitt and another CFMEU delegate would pocket $5000 each. Leavitt, a former CFMEU health and safety representative, who arrived at Wednesday’s hearing admitting he was hungover, told the inquiry he used cocaine to “zone in” on safety paperwork, and conceded he may have skimmed thousands from the souvlaki catering rort. Bandidos and former Rebels bikie Joel Leavitt arrives at the Big Build royal commission on Wednesday. Penny Stephens Under questioning from counsel assisting Chris Carr, SC, Kearney confirmed BK Labour Hire – the firm which numerous witnesses have said was placed onto the $110 million Gap Road level crossing removal project after union pressure – received $256,000 in consulting invoices from Myles. Myles lost his senior CFMEU role in 2024 following The Age’s Building Bad investigation that year. Last week, witnesses told the inquiry that Myles demanded BK Labour Hire be appointed at Gap Road and boasted of a “direct line” to former premier Jacinta Allan’s office.





Leavitt had also earlier been warned that refusing to answer questions carried a two-year jail sentence. That warning came after Leavitt recited a memory-loss claim eight times in five minutes, and blamed trauma from being shot in the leg at a Rebels clubhouse in 2023. Loading “How do you think you would act if you’ve ever been shot?” Leavitt asked Kourakis at one point during this questioning. “Fortunately, I can’t answer that,” Kourakis said in response.



BK Labour Hire’s Kearney denied knowing of Leavitt’s outlaw motorcycle gang ties when he first employed him on a rail project in Hallam in 2021, claiming hiring deals were “done between the CFMEU and Laing O’Rourke” and saying: “I didn’t even know who he was.” The commission heard earlier this week that the union had campaigned for months to get Leavitt hired by Laing O’Rourke. Financial records tendered on Wednesday showed BK Labour Hire went from losing more than $300,000 each year in 2020 and 2021 to clearing more than $24 million in profit between 2022 and last year. By 2023, when Kearney and his business partners were considering selling their firm, accountants valued BK Labour Hire at $43.5 million.



Kourakis noted that after winning its first contract with Laing O’Rourke, in future tenders “you won every time” – a point Kearney accepted. “You’re charging more than the industry average and still winning almost every time. It’s pretty remarkable, isn’t it, Mr Kearney?” Carr said. Before Kearney took the stand, the commission heard how major contractor Acciona allowed Leavitt to hand out taxpayer-funded jobs to his associates on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade, and sought his permission before hiring workers. Text messages tendered by Carr showed Acciona site superintendent Tim Alford telling Leavitt: “I don’t care [about] bringing your mates on and putting them in spotting roles and finding homes, but they all need to do their jobs.”



In another exchange, Leavitt messaged Alford: “Hey Tim, can you send Cycon [Civil] a request for two people at Diamond Creek and one person for Alpington (sic)?” Cycon Civil is a labour hire and civil firm whose ties to the CFMEU and payments to underworld figure Mick Gatto have previously been reported by The Age. Carr also showed tendered as evidence a text message from a site superintendent seeking Leavitt’s permission to place onto a job a worker from Women in Construction – a firm run by a man convicted of domestic violence whose labour hire licence was revoked earlier this year. Other texts showed Leavitt promising work with Cycon Civil and labour hire firm OCC to a Rebels bikie named “Corbo”, and offering to have the bikie’s partner hired by Women in Construction. It prompted Carr to observe that Leavitt was running “an employment agency for Rebels and their partners”.



The commission also examined March 2023 texts between Leavitt and a fellow CFMEU safety delegate arranging a free souvlaki lunch for 600 Hurstbridge workers, with Leavitt writing: “So just make up a quote that hits 20k, and we will collect the other nine off the subbies”. Texts between bikie Joel Leavitt and Acciona’s Tim Allford. In a follow-up message, Leavitt wrote the pair would get “five each”, before sending a $20,000 invoice to Alford for a meal that a cash register receipt showed cost $9000. “Can I take it that you’re not surprised that you might have engaged in that conduct?” Kourakis asked. “I’ll accept that. I’m not surprised that I could of,” Leavitt replied.
