Cameron Bancroft says the entire Australian team knew he was using sandpaper to achieve reverse swing during the 2018 tour of South Africa, backing Usman Khawaja’s account of events and saying he felt betrayed and angered by Pat Cummins’ denials last week.

Bancroft, in a 4000-word piece released in The West Australian on Wednesday evening, said he failed to provide a “complete and truthful” account of events when investigated by Cricket Australia in 2018, withholding important details about when the use of sandpaper began, how long it continued, and the awareness of the rest of the travelling party.

Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images

“It was not just the three of us – Steve Smith, David Warner and I – who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team,” he wrote.

“I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.”

World.title: ‘I couldn’t walk’: The moment Rose Byrne knew she’d gone too far for her new thriller
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a point in every crime thriller when the puzzle pieces start to click together – new evidence is unearthed, new testimony is recorded, a new suspect appears and turns the case on its head. In each episode of new thriller The Good Daughter, each assembled piece reveals only more loose ones, widening the scope of an addictive and emotional story set in the American South until just about every resident of the town of Pikeville is in the crosshairs. At the heart of the story, adapted from legendary crime writer Karin Slaughter’s 2017 book, are sisters Samantha and Charlotte “Charlie” Quinn, played by Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy. As girls, they were raised by a sharp, cerebral mother as interested in Emily Dickinson as she was in studying the science of weather patterns. Editor's pick ★★★★

Review Is there a better villain on TV right now than David Tennant? Their father, Rusty, played by Brendan Gleeson, is the town’s notorious defence attorney and has a list of enemies a mile long for taking on cases without neat moral boundaries. He’s a larger-than-life figure, a kind of funhouse-mirror version of Atticus Finch who keeps the town – and his girls – in line with a dirty mouth and sly smile. “[Slaughter] has a richness of character and a detailed place in the American South,” says Byrne. “And she’s an absolute force to work with. It was interesting having the author on set because [she’s had] these characters for decades in her head.” Loading Fahy agrees. “Karin’s pretty unflinching,” she says. “She’s really not afraid to go anywhere with a character. And there’s not really any topic of conversation that she’s not willing to put under a microscope.”



She’s an expert at surprise, at building in twists and reveals and herrings of all colours in characters you care deeply about. “You really can’t get ahead of her plot-wise.” We meet the Quinns, in episode one’s opening flashback, on the day the violent ripples of their father’s work floods their doorstep. Rose Byrne plays Samantha Quinn, who returns home to help on a court case, in The Good Daughter. Thirty years after experiencing the town’s brutality first-hand, the sisters are splintered. While Sam is practising sterile and safe patent law in New York City, Charlie has stuck around in town to follow in their father’s footsteps, hauling teenagers in front of the judge to face their petty crimes, messing around on her estranged husband and knowing the rules just well enough to break them. Related Article Australian TV Another spiky and difficult female detective? That’s just the way Anna Samson likes it “I was involved with casting and we were so lucky to get Meghann, who brings such a lightness of touch to a character that is very tightly locked up and is hard to reach for the people around her – and the audience,” says Byrne, who served as an executive producer on the series. “Charlie is the heart and soul of this story.” After witnessing a school shooting, Charlie senses there’s more to the story than what Pikeville’s corrupt cops are telling the community – but she can’t argue the case alone. When her sister returns home, the layers of their personal history unravel alongside this complex new case.



The sisters are like magnets with opposing fields; they push at and test each other, denying the fact they’re fated to face the world and their shared trauma shoulder-to-shoulder. When one stays, the other runs. One sister deals with her pain by enforcing control over every element of her life, while the other attracts chaos. Meghann Fahy and Brendan Gleeson as Charlie and Rusty Quinn in The Good Daughter. The youngest of three sisters, Slaughter wove the specificities of a sisterly bond into every line of her book, and the series’ scripts – all of which she wrote. She also served as a showrunner and an executive producer. “Karin’s dialogue is so specific. It does a lot of the heavy lifting in terms of who the characters are,” says Fahy. “There’s a very particular way that Charlie speaks and there’s a very particular way that Sam speaks. When we were in scenes that were quite snappy and going back and forth, you do start to slip into the rhythm of these people because it’s so clearly there on the page.” Related Article Streaming The 10 best Rose Byrne performances to watch after her Golden Globes win For as much as Sam tries to plaster over her past, her scars are visible on the surface. The violence in her childhood left her disabled and walking with a limp, and affected her speech. Fresh off her Golden Globe win and Oscar nomination for last year’s If I Had Legs I’d Kick You, Byrne grabbed the opportunity with both hands – but might’ve accidentally gone a little too method.



“I worked with a PT trainer who works in rehab with people with injuries to establish [Sam’s] walk, and then with another person with dysarthria [to accurately portray] how she spoke,” says Byrne. “It had quite a consequence. I was in Melbourne on a holiday with my family and all of a sudden … my back seized up and I couldn’t walk and I had to lie down for two days. “I saw this osteopath, and they said, ‘What have you been doing?’ I said, ‘Well, I was playing a person with a limp. I did it every day for eight weeks.’” Rose Byrne (left) and Meghann Fahy arrive at the premiere of The Good Daughter in New York. AP Photo/Christopher Smith Turns out that’s the precise amount of physical adjustment it takes to fundamentally change how your body operates. Alongside Byrne and Slaughter, a largely female creative team brought The Good Daughter to life with care and thoughtfulness. Oscar-nominated Steph Green directed the entire series, which was also overseen by Australian super-producer Bruna Papandrea, co-founder of Reese Witherspoon’s production company, Pacific Standard. “It was a very sensitive topic we were covering and it felt like we were just in really great hands the whole time,” says Byrne, referring to the crew as an “incredible coven”. Her character, Sam, is in many ways a literary classic – the prodigal child returning home to face their family’s demons – and in others, an entirely modern invention. “It’s something we’ve seen countless times with men, but not as much with women,” says Byrne. “It felt very fresh in that sense that it was about a woman doing that.”

Jamal Fogarty could make an immediate switch to Wests Tigers as the joint-venture club prioritises the signature of the Manly halfback above that of Josh Addo-Carr. Fogarty is contracted to the Sea Eagles until the end of 2028, but has been given permission to leave early. The Sea Eagles are looking to free up salary cap space with Fogarty, Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor among the players the club is prepared to release early. Jamal Fogarty could be heading to Concord. Getty Images The Tigers believe Fogarty’s experience could be invaluable after the departure of Jarome Luai to Parramatta. Coach Benji Marshall has several playmaking options at his disposal, including Adam Doueihi, Latu Fainu, Javon Andrews and Jock Madden. However, Fogarty has been identified as the controlling No.7 the club requires to break a finals drought stretching back to 2011.



Any move is likely to be subsidised by Manly, who are trying to reshape their roster. The Sea Eagles have a surplus of halves with Fogarty, Brooks, Joey Walsh and Onitoni Large on their books. The northern beaches outfit recently released Blake Wilson to the Perth Bears, but are for more salary cap wiggle room. Fogarty – who has made 140 NRL appearances for the Titans, Raiders and Sea Eagles – isn’t the only player of interest to the Tigers. Out-of-favour Eel Addo-Carr could also be making the move to Concord, despite a player swap with Heamasi Makasini falling through. Parramatta were keen on taking Makasini for one season in exchange for Addo-Carr, on the understanding the young centre would return to the Tigers for 2028. The deal fell over at the last minute after the Tigers decided they wouldn’t part with Makasini, but their interest in Addo-Carr remains. However, those chats will be put off until they get a definitive answer on Fogarty. In other signing news, South Sydney has shored up their coaching staff by extending Wayne Bennnett’s contract until the end of 2028. Assistant Ben Hornby has also been given a one-year extension, while Kangaroos assistant Ben Te’o has been signed for three years.



The seven-time premiership-winning coach will become the Rabbitohs’ second-longest serving coach at the end of this contract, with the scope to further extend his career beyond the 2028 season. Related Article NRL 2026 Gould receives medical attention after feeling faint at Langmack memorial “Wayne Bennett is still hungry for success and has the complete respect of everyone connected with the Rabbitohs organisation,” Rabbitohs chairman Nick Pappas said. “Wayne has proven results over an extended period of time and is able to extract the best out of his players. We are confident that he can lead the Rabbitohs to premiership success during his tenure. “Ben Hornby has done a tremendous job over the past seven seasons and has become one of the most sought-after young coaches in the game. Personally, I am delighted that Ben is extending his tenure with us as he is a key contributor to the coaching and management of our playing squad. “And last, but by no means least, I know that everyone at the club is delighted to be welcoming back Ben Te’o. Ben’s significant role in the club securing its 21st premiership in 2014 has been followed by an impressive start to his coaching career.”

Recently disendorsed Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann chased down a man he alleges defaced his corflutes in a video that shows them zigzagging across a football oval. Lindemann aggressively yells,“Is this democracy, mate?” as he chases the alleged offender across Robertson Reserve in Williamstown. Loading At numerous points the man attempts to change direction and get away from the candidate, but Lindemann follows him closely. “You’re shitting yourself, mate” Lindemann says in the video. “You’ve been caught mate. Vandalling [sic] my boards. What type of person are you?



“Did you put Nazi signs on my board? That’s a Commonwealth federal offence, mate. “Is it nice being caught … This is gonna go on everything you see, mate.” When contacted, Lindemann said he could not comment because it was a police matter. There is no specific offence for vandalising political signage, although normal laws around property damage still apply.



Lindemann is running as an independent after being disendorsed by the Liberal Party last week over comments he made about Indigenous Australians on a Facebook account named after his yacht. Police have been contacted for comment but were unable to verify the information without a specific date, which Lindemann did not provide. The date of the video is unknown, but in early November, 3AW’s Rumour File reported a frustrated candidate had chased someone defacing their signs. It has been circulating in group chats across Williamstown and surrounding areas as Lindemann has dug in and continued to campaign to unseat Labor MP Melissa Horne. Paul Lindemann has been posting on Facebook under an account called Biddy Hu Biddy Hu, named after his yacht.



The account was revealed by The Age and came a day after this masthead also reported he had been suspended for six weeks by Basketball Victoria because of his behaviour as a coach towards an under-14s female basketball player from an opposing team. Lindemann has been spotted handing out flyers at railway stations and on at early voting centres. Signs have also appeared around the electorate asking people to “Vote 1 Team Paul”. The signs don’t have the Victorian Liberal logos but are a similar shade of blue. A sign for Paul Lindemann, who is now running as an independent. On Wednesday, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson was asked about Lindemann’s decision to keep using the party’s traditional colour.



She did not say whether it was misleading or whether the party would ask for the signs to be taken down. “That’s a matter for his team. He’s not a candidate for Liberal Party,” Wilson said. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Liberals dump candidate over Indigenous slurs on secret Facebook account Williamstown is a heartland seat for Labor and was held by former premiers Joan Kirner and Steve Bracks during their time in parliament. Government minister Horne retained the seat four years ago with a two-party-preferred margin of 13.4 per cent.

World.title: When will house prices stop falling?
World.content:
Economic forecasters all agree that house prices should start to rise again at some point next year.

But first they'll have to stop falling.

Cotality said prices fell 0.4 percent in October, their seventh consecutive monthly fall.

Gareth Kiernan, chief forecaster at Infometrics, said it was likely that house values would not level off on a month-on-month basis until the second quarter of next year.

But it could be even later than that.

"That forecast is a bit of an act of faith at the moment, and it relies on a sustained fall in fuel prices into the US$80 to $90 a barrel range, improvements in employment growth, and clarity on what the peak in interest rates is.

"From a more pragmatic point of view, stock levels are high, particularly in Auckland and - to a lesser extent - Canterbury, so until that stock of available homes is reduced and there is more competition between buyers, prices will continue to come under downward pressure.

"On that basis, I'd say there's a risk that price falls continue for longer - both in terms of supply remaining elevated, meaning stock takes a long time to work through, as well as weak buyer numbers because broader macroeconomic conditions remain unfavourable for longer."

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said his forecasts were for an increase in values early in the new year but he said the most recent momentum was not encouraging. Sales fell by about a third in October, according to the most recent Real Estate Institute update.

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Economist Shamubeel Eaqub described that fall as "extraordinary" and said it was noticeable that the drop in activity was spread across the country. He said house sales were a good barometer of the domestic economy.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said the seven monthly falls were not seasonally adjusted and it was normal for prices to fall in winter.

"As we get the November, December, January numbers, they might start to take up a little bit on a monthly basis … So, that is in the back of my mind. But even if you take that away and look on an annual basis, nationally we're still down 2.3 percent on the latest numbers anyway. For me, that's probably the measure to focus on."

He said the annual change could turn positive in about March or April next year but prices might drift lower for the next few months, as the country navigated economic uncertainty and rising interest rates, as well as stubbornly high unemployment.

"It does feel as if it's going to be more of the same for the next little while at least."

He said it was likely to be the second or third quarter of next year before an upturn became evident.

"There's an element as well of we're talking about a national average, but nobody buys the national average… in the past 12 months in Christchurch, for example, values are up 3 percent, Invercargill's up 4 percent. But if you look purely at the national average, Auckland is a big part of that and Auckland is down 4 percent year-on-year."

With growing supply in Auckland and a patchy economic recovery, the next three months was likely to be subdued for the property market in the biggest city, he said.

"The national figure will probably stay pretty subdued as well. And then you think about Wellington too, the governmental uncertainty that will end at some point and maybe you can argue if we swap sides and we go to the left bloc, it might give a bit of confidence to the Wellington market … if we stick with what we've got now, it's hard to see Wellington recovering particularly quickly either, and that comprises a reasonably large share of the national average too."

But he said the economy was recovering and things would slowly pick up.

"In plain English, it's sort of like, don't expect it straight away. It won't happen overnight, but it will happen. But it does feel like it's more of a story for next year, and even when it does happen, there's a growing acceptance that, you know, the next recovery will be pretty lacklustre too, with more housing supply, with possible tax changes, with DTIs…

'When values do start to turn around, it might not be exactly racing away."

World.title: Threat of strong, unusual currents after tsunami activity has passed, NEMA says
World.content:
A tsunami advisory issued on Wednesday afternoon has been cancelled after strong currents were picked up on tidal gauges at Napier and Gisborne, but with no sign of an earthquake.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) issued an advisory about 5.40pm, saying strong currents and unpredictable surges at the shore could be expected in coastal areas on the East Coast of the North Island.

No evacuations took place and the advisory was cancelled 15 minutes later.

In its initial advisory, NEMA said it didn't know what had caused the alert, but said it was possible there had been an underwater landslide.

NEMA deputy chief executive John Price said there was no current threat to New Zealand's shoreline.

He said surges of up to 60cm on tidal gauges earlier on Wednesday evening triggered a notification to the agency, and the activation of the tsunami expert panel in addition to an advisory to civil defence partners that urged people in or near the East Coast shore to leave.

Scientists on the panel had since concluded the threat had passed, Price said, but something had happened.

"There has been no indication that there was an earthquake, but something has occurred that has fluctuated the tidal gauges on the East Coast, predominantly Hawke's Bay and Tai Rāwhiti, Gisborne."

He said Earth Sciences New Zealand was working to find out what was behind the waves, suggesting an underwater landslide or changes in the weather could be responsible.

Price said no mobile or public alert was sent out, with only emergency services, emergency management and civil defence partners receiving the "precautionary alert".

"One of the things is you don't want to activate the public where you don't need to, but we needed to make sure we were doing all the due diligence to ensure we could investigate what was happening.

"It's better to be precautionary and preventative than wait too early for a response."

RNZ is New Zealand's statutory civil defence lifeline radio broadcaster, providing vital information and updates as they come to hand. All frequencies can be found here.

World.title: Autism expert condemns school over boy allegedly forced to empty clogged toilet bare-handed
World.content:
Correction: Autism NZ received over 3500 enquiries in the year to 30 June 2026 not 35,000 as the copy originally stated.

An autism expert says a seven-year-old allegedly being forced to empty the contents of a clogged Bay of Plenty school toilet into a bucket without gloves is tantamount to child abuse.

Megan* said her son, who was on a waiting list for further formal autism and ADHD evaluation, was also made to wait with his nose against the wall for hours as "punishment" for clogging the toilet.

Autism NZ spokesperson Kirsty Whalen-Stickley said what the mother said her son was subjected to was "completely unacceptable".

"It constitutes abuse and is not helpful for any child, regardless of what needs they may have. To put a vulnerable child in that position is horrific. I haven't heard something quite that awful in a very long time."

After the incident at Paengaroa School last Thursday, the boy's parents removed him and his older brother from the school.

But she wanted a public apology and for the school's principal and the staff member involved to be stood down.

"If [the principal] had just been accountable and actually made [the staff member] apologise to my child, we would have left the school quietly and happily."

It had been over one year since Megan was first told her son Elijah* presented with several features suggestive of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He was on a waiting list and had not received a formal diagnosis.

She said that as a young parent, she felt unsupported advocating for her son.

She left her most recent parent-teacher conference in tears, and she had not been to one since.

"I left crying because of the way they spoke about my son. I understood their concerns, but it was harsh. Not one positive thing was said about him.

"As a mother, it's heartbreaking to listen to someone speak about your child that way. If you met my son, he has the biggest heart. He will go out of his way to help anyone."

Kiwi stand-down

She said this year, Paengaroa School provided Elijah with a teacher aide.

"She has been amazing, helping him to have more confidence and with socialising. She has made him more open to learning, and she's made him enjoy going to school. I cannot thank this woman enough. She has a beautiful soul. She has helped him in every aspect possible."

But she said even with a diagnosis, Elijah would not qualify for government funding.

That meant the aide was not with him in the classroom all the time, and Megan said she would often be asked to collect her son during the school day, when the aide was not there.

"At least every fortnight I'd have a phone call. They would tell me he's sick, he's tired, he needs to come home. I'd get him home, and there'd be nothing wrong with him, and he'd say, 'Mum, they just said I was being too much today, so they sent me to the office'."

Whalen-Stickley said that situation was so common there was a name for it.

"The colloquial term that gets tossed around is a Kiwi stand-down, and it's the idea that the child hasn't been formally stood down or excluded from a class but is regularly being excluded because the parents are being asked to pick them up.

"Every child has the right to access education, and if that is happening on a regular basis, it should be escalated to the Ministry of Education because it is common practice, but it is not acceptable practice. It is illegal."

Megan said she had offered to help pay for her son to have an aide and wished the school had communicated with her more about what was happening in the classroom.

Whalen-Stickley said educators were generally trying their best.

She said even schools with students with the highest, most severe learning and disability needs, who qualified for learning support under the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme, struggled.

"Teacher aide funding is very limited, and we hear regularly from teachers that they desperately need more support in the classroom.

"It's very difficult funding to get, and even students who do have teacher aide funding, often schools and teachers are having to make decisions to distribute that teacher aide time across the many kids who need support rather than being able to dedicate that time to the individual child who's actually funded to have the teacher aide because there's just so much need."

More funding needed

She said a government-funded programme Autism NZ used to run, Tilting the Seesaw, allowed teachers, parents, and other school staff to make a plan for a child who needed extra support in school.

"They didn't have to have a diagnosis in order to access that programme, and it was incredibly positive and successful, but unfortunately the funding for that programme has been cut.

"We're looking at providing alternative programmes that are similar so that teachers are getting the resources, strategies, and support they need and not having to have a diagnosis, as a threshold for access is super important."

Whalen-Stickley said wait times varied between regions, but it could take anywhere from just a few months to years to get an autism diagnosis.

"There's a huge demand for diagnosis, and the current services are generally not meeting that demand.

"Some people pursue a diagnosis privately, but the costs can be very high, into the thousands of dollars, so it's really not achievable for a lot of people and a lot of families."

She said they had to stop adding people to the wait list for Autism NZ's own Wellington-based diagnosis clinic because they were too overwhelmed.

She said Autism NZ received over 3500 enquiries in the year to 30 June 2026, relating to requests for support and information about getting a diagnosis.

"In New Zealand we have a bit of an ambulance at the bottom of the cliff approach to support. That is starting to change with more early intervention programmes like our Early-Years Support Pathway, which was funded by the Social Investment Agency, which is great, but it's very limited in one specific area.

"If we're constantly supporting children, adults, and families after they've experienced crisis, we're not putting the support in the right place, and we need to get the right support at the right time before someone reaches crisis point."

She said more funding was needed to support children like Elijah.

"In this instance, it seems like what has happened is the lack of support is going to lead to further trauma and far more challenges for the student and the family, which is just really sad. "

Health NZ acknowledges frustrations

In a statement to RNZ, Health NZ national chief mental health and addiction Leeanne Fisher acknowledged Megan's and Autism NZ's frustrations.

"Demand for ADHD and autism assessment and support has increased substantially, and we recognise this is putting pressure on services and contributing to long waits in some areas. We are continuing to work on ways to improve access and make the best use of available resources, including strengthening referral pathways and working across primary, specialist, and community services.

"Addressing this increased demand requires sustained investment and a coordinated response across health, education, and community services, alongside work to make the best use of existing specialist capacity."

She said families did not need to wait for a diagnosis before seeking support from their GP, school, or early childhood provider.

"Support can involve health, education, and community services, recognising that children referred for neurodevelopmental concerns often have a range of overlapping needs."

Ministry investing in specialised support

Ministry of Education learning support deputy secretary Bridget White said it has been investing in specialist support, including increasing the number of hours teacher aides spend in schools.

"We acknowledge that families' experiences of accessing support can vary and are committed to improving the responsiveness and capacity of the learning support system.

"We are continuing to strengthen the learning support system to ensure children receive help as early as possible and that transitions from early learning to school are well supported. Budget 2025 included significant investment in learning support across the education system. This investment includes additional specialist roles, increased teacher aide hours being phased into schools, and further investment in specialist services to better support learners, schools and whānau. Many of these initiatives began from the start of the 2026 school year and will continue to be expanded over the coming years.

"From 2027, the Ministry will also fund professional learning and development for teacher aides and other support staff working with neurodiverse learners, focused on inclusive practice and strengthening learning environments that support ākonga participation, belonging and learning."

On Kiwi stand-downs, White iterated that schools could not exclude students or send them home early on the basis of their disability.

"When the Ministry becomes aware of a barrier to enrolment or attendance, we work with students, their parents and whānau, and schools to return students to regular attendance as soon as possible. Through this work, the Ministry does not investigate whether the student has a disability specifically, but responds to the learning support needs of the student."

She said if complaints were not resolved by the school, they could be made to the Ministry of Education and then the Ombudsman.

But Megan said she was speaking out in the hope that no other child had the same experience as her son.

Paengaroa School and the Ministry of Education both said they were investigating "concerns raised", but could not comment further while the investigation was ongoing.

World.title: US Ambassador Jared Novelly labels Auckland mayor Wayne Brown a 'boomer'
World.content:
Audio player for " US Ambassador to NZ lashes out at Auckland mayor " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/world/2661871%2Fus-ambassador-jared-novelly-labels-auckland-mayor-wayne-brown-a-boomer

US Ambassador to NZ lashes out at Auckland mayor Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

The US Ambassador to New Zealand has suggested Auckland's mayor is too close to the Chinese government.

On Wednesday afternoon Jared Novelly took to social media to label Wayne Brown a "boomer" and question his intelligence after Brown declared "democracy's had its day".

Brown returned from a trip to communist China remarking about the country's economic growth, saying it's time for something other than democracy.

"It's an unfathomable system… and look at the election in America… produced a sort of non-working government. Europe hasn't had a good election for years," he told Stuff.

Brown told Morning Report New Zealand's election result also exposed democracy's problems.

He said he was not pushing for the adoption of China's Communist system but "it would be nice to have the results of China".

US Ambassador Jared Novelly blasted Brown via social media. (His post is copied in full below).

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown. (File photo) RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Novelly went further in an interview with Checkpoint's Lisa Owen, saying Brown's relationship with China was troubling.

He said it seemed Brown had been "captured" by the Chinese during his trip there: "where they approach people in positions of political power, and they can't win the hearts and minds of the people, but they can win the hearts and minds of a person."

Novelly said he would welcome a discussion with Brown to present some alternative viewpoints.

"But you know, it might be tough to get through the red flag on his door."

Brown's comments that New Zealand should sell its Five Eyes seat to Japan were "egregious and insulting", Novelly said, adding that the mayor should apologise to all Five Eyes partners.

"He probably needs to apologise to the Age of Enlightenment as well."

He said the intelligence alliance comprising New Zealand, the US, Australia, Canada, and the UK was sacred, and Brown's comments showed he was unaware of its importance.

"I would hope that those who are in the know would pull him aside, kind of quietly, and correct him on what's really happening and what a Five Eyes partner means."

Novelly acknowledged China was an important business partner for both the US and New Zealand, but warned China was dangerous in certain circumstances.

"You should know who's on the other side of those tables, and an intelligence briefing really would do the mayor good."

Novelly also celebrated that New Zealand and the US had recently gone to the polls, and noted the difference between a regime like China's, and an administration.

"Administrations change, and we as the electorate have a capability of changing those administrations, and that's not the case in a regime," he said.

"Maybe the mayor's looking to establish a regime in Auckland for himself, but there is certainly a benefit from different viewpoints, and those viewpoints can change over time."

The ambassador hoped Brown's comments were a flash in the plan.

"In America we've had mayors of major cities get caught smoking crack before too, so you know, maybe that's what he did."

Brown's office said the mayor will not comment on the ambassador's criticism of his statement about democracy.

'Ok, Boomer!' - US Ambassador Jared Novelly

Here's Novelly's social media post in full.

"Ok, Boomer! @mayor.auckland Wayne Brown.

"I suppose New Zealand government requires a minimum level of intelligence to receive an intelligence briefing; it's obvious from his statements the mayor hasn't made the cut.

"Sure, democracy can be messy, slow, and frustrating. So can Auckland traffic. But no one would recommend getting rid of the traffic lights.

"The United States and New Zealand didn't build two successful democracies by deciding that giving people a say was too much trouble.

"Economic growth matters. So do freedom, accountability, and the right to vote your leaders out.

World.title: Xero remains tight-lipped over cuts to New Zealand and Australian jobs
World.content:
Software accounting firm Xero is refusing to answer questions about whether it is cutting its New Zealand and Australian workforces.

The NZ Herald reported an insider saying New Zealand software engineers and some Australian staff had been called into a meeting on Wednesday.

It said the affected staff would be given an option to reapply for a reduced number of roles or "receive an opt-out package".

Xero remained tight-lipped in response to RNZ's requests and said it would not comment on "individual employees or internal processes".

"Xero evolves the structure of its global teams, as needed, to best support our customers, business needs and strategy. We share any proposed changes through the appropriate internal channels and operate in compliance with our legal obligations," the spokesperson said.

A former Xero employee, who was made redundant three years ago, told RNZ the company had moved executive roles offshore and to the United States after San Francisco based chief executive Sukhinder Singh Cassidy took over the role at the beginning of 2023.

Soon after Singh Cassidy's appointment the New Zealand founded company said it would be slashing about 800 roles from its 4500 global staff.

"The first round of cuts helped to 'right size' the business and make them look good on paper," he said.

"More and more they are extending into areas where they want to encourage growth. They have kind of topped out in New Zealand whereas the States and UK give them the opportunity to expand more".

He said in addition to relocating functions and roles to new more cost effective locations, the firm was looking to embrace AI as a part of a strategy "to create opportunities for further efficiencies in workflow".

"Which in everyday language would mean fewer people and therefore lower costs across the business," he said.

According to the company's interim report, released last Tuesday, Xero's profit for the half year ending September fell to $18.6 million, a $116.2 mil drop from profits posted for the same time the previous year.

The report attributed most of the drop to the incorporation of payments platform Melio, which currently ran at a loss, and the absence of large foreign exchange gains on term deposits that were realised in the prior year.

World.title: 'Many flags, one umbrella': How rugby league is bringing communities together
World.content:
"Our culture is forever."

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.

Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408527133112

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.

The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

Geoffery Matautia / Southsides

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.

"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.

"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."

Josh Thomas / Flicksbyjosh / Wahs Fits

Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.

It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'

"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."

Geoffery Matautia / Southsides

But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.

Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.

Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.

Josh Thomas / Flicksbyjosh / Wahs Fits

And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.

"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.

"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."

"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

Geoffery Matautia / Southsides

Williams hopes the celebrations also challenge the assumption that seeing people convoy with Māori flags means a protest is underway.

"That's been really awesome to celebrate as a people carrying that flag. And I hope it changed the mindset of the public as well to those who check out the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and go, oh, are they protesting?

"It's like, no, we're celebrating ... we're not always fighting with this flag. And so I love that we can now use it for celebration and not just for progression forward."

Williams said one of the most memorable moments came during the final, when supporters from different Pacific nations came together under a shared identity as people of Aotearoa.

"It was a real different vibe. It was something I'd never seen before. So it was all these flags now coming together ... We represent these islands, but now we represent, where we are from, here, Aotearoa. And we're all on board this one waka, many flags, and it really blew me away."

Geoffery Matautia / Southsides

Lefaoali'i associate professor Dion Enari (Sāmoa), whose research explores sport as a space for Indigenous cultural reclamation, told RNZ that sport provides an important platform for Māori and Pacific communities to express their languages and cultures.

"Sport really is a space for us to navigate and negotiate and platform our languages and our cultures. So, yes, sport is a massive vehicle for us to do so."

Enari said this is particularly important for generations of Māori and Pacific people born and raised in the diaspora, who can use sporting spaces to reconnect with their cultural identity.

He said athletes carry their communities and cultural identities with them, both on and off the field.

"It's a very strong message to mainstream society that our athletes will come with their communities and our athletes won't leave their culture at the door. Our athletes won't leave their culture at the locker room."

"They will embody their culture in all of the glory that comes with it, going onto the rugby field, going off the rugby field, preparing before the game and well after the game is finished being played."

Josh Thomas / Flicksbyjosh / Wahs Fits

Williams said the connection between culture and sport is something that exists long after the tournament.

"We live and breathe our culture before, during, after the Rugby League World Cup, and we're forever winning."

"It's not like, OK, all of a sudden I'm going to put on my culture hat during the Rugby League World Cup and be all cultural. No, we live and breathe our culture before, during, after the Rugby League World Cup, and we're forever winning."

"It's not like, oh, we're going to lose because we lost the game. Heck no. No way, because our culture is not dependent on winning sports. It's not even in the same kōrero."

Geoffery Matautia / Southsides

Williams said that of course winning sports is great.

World.title: Zuru quizzed over size of Lego wording on boxes
World.content:
Lawyers for Zuru say the toy company's use of the Lego trademark on packaging is to compare two brands, rather than make shoppers think they're buying Lego.

It's the second day of Lego's appeal of a 2025 Court of Appeal decision, which said Zuru - owned by New Zealand rich-listers Mat and Nick Mowbray - hadn't infringed the global toy giant's trademark on a box of toy bricks.

The heart of the dispute centres on a simple phrase that had been printed on packaging of Zuru's Max Build More brick building kits: "LEGO® BRICK COMPATIBLE".

Zuru's lawyer Julian Miles KC told the Supreme Court that Zuru was using comparative advertising, rather than telling consumers this was a Lego product.

"It is literally just a comparison of the two marks, and can never be a suggestion that when they open up a Max box... they are expecting it to be Lego, which is where a classic trademark infringement would occur."

Miles said that Parliament had permitted comparative advertising when it passed the Trade Marks Act in 2002, which has a section allowing the use of a registered trademark, so long as the ad follows honest commercial practices, and does not take unfair advantage of, or damage the brand's reputation.

Miles said comparative advertising "worked for the consumer".

"So long as the advertising is accurate, so long as it's passing on information that is valuable and helpful to the consumer, that is what comparative advertising is all about."

He referred to the Court of Appeal's decision in his arguments, including that the use of the phrase, "LEGO BRICK COMPATIBLE", was descriptive.

Lego was being used as an adjective in the phrase, Miles said, and was describing the type of brick.

One of Lego's key arguments in court on Tuesday was that Zuru was leveraging Lego's brand by using its trademark on packaging, boosting Zuru's own reputation in the process and undermining the integrity of Lego's brand.

Chief Justice Helen Winkelmann questioned Miles on the way the Lego comparison had been written in large letters on the box.

"You could just have a situation in plain black text, this is compatible with - a list of products it's compatible with - and that doesn't look like it's use of a trademark, it just looks like it's a piece of information being provided."

Zuru co-owner Nick Mowbray. Supplied / Zuru

Justice Neil Campbell said it wasn't that Zuru couldn't mention Lego anywhere, but that the brand name was "four times bigger" than information underneath, and would be the first thing a shopper sees.

Miles said Zuru was factually stating the toy bricks worked with Lego, when other brands didn't - the sentence didn't erode the distinctiveness of Lego's brand or dent its reputation.

This case has made its way through all of the lower courts over a number of years.

Following objections by Lego to Zuru's initial use in 2018, Zuru brought a case to the High Court in 2021 to keep using the phrase 'LEGO BRICK COMPATIBLE' on its packaging.

In 2023, the High Court agreed Zuru had infringed Lego's trademark, whereas the Court of Appeal ruled that it hadn't.

World.title: Memorial garden unveiled for patients who died at Lake Alice
World.content:
Audio player for " Memorial garden unveiled for patients who died at Lake Alice " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/community/2664333%2Fmemorial-garden-unveiled-for-patients-who-died-at-lake-alice

Memorial garden unveiled for patients who died at Lake Alice Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

As rain fell over Whanganui, several dozen people gathered to remember the lives of 12 people who died while patients at the former psychiatric hospital, Lake Alice.

The 12 are buried in unmarked graves at Aramoho Cemetery and the Whanganui District Council has on Wednesday unveiled a memorial garden and seat there in their memory.

It's now accepted that young people were tortured at Lake Alice's child and adolescent unit in the 1970s. The adult section of the hospital operated for far longer, closing in 1999 after almost 50 years.

As the rain relentlessly beat down on the sea of umbrellas shrouding the unveiling, Peter Manins reflected on why he made the long journey from Dunedin - to remember his "dear uncle" Frank Ginn.

"My uncle was a dearly loved youngest brother of my mother and her sisters and brothers. They were five, and Frank was the youngest of them.

"When he was in his early 20s, I think, he was committed to Lake Alice hospital."

The family thought he was treated okay, although they'd later heard about questionable practices there.

"As a boy of about the age of 10 and 11 I remember travelling here from Wellington, where my family lived," Manins said.

"We would visit uncle Frank and sometimes in the school holidays my mother and father would come up here and we would pick him up. My parents were teachers, so we had the school holidays off.

"Uncle Frank would come and stay home with us in Wellington for a week or two. He was always happy to go back."

Sarah Carson and Sally Anderon remember former Lake Alice patient Fred Emerson. Jimmy Ellingham

Sally Anderson was also paying her respects to a family member - her uncle Fred Emerson, who she thought died in the 1980s.

"As a family we're really surprised that he was in an unmarked grave and thought it was important we came today to recognise that and the other people who were in the same situation."

Anderson has fond childhood memories of her uncle Fred.

"He used to do a lot of wood crafts and stuff like that. He lived with his parents and when we went and stayed with them he let us help with that. He was quite a caring person."

Robyn Dandy is a survivor of the child and adolescent unit, as was her late brother, Michael. She's thankful the council's created a memorial.

"It honestly feels to me like there is now some sort of peace for them, hopefully, but it's just like they were planted in the place. It feels like it was a horrible thing to do to them."

Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe stands next to the memorial seat. Jimmy Ellingham

Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe is researching the 12 people's histories. He said they deserved to be remembered as individuals, and a seat was an appropriate memorial because it allowed people to sit and contemplate.

"It's doing the right thing for those who couldn't speak for themselves. The council and my role as mayor - we're custodians of the Aramoho Cemetery, and there are people here who have unmarked graves.

"They have an identity and they deserve dignity and respect."

Council parks team leader Lynn Te Ngahue and her team led the 30 people who attended the unveiling on a walk around the cemetery to lay flowers at the 12 unmarked graves.

"It's been quite profound for me. I had very little to do with Lake Alice in my lifetime and to understand what went on there and the recognition and the healing that's required has been really significant for myself and my team," she said.

The only trace of the Lake Alice hospital, near Bulls and Marton, about 30 minutes away from Whanganui, is an old water tower, and a memorial there installed earlier this year.

The Whanganui District Council received money for its memorial from the government's survivor support and recognition fund, set up on the recommendation of the Royal Commission into abuse in care.

World.title: Breaking: Bancroft says 'whole team' knew about sandpaper in explosive claims
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft claims the entire Australian team knew about their 2018 sandpaper plot, in an explosive article that will cast another dark cloud over the Test team.

Bancroft, who was banned with Steve Smith and David Warner over the tactic, said the entire team knew about the plan despite claims from current Test skipper Pat Cummins to the contrary.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in an article for the West Australian.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference."

Loading

World.title: Sandpapergate coach has 'nothing to hide' after forum announced
World.content:
Former Australian Test coach Darren Lehmann, who led the side during the Sandpapergate incident in 2018, has said he has "nothing to hide" after a new forum into the saga was announced.

Cricket Australia on Wednesday announced a voluntary forum for players and staff involved in the Test match at Cape Town, where Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, to discuss their recollection and perspective of the incident.

Warner wants Sandpapergate 'public inquiry' as CA announces safe-space forum Cricket Australia has announced a new forum for players and staff to discuss the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, but whether it will achieve anything has already been questioned.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were suspended for their roles in the ball-tampering, but the saga was thrust back into the spotlight last week following the release of Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr.

In the book, Khawaja says he knew the ball-tampering was happening, while former player Chadd Sayers has since claimed he believes everyone knew.

Australia's bowling unit has consistently denied they knew about sandpaper being used on the ball.

Lehmann, who has also denied knowing about the ball-tampering plot, has said he supports Cricket Australia's forum.

Darren Lehmann says he will be happy to be part of Cricket Australia's Sandpapergate forum. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Asked if he would be happy to participate while on the ABC Sport broadcast of Australia's third ODI against England, Lehmann said: "Yeah [I would speak to them], I've got nothing to hide."

"I think this gives everyone who didn't get a chance to speak [a chance now].



"It gives everyone a bit of clarity for the Cricket Australia board to make a decision from there [once people are heard]. I think it's a good thing."

The reaction to Khawaja's chapter about Sandpapergate has led to a turbulent fortnight for Australian cricket.

In the book, Khawaja said the whole team should have taken responsibility for the incident and the brunt of punishment should not have been put on Bancroft, Smith and Warner.

Khawaja said he knew the ball-tampering was happening, and even told Bancroft to be careful.

Since the book's release, there has been a frenzy over who knew what and whether the entire team knew of the ball-tampering.

Warner said the claims detailed in Khawaja's book are "100 per cent accurate", and has accused Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation as "botched".

Former Test player Chadd Sayers, who was in the 2018 touring squad, says 'everyone knew' about the use of sandpaper.

Loading...

Current Test captain Pat Cummins held a 70-minute press conference in the wake of the book release, repeating the bowlers' stance that they knew nothing of the ball-tampering, and said his friend had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, said the announcement of a forum by Cricket Australia let him "see some light at the end of the tunnel".

"I haven't been great [for me since the topic re-emerged]," he said.

"People close to me know that. It happened in 2018, it's a long time ago.

"[I] went through health troubles then, and a triple bypass; mentally I wasn't great either.

"The last couple of weeks have been tough, but that's for everyone involved."

World.title: Thieves steal 1948 Caulfield Cup from Caulfield Racecourse
World.content:
Thieves have smashed their way into Caulfield Racecourse and stolen the 1948 Caulfield Cup.

That theft is believed to be one in a string of break-ins at the track during Melbourne's Spring Racing carnival.

Victoria Police confirmed this afternoon that an alleged offender or offenders entered the Caulfield premises on four occasions between November 4 and 11.

Red Fury won the 1948 Caulfield Cup. (Supplied)

"Alcohol and trophies, including the Caulfield Cup, were allegedly stolen during the course of offending," the police spokeswoman said.

"A 39-year-old was arrested at a residence on Orrong Road in Elsternwick on 16 November.

"He was charged with attempted burglary and possess drug of dependence (methylamphetamine)."

The police spokeswoman said the Elsternwick man was charged and bailed to attend Moorabbin Magistrates Court on March 1 next year.

A broken display at Flemington Racecourse where three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva were stolen on November 16. (ABC News)

It comes after another brazen heist at Flemington this week, where thieves disguised as construction workers stole three Melbourne Cups won consecutively by legendary mare Makybe Diva in 2003, 2004 and 2005.

"Detectives are investigating if (the Caulfield Cup) incident is linked to the theft of the three Melbourne Cup trophies on 16 November," the police spokeswoman said.

A Melbourne Racing Club spokesman said the cup was stolen along with some bottles of wine and some other "low-value" items.

"The club has been requested by Victoria Police not to speak to the media during the investigation," a MRC spokesman said.

"As this is an active police investigation, the Club can make no further comment at this stage."

It is understood the 1948 Caulfield Cup, won by then five-year-old Australian thoroughbred Red Fury, had been kept in a secure area of the racecourse off-limits to the public.

The cup, worth $55,000, was sold in March and was on loan to the MRC during this year's racing festivities.

Victoria Police has been contacted for comment.

The 2026 theft is not the first time the cup has been stolen.

A painting of Red Fury with jockey William Briscoe with the Caulfield Racecourse grandstand in the background. (Supplied: Leski Auctions)

Three men were committed for trial over the theft of the same 1948 cup, less than two years after Red Fury's racetrack success.

In 1950, The Argus newspaper reported that the cup was stolen from the now-defunct Ress-Astoria Hotel in central Melbourne when it had a value of 200 pounds (about $15,500 in 2026, adjusted for inflation).

One of the men accused of the theft was later acquitted.

World.title: 'Why are they selling pies?' What surprised O'Connell about AFL footy
World.content:
When Irish AFLW import Siofra O'Connell arrived in Australia, she wasn't entirely sure what to expect.

She had watched AFL games on TV, time zone permitting, and braced herself for the transition from limited-contact Gaelic football to the heavy contact of Australian Rules.

"I was like, 'This is chaos,'" O'Connell told ABC Sport, who signed for Carlton in December 2024. "It's been a learning curve."

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

But then all the quirks and traditions came along with the more than 130-year-old sport.

"I was like, 'Why are they selling pies at a game?' O'Connell laughed. "That was very eye-opening … The chicken and chips is a big one.

"And even the fact that there's alcohol on the ground. You're only allowed it outside the stadium (in Ireland). You can't bring it to your seat.

"So when I went to my first AFL game, and people were a bit tipsy beside me, I didn't know what was going on."

Siofra O'Connell was surprised by the food choices at AFL games. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Media)

Just how much Melbourne is "an AFL city" also took O'Connell by surprise.

"You start getting used to that as well, in a way, because it's on the TV every night of the week almost, and from March to November," she said.

And playing at a big Victorian club like Carlton inevitably puts you in the headlines.

"I work one day a week in the club shop … and that opened my eyes to the supporters and the fan base, and how big the club is," she said.

"You can appreciate it a lot more when it's post-game, and you're engaging with the fans … I'm so not used to all the numbers and spectators. So, it's just amazing to hear a crowd."

Carlton beat Hawthorn in the semifinal to send them to a preliminary final match-up with Melbourne. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

There was a crowd of over 5,000 for the Blues' qualifying final against North Melbourne, and then about 4,000 for the semifinal against Hawthorn.

"You see the number on the board, and I never would have dreamt that there'd be 5,000 at a game before. (In Ireland), We might go to a game, and we have great support at home, but it's just not as big.

"And the platform isn't as vocal as it is (in Australia)."

Darcy Vescio sealed the semifinal victory for the Blues in their 100th game. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

That crowd made itself known for the Blues' win over the Hawks in inaugural player and fan-favourite Darcy Vescio's 100th game.

The two-time All Australian sealed the victory with their second goal of the night, prompting the stands to fill with signs celebrating the beloved player.

In the lead-up to the game, Carlton organised speeches honouring Vescio and had special shirts made to mark the occasion.

"Being able to celebrate Darcy today, and seeing that players are getting to 100 games, I just didn't realise how big an achievement it was coming in last season," O'Connell said.

"Because we don't celebrate these kinds of things at home. To see that it's so special, and it's for that person for the week … You're just so excited to go out and play with them, and it lifts you. It lifts your spirits."

World.title: Rockliff says 'no surprise' if Hobart stadium cost exceeds $1.13b estimate
World.content:
Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has told parliament the final cost of Hobart's planned stadium will be made public next week, while avoiding questions about whether he'll stick to the $875 million public spending cap.

The last cost estimate of the stadium put it at $1.13 billion, but that was from about a year ago.

Since then, world events have resulted in prices going up, and it seems Tasmanians can expect the same for the waterfront, 23,000-seat, roofed stadium.

The roofed stadium at Macquarie Point is a condition of Tasmania being granted entry to the AFL competition. (Supplied: MPDC)

Under questioning in parliament, Mr Rockliff said he would be "very surprised" if the cost hadn't escalated.

"I'm not aware of the cost, however everything has gone since the 28th of February where there was an invasion in Iran," he said.

"Houses have gone up, buildings have gone up … there'd be no surprise if there was some cost escalation.

" I don't know the figure … but that is no reason to kill this project. "

An artist's impression of the Macquarie Point stadium's entry gate four. (Supplied: Mac Point Site Master Plan Report)

Over the past two days, Mr Rockliff has repeatedly faced questions as to whether he will stick to the $875 million public spending cap or bring it back to parliament for approval to exceed it.

It was a commitment he made to Upper House MLC Bec Thomas last year to secure her support for the project.

But Mr Rockliff was evasive, saying only that budgets go before the parliament.

Rosalie Woodruff: "I just want a simple yes or no for Tasmanians. Will the premier come back to parliament to ask … or are you just going to break the promise you made?" Jeremy Rockliff: "We have budgets alright and the budget's gone through the parliament. There'll be a budget go through the parliament as well."

Asked again later in the sitting, Mr Rockliff said the parliament had already spoken on the project.

"The parliament has overwhelmingly voted on this project and made that call, and I know you don't like it."

Liberals' vote hits 25-year low as One Nation continues Tasmanian surge Support for the Liberal government in Tasmania has fallen to its lowest result in an EMRS poll since 2001, as Labor and One Nation appear to make inroads by focusing on healthcare and cost of living — the two biggest issues on voters' minds.

The government has also been under pressure to reveal the final cost of the stadium before parliament rises for the year.

It is facing a motion, which is likely to get up, from independent Kristie Johnston to release the cost by tomorrow evening.

The preferred builder, BESIX Watpac, has given Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) its updated cost, but the government says that is not the final price.

That final costing was due to be made public in early December, but in question time today, Mr Rockliff said the MPDC is now working to have it ready by Monday.

"This is the most scrutinised project in Tasmania's history, and we need to get on with it," he told parliament.

"There is a view it should be released before this house rises, so we are working with the MPDC to condense the next two weeks' work into one week.

"Notwithstanding that, it's likely to create significant challenges, and possibly more costs, but we will have the updated costings by Monday next week.

" We'll get those out, and I'm sure we'll give everyone in this house plenty to talk through next week. "

Independent wants details of contract

The government says the final cost is likely to be made public Tuesday, but for Ms Johnston that's not enough.

"It's important we get [the BESIX Watpac] lump sum design and construct offer price," Kristie Johnston said.

"It's also important that we get the full project number, which the premier has committed he will deliver to the parliament.

"Combined these two prices tell us a lot. It tells us about what's included in the contract, what's not included in the contract and importantly what's still yet to come when it comes to the final project number."

Labor appears likely to support the motion.

"We support scrutiny and transparency. That's why we said we'd support the motion," Labor Leader Josh Willie said.

"The government has said there are probity issues, but the figure will be revealed.

" We need to make sure people's intentions are clear. Kristie Johnston does not support the stadium. She wants to kill the stadium. "

Funding uncertainty

Even once the figure is revealed, the question of how much taxpayer money is going towards it will not go away.

Ms Thomas said she expected the government to honour her agreement.

"The government made a clear commitment, a written commitment, to the parliament and the people of Tasmania that it would cap the state's contribution at $875 million," she said.

"If any additional funding is required, the government is committed to seek it from additional sources," she said.

" If the government can't seek that funding from additional sources, the contract ought not be signed. "

Loading...

Greens Leader Rosalie Woodruff said if the taxpayer spend was more that $875 million, the premier had to bring parliament back and put the question again.

"Parliament can exercise its right to make the government bring it back for approval if we had the numbers," she said.

"We've seen signatures from across MPs who voted for and against the stadium, wanting the premier to bring it back to parliament and consider whether the stadium bill needs to be reassessed."

World.title: Warner wants Sandpapergate 'public inquiry' as CA announces safe-space forum
World.content:
Cricket Australia (CA) has announced a new forum for players and staff to discuss the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, but whether it will achieve anything has already been questioned.

CA CEO Todd Greenberg and board member David Boon announced the forum on Wednesday, following a turbulent fortnight for the game.

The notorious 2018 Cape Town Test match where Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, leading to his suspension as well as that of captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner, was thrust into the spotlight after Usman Khawaja revealed he knew about the ball tampering in his new memoir, Sabr.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. That is all for our live coverage Thank you for joining us this afternoon. Cricket Australia has announced a new forum for people to discuss their recollections and perspectives of the Sandpapergate saga. Meanwhile, Usman Khawaja and David Warner have questioned if the forum will achieve anything if all the information is not made public. This is where we end our live coverage of the media conference and the reaction. You can get all the latest sport news and analysis on the ABC Sport website. Sport Khawaja and Warner both say they want to move on from Sandpapergate David Warner says he does not want any more penalties handed to players or staff in relation to Sandpapergate. The former Test opener says he would like to see "transparency and accountability". Both he and Khawaja have also said they want all of Australian cricket to be able to move on from this scandal. Warner "I think everyone just wants to see cricket played on our TV. It's about the Australian public, the fans of the game. " Yes, people want to talk about moving on, but in this safe environment, we want every single person that was there to be able to speak." Khawaja "We all want to move on. There's no clearer thing from everyone that we want to move on. The question is, will this allow us to move on. That's the question that has to be asked." Khawaja says he has heard some former CA staff 'aren't allowed to talk' Usman Khawaja is speaking again. He has taken issue with the findings of the forum potentially not being fully available to the public. Todd Greenberg said in the press conference that Cricket Australia would need to wait until the conclusion of the forum before deciding what information was made public. Khawaja said he had a lot of respect for Greenberg, but worried about what the point of the forum was if all the information was not made public. At the end of the day, if you're going to cherry-pick what is said in this report, the board can choose whatever they want to come in or come out. Are we just going around in a circle? Khawaja then references his understanding that some people "aren't allowed to talk" about Sandpapergate. What he means there is not clear. "Plenty of guys, including staff who have left CA, from all reports I've heard, aren't allowed to talk about the situation. Are they allowed to talk about it in this forum? I don't know. But how are we supposed to get the truth if they can't talk about it?" Show more

Since then, former player Chadd Sayers says be believed everyone in the team knew about the tampering, something strongly denied by the bowling unit, including current captain Pat Cummins.

The new forum will be voluntary, and has been described as a "safe space" for players and former staff to discuss their recollections and perspectives on Sandpapergate.

Loading...

Greenberg said this forum was not an investigation, there would not be a new investigation, and there would be no penalties or sanctions to come out of the forum.

"The game is genuinely hurting at the moment. It's not good for anyone," Greenberg told media in Hobart, ahead of Australia's third ODI against England.

"We need to find a path through and we need some time to heal. As part of this process, and so that all parties who wish to can tell their version of events, we have set up now an independent forum."

Asked if the public would find out what is discussed in the forum, Greenberg did not commit to making anything public.

"Ultimately, that will be a matter when we get through the end of this with the Cricket Australia board on what we can disclose," he said.

"And we will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward."

Warner wants 'public inquiry' as Khawaja questions value of forum

Greenberg and Boon's press conference on Wednesday came just as Fox Cricket, broadcaster of Australia's ODI match with England, went to air.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner have responded to Cricket Australia's announcement of a Sandpapergate forum. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Khawaja and Warner both appeared on Fox commentary and responded immediately to the press conference.

Both men questioned whether the forum would achieve the desired result of bringing closure to the ugly chapter in Australian cricket if CA was the one who chose what information was made public.

Warner said he wanted a public inquiry into Sandpapergate.

"Are we going to get down to what the public want, [which] is the truth?" Warner said.

"Where do we actually end here, because it is upon the board to review what they want to be published. Yes that's a safe space, but is everyone able to talk?

"I would have liked an open public inquiry and the people that were there at the time can come forward and speak.

Khawaja said he had a lot of respect for Greenberg and believed CA had its heart in the right place with the forum, but he too worried about what the point of the forum was if all the information was not made public.

"At the end of the day, if you're going to cherry-pick what is said in this report, the board can choose whatever they want to come in or come out. Are we just going around in a circle?" he said.

"We all want to move on. There's no clearer thing from everyone that we want to move on. The question is: will this allow us to move on? That's the question that has to be asked."

Since the book's release, there has been a frenzy over who knew what and whether the entire team knew of the ball tampering.

Warner said the claims detailed in Khawaja's book are "100 per cent accurate", and has accused Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation of being "botched".
